sections.heading: Wall-clock time is not the same thing as CPU time
sections.body: Big-O tells you how an algorithm's cost SCALES, but a science fair judge will eventually ask 'how fast is it really,' and that requires an actual clock. There are at least three different clocks a program can read, and they answer different questions. Wall-clock time is elapsed real-world time between two instants; it includes everything happening on the machine, including other processes, disk waits, and network stalls. CPU time (user+system) counts only the seconds the CPU spent executing your process, so it ignores time your process spent asleep or preempted. For a single-threaded, CPU-bound sort or search, CPU time is closer to what the algorithm's complexity predicts; for anything with I/O or concurrency, wall-clock time is what a user actually experiences. Neither is 'the' right answer -- the right one depends on the question being asked.

sections.heading: Why time.time() lies to you
sections.body: Python's time.time(), C's time(), and similar calendar-clock APIs read the system's wall-clock, which is NOT monotonic: it can jump backward or forward when the OS's NTP (Network Time Protocol) daemon steps the clock to correct drift against a reference server, or when a user changes the system clock. A benchmark that happens to straddle an NTP step can report a negative duration or a wildly inflated one. Calendar clocks are also often coarser than the CPU's real timing resolution -- historically ~15.6 ms on Windows and much finer but still non-monotonic on Unix. The fix is a MONOTONIC clock that is guaranteed to only move forward and is not subject to time-of-day adjustments: Python's time.perf_counter(), Java's System.nanoTime(), and the POSIX call clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) all read a dedicated hardware counter for exactly this purpose. perf_counter() in particular is explicitly documented as the highest-resolution monotonic clock available and the one to use for interval measurement.

sections.heading: Resolution is a floor, not a detail
sections.body: Every clock, monotonic or not, has finite resolution -- the smallest time difference it can distinguish. If an operation takes 200 nanoseconds but your clock's resolution is on the order of microseconds, a single call will read as 0, or as one tick, or as two ticks essentially at random: pure quantization noise, not signal. The standard fix is to never time one iteration -- time a LOOP of N iterations (N chosen so the total is comfortably above the clock's resolution, often N = 10^5 to 10^7) and divide the total elapsed time by N. This amortizes both the quantization error and the fixed overhead of the timer call itself across many repetitions, and it is exactly what Python's timeit module and Java's JMH do internally by default rather than trusting a single call.

sections.heading: A hardware-independent second measurement
sections.body: Wall-clock and CPU time are inherently tied to the machine you happened to run on -- a different CPU clock speed, cache size, or thermal state changes the number. To make a claim that survives being re-run on a different laptop, pair the timer with an INSTRUMENTED COUNT: the number of comparisons, swaps, array accesses, or recursive calls the algorithm actually performed, counted in software regardless of hardware speed. Two machines will disagree on seconds but should agree closely on comparison counts for the same algorithm and input, which is what lets you argue the algorithm itself -- not your laptop -- is the reason for a speed difference.

lessons.workedExample: A student benchmarks insertion sort on an array of 5,000 integers. A single call wrapped in time.time() before and after reports 0.0 seconds on one run and 0.001 on the next -- useless noise, partly because time.time() has coarse resolution and partly because it is not protected from a background NTP adjustment. Switching to time.perf_counter() and wrapping the sort in a loop that repeats it 50 times, then dividing the total by 50, gives a stable 0.0184 seconds per sort across five separate trials. The student also instruments the comparison operator to increment a global counter, and finds ~12.4 million comparisons regardless of which machine runs it -- a number that will match a friend's report from a different laptop even though the friend's seconds-per-run differs because their CPU is older.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has run benchmarks before will ask exactly one gating question: 'which clock did you use, and why?' A student who answers 'time.time() in Python' has revealed they never hit the NTP-step or resolution problem, which is an immediate credibility loss. Naming perf_counter() or clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) specifically, and explaining that comparison counts were tracked as a second, hardware-independent measurement, signals the student understands that a benchmark's TIME is machine-specific but its OPERATION COUNT is not -- exactly the distinction a judge is probing for.

questions.prompt: Why is time.time() (a calendar wall-clock read) considered unreliable for benchmarking short operations?

options.text: It only works on Windows machines
It can jump when the OS steps the clock via NTP, and its resolution may be coarser than the operation being timed
It cannot be called more than once per program
It measures CPU temperature instead of elapsed time

explanations.a: Wall-clock APIs exist on every OS; the problem is not platform-specific availability.
explanations.b: Correct -- NTP corrections can step the wall-clock non-monotonically, and its tick resolution can be far coarser than a nanosecond- or microsecond-scale operation, producing quantization noise or even negative deltas.
explanations.c: It can be called any number of times; call frequency is not the issue.
explanations.d: Wall-clock APIs read time, not thermal sensors.

questions.prompt: An operation takes roughly 200 nanoseconds. What is the correct way to measure it with a clock that has microsecond-level resolution?

options.text: Time it once and trust the reading
Run it in a loop of many iterations, time the whole loop, and divide by the iteration count
Switch to time.time() instead
Multiply the single-call reading by 1000

explanations.a: A single 200 ns call is below the clock's resolution floor and will read as essentially quantization noise, not a real measurement.
explanations.b: Correct -- amortizing across a large loop (e.g. 10^5-10^7 iterations) pushes the total well above the clock's resolution, and dividing recovers a meaningful per-iteration estimate.
explanations.c: time.time() has coarser resolution and the NTP-step problem, making the situation worse, not better.
explanations.d: There is no fixed multiplier that recovers a value the clock never actually resolved.

questions.prompt: Match each timing concept to its correct description.

right.text: Total elapsed real-world time, including waits and other processes
Only the seconds the CPU actually spent executing this process
Guaranteed to move only forward, immune to NTP time-of-day steps

questions.explanation: Wall-clock time reflects everything happening on the machine during the interval; CPU time isolates only this process's execution seconds; a monotonic clock like perf_counter or clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) is designed specifically to be immune to the time-of-day corrections that make calendar clocks unsafe for interval measurement.

questions.prompt: Why pair a timer measurement with an instrumented operation count (e.g. comparisons or swaps)?

options.text: Because operation counts are always more accurate than seconds
Because operation counts are hardware-independent and let a claim survive being re-run on a different machine
Because timers cannot be used on algorithms with loops
Because judges never trust timing data

explanations.a: Neither measurement is universally 'more accurate' -- they answer different questions; accuracy claims about seconds are not the point.
explanations.b: Correct -- two different laptops will disagree on seconds due to CPU speed and cache differences, but should closely agree on the number of comparisons or swaps an algorithm performs on the same input, which isolates the algorithm's cost from the machine's.
explanations.c: Timers work fine on looped code; that is in fact how sub-resolution operations are measured at all.
explanations.d: Judges do trust timing data; the point is to supplement it, not replace it.

lessons.label: Warm-Up, JIT, and the Optimizer That Deletes Your Benchmark

sections.heading: The first run is lying to you
sections.body: If you time an algorithm's very first invocation, you are not measuring the algorithm -- you are measuring the cost of getting the machine ready to run it. In a language like Java or C#, methods start out INTERPRETED, and the JIT (just-in-time) compiler only promotes a method to optimized native code after it has been called enough times to look 'hot.' HotSpot's tiered compilation ladder runs a method through five levels, from pure interpretation up to C2, the fully-optimizing compiler; the classic non-tiered default threshold for triggering compilation (-XX:CompileThreshold) is 10,000 invocations, and tiered thresholds are lower per-tier but still in the thousands. A benchmark that calls a method only a few hundred times may be measuring the interpreter or the lightly-optimizing C1 tier, not the steady-state performance the code would reach in a long-running production process -- which can differ by an order of magnitude.

sections.heading: Other confounds hiding in the first few runs
sections.body: JIT warm-up is the most famous first-run confound but far from the only one. Interpreter and import/module-loading startup cost gets bundled into a 'first call' timing in Python just as much as in Java. Instruction and data CACHES start cold -- the first pass through a function's code and data has to fault everything in from main memory, and subsequent passes benefit from cache residency that a single timed call never sees. Branch predictors similarly need repeated exposure to a loop's actual branch pattern before they predict it well; an untrained predictor mispredicts far more often, and each misprediction costs a pipeline flush on modern CPUs. All of these effects push in the same direction: the first iterations of ANY benchmark loop are systematically slower than the steady state, for reasons that have nothing to do with the algorithm's asymptotic behavior.

sections.heading: The optimizer that deletes your benchmark: dead-code elimination
sections.body: There is a second, opposite failure mode that is arguably more dangerous because it produces a benchmark that runs suspiciously FAST. If a compiler's optimizer (in C, C++, Java's JIT, or even Python's peephole optimizer in narrower cases) can prove that a computed value is never used, it is permitted to remove the computation entirely -- this is called DEAD-CODE ELIMINATION, and it is a legitimate and desirable optimization in real programs. But inside a microbenchmark, if you compute result = mySort(data) and never read result afterward, an aggressive optimizer can legally delete the entire sort, and your 'O(n^2) loop' benchmark reports 0 nanoseconds. This is not a hypothetical: it is one of the single most common ways student and even published microbenchmarks silently measure nothing at all.

sections.heading: The disciplined response: purpose-built harnesses
sections.body: The field's answer to both problems is threefold. First, discard warm-up iterations: run the code some number of times before you start recording, so the JIT has already promoted the method and the caches are already populated, then time only the iterations AFTER that point. Second, consume every result -- assign it to a variable read by something the optimizer cannot see through (printing it, summing it into an accumulator, or using a library 'blackhole' primitive), so dead-code elimination has nothing to remove. Third, and most importantly, prefer a purpose-built benchmarking harness over a hand-rolled for-loop with a stopwatch: JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) for the JVM, pyperf for Python, and even Python's own timeit module all implement warm-up, result-consumption, and statistical repetition correctly by default, because getting all three right by hand, every time, is exactly the kind of thing humans reliably get wrong.

lessons.workedExample: A student benchmarks a binary search function in Java by calling it once inside a loop of 100 iterations and averaging. The reported time is suspiciously low: 2 nanoseconds per call, far below what array indexing and comparisons should cost even in principle. Investigating, they find they never used the search's return value -- the JIT's C2 compiler proved the result was dead and eliminated the call entirely after promoting the method. Switching to JMH, which forces every benchmarked value into a 'blackhole' so it cannot be eliminated, and which automatically runs warm-up iterations before the timed measurement phase begins, the same method now reports 18 nanoseconds per call on a warmed-up JIT -- a number nine times larger and the one that actually reflects the algorithm's cost.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has been burned by a benchmark before will ask 'did you discard your warm-up iterations, and how do you know the compiler didn't just delete the thing you were timing?' A student who has never encountered dead-code elimination will report a number that looks impossibly fast and have no explanation for why. Naming the specific mechanism -- the JIT promoting hot methods after thousands of invocations, and the optimizer's right to remove unused computations -- and naming a harness (JMH, pyperf, timeit) that handles both correctly by construction, is the difference between a benchmark a judge can trust and one that quietly measured nothing.

questions.prompt: A student's Java microbenchmark of a search function reports an implausibly low time, near 0 nanoseconds. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The JVM's JIT compiler eliminated the search call because its result was never used
The clock used has too much resolution
Binary search is simply that fast on any input size
The benchmark ran on a faster CPU than expected

explanations.a: Correct -- dead-code elimination is a legitimate optimization that removes computations whose results are never read, and an unused search result is a classic trigger.
explanations.b: Excess clock resolution does not cause implausibly low readings; insufficient resolution causes quantization, not disappearance of real work.
explanations.c: Binary search is fast asymptotically, but it still performs real memory accesses and comparisons that cost more than a few nanoseconds; near-zero is a red flag, not expected behavior.
explanations.d: A faster CPU changes the constant factor modestly; it cannot make real work reported at essentially zero time.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a properly-run JVM microbenchmark from first to last.

items.text: Method runs interpreted; caches and branch predictor are cold
JIT compiler promotes the method to optimized native code after enough invocations
Warm-up iterations are discarded and not counted toward the reported result
Steady-state iterations are timed and their results consumed to prevent dead-code elimination

questions.explanation: A method begins interpreted with cold caches, gets promoted by the JIT after crossing its invocation threshold, and only then does the harness stop discarding iterations and begin recording -- with every result consumed so the optimizer cannot remove the work it is supposed to be measuring.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many invocations does HotSpot's classic (non-tiered) CompileThreshold require before a method is JIT-compiled by default?

options.text: About 10
About 10,000
About 10 million
Exactly 1, on the first call

explanations.a: Ten invocations is far too few to trigger JIT compilation; this would leave nearly everything interpreted.
explanations.b: Correct -- the classic default CompileThreshold is 10,000 invocations, which is why benchmarks with only a few hundred calls typically never reach compiled, steady-state performance.
explanations.c: Ten million overstates the threshold by three orders of magnitude for the classic compiler.
explanations.d: Compilation is deliberately delayed, not immediate, precisely because most methods are called too rarely to be worth optimizing.

questions.prompt: Why is a purpose-built harness like JMH or pyperf generally preferred over a hand-rolled timing loop?

options.text: It handles warm-up discarding, result consumption, and repeated statistical trials correctly by default
It always produces smaller numbers
It disables the JIT compiler entirely
It is required by law for published benchmarks

explanations.a: Correct -- these harnesses are specifically engineered to discard warm-up, force result consumption to defeat dead-code elimination, and run enough repetitions for sound statistics, which is easy to get wrong by hand.
explanations.b: There is no guarantee of smaller numbers; the goal is a correct number, not a small one.
explanations.c: Disabling the JIT would defeat the purpose of measuring realistic, compiled steady-state performance.
explanations.d: There is no such legal requirement; the reason to prefer these tools is methodological soundness, not compliance.

lessons.label: Designing the Input Sweep

sections.heading: Why n should double, not add
sections.body: To confirm an algorithm's complexity empirically, the standard approach is a LOG-LOG PLOT: graph log(time) against log(n), because if time really does scale as n^k, then log(time) = k*log(n) + c is a straight line whose SLOPE is the exponent k. Fitting a reliable slope requires the x-axis to span several 'decades' (factors of 10, or in binary terms, several doublings) -- a handful of closely-spaced points clustered near n=1000 cannot distinguish a slope of 1 from a slope of 1.3. This is why the input sizes in a sweep should be chosen GEOMETRICALLY rather than arithmetically: n = 2^10, 2^12, 2^14, ..., 2^22 (roughly 1,024 up to about 4.2 million) spreads points evenly across the log axis, whereas n = 1000, 2000, 3000, ..., 10000 bunches all the interesting large-n behavior into one corner of a log-log plot and wastes most of the sweep at a scale too small to distinguish exponents.

sections.heading: Pushing n far enough that asymptotics dominate
sections.body: A second reason to sweep across a wide range is that at SMALL n, constant factors and lower-order terms often dominate the runtime, masking the asymptotic term you actually want to measure. An O(n log n) algorithm with a large constant can look slower than an O(n^2) algorithm with a tiny constant when n is only 50 -- the crossover point where the asymptotic term takes over can require n in the thousands or more depending on the algorithm. The top of the sweep should therefore be pushed high enough that the highest-order term clearly dominates the lower-order ones and the log-log slope has stabilized across the last several points; if the measured slope is still drifting as n grows, the sweep has not gone high enough yet to trust the fit.

sections.heading: Input class as a controlled variable, not an afterthought
sections.body: n is not the only variable that matters -- the SHAPE of the input can change an algorithm's runtime by orders of magnitude independent of size. Quicksort with a naive pivot choice is O(n log n) on random data but degrades to O(n^2) on already-sorted or reverse-sorted input; insertion sort is O(n^2) worst-case but O(n) on nearly-sorted data. A rigorous sweep therefore fixes several distinct INPUT CLASSES and runs the full n-sweep on each one separately: uniform random, already sorted, reverse sorted, few-unique-values (many duplicates), and an adversarial input specifically constructed to trigger an algorithm's known worst case (such as the median-of-three killer sequences designed to defeat common quicksort pivot heuristics). Reporting only 'random input' results hides exactly the worst-case behavior a judge is most likely to ask about.

sections.heading: Reproducibility: fixed seeds and pre-generated inputs
sections.body: Randomized input classes must be reproducible, or a claimed result cannot be checked by anyone else. The fix is to FIX THE RANDOM SEED (e.g. Python's random.seed(12345) or numpy's np.random.default_rng(12345)) before generating each input, and to record that seed alongside the results so a second run -- by the same student or a skeptical judge -- produces the identical array. Equally important is generating every input OUTSIDE the timed region: if array construction, shuffling, or file parsing happens inside the same clock interval as the algorithm under test, the benchmark is measuring generation cost plus algorithm cost conflated together, which silently distorts the very slope the sweep exists to measure.

lessons.workedExample: A student sweeps a candidate O(n log n) sort across n = 2^10, 2^12, ..., 2^22, generating each array with numpy's default_rng(seed=42) BEFORE starting the timer, then timing only the sort call itself. They repeat the entire sweep on five input classes: uniform random integers, already sorted, reverse sorted, an array of only 3 distinct values repeated, and a known quicksort-killer sequence. The random and few-unique classes both show a log-log slope of about 1.1 (consistent with n log n), but the reverse-sorted class run through a naive-pivot quicksort shows a slope of nearly 2.0 -- clear evidence of the O(n^2) worst case the theory predicts, visible only because the student tested more than the 'random' input class.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows quicksort's worst case will ask, almost reflexively, 'what happens on sorted input?' -- and a student who only benchmarked random arrays has no answer. Presenting a log-log slope fit across a genuinely wide, geometrically-spaced n range, on multiple named input classes with a fixed and disclosed random seed, shows the student understands that an algorithm's complexity is a claim about behavior across BOTH size and input shape, not a single flattering number from one convenient test.

questions.prompt: Why should input sizes in a complexity-confirming sweep be spaced geometrically (e.g. powers of 2) rather than arithmetically (e.g. adding 1000 each time)?

options.text: Geometric spacing is faster to type in code
It spreads points evenly across a log-log plot, which is needed to fit a reliable slope (the complexity exponent) across several decades of scale
Arithmetic spacing is not supported by most timing libraries
Geometric spacing avoids the need for a random seed

explanations.a: Typing convenience is not the reason; the reason is statistical and visual on a log-log axis.
explanations.b: Correct -- the exponent k in time ~ n^k appears as the slope of a log(time) vs log(n) line, and fitting that slope reliably requires points spread across several decades, which arithmetic spacing fails to provide at large n.
explanations.c: Timing libraries do not care how n values are chosen; this is a methodology issue, not a tooling limitation.
explanations.d: Random seeding is a separate concern about reproducibility of randomized inputs, unrelated to how n is spaced.

questions.prompt: Match each input class to the behavior it is specifically designed to reveal.

right.text: Naive quicksort-style pivot degradation to O(n^2)
A specifically engineered sequence that triggers an algorithm's documented worst case
Comparison-heavy behavior when many elements are equal (e.g. duplicate-heavy partitioning)

questions.explanation: Already-sorted input is the classic trigger for naive quicksort's worst case; adversarial inputs are deliberately constructed (like median-of-three killer sequences) to hit a known worst case directly; and inputs with many duplicate values stress comparison and partitioning logic differently than uniformly distributed random data.

questions.prompt: Why must input generation (e.g. building or shuffling the array) happen OUTSIDE the timed region of a benchmark?

options.text: Because random number generation is illegal to time
Because including it conflates generation cost with algorithm cost, distorting the measured complexity
Because it makes the code harder to read
Because it changes the fixed random seed

explanations.a: There is no such prohibition; the concern is methodological accuracy, not legality.
explanations.b: Correct -- if generation time is included in the timed interval, the reported number is generation cost plus algorithm cost combined, which can have a different growth rate than the algorithm alone and will bias the fitted slope.
explanations.c: Code readability is unrelated to where the timer starts and stops.
explanations.d: Where generation happens relative to the timer has no effect on what seed value was used.

questions.prompt: A student sweeps n from 50 to 500 in steps of 50 and finds an O(n log n) algorithm looks slower than an O(n^2) one. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The O(n log n) algorithm's asymptotic advantage has not yet overtaken constant-factor and lower-order-term effects at such small n
O(n log n) is actually always slower than O(n^2)
The clock used must be broken
The input class used must have been adversarial

explanations.a: Correct -- at small n, constant factors and lower-order terms can dominate; the sweep needs to extend to larger n before the asymptotic term reliably takes over and the log-log slope stabilizes.
explanations.b: This contradicts the definition of Big-O; for sufficiently large n, O(n log n) will always overtake O(n^2).
explanations.c: A crossover at small n is an expected, well-understood phenomenon and does not imply broken instrumentation.
explanations.d: Nothing in the scenario indicates an adversarial input; the described effect happens even on ordinary random input at small sizes.

lessons.label: Trials, Noise, and Honest Statistics

sections.heading: One run is an anecdote; report a distribution
sections.body: A single timed run of an algorithm is a sample from a noisy process, not a fact about the algorithm. The discipline is to run each configuration many times -- commonly dozens to hundreds of trials -- and report a SUMMARY STATISTIC chosen for what it means, not just what is convenient. For CPU-bound, deterministic work (a sort on a fixed input, say), the MINIMUM across trials is often the best estimate of the algorithm's true cost, because nearly every source of noise (a context switch, a cache eviction, a GC pause) can only make a run SLOWER than its best-case execution, never faster -- so the fastest observed run is the closest empirical approximation to the noise-free time. The MEDIAN is a more robust general-purpose choice when trials include occasional large outliers you don't want to explain away, because it ignores tail values entirely. The MEAN, in contrast, is fragile here: a single trial that happens to catch a garbage-collection pause or a thermal-throttling dip can pull the average far from every other run, precisely because the mean weights every value, including the worst ones.

sections.heading: Spread matters as much as the center
sections.body: Reporting only one number without a sense of its spread hides whether that number is stable or a fluke. The standard companions are the INTERQUARTILE RANGE (IQR, the span from the 25th to 75th percentile, which like the median ignores extreme tails) and ERROR BARS on a chart, typically showing the standard deviation or a percentile range around the reported statistic. Critically, a standard deviation computed from THREE runs is close to meaningless -- with n=3, a single unlucky trial swings both the mean and the standard deviation dramatically, and there are only 2 degrees of freedom informing the spread estimate. A trustworthy spread claim needs enough trials (commonly 20-30 or more) that the summary statistic itself stops moving much from one batch of trials to the next; if re-running the whole experiment changes the reported number by more than the claimed uncertainty, the trial count was too low.

sections.heading: Naming the actual sources of noise
sections.body: Benchmark noise is not mysterious -- it comes from specific, nameable mechanisms. THERMAL THROTTLING reduces clock speed once a CPU's temperature crosses a limit, so a long benchmark run can slow down partway through as the chip heats up. TURBO BOOST does the opposite for short bursts, temporarily raising clock speed above the sustained rating, so a short benchmark can look faster than a long one on the identical hardware. OTHER PROCESSES sharing the machine compete for CPU time, cache space, and memory bandwidth in ways that vary run to run. GARBAGE COLLECTION pauses in managed languages (Java, Python, JavaScript) periodically halt the program for cleanup, and one unlucky pause landing inside a timed interval can dominate that trial's reported time. ASLR (address space layout randomization), a security feature that randomizes where a program's memory is placed, can shift which cache lines and pages get used from run to run, changing cache-hit rates for structurally identical code.

sections.heading: When methodology alone reverses a conclusion: Mytkowicz et al., ASPLOS 2009
sections.body: The canonical demonstration that these confounds are not academic hair-splitting is Todd Mytkowicz, Amer Diwan, Matthias Hauswirth, and Peter Sweeney's paper 'Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong!' (ASPLOS 2009). The authors showed that two factors with no logical connection to an algorithm's performance -- the LINK ORDER in which object files are assembled into an executable, and the SIZE of UNIX environment variables (which shifts the starting memory address of the stack and therefore data alignment) -- were each, on their own, large enough to change measured performance rankings between competing systems, in some cases REVERSING which of two configurations looked faster in a published result. Their proposed fix, causal analysis paired with setup randomization (deliberately varying link order and environment size across trials rather than holding them fixed at whatever the build system happened to produce), is now cited as a standard caution: an unlucky, unexamined default setup can produce a benchmark result that looks rigorous but is actually measuring memory-layout accidents, not algorithmic difference.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs the same sort 30 times on identical input and gets times mostly clustered around 14.2 to 14.6 milliseconds, but one trial reports 41 milliseconds. Reporting the MEAN of all 30 trials gives 15.1 ms, visibly dragged upward by that single outlier -- likely a garbage-collection pause or an OS scheduler preemption landing mid-run. Reporting the MEDIAN instead gives 14.4 ms, matching the bulk of the distribution, and reporting the MINIMUM gives 14.2 ms, the closest approximation to the noise-free cost. The student presents all three alongside the IQR (14.3-14.5 ms) and explicitly states which statistic (median) they used for their headline claim and why -- rather than quietly picking whichever of the three numbers looked best.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge trained to spot weak statistics will ask 'how many trials, and why that summary statistic?' A student who ran 3 trials and reported a standard deviation has, without realizing it, reported a number with almost no information content. Citing Mytkowicz et al.'s ASPLOS 2009 finding that link order and environment-variable size alone reversed a published performance ranking demonstrates the student understands that noise is not just random jitter to average away -- it can be a systematic, unexamined confound that silently produces a false conclusion, which is exactly the failure mode rigorous trial design exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: For CPU-bound, deterministic work, why is the MINIMUM across many trials often a good estimate of an algorithm's true cost?

options.text: Because nearly all noise sources can only slow a run down, never speed it up, so the fastest observed run is closest to the noise-free time
Because the minimum is always the largest value in a data set
Because minimum values are immune to garbage collection
Because judges prefer smaller numbers

explanations.a: Correct -- context switches, cache evictions, GC pauses, and thermal effects add delay; they essentially never make a run finish faster than its true best-case cost, so the minimum across trials approximates that noise-free floor.
explanations.b: The minimum is definitionally the smallest value, not the largest.
explanations.c: The minimum trial can still be affected by GC; it is simply the trial least affected among those observed, not immune by definition.
explanations.d: Statistical choice of summary statistic is about what the number means, not about aesthetic preference.

questions.prompt: Why is a standard deviation computed from only 3 trials essentially meaningless?

options.text: Because standard deviation cannot be computed for fewer than 10 values
Because with so few trials, a single unlucky run swings both the estimate and its reported spread dramatically, and there is almost no basis for judging stability
Because 3 trials always produce a standard deviation of zero
Because standard deviation only applies to normally-distributed data

explanations.a: Standard deviation is mathematically computable from as few as 2 values; the issue is reliability, not computability.
explanations.b: Correct -- with n=3 there are only 2 degrees of freedom, and one outlying trial dominates both the mean and the spread estimate, so the reported number carries very little real information about the algorithm's stability.
explanations.c: There is no reason 3 trials would force a standard deviation to zero; that would only happen if all 3 values were identical.
explanations.d: Standard deviation can be computed regardless of distribution shape; the objection here is about sample size, not distributional assumptions.

questions.prompt: Match each noise source to its mechanism.

right.text: CPU reduces clock speed once temperature crosses a limit
CPU temporarily raises clock speed above sustained rating for short bursts
Managed-language runtime periodically halts execution for memory cleanup
Randomizes memory layout, shifting cache-line and page alignment run to run

questions.explanation: Thermal throttling and turbo boost are opposite clock-speed effects tied to temperature and burst duration; GC pauses are runtime-managed memory cleanup that can land inside a timed interval; ASLR is a security feature that randomizes memory addresses, indirectly affecting cache behavior between runs.

questions.prompt: What did Mytkowicz, Diwan, Hauswirth, and Sweeney's ASPLOS 2009 paper demonstrate?

options.text: That factors unrelated to algorithm logic, like link order and environment variable size, could shift measured performance enough to reverse a published ranking
That all benchmarking is fundamentally impossible
That only Java benchmarks suffer from measurement bias
That minimum is always a worse statistic than mean

explanations.a: Correct -- the paper showed link order and UNIX environment variable size, both logically unrelated to algorithmic performance, were each large enough on their own to change or reverse measured performance rankings, motivating causal analysis and setup randomization as fixes.
explanations.b: The paper's message is that benchmarking requires controlling for hidden confounds, not that it is impossible; it proposes concrete remedies.
explanations.c: The paper's findings and its proposed remedies (causal analysis, setup randomization) are general methodological concerns, not limited to one language.
explanations.d: The paper does not make a general claim ranking minimum against mean; its focus is on hidden environmental confounds, a separate topic from choice of summary statistic.

lessons.label: Separating the Algorithm from the Machine and the Language

sections.heading: The interpreter tax and why 'my algorithm is faster' can be a lie about languages
sections.body: A naive comparison -- 'my C implementation of algorithm A beats my Python implementation of algorithm B, so A is faster' -- routinely confuses the algorithm with the LANGUAGE it was written in. Interpreted languages like pure Python or Ruby typically run raw, hand-written loops on the order of 10 to 100 times slower than the equivalent compiled C or Rust code, purely from interpreter dispatch overhead, dynamic typing checks, and the lack of ahead-of-time optimization -- a gap that has nothing to do with which algorithm is asymptotically better. A test comparing an O(n log n) algorithm in Python against an O(n^2) algorithm in C can easily show the WORSE algorithm finishing faster in wall-clock seconds simply because the 10-100x language penalty outweighs the algorithmic difference at the tested input size, which is exactly backwards from what the comparison was supposed to show.

sections.heading: Hidden C underneath a Python API
sections.body: A closely related trap is comparing 'my Python code' against 'a library's Python code' and concluding the library's ALGORITHM is better, when the real difference is that the library's inner loop is written in C (or Fortran, or hand-vectorized assembly) and merely exposed through a thin Python wrapper. NumPy's array operations, Python's built-in sorted() (Timsort implemented in C), and most of pandas fall into this category: the Python-level API is not where the time is spent, and a fair comparison of 'my algorithm vs. this library's algorithm' needs to either implement both in the same language and runtime, or explicitly acknowledge that the comparison also includes an implementation-language effect, not a pure algorithmic one.

sections.heading: Allocator behavior and memory pressure as silent confounds
sections.body: Even within a single language, the memory ALLOCATOR can dominate a measurement that was intended to isolate an algorithm. Repeatedly allocating and freeing many small objects (as a naive linked-list-heavy implementation might) stresses the allocator and can trigger heap fragmentation, extra system calls, or -- in managed languages -- more frequent garbage collection cycles, all of which show up as 'algorithm time' in a naive benchmark even though they are properties of the memory manager, not the algorithm's logic. Similarly, MEMORY PRESSURE -- how much of the working data set fits in cache versus must be fetched from main memory -- can make the identical algorithm look dramatically different depending on whether a competing process on the same machine is also consuming cache and memory bandwidth during the run.

sections.heading: Three disciplines that separate the algorithm from its wrapper
sections.body: The standard defenses are threefold. First, report OPERATION COUNTS (comparisons, allocations, cache-relevant accesses) alongside wall-clock seconds, because operation counts are language- and machine-independent in a way raw time is not -- this was covered in the first lesson of this unit and is worth repeating here because it directly defeats the language-confound problem. Second, PROFILE the code with a tool built for the purpose -- perf on Linux, or cProfile in Python -- to confirm empirically where time is actually being spent, rather than assuming; a profiler will reveal if 90% of 'algorithm time' is actually sitting inside malloc/free or a library's internal C loop. Third, RE-RUN THE ENTIRE SWEEP ON A SECOND, DIFFERENT MACHINE. If the algorithm's log-log slope (its measured complexity exponent) stays essentially the same on both machines while the absolute seconds-per-operation constant differs, that is strong evidence the SHAPE of the curve reflects the algorithm and the CONSTANT reflects the hardware -- exactly the separation a rigorous claim needs to make explicit.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares their own quicksort, written in pure Python, against Python's built-in sorted(). Their quicksort loses badly -- 40 times slower on the same 100,000-element array. Before concluding quicksort is a worse algorithm, they profile with cProfile and confirm that both implementations perform a similar number of comparisons (both are O(n log n) on this input), but sorted() calls down into Timsort's C implementation while their quicksort runs as interpreted Python bytecode line by line. They then reimplement their partition step in a small C extension and the gap shrinks to roughly 3x -- consistent with residual constant-factor and cache-behavior differences between the two algorithms, not a 40x language penalty masquerading as an algorithmic one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will ask 'is that a language you're seeing, or an algorithm?' whenever a comparison crosses a language or library boundary -- and 'my pure-Python code was slower than NumPy's' is a trap many students fall into without noticing. Showing operation counts alongside wall-clock time, a profiler trace confirming where cycles actually went, and a second machine's sweep with an unchanged log-log slope but a different constant, demonstrates the student has actively isolated the algorithm's contribution from the machine's and the language's -- which is precisely the distinction that separates a real empirical claim from an artifact of implementation choices.

questions.prompt: A student's O(n log n) algorithm written in pure Python runs slower in wall-clock seconds than a worse, O(n^2) algorithm written in C, at the tested input size. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The interpreted-language penalty (commonly 10-100x versus compiled code) is outweighing the algorithmic advantage at this input size
O(n log n) is mathematically slower than O(n^2)
The student's clock must have been miscalibrated
C code cannot implement O(n^2) algorithms
Python cannot run algorithms of complexity better than O(n^2)

explanations.a: Correct -- interpreted languages commonly carry a 10-100x constant-factor penalty versus compiled code, which can dominate wall-clock time at input sizes where the algorithmic gap hasn't yet grown large enough to overcome it.
explanations.b: This directly contradicts the definition of Big-O notation; O(n log n) is asymptotically better than O(n^2) by definition for sufficiently large n.
explanations.c: Nothing in the scenario suggests a clock problem; the effect described is a well-known, expected language-performance gap.
explanations.d: C can implement algorithms of any complexity class; the language does not restrict which algorithms can be written in it.
explanations.e: Python can implement any algorithm regardless of its complexity class; the language affects the constant factor, not which algorithms are expressible.

questions.prompt: Why can comparing 'my Python code' to 'NumPy's Python API' overstate NumPy's algorithmic advantage?

options.text: Because NumPy's core operations are implemented in C, so the comparison partly measures a language difference, not a pure algorithm difference
Because NumPy always uses a worse algorithm
Because Python code cannot be profiled
Because NumPy arrays cannot hold the same data as Python lists

explanations.a: Correct -- NumPy's Python-level API is a thin wrapper around C (and often vectorized/BLAS) implementations, so a naive comparison conflates a language/implementation effect with any genuine algorithmic difference.
explanations.b: NumPy frequently uses well-established, efficient algorithms; the point is that its speed advantage over naive Python often comes from implementation language, not necessarily a different algorithm.
explanations.c: Python code, including code calling into NumPy, can be profiled with tools like cProfile; profiling is in fact how this confound gets detected.
explanations.d: NumPy arrays can represent the same numeric data as Python lists; data representation is not the source of the confound described.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in the recommended discipline for confirming a performance difference is really about the algorithm.

items.text: Report operation counts alongside wall-clock seconds
Profile with a tool like perf or cProfile to confirm where time is actually spent
Re-run the full sweep on a second, different machine
Compare the log-log slope across machines to confirm the curve's shape is stable while its constant differs

questions.explanation: The discipline starts with a language-independent operation count, then uses profiling to empirically confirm where cycles are actually going rather than assuming, then validates on a second machine, and finally checks that the exponent (slope) held steady across machines even if the constant did not -- which is the actual evidence that the algorithm, not the hardware, explains the curve's shape.

questions.prompt: Why might repeated small allocations make an algorithm's benchmark look slower than its logic alone would predict?

options.text: Because the memory allocator's overhead, fragmentation, or triggered garbage collection gets counted as algorithm time in a naive benchmark
Because small allocations always cause a segmentation fault
Because allocators only work correctly on machines with more than 16 GB of RAM
Because Big-O notation ignores memory entirely

explanations.a: Correct -- frequent small allocations and deallocations can stress the allocator (fragmentation, extra system calls, more frequent GC), and a naive timer includes that overhead as if it were purely the algorithm's own cost.
explanations.b: Small allocations do not inherently cause crashes; the concern here is a performance confound, not a correctness bug.
explanations.c: Allocator behavior is unrelated to total system RAM in this way; the issue is allocation pattern, not machine memory capacity.
explanations.d: Big-O notation can describe space complexity too, but that is a separate concern from the runtime confound described here -- the issue is a benchmarking artifact, not a notational gap.

lessons.label: A Benchmark Protocol a Judge Cannot Poke Holes In

sections.heading: Pre-registering the hypothesis before running anything
sections.body: Every lesson in this unit has covered one piece of methodology in isolation; the discipline that ties them together is committing to a written protocol BEFORE the first trial runs, not after the data is in. The single most important item in that protocol is a stated HYPOTHESIS with a predicted exponent: 'I expect this sort to show a log-log slope near 1.0 (O(n log n)) on random input, and near 2.0 on already-sorted input if it uses a naive pivot.' Writing the prediction down first, and only then running the sweep, is what statisticians call PRE-REGISTRATION -- and it matters because it is the difference between the data CONFIRMING a claim made in advance and a student noticing a pattern after the fact and constructing a story to fit it, a well-documented bias sometimes called HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known). A matching curve found after pre-registering the prediction is real evidence; the same matching curve found by picking whichever exponent looked closest after the fact is not.

sections.heading: The full checklist: what must be nailed down in advance
sections.body: Beyond the hypothesis, a defensible protocol fixes every variable this unit has named as a confound, in writing, before data collection: the CONTROLLED VARIABLES (which input classes will be tested: random, sorted, reverse-sorted, few-unique, adversarial), the FIXED RANDOM SEEDS used to generate each input class, the exact LANGUAGE, COMPILER OR INTERPRETER VERSION, and LIBRARY VERSIONS involved (a different Python minor version or a different NumPy release can itself shift constants), the HARDWARE and OPERATING SYSTEM specification (CPU model, RAM, OS version -- since the earlier lessons showed even link order and environment variable size can matter), the TRIAL COUNT (e.g. 30 repetitions per configuration) and which SUMMARY STATISTIC (median, minimum) will be reported, decided before seeing the data so as not to cherry-pick whichever statistic flatters the result.

sections.heading: Retaining raw data and publishing code
sections.body: A protocol is only as trustworthy as its paper trail. RAW DATA -- every individual trial's timing and operation count, not just the summary statistics -- should be retained and available, because a skeptical judge or a re-analysis may want to check whether the reported median genuinely represents the distribution, or whether an unusual number of trials were silently dropped as 'outliers.' Equally, the BENCHMARK CODE ITSELF should be published (or at minimum available on request) rather than only the resulting chart, because a chart alone cannot reveal whether warm-up iterations were discarded, whether results were consumed to defeat dead-code elimination, or whether input generation happened inside or outside the timed region -- all of which this unit has shown can silently change a result by an order of magnitude or more.

sections.heading: What reproducibility actually requires
sections.body: The end goal of all this record-keeping is REPRODUCIBILITY: a specific, testable claim that a DIFFERENT person, on a DIFFERENT (but comparably specified) machine, using the PUBLISHED code, fixed seeds, and stated protocol, should be able to re-run the experiment and recover the same qualitative conclusion -- the same approximate log-log slope, the same relative ranking between algorithms or input classes -- even if the exact seconds differ because their CPU is not identical to the original author's. This is a strictly higher bar than 'I ran it and it worked on my machine once': it requires that every methodological choice in this unit -- the clock, the warm-up, the input sweep, the trial count, the summary statistic -- be documented clearly enough that someone else's rerun is a genuine TEST of the claim rather than a repetition of whatever the original author happened to do.

lessons.workedExample: Before running a single trial, a student writes: 'Hypothesis: our merge sort implementation will show a log-log slope of approximately 1.0-1.1 across all five input classes (random, sorted, reverse-sorted, few-unique, adversarial), since merge sort's complexity is O(n log n) regardless of input order. Protocol: Python 3.12.4, seed=2026 for all random generation, n from 2^10 to 2^22, 30 trials per configuration, median reported with IQR, hardware: [specific CPU/RAM], code and raw CSV published to a public repository.' After running the sweep, the slope comes out between 1.05 and 1.15 across all five classes, matching the pre-registered prediction -- and because the prediction was written down first, this result is confirmation rather than a story invented to explain whatever number happened to come out.
lessons.judgeFraming: The single most damaging question a judge can ask is 'did you predict this result before you ran it, or did you notice the pattern afterward?' A student who pre-registered a specific exponent, fixed every confound this unit named in writing beforehand, and can hand over raw per-trial data and runnable code on request has built a claim that survives scrutiny. A student who ran the experiment first and then wrote a hypothesis that happens to match whatever came out has, whether they intend it or not, committed HARKing -- and an experienced judge will recognize the difference immediately.

questions.prompt: Why does writing a hypothesis with a predicted exponent BEFORE running the sweep matter more than writing it after seeing the data?

options.text: It prevents HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) and makes a matching result genuine confirmation rather than a post-hoc story
It makes the code run faster
It is required by the checkpoint's JSON schema
It eliminates the need for multiple trials

explanations.a: Correct -- pre-registering the predicted exponent before seeing results is what distinguishes real confirmation from HARKing, where a story is constructed to fit whatever pattern happened to appear after the fact.
explanations.b: Writing a hypothesis has no effect on runtime performance; it is a methodological, not a computational, step.
explanations.c: This is a scientific methodology practice, unrelated to any technical file-format requirement.
explanations.d: Pre-registration and trial count address different problems -- one is about avoiding post-hoc bias, the other is about controlling noise; neither substitutes for the other.

questions.prompt: Order these protocol steps in the sequence a rigorous benchmarking process should follow.

items.text: Write a hypothesis predicting a specific exponent, before running any trial
Fix all controlled variables in writing: input classes, seeds, versions, hardware spec, trial count, summary statistic
Run the sweep and record every individual trial's raw data
Publish the code and raw data alongside the summary result

questions.explanation: A defensible protocol states the prediction first, locks down every controlled variable this unit identified as a confound before collecting any data, runs the sweep while retaining raw per-trial results, and finally makes both the code and that raw data available so the result can be independently checked.

questions.prompt: Why should raw, per-trial data be retained rather than only the summary statistic (e.g. the reported median)?

options.text: So a skeptical reviewer can check whether the summary genuinely represents the distribution, rather than trusting a number with no visible trail
Because summary statistics are illegal to publish alone
Because raw data always shows a smaller number than the median
Because the median cannot be recomputed from raw data

explanations.a: Correct -- raw data lets someone verify the summary statistic was computed honestly and wasn't distorted by silently dropped trials or a poor choice of statistic.
explanations.b: There is no such prohibition; the issue is trustworthiness and verifiability, not legality.
explanations.c: Raw data has no systematic relationship making it smaller than the median; this claim does not follow from the concept.
explanations.d: The median is, by definition, computable directly from the raw data; retaining raw data makes recomputing it possible, not impossible.

questions.prompt: What does 'reproducibility' require in this context, beyond the original author's own single successful run?

options.text: That a different person, on a comparably specified but different machine, using the published code and stated protocol, can recover the same qualitative conclusion
That the exact same number of seconds is produced on any machine
That no other researcher is ever allowed to question the result
That the code only needs to run once successfully on the author's own laptop

explanations.a: Correct -- reproducibility means an independent rerun, on different but comparable hardware, following the documented protocol, recovers the same qualitative pattern (e.g. the same approximate slope or ranking), even if exact seconds differ.
explanations.b: Exact second-for-second matches across different hardware are not required or expected; the qualitative conclusion (shape of the curve, relative ranking) is what should reproduce.
explanations.c: Reproducibility is precisely what invites and enables outside scrutiny, not what forecloses it.
explanations.d: A single successful run on the author's own machine is exactly the weaker standard that pre-registration and published protocol are meant to move beyond.

lessons.label: Runtime vs. n, and Why Linear Axes Betray You

sections.heading: The same data, three different-looking stories
sections.body: Take three functions, t = 5n (linear), t = n log2(n) (linearithmic), and t = n^2 / 200 (quadratic), and evaluate them at n = 10, 100, 1000. On plain linear-linear axes over that range, all three produce what a viewer's eye reads as roughly 'a curve going up and to the right' — the small-n region (n = 10 to 100) is squeezed into a few pixels near the origin while the n = 1000 point dominates the frame. This is not a rendering accident; it is a mathematical property of linear axes: equal PIXEL distances represent equal VALUE distances, so a function whose values span three orders of magnitude (50 to 5000 for linear here, ~33 to ~10,000 for n log n, ~0.5 to 5000 for quadratic) forces almost all of its interesting early behavior into a sliver near zero. A chart-reader who only looks at the overall silhouette, without checking the axis tick labels, can be shown two algorithms that look nearly identical at small n and wildly different at large n using the exact same linear scale — the visual impression depends entirely on which n-range the chart-maker chose to display.

sections.heading: The n-range is an editorial choice, not a neutral window
sections.body: Because linear axes compress small values, the chart-maker's choice of x-axis range is itself an argument. Plot only n = 1 to 50 and an O(n^2) algorithm's curve looks gently rising, barely distinguishable from linear — the quadratic term is small relative to constants at low n. Extend the same chart to n = 1 to 100,000 and the quadratic curve goes vertical while the linear curve stays a nearly flat line along the bottom. Neither chart is fabricated; both use real data. But a chart restricted to the 'flattering' range for one algorithm is a common way benchmark results get misrepresented, deliberately or not, in papers, blog posts, and marketing claims about 'faster' algorithms.

sections.heading: What an honest runtime chart discloses
sections.body: Three disclosures separate an honest empirical-runtime chart from a misleading one. First, AXIS RANGE: the chart should either span enough of n to reach the regime that matters, or explicitly say why it doesn't. Second, the ZERO-BASELINE QUESTION: unlike many statistical charts where truncating the y-axis at a nonzero value is a well-known distortion, runtime axes usually SHOULD include zero, because a truncated y-axis can make a modest runtime difference look like a dramatic one. Third, the CAPTION METADATA: a runtime number is meaningless without stating the unit (milliseconds? CPU cycles?), the machine (which processor, how much RAM, was anything else running), and the trial count (a single run is noise; benchmarking convention, following tools like Google's own benchmark libraries, is to report the median or mean of many repeated trials with variance shown, because OS scheduling jitter and cache warm-up effects can swing a single trial by 10-30%).

lessons.workedExample: A blog post claims 'Algorithm X beats Algorithm Y' showing a chart from n=1 to n=200, both curves looking flat and nearly overlapping, with X very slightly below Y. A skeptical reader checks the y-axis: it runs from 0 to 2 milliseconds, and the caption gives no trial count or machine spec. Re-running both algorithms out to n=100,000 reveals X is O(n^2) and Y is O(n log n) — at n=200 the constant factors dominate and the curves are nearly indistinguishable, but by n=100,000 X takes 40 times longer. The original chart was not falsified, but its n-range was too small to reach the regime where the asymptotic difference actually shows up, making a real long-run disadvantage invisible.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen a hundred fair projects knows that 'our algorithm is faster, see this chart' is the single most common unsupported claim at a science fair. Asking 'what n-range does this cover, and why did you stop there' immediately separates a student who chose the range to reach the asymptotic regime from one who copied whatever range ran fastest on their laptop. A student who can also state the number of trials and the machine used shows they understand that a runtime number without that context is not a scientific measurement at all.

questions.prompt: Why do O(n), O(n log n), and O(n^2) curves often look like the same 'rising curve' on a small linear-linear plot?

options.text: Because the three complexity classes are mathematically equivalent at small n
Because linear axes compress small-n values near the origin, hiding the differences that only appear at larger n
Because runtime charts always round to the nearest millisecond
Because computers execute all three algorithms at the same speed below n=1000

explanations.a: They are not equivalent; the classes diverge as n grows, but linear axes visually hide that divergence at small scales.
explanations.b: Correct — on linear axes, equal pixel distances equal equal value distances, so with a small n-range and small constants, the growth-rate differences have not yet produced large enough value gaps to be visible.
explanations.c: Rounding is unrelated; the effect happens even with exact, unrounded values.
explanations.d: Computers do not execute at identical speeds across complexity classes; the underlying operation counts genuinely differ, the chart just fails to reveal it at that range.

questions.prompt: A runtime chart's y-axis is truncated to start at 8ms instead of 0ms, making a 9ms vs 10ms difference look like a doubling. What is the most accurate description of this issue?

options.text: It is standard practice and always improves readability
It visually exaggerates a small absolute difference, which is why runtime axes are usually best kept zero-baselined
It only matters for O(n^2) algorithms
It has no effect since the underlying data is unchanged

explanations.a: It is not standard best practice for runtime magnitude comparisons; it is a well-documented way charts mislead.
explanations.b: Correct — truncating the baseline inflates the visual ratio between bars or points even though the true ratio (10/9) is much smaller, so runtime charts generally should include a zero baseline.
explanations.c: The distortion applies regardless of which complexity class is being charted.
explanations.d: The data may be unchanged, but the READER's perception of the difference is changed, which is the entire problem with a misleading chart.

questions.prompt: Match each caption element to what it protects against.

right.text: Comparing numbers that are actually on incompatible scales
Results that don't reproduce on different hardware
A single noisy run mistaken for a stable measurement

questions.explanation: Without a stated unit, readers can't tell milliseconds from cycles from seconds. Without hardware specs, results can't be reproduced or compared across machines. Without a trial count, a single run's OS-scheduling noise or cache-warmup effect can be mistaken for the algorithm's true behavior.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for producing an honest runtime-vs-n chart, from first to last.

items.text: Choose an n-range wide enough to reach the regime where growth-rate differences matter
Run each algorithm many trials per n value on a fixed, documented machine
Plot with a zero-baselined y-axis
Caption the chart with units, machine spec, and trial count

questions.explanation: You first decide what range of n is worth measuring, then collect the actual timing data with enough repetition on known hardware, then render it honestly (zero baseline), then document the metadata so a reader can judge and reproduce the result.

lessons.label: Log-Log Plots and the Slope Trick

sections.heading: Deriving why the slope IS the exponent
sections.body: Suppose an algorithm's runtime genuinely follows a power law, t = c * n^k, where c is a constant (setup cost, per-operation cost) and k is the exponent we want to discover (1 for linear, 2 for quadratic, 3 for cubic). Take the logarithm of both sides: log(t) = log(c * n^k) = log(c) + log(n^k) = k * log(n) + log(c). This is exactly the equation of a straight line, y = m*x + b, if we let y = log(t), x = log(n), the slope m = k, and the intercept b = log(c). This is the single most useful fact in empirical algorithm analysis: PLOT log(t) AGAINST log(n) and a genuine power-law relationship becomes a straight line whose SLOPE is the exponent you are trying to identify, and whose Y-INTERCEPT (at log(n) = 0, i.e., n = 1) recovers the constant factor c. A log-log plot converts the hard visual problem 'is this curve n^1.9 or n^2.0' into the much easier problem 'what is the slope of this line,' which can be read off directly or fit numerically.

sections.heading: Reading exponents off the slope
sections.body: In practice you read the slope by picking two well-separated points on the line and computing rise over run in log-space: if doubling n from 1000 to 2000 moves log(t) up by exactly log(2) (about 0.301), the slope is 1 and the algorithm is linear. If the same doubling moves log(t) up by 2*log(2) (about 0.602), the slope is 2 and the algorithm is quadratic. A slope near 1 signals O(n), a slope near 2 signals O(n^2), a slope near 3 signals O(n^3), and non-integer slopes (like 1.585) are the signature of divide-and-conquer algorithms whose recurrence yields a fractional exponent, such as Karatsuba multiplication's O(n^log2(3)). The intercept matters too: two O(n^2) algorithms will both show slope 2, but the one with the larger intercept (larger c) is uniformly slower by a constant factor, which the slope alone cannot reveal — you need both numbers from the fitted line.

sections.heading: The subtlety: O(n log n) is not perfectly straight
sections.body: The one common complexity class that does NOT produce a straight log-log line is O(n log n), because it is not a pure power law — the log(n) factor grows, just extremely slowly. Written out, log(t) = log(c * n * log n) = log(n) + log(log n) + log(c). The log(log n) term is not a constant, so the 'slope' at any given point (the local derivative of log(t) with respect to log(n)) is actually 1 + 1/ln(n), which is always slightly above 1 but shrinks toward 1 as n grows. Concretely, the LOCAL SLOPE drifts slowly downward from roughly 1.13 to roughly 1.10 across a typical benchmarking decade of n (for example, from n = 10^3 to n = 10^4), then keeps drifting toward 1 only across many more decades. This is exactly the diagnostic that separates a true O(n log n) sort (like merge sort or an efficient quicksort) from a true O(n) algorithm on a log-log chart: a linear algorithm's slope stays flat and unchanging across every decade, while an n log n algorithm's slope creeps downward toward 1, however gently, as you extend the n-range further to the right.

lessons.workedExample: A student benchmarks their sorting implementation at n = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6 and plots log(t) vs log(n). Between n=10^3 and n=10^4, the line's slope measures about 1.13; between n=10^4 and n=10^5, the slope measures about 1.10; between n=10^5 and n=10^6, about 1.08. Because the slope is creeping downward toward 1.0 decade over decade rather than staying perfectly flat at 1.0, the student concludes the algorithm is NOT O(n) despite looking nearly linear over any single decade, and identifies it as O(n log n) — consistent with merge sort's known behavior, since log2(10^6) ≈ 20 while log2(10^3) ≈ 10, giving the expected small downward drift in the effective per-decade slope as the growing log(n) factor's relative contribution shrinks.
lessons.judgeFraming: Any judge with a CS background will ask 'how do you know it's O(n log n) and not O(n)' the moment they see a log-log chart with a nearly-straight line, because the two ARE visually almost indistinguishable over a single decade. A student who can point to the slight downward drift toward 1 in local slope across multiple decades — and explain it comes from the log(n) factor's derivative, 1/ln(n) — demonstrates they understand the mathematics behind the chart rather than having pattern-matched 'straight line on log-log means power law' without appreciating its one major exception.

questions.prompt: If t = c * n^k, what does the slope of log(t) vs log(n) equal?

options.text: The constant c
The exponent k
The value of n
Always exactly 1, regardless of k

explanations.a: The constant c appears in the intercept (log c), not the slope.
explanations.b: Correct — taking logs of t = c*n^k gives log(t) = k*log(n) + log(c), a line with slope k, so the slope directly reveals the exponent.
explanations.c: n is the x-axis variable itself, not the slope.
explanations.d: The slope equals k, which varies by algorithm — only a true linear algorithm has slope exactly 1.

questions.prompt: Why does O(n log n) fail to produce a perfectly straight line on a log-log plot?

options.text: Because n log n is not a power law; the log(n) factor makes the local slope drift slowly toward 1 rather than staying fixed
Because log-log plots cannot display any function containing a logarithm
Because n log n runtimes are always measured with more error than other classes
Because it is actually a straight line, and any apparent curve is a plotting bug

explanations.a: Correct — log(t) = log(n) + log(log n) + log(c) has a non-constant local slope, 1 + 1/ln(n), which drifts slowly upward from about 1.1 toward 1 more slowly, and toward higher values at smaller n, rather than being fixed.
explanations.b: Log-log plots can display functions with logarithms fine; the issue is that this particular function isn't a pure power law, not a display limitation.
explanations.c: The drift is a real mathematical property of n log n, not a measurement artifact.
explanations.d: It is genuinely not a perfectly straight line; the near-straightness is only an approximation over a limited range.

questions.prompt: Match each measured log-log slope to the complexity class it indicates.

left.text: Slope stays flat at ~1.0 across every decade
Slope stays flat at ~2.0 across every decade
Slope creeps slowly downward toward 1.0, e.g. 1.18 down to 1.10 across decades

right.text: O(n)
O(n log n)

questions.explanation: A flat slope of 1 is a pure linear power law. A flat slope of 2 is a pure quadratic power law. A slowly downward-drifting slope toward 1, never fully flat, is the signature of the log(n) factor in O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Order the derivation steps that show the slope of a log-log plot equals the exponent k in t = c*n^k.

items.text: Start with t = c * n^k
Take the logarithm of both sides
Expand using log(c * n^k) = log(c) + k*log(n)
Recognize the result as a line, log(t) = k*log(n) + log(c), with slope k

questions.explanation: You begin with the assumed power-law model, apply log to both sides, expand the logarithm of a product/power into a sum, and the resulting equation is linear in log(n) with slope k and intercept log(c).

lessons.label: Semi-Log Plots and Exponential Growth

sections.heading: Why exponential runtime becomes a straight line on semi-log-y
sections.body: Consider an exhaustive search algorithm, such as brute-force checking every subset of an n-element set, whose runtime is t = c * 2^n. Take the logarithm of just the y-value (runtime), leaving n itself on a plain linear x-axis — this is a SEMI-LOG-Y plot (also written log-linear). Then log(t) = log(c * 2^n) = n * log(2) + log(c). This is a straight line in n, with slope log(2) (about 0.301 in base 10, or 1 in base 2 if you use log base 2) and intercept log(c). The key structural fact is that ANY exponential function b^n, for any base b, produces a straight line on semi-log-y, because the exponent n appears multiplied by log(b) rather than raised as a power. This gives a clean visual test: plot log(runtime) against plain n, and if the result is a straight line, the algorithm's growth is exponential in the base implied by the slope.

sections.heading: Why every polynomial curves away on the same axes
sections.body: Contrast this with any polynomial, t = c * n^k for fixed k. On semi-log-y, log(t) = k*log(n) + log(c) — the right-hand side has log(n), not n, so as a function of n (not log n) this is NOT linear; it grows much more slowly than n does, meaning the polynomial's semi-log-y curve bends downward and flattens as n increases, visually curving away from any straight line. This gives the single most consequential visual test in the whole field: on semi-log-y axes, exponential algorithms are straight lines and polynomial algorithms curve downward and flatten. A chart-reader who sees a curve that keeps flattening as n grows, rather than continuing straight, is looking at a polynomial (or slower) algorithm; a chart-reader who sees a genuinely straight line all the way across is looking at true exponential growth — this is exactly how researchers empirically distinguish, for example, a provably exponential brute-force SAT solver from a polynomial-time approximation, without needing a formal proof of the underlying complexity class.

sections.heading: The mirror case: semi-log-x for logarithmic algorithms
sections.body: The complementary transform, SEMI-LOG-X, puts log(n) on the x-axis while leaving runtime t on a plain linear y-axis. This is the right tool for algorithms like binary search, whose runtime is t = c * log(n) + d. On a plain linear-linear plot, binary search looks almost flat and unchanging even as n grows by factors of a million, because log(n) grows so slowly it is easy to mistake for a constant — doubling n from 10^6 to 2*10^6 only adds log10(2) ≈ 0.301 to the base-10-logged count, barely visible against the y-axis scale needed to show any interesting variation. On semi-log-x, however, since t is already linear in log(n), the same data becomes an honest, clearly-sloped straight line, making the logarithmic growth rate visible rather than compressed into apparent flatness. Choosing the right axis transform is therefore not cosmetic: semi-log-y is the honest choice for suspected exponential behavior, semi-log-x is the honest choice for suspected logarithmic behavior, and plain linear-linear axes flatten precisely the algorithms (like binary search) whose growth is slowest and most valuable to distinguish from true constant time.

lessons.workedExample: A student times a brute-force subset-sum solver at n = 10, 15, 20, 25, getting roughly 0.001s, 0.03s, 1s, 33s. Plotted on linear-linear axes, the last point dwarfs the rest and the chart looks like a hockey stick with no useful information for n < 20. Re-plotted on semi-log-y (log(t) vs plain n), the four points fall almost exactly on a straight line with slope close to log10(2) ≈ 0.301 per unit n, confirming t doubles for each additional element — direct visual evidence of O(2^n) growth. The student contrasts this with their O(n^2) baseline, whose semi-log-y plot visibly curves and flattens over the same n-range, giving a clean side-by-side demonstration of exponential versus polynomial growth using the same axis choice.
lessons.judgeFraming: Distinguishing exponential from polynomial growth is the most consequential classification in complexity theory — it is the line between 'solvable at scale' and 'only solvable for toy inputs,' the practical heart of P vs NP intuition. A judge will want to see that a student chose semi-log-y specifically BECAUSE they suspected exponential behavior, and can explain that a straight line there means true exponential growth while a flattening curve rules it out — not just that they made 'a log chart' without understanding which axis transform tests which hypothesis.

questions.prompt: On a semi-log-y plot (log of runtime vs. plain n), what does a true exponential algorithm t = c*2^n look like?

options.text: A straight line
A curve that flattens as n grows
A curve that steepens without bound relative to a straight line
Indistinguishable from a polynomial

explanations.a: Correct — log(c*2^n) = n*log(2) + log(c) is linear in n, so exponential growth becomes a straight line on semi-log-y.
explanations.b: Flattening curves on semi-log-y are the signature of polynomials, not exponentials.
explanations.c: An exponential doesn't steepen relative to the straight line predicted by its own log-transform; it produces exactly that straight line.
explanations.d: Semi-log-y is specifically the tool that separates the two: exponentials are straight, polynomials flatten.

questions.prompt: Why does binary search look almost flat on a plain linear-linear plot even though its runtime does grow with n?

options.text: Because binary search runtime is actually constant, not logarithmic
Because log(n) grows so slowly that large multiplicative increases in n produce tiny additive increases in runtime, which a linear axis compresses into apparent flatness
Because linear axes cannot display any algorithm faster than O(n)
Because binary search's runtime decreases as n grows

explanations.a: Binary search is O(log n), not O(1); it does grow, just very slowly.
explanations.b: Correct — since t = c*log(n) + d, even huge jumps in n produce small jumps in log(n) and thus small jumps in t, which look flat unless plotted against log(n) itself on semi-log-x.
explanations.c: Linear axes can display any function; the issue is visual compression of slow growth, not an inability to render it.
explanations.d: Binary search runtime increases (slowly) with n; it does not decrease.

questions.prompt: Match each suspected growth type to the axis transform that renders it as an honest straight line.

left.text: Suspected logarithmic growth, t = c*log(n) + d

right.text: Semi-log-y (log t vs. plain n)
Semi-log-x (plain t vs. log n)
Log-log (log t vs. log n)

questions.explanation: Exponential growth becomes linear when only the y-axis is logged (log t = n*log b + log c). Logarithmic growth becomes linear when only the x-axis is logged (t is already linear in log n). Power-law growth becomes linear only when BOTH axes are logged (log t = k*log n + log c).

questions.prompt: On semi-log-y axes, how does an O(n^2) algorithm's curve typically behave as n increases?

options.text: It stays a perfectly straight line, just like an exponential
It curves and flattens, growing more slowly relative to a straight line
It becomes vertical
It becomes indistinguishable from O(log n)

explanations.a: Only exponentials are straight on semi-log-y; a quadratic is not.
explanations.b: Correct — log(c*n^2) = 2*log(n) + log(c) grows only as fast as log(n), which flattens relative to n itself, so the semi-log-y curve visibly bends downward and flattens.
explanations.c: It flattens rather than becoming vertical; a vertical shape would suggest unbounded growth in a tiny n-range, not what a polynomial produces on this transform.
explanations.d: It remains distinguishable — both flatten, but a quadratic's log(t) grows as 2*log(n), still faster than a true logarithmic algorithm's log(t), which grows only as log(log n), i.e., even more slowly than log(n) itself — unbounded, but so slowly that at any practical n-range it is effectively indistinguishable from flat on this transform.

lessons.label: Fitting an Empirical Curve to a Complexity Class

sections.heading: Least-squares fitting on log-transformed data
sections.body: Eyeballing a log-log slope gets you in the right neighborhood, but a defensible empirical claim needs a fitted number with an uncertainty range. The standard method is ordinary least-squares linear regression, applied AFTER the log transform: take your (n, t) measurement pairs, compute (log n, log t) for each, and fit a line log(t) = k*log(n) + log(c) by minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals.
