questions.prompt: Order the steps of the average-case quicksort comparison-count derivation from first to last.

items.text: Define indicator variable X_ij = 1 if ranks i and j are ever compared, 0 otherwise
Observe that i and j are compared iff one of them is the first pivot drawn from the rank range [i, j]
Compute that probability as 2/(j - i + 1) and sum it over all pairs i < j
Simplify the resulting double sum to approximately 2n*ln(n), then convert to ~1.39n*log2(n)

questions.explanation: The derivation proceeds from defining the indicator variables, to identifying exactly when a pair is compared, to computing and summing that probability across all pairs (which involves the harmonic number H_n), to simplifying the final expression into the familiar ~1.39n*log2(n) figure.

lessons.label: Recursion Depth, Tail Calls, and Stack Safety

sections.heading: A crash, not just a slowdown
sections.body: Textbook recursive quicksort makes two recursive calls per partition -- sort the left side, then sort the right side -- and on adversarial input (the same sorted-array-with-first/last-pivot case that drives the Theta(n^2) worst case) the recursion tree degenerates into a straight chain of depth Theta(n): each call partitions off exactly one element and recurses on the remaining n-1. Every recursive call consumes a frame on the call stack, and the call stack has a FIXED, finite size set by the runtime (often a few megabytes, translating to on the order of tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand frames depending on frame size and language). For n in the hundreds of thousands or millions -- entirely ordinary input sizes -- an unmodified quicksort on adversarial or even just unluckily-ordered data does not merely run slowly, it CRASHES: a StackOverflowError in Java, a RecursionError in Python, a segmentation fault in unchecked C. This is a qualitatively different failure mode than a slow sort finishing late; the program terminates abnormally, which is why production sort implementations treat stack depth as a correctness property to guarantee, not just a performance detail to hope goes well.

sections.heading: The standard fix: recurse on the smaller half, loop on the larger
sections.body: The fix requires no change to the partitioning logic at all -- only to which recursive call is made explicitly and which is turned into a loop. After partitioning, compare the sizes of the two resulting subarrays; make a genuine RECURSIVE call on the SMALLER one, and instead of recursively calling on the larger one, update the current function's own bounds to cover the larger subarray and LOOP back to partition it again (an explicit `while` around the partition-and-compare step, rather than a second recursive call). Because the smaller of the two partitions is at most half the current subarray's size, each ACTUAL recursive call at least halves the problem, bounding the recursion depth at log2(n) regardless of how unbalanced any individual partition is -- even in the fully degenerate case where one side is empty and the other is n-1, the recursive call goes on the empty (trivially small) side, and the large n-1 side is handled by looping in the same frame. This technique is sometimes described loosely as 'tail-call-like,' though it is not automatic tail-call elimination by the compiler -- it is the programmer manually converting what would be a tail-recursive call into an explicit loop, guaranteeing the stack bound rather than hoping the language runtime optimizes it away (most mainstream languages, including Java, Python, and C++, do NOT guarantee tail-call optimization at all).

sections.heading: Fully iterative quicksort, and the contrast with merge sort
sections.body: Pushing this idea to its conclusion, quicksort can be written with NO recursion whatsoever: maintain an explicit STACK data structure (typically an array or a language's built-in stack/list) holding the (lo, hi) bounds of subarrays still needing partitioning; push the initial (0, n-1) range, then loop, popping a range, partitioning it, and pushing its two resulting sub-ranges back onto the stack (optimally pushing the LARGER one first so the smaller is processed next, keeping the explicit stack's maximum size bounded the same way the recursion-depth fix does). This trades the implicit call stack for an explicit heap-allocated one, which some environments prefer since it can be resized dynamically rather than hitting a fixed OS-level limit. Contrast this entire concern with merge sort, whose recursion ALWAYS splits at the exact midpoint regardless of data -- its call-stack depth is unconditionally Theta(log n) with no adversarial input able to change that, so merge sort never needed a smaller-first rewrite in the first place. This depth-bounding idea reappears directly in INTROSORT (David Musser, 1997): introsort runs quicksort but tracks recursion depth explicitly, and once depth exceeds a threshold like 2*log2(n) -- signaling the partitions have stopped halving well -- it abandons quicksort for that subarray and switches to heapsort instead, using depth itself as the worst-case tripwire rather than waiting for a stack overflow to prove something has gone wrong.

lessons.workedExample: Quicksort a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements with a naive first-element pivot and NO smaller-first fix: every partition splits off one element, so the recursion chains 999,999 levels deep, exhausting a typical several-megabyte call stack (which holds on the order of tens of thousands of frames) long before the sort finishes -- a stack overflow, not a slow result. Now apply the smaller-first fix: at the very first partition, one side has 0 elements and the other has 999,999. The algorithm makes a trivial recursive call on the 0-element side (which returns immediately) and LOOPS in the same frame to handle the 999,999-element side by partitioning it again -- repeating this pattern, the actual call-stack depth never exceeds log2(1,000,000) ~= 20 frames, regardless of how many times a partition is maximally unbalanced, because every genuine recursive call is guaranteed to at least halve the problem size.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has actually shipped sorting code in a systems or embedded context will ask about stack depth specifically because it is a real production incident category -- 'my sort worked in testing on small inputs and crashed in production on large ones' is a story many engineers have lived, and recognizing that the failure mode is a hard CRASH rather than a graceful slowdown shows you understand why this is treated as a correctness issue, not a nice-to-have optimization. A sharper judge will ask you to name the exact fix (recurse smaller, loop larger) and explain WHY it bounds depth at log2(n) even when partitions are maximally unbalanced -- the key insight being that only the SMALLER side ever gets a real recursive call, so that call alone halves the remaining problem. Connecting this forward to introsort's use of recursion depth as an explicit tripwire for switching to heapsort shows you see this not as an isolated trick but as a reusable idea in real-world hybrid sort design.

questions.prompt: Why can naive recursive quicksort actually CRASH on large adversarial input, rather than just run slowly?

options.text: Because partitioning corrupts array memory on large inputs
Because the recursion depth can reach Theta(n) on adversarial input, exceeding the call stack's fixed, finite size
Because quicksort requires more memory for the array itself than the system has available
Because integer overflow occurs when comparing large arrays

explanations.a: Partitioning is a standard in-place rearrangement; it does not corrupt memory regardless of input size.
explanations.b: Correct -- on adversarial input the recursion tree can degenerate into a Theta(n)-deep chain, and since the call stack has a fixed capacity (often bounding it to tens of thousands of frames), a sufficiently large n overflows it, producing a hard crash.
explanations.c: The array itself takes Theta(n) space regardless of pivot quality; the crash risk specifically concerns the CALL STACK from recursion depth, not the array's own storage.
explanations.d: This failure mode has nothing to do with integer overflow; it is specifically about exhausting the call stack via recursion depth.

questions.prompt: How does the 'recurse on the smaller half, loop on the larger' fix guarantee recursion depth of at most log2(n)?

options.text: It always splits the array exactly in half at the midpoint, like merge sort
Every genuine recursive call is made on the smaller partition, which is at most half the current size, so each real recursive call at least halves the problem
It caches previous partition results to avoid redundant recursive calls
It limits the array to at most log2(n) elements before switching to insertion sort

explanations.a: Quicksort's partition point still depends on the pivot and data, not a fixed midpoint -- the fix works even when the split is maximally unbalanced.
explanations.b: Correct -- because the recursive call always targets the smaller of the two partitions (at most half the current subarray), the number of genuine recursive calls before reaching a base case is bounded by log2(n), while the larger partition is handled by looping in the same stack frame instead of recursing.
explanations.c: There is no caching or memoization involved; the technique is purely about which call is recursive versus iterative.
explanations.d: This describes a different, unrelated small-array optimization (switching to insertion sort below a size threshold), not the smaller-first recursion technique.

questions.prompt: Match each sorting-related concept to its stack-depth behavior.

right.text: Can reach Theta(n) call-stack depth on adversarial input
Guaranteed at most log2(n) call-stack depth regardless of partition balance
Always Theta(log n) depth, since splits are always at the array midpoint
Tracks recursion depth explicitly and switches to heapsort once a threshold like 2*log2(n) is exceeded

questions.explanation: Naive quicksort's depth is unbounded up to Theta(n) on adversarial input; the smaller-first fix caps it at log2(n); merge sort never had this problem because its split is always positional; and introsort (Musser, 1997) uses recursion depth as an explicit worst-case tripwire, falling back to heapsort when quicksort's recursion runs too deep.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the fully iterative, explicit-stack quicksort.

items.text: Push the initial (lo, hi) range covering the whole array onto an explicit stack
Pop a (lo, hi) range from the stack and partition that subarray
Push the two resulting sub-ranges back onto the stack, larger one first
Repeat popping and partitioning until the stack is empty

questions.explanation: The explicit-stack version replaces the call stack with a programmer-managed stack of index ranges: seed it with the full array range, then repeatedly pop a range, partition it, and push the resulting sub-ranges (larger first, to keep the maximum stack size bounded) until no ranges remain.

units.label: Searching and Selection: Binary Search and Order Statistics

lessons.label: Binary Search Done Right: the Invariant and the Bugs

sections.heading: Deriving the loop from a single invariant
sections.body: Binary search is easy to describe and shockingly easy to get wrong, because most people write it from memory instead of deriving it from a stated invariant. The invariant that makes every line of the loop mechanical is: "if the target is present in the array, it lies in the half-open range [lo, hi)." Initialize lo = 0 and hi = n so the invariant holds trivially over the whole array. Each iteration, as long as lo < hi, compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, which sits strictly inside [lo, hi). Compare arr[mid] to the target: if arr[mid] equals the target, you are done. If arr[mid] is less than the target, the target (if present) must be in [mid + 1, hi), so set lo = mid + 1. If arr[mid] is greater, the target must be in [lo, mid), so set hi = mid. Every branch preserves the invariant by construction, so termination correctness is not a separate proof you bolt on afterward -- it falls out of the invariant automatically. When lo == hi the range is empty and the search has exhausted every candidate.

sections.heading: Comparisons needed and the matching lower bound
sections.body: Each comparison discards roughly half the remaining candidates, so after k comparisons at most n / 2^k elements remain feasible; setting that to 1 gives k >= log2(n), so binary search finishes in about floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons in the worst case. This is not just an upper bound on ONE algorithm -- it is the best that ANY comparison-based search over a sorted array can do. Model the search as a binary decision tree: each internal node is a comparison, each leaf is an outcome (found at some index, or confirmed absent). A tree distinguishing n+1 outcomes (n found positions plus "not present") needs at least n+1 leaves (one per outcome), and a binary tree with L leaves has depth at least ceil(log2 L); with L = n+1 this gives depth at least ceil(log2(n+1)). That establishes the matching Omega(log n) lower bound: no comparison-based algorithm can search a sorted array of size n in fewer than roughly log2 n comparisons, so binary search is asymptotically optimal, not merely a fast heuristic.

sections.heading: Two famous humiliations
sections.body: Jon Bentley, in his book Programming Pearls, reported running binary search as a workshop exercise for professional programmers over many years and finding that the overwhelming majority -- by his account, roughly 90 percent -- could not produce a correct implementation even when given ample time, most commonly failing at the boundary conditions (off-by-one errors in lo/hi/mid updates, or infinite loops when mid is computed wrong). The second humiliation came decades later and hit production code: in June 2006, Joshua Bloch, then at Google, published a widely read post titled "Extra, Extra -- Read All About It: Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken," revealing that Java's own java.util.Arrays.binarySearch had shipped for roughly nine years with the classic bug -- computing mid as (low + high) / 2, which overflows a 32-bit int when low + high exceeds about 2^31 - 1 on arrays large enough to reach it. The fix is either low + (high - low) / 2, which cannot overflow because the difference is bounded by the array size, or the unsigned-shift trick (low + high) >>> 1 in languages with an unsigned right shift.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose n = 2^31 - 2 (near Java's array-size ceiling) and a search step has low = 2^30 and high = 2^31 - 2. The naive mid = (low + high) / 2 computes low + high = 2^30 + 2^31 - 2, which is about 3.2 billion -- past Java's signed 32-bit int max of 2,147,483,647 -- so it silently wraps to a large negative number before the division, corrupting mid into a nonsensical negative index and eventually throwing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or looping incorrectly. Computing mid = low + (high - low) / 2 instead gives high - low = 2^31 - 2 - 2^30, a value that fits comfortably in a positive int, so the addition to low never overflows. This is exactly the class of array size where Bloch's bug bit real Java programs, though it took nine years to be noticed because most arrays never got that large.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has implemented binary search before knows exactly where the bugs hide -- the mid computation, the choice between < and <=, and whether bounds are open or closed -- and will ask you to write it live or trace it on a small example with duplicates or a target at the very first or last index. Reciting "it's log n" without being able to derive the loop from the [lo, hi) invariant, or without knowing that (low+high)/2 is a real historical bug rather than a textbook gotcha, signals memorized rather than understood knowledge. Naming Bentley's and Bloch's findings shows you know the algorithm is a genuine engineering hazard, not a trivial exercise.

questions.prompt: What invariant does the standard [lo, hi) binary search loop maintain at the start of every iteration?

options.text: arr[lo] is always less than the target
If the target is present in the array, it lies within the range [lo, hi)
mid always equals the index of the target
The array has already been partially sorted by the search

explanations.a: This is not guaranteed and is not the invariant used to derive the loop; arr[lo] can be anything relative to the target as long as it lies outside the surviving range.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is precisely the invariant that lets every branch of the loop be derived mechanically rather than memorized.
explanations.c: mid is only checked against the target each iteration; there is no guarantee it lands on the target until (and unless) it does.
explanations.d: Binary search does not sort or modify the array; it only narrows a search range within an already-sorted array.

questions.prompt: What was the root cause of the binary search bug Joshua Bloch reported in 2006 in java.util.Arrays.binarySearch?

options.text: Using < instead of <= in the loop condition
Computing mid as (low + high) / 2, which can integer-overflow for large arrays
Comparing objects with == instead of .equals()
Failing to handle an empty array as input

explanations.a: The loop condition was not the reported defect; the bug was arithmetic, in the mid computation.
explanations.b: Correct -- low + high can exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE for large arrays, silently overflowing and producing a corrupted mid index.
explanations.c: The bug is about integer arithmetic on indices, not object comparison semantics.
explanations.d: Empty-array handling was not the defect Bloch identified; the array had to be large enough for low+high to overflow, which requires a sizable array, not an empty one.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of professional programmers did Jon Bentley report as unable to write a correct binary search in his workshop exercise?

options.text: About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 90 percent
Nearly 0 percent -- almost everyone succeeded

explanations.a: This inverts the reported figure -- roughly 10 percent succeeded, not 10 percent failed.
explanations.b: The failure rate Bentley reported was substantially higher than half.
explanations.c: Correct -- Bentley reported that roughly 90 percent of professional programmers given ample time could not produce a correct implementation, usually failing at boundary handling.
explanations.d: The exercise is famous precisely because success was rare, not because almost everyone got it right.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one iteration of the [lo, hi) binary search loop, starting from the loop-condition check.

items.text: Check that lo < hi; if not, stop
Compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
Compare arr[mid] to the target
Narrow to [mid + 1, hi) or [lo, mid) based on the comparison

questions.explanation: Each iteration first checks the loop condition, then computes a safe mid strictly inside the current range, compares the target against arr[mid], and finally narrows lo or hi according to that comparison -- exactly the sequence that keeps the [lo, hi) invariant true.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what it establishes about binary search.

right.text: Omega(log n) lower bound for any comparison-based search
Avoids the integer-overflow bug from (low + high) / 2
Lets every loop branch be derived mechanically rather than memorized

questions.explanation: The decision-tree argument over n+1 possible outcomes shows no comparison-based algorithm can beat about log2(n) comparisons; computing mid via low + (high-low)/2 keeps the intermediate sum bounded and overflow-free; and stating the [lo, hi) invariant up front is what makes the loop's update rules mechanical rather than something to memorize.

lessons.label: Lower Bound, Upper Bound, and Searching for Ranges

sections.heading: An insertion point instead of a yes/no answer
sections.body: Textbook binary search returns "found at index i" or "not found," but that framing is the wrong primitive for most real problems, and reaching for it first is the beginner's mistake. The more useful primitive returns an INSERTION POINT: the index where the target could be inserted while keeping the array sorted. Python's bisect module calls the two variants bisect_left and bisect_right; C++'s standard library calls the same pair lower_bound and upper_bound. lower_bound(x) returns the index of the first element that is >= x (equivalently, the leftmost position at which x could be inserted). upper_bound(x) returns the index of the first element that is > x (the rightmost position at which x could be inserted, i.e., just past any run of elements equal to x). Both are computed with the same [lo, hi) loop from ordinary binary search, differing only in whether the comparison uses < or <=: lower_bound moves lo = mid + 1 when arr[mid] < x, while upper_bound moves lo = mid + 1 when arr[mid] <= x. Both always return a valid index in [0, n], even when x is absent -- there is no found/not-found branch to get wrong.

sections.heading: One primitive, four answers
sections.body: The reason this formulation is worth memorizing over ordinary binary search is that a single pair of calls answers a whole family of range questions without any extra logic. "First element >= x" is exactly lower_bound(x). "Count of x in the array" is upper_bound(x) minus lower_bound(x) -- the width of the run of equal elements, zero if x is absent. "Predecessor of x" (largest element strictly less than x) is the element at lower_bound(x) - 1, if that index is >= 0. "Successor of x" (smallest element strictly greater than x) is the element at upper_bound(x), if that index is < n. All four questions -- membership, counting, predecessor, successor -- reduce to arithmetic on two insertion points, with no special-casing for "not found." This is why competitive programmers and library authors treat lower_bound/upper_bound as the actual primitive and treat classic yes/no binary search as a derived convenience: check whether arr[lower_bound(x)] == x (guarding the out-of-range case first).

sections.heading: Why this matters most exactly where plain binary search breaks: duplicates
sections.body: Consider a sorted array with a run of duplicate keys, say [2, 4, 4, 4, 4, 7, 9], searching for x = 4. Ordinary found/not-found binary search will report SOME index where arr[mid] == 4 -- but which one depends on implementation details of how mid is computed and which half is chosen on ties, and it is not guaranteed to be the first or last occurrence. If a caller then wants "how many 4s are there" or "what is the first index of 4," an arbitrary hit in the middle of the run gives no way to answer without additional linear scanning outward -- which silently degrades an O(log n) algorithm to O(n) in exactly the case duplicates create. lower_bound(4) deterministically returns index 1 (the first 4) and upper_bound(4) deterministically returns index 5 (just past the last 4), so the count is 5 - 1 = 4, correct and O(log n), with no scanning. This duplicate-key case is precisely where the found/not-found formulation quietly breaks and the insertion-point formulation stays correct.

lessons.workedExample: Given the sorted array [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 8, 9] (n = 8), find the count of 5s and the predecessor/successor of 5. lower_bound(5) binary searches for the first index with arr[i] >= 5, landing at index 4 (the first 5). upper_bound(5) searches for the first index with arr[i] > 5, landing at index 6 (the 8). Count of 5s = 6 - 4 = 2, matching the two 5s at indices 4 and 5. The predecessor of 5 is arr[lower_bound(5) - 1] = arr[3] = 3, the largest element strictly less than 5. The successor of 5 is arr[upper_bound(5)] = arr[6] = 8, the smallest element strictly greater than 5. All four answers came from two binary searches and simple index arithmetic, with no separate found/not-found logic and no scanning through the run of 5s.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson will ask you to find the count of a value that appears many times, or the predecessor of a value not in the array, and watch whether you reach for lower_bound/upper_bound automatically or start writing custom scan logic. The tell that you understand the primitive is naming WHY it subsumes found/not-found search (insertion points are always well-defined, so there is no not-found branch to get wrong) and being able to state, without hesitation, that count = upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x). A judge may also probe the duplicate-key case specifically, since that is where naive binary search implementations silently give inconsistent answers.

questions.prompt: What does bisect_left(x) (equivalently, lower_bound(x)) return?

options.text: The index of the first element strictly greater than x
The index of the first element that is greater than or equal to x
True if x is present, false otherwise
The index of the last element less than or equal to x

explanations.a: That description is upper_bound(x), not lower_bound(x).
explanations.b: Correct -- lower_bound(x) is the leftmost insertion point, the first index whose element is >= x.
explanations.c: lower_bound returns an index (an insertion point), not a boolean; it is always well-defined even when x is absent.
explanations.d: That would describe something closer to a predecessor search, not lower_bound.

questions.prompt: In a sorted array, how do you compute the count of occurrences of value x using lower_bound and upper_bound?

options.text: lower_bound(x) - upper_bound(x)
upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x)
upper_bound(x) + lower_bound(x)
You cannot compute a count this way; you must scan the array

explanations.a: This subtracts in the wrong order and would produce a negative or nonsensical value, since upper_bound(x) >= lower_bound(x) always.
explanations.b: Correct -- upper_bound(x) is the first index past the run of x's, and lower_bound(x) is the first index of the run, so their difference is the run's length, i.e. the count.
explanations.c: Adding the two insertion points has no meaningful interpretation as a count.
explanations.d: This is exactly the point of the primitive: no scanning is needed, only two O(log n) searches and a subtraction.

questions.prompt: Why does ordinary found/not-found binary search break down specifically when the array contains duplicate keys?

options.text: Binary search cannot run at all on an array with duplicates
It returns some index within the run of equal elements, but not necessarily the first or last, making counting or boundary queries unreliable without extra scanning
Duplicates make the array technically unsorted
It always returns the last occurrence, which is fine for counting but not for predecessor queries

explanations.a: Binary search still runs and terminates correctly; the issue is which index within a duplicate run it happens to report, not whether it runs.
explanations.b: Correct -- an arbitrary hit inside the run gives no first/last boundary, so counting or range queries would require additional linear scanning outward, degrading to O(n).
explanations.c: A sorted array can absolutely contain duplicate keys and remain sorted; sortedness only requires non-decreasing order.
explanations.d: Which specific index within the run gets returned depends on implementation details of mid computation and tie-breaking, not a guaranteed last occurrence.

questions.prompt: For the sorted array [2, 4, 4, 4, 7, 9], order these steps to compute the count of 4s using the insertion-point method.

items.text: Compute lower_bound(4), landing at index 1 (first element >= 4)
Compute upper_bound(4), landing at index 4 (first element > 4)
Subtract: count = upper_bound(4) - lower_bound(4) = 3

questions.explanation: You first find the leftmost insertion point for 4 (index 1), then the rightmost insertion point (index 4, just past the run of three 4's), and only then subtract to get the count of 3.

questions.prompt: Match each range query to how it is computed from lower_bound(x) (= L) and upper_bound(x) (= U) on a sorted array arr of length n.

right.text: arr[L] == x, after checking L < n
arr[L - 1], if L - 1 >= 0
arr[U], if U < n

questions.explanation: Membership reduces to checking whether the element at the lower-bound insertion point equals x (with a bounds guard); the predecessor is the element just before the lower-bound insertion point; and the successor is the element at the upper-bound insertion point, i.e. just past any run of x's.

lessons.label: Binary Search on the Answer

sections.heading: The generalization: searching a predicate, not an array
sections.body: The core operation in binary search is not really "search a sorted array" -- it is "find where a monotone boolean predicate flips from false to true." Once stated that way, the array is optional. Suppose P(x) is a predicate over a numeric range (integers or reals) such that P is false for every x below some threshold t and true for every x at or above t -- a false...false,true...true pattern with no array in existence, just a function you can evaluate at any point. Binary search over that range, evaluating P(mid) each step, locates t in O(log(range)) evaluations of P, exactly as if the range were a sorted array of P's values. This is called binary search on the answer, and it is one of the most reused techniques in competitive programming because an enormous range of optimization problems -- minimize the largest chunk, minimize the maximum load, find the smallest feasible value -- can be recast as: is answer <= x feasible? Then binary search x.

sections.heading: Canonical problems and the discipline of proving monotonicity first
sections.body: Three canonical instances make the pattern concrete. Minimum ship capacity to ship packages within D days (LeetCode 1011): P(capacity) = "can all packages be shipped within D days using this capacity, greedily loading each day until the next package would exceed capacity?" is false for small capacities and true for large ones, monotone by the argument that any capacity that works also works with a strictly larger capacity, since a greedy day-by-day loader only ships more per day as capacity grows. Minimum eating speed Koko can use to finish all banana piles within H hours (LeetCode 875): P(speed) = "can Koko finish all piles at this speed within H hours?", monotone because a faster eating speed only reduces or holds equal the hours needed per pile. Minimum-maximum page allocation (assign contiguous book pages to k students minimizing the maximum pages any one student gets): P(maxPages) = "can the books be partitioned into <= k contiguous groups each summing to at most maxPages?", monotone because raising the cap only makes partitioning easier. In every case, the discipline is to PROVE monotonicity before reaching for binary search -- if P is not actually false...false,true...true (it can flicker back and forth), binary search silently returns a wrong or arbitrary answer with no error, because the algorithm has no way to detect that its core assumption was violated.

sections.heading: The floating-point variant: fixed iteration count instead of a loop condition
sections.body: When the answer range is real-valued rather than integer, the usual lo < hi loop condition never naturally terminates, because there is always another real number between lo and hi. The standard fix is to iterate a FIXED number of times -- commonly around 100 iterations -- rather than looping while lo < hi. Each iteration halves the interval width, so after 100 iterations the interval has shrunk by a factor of 2^100, which is astronomically finer than double-precision floating point's roughly 2^-52 relative precision; the loop is guaranteed to converge to the limits of floating-point representation long before 100 iterations complete, so a fixed count is both safe and simpler than trying to reason about an epsilon-based stopping condition, which is easy to get wrong (too loose an epsilon undershoots precision; too tight one causes infinite looping due to floating-point rounding making lo and hi never exactly converge).

lessons.workedExample: Koko must eat all banana piles [3, 6, 7, 11] within H = 8 hours, eating at a constant integer speed per pile (ceil(pile / speed) hours per pile). Binary search speed over [1, max(piles)] = [1, 11]. P(speed) = sum of ceil(pile/speed) for all piles <= 8. Testing speed = 4: ceil(3/4)+ceil(6/4)+ceil(7/4)+ceil(11/4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8, which is <= 8, so P(4) is true. Testing speed = 3: ceil(3/3)+ceil(6/3)+ceil(7/3)+ceil(11/3) = 1+2+3+4 = 10, which exceeds 8, so P(3) is false. Since P is false for speed 3 and true for speed 4 with no flips elsewhere in this monotone range, binary search converges on 4 as the minimum feasible eating speed in O(log(max pile) * n) time rather than testing every speed from 1 upward.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will want to hear you say, unprompted, that the technique requires proving P is monotone BEFORE applying it -- not just noticing the pattern looks similar to array binary search. Expect a probe like "what if the feasibility function isn't actually monotone here -- what happens?" (silent wrong answer, no crash, no error signal) and a probe on the floating-point case asking why you would iterate a fixed 100 times instead of using an epsilon-based while loop. Naming a canonical problem (ship capacity, Koko eating speed, or page allocation) by its actual constraints, rather than describing it vaguely, signals you have implemented this pattern rather than just recognized its name.

questions.prompt: What must be true of a predicate P over a numeric range before binary search on the answer can correctly locate its threshold?

options.text: P must be true for at least half of the range
P must be monotone: false for all values below some threshold and true for all values at or above it
P must be evaluable in O(1) time
The range must contain an actual sorted array of values

explanations.a: The proportion of true values is irrelevant; what matters is that all false values precede all true values with no flips.
explanations.b: Correct -- monotonicity (false...false,true...true with a single flip point) is the exact precondition; without it binary search can silently converge to a wrong answer.
explanations.c: P can take any evaluation cost; a slower P only affects the overall time complexity, not correctness of the search.
explanations.d: The entire point of the generalization is that no array needs to exist -- P is evaluated directly at any candidate value in the range.

questions.prompt: In the floating-point variant of binary search on the answer, why is a fixed iteration count (e.g., about 100) typically used instead of looping while lo < hi?

options.text: Because floating-point comparisons are undefined in most languages
Because lo < hi may never become false for real numbers, but a fixed count comfortably exceeds the iterations needed to reach double-precision limits
Because fixed iteration counts run faster on all hardware
Because the predicate P cannot be evaluated more than 100 times without overflow

explanations.a: Floating-point comparisons are well-defined; the issue is termination of the loop condition, not comparison validity.
explanations.b: Correct -- there is always another real number between lo and hi, so the loop may never naturally terminate on that condition, while ~100 halvings vastly exceeds double precision's ~2^-52 relative resolution.
explanations.c: The fixed count is chosen for correctness and simplicity of termination, not for raw speed; both approaches do similar work per iteration.
explanations.d: There is no overflow constraint on evaluating P; the 100 count is about interval precision, unrelated to overflow.

questions.prompt: What happens if you apply binary search on the answer to a predicate that is NOT actually monotone (it flips true/false/true across the range)?

options.text: The algorithm throws a runtime exception alerting you to the violated assumption
It silently converges to some value with no indication that the result may be wrong
It automatically falls back to a linear scan
It always returns the correct global answer regardless, just more slowly

explanations.a: There is no built-in check for monotonicity; the algorithm has no way to detect that its core assumption is violated.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is precisely why monotonicity must be proven before applying the technique: a non-monotone P yields a silently wrong or arbitrary threshold with no error signal.
explanations.c: There is no automatic fallback mechanism; binary search on the answer proceeds exactly as designed regardless of whether the precondition holds.
explanations.d: Correctness is not guaranteed at all without monotonicity -- the result can be any value where the predicate happened to look like a flip near mid.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving the Koko eating-speed problem via binary search on the answer.

items.text: Define P(speed) = total hours to eat all piles at this speed <= H
Prove P is monotone: faster speed only reduces or holds hours needed
Binary search speed over [1, max(piles)], evaluating P(mid) each step
Converge on the minimum speed for which P is true

questions.explanation: You first define the feasibility predicate, then establish that it is monotone (a prerequisite, not an afterthought), then run the binary search evaluating the predicate at each midpoint, and finally arrive at the minimum feasible speed where the predicate flips to true.

questions.prompt: Match each canonical binary-search-on-the-answer problem to its feasibility predicate P(x).

left.text: Minimum ship capacity within D days
Minimum eating speed within H hours
Minimum-maximum page allocation to k students

right.text: P(capacity) = all packages ship within D days at this capacity
P(speed) = all piles eaten within H hours at this speed
P(maxPages) = books partition into at most k contiguous groups, each <= maxPages

questions.explanation: Each problem's feasibility predicate is monotone in its respective parameter: larger capacity or speed only makes the day/hour constraint easier to satisfy, and a larger max-pages cap only makes the k-way partition easier to achieve.

lessons.label: Binary Search Where the Array Isn't Sorted (or Isn't There)

sections.heading: Rotated sorted arrays: at least one half is always sorted
sections.body: A rotated sorted array -- take a sorted array and cyclically shift it by some unknown offset, e.g. [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] rotated from [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] -- is not sorted globally, so a naive binary search comparison against arr[mid] tells you nothing by itself. The key structural fact that rescues binary search is: at every step, at least one of the two halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] IS sorted (a contiguous rotation of a sorted array, when split at any point, always leaves at least one piece internally sorted, since the single "break" between the rotated end and the original start can only fall in one half). The algorithm is: compute mid, determine which half is sorted by comparing arr[lo] to arr[mid], then check whether the target lies within that sorted half's range; if it does, recurse into it, otherwise recurse into the other half (which must contain the target if it exists at all). This preserves O(log n) time because each step still discards half the array, exactly as ordinary binary search does, just with an extra O(1) check to determine which half is safe to reason about.

sections.heading: Duplicates break the sortedness test
sections.body: This technique depends on being able to tell WHICH half is sorted using a single comparison like arr[lo] < arr[mid], arr[lo] > arr[mid], or arr[lo] == arr[mid]. With distinct elements, arr[lo] == arr[mid] can only happen when lo == mid, which is unambiguous. But if duplicates are allowed, arr[lo] == arr[mid] can also occur when lo != mid, and in that case you genuinely cannot tell from that one comparison whether the left half is sorted, the right half is sorted, or both -- the identical values could arise from either side of the rotation break. The only safe fallback when arr[lo] == arr[mid] != informative is to shrink the search by one from either end (e.g., lo += 1) and retry, which in the worst case (an array of nearly all-identical values, like [2,2,2,2,2,2,2,0,2,2,2,2]) degrades the algorithm to discarding only one element per step -- dragging the worst case from O(log n) all the way back to Theta(n). This is a genuinely different complexity class, not just a slower constant, and it is the textbook example (LeetCode's "Search in Rotated Sorted Array II") of how duplicates can silently destroy an algorithm's asymptotic guarantee.

sections.heading: When there is no array at all: exponential search and interpolation search
sections.body: Exponential search (also called galloping search, studied by Jon Bentley and Andrew Chi-Chih Yao in 1976) handles the case where you must search a sorted but UNBOUNDED or unknown-length sequence -- for instance, a stream where you can index arr[i] but don't know n in advance. The method: starting from index 1, repeatedly double the bound (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) until either the sequence ends or arr[bound] overshoots the target, then run an ordinary binary search restricted to the range between the previous and current bound. If the target's true index is i, doubling takes about log2(i) steps to overshoot, and the subsequent binary search over a range of about that same size costs another log2(i) comparisons, giving a total of roughly 2*floor(log2 i) comparisons -- worse by a constant factor than binary search over a known array of size i, but the only option when n itself is unknown. Interpolation search takes a different tack on ordinary arrays: instead of always probing the midpoint, it estimates where the target SHOULD be using linear interpolation between arr[lo] and arr[hi], the way a person flipping through a phone book jumps toward the back for a name starting with "W." On uniformly distributed keys this achieves an expected O(log log n) -- provably, per Yao and Yao's 1976 analysis -- far better than binary search's O(log n), but on skewed or adversarially clustered distributions the interpolation estimate can be consistently wrong, degrading the worst case to Theta(n), the same as a linear scan.

lessons.workedExample: Search for 0 in the rotated array [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] (n=7). mid = 3, arr[mid] = 7. Compare arr[lo]=4 to arr[mid]=7: since 4 < 7, the left half [lo..mid] = [4,5,6,7] is sorted. Is 0 within [arr[lo], arr[mid]] = [4,7]? No, so the target must be in the other half: set lo = mid+1 = 4, hi stays 6. Now mid = 5, arr[mid] = 1. Compare arr[lo]=0 to arr[mid]=1: 0 < 1, so [0,1] (indices 4-5) is sorted. Is 0 within [arr[lo],arr[mid]] = [0,1]? Yes, so recurse into that sorted half: hi = mid = 5. Now lo=4, hi=5, mid=4, arr[mid]=0, which matches the target -- found at index 4 in 3 comparisons, the same order as ordinary binary search on 7 elements (about floor(log2 7)+1 = 3).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will likely ask you to trace the rotated-array search by hand on a small example and explain, at each step, WHY you can be sure one particular half is sorted -- the answer must reference the single-break structural property, not a guess. A sharper follow-up asks what happens with duplicates, and the correct answer names the specific worst-case degradation to Theta(n), not a vague "it gets slower." If you bring up exponential or interpolation search unprompted when discussing arrays that aren't fully known or fully random-access, that signals you understand binary search as a family of related techniques rather than one fixed recipe, and citing the O(log log n) versus Theta(n) split for interpolation search under different data distributions shows you grasp that its performance is data-dependent, not universal.

questions.prompt: What structural fact makes binary search still possible on a rotated sorted array?

options.text: The whole array remains fully sorted after rotation
At every step, at least one of the two halves around mid is internally sorted
Rotation always places the target in the first half
The array must be re-sorted before searching

explanations.a: Rotation is exactly what breaks global sortedness; the array as a whole is not sorted after rotation.
explanations.b: Correct -- because there is only a single rotation break point, splitting the array at any mid always leaves at least one of the two resulting halves internally sorted.
explanations.c: There is no such guarantee; the target can be in either half depending on where the rotation break and the target both fall.
explanations.d: The entire point of the technique is to avoid re-sorting; it exploits the rotated structure directly in O(log n) time.

questions.prompt: Why do duplicate values degrade rotated-array search from O(log n) to Theta(n) in the worst case?

options.text: Duplicates make the array too large to fit binary search's assumptions
When arr[lo] == arr[mid] with duplicates present, you cannot determine which half is sorted, forcing a one-element-at-a-time shrink in the worst case
Duplicates require re-sorting the array before each search
Duplicates cause the algorithm to enter an infinite loop that must be manually terminated

explanations.a: Array size is unrelated to this degradation; the issue is ambiguity in determining which half is sorted, not scale.
explanations.b: Correct -- when arr[lo] equals arr[mid] and duplicates are allowed, this equality no longer reliably indicates lo == mid, so the safe fallback is to shrink the range by one element at a time, which can cost Theta(n) in adversarial cases like an array of nearly identical values.
explanations.c: No re-sorting occurs or is needed; the algorithm still searches the rotated structure directly.
explanations.d: A correct implementation terminates (via the one-at-a-time shrink), just slowly in the worst case -- it does not infinite-loop by design.

questions.prompt: On uniformly distributed keys, what expected time complexity does interpolation search achieve, compared to binary search's O(log n)?

options.text: O(log log n), better than binary search
O(n), the same as a linear scan
O(log n), identical to binary search
O(1), constant time regardless of array size

explanations.a: Correct -- Yao and Yao's 1976 analysis established O(log log n) expected time for interpolation search on uniformly distributed keys, better than binary search's O(log n).
explanations.b: O(n) describes interpolation search's worst case on skewed or adversarially clustered data, not its behavior on uniformly distributed keys.
explanations.c: Interpolation search is provably better than plain O(log n) specifically under the uniform-distribution assumption; it is not merely equivalent.
explanations.d: Constant time is not achievable for comparison/probe-based search over an arbitrary-size sorted array; interpolation search still scales with n, just more slowly than log n on average.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of exponential (galloping) search for a target in a sorted sequence of unknown length.

items.text: Start with bound = 1
Repeatedly double the bound until the sequence ends or arr[bound] overshoots the target
Run ordinary binary search restricted to the range between the previous and current bound

questions.explanation: Exponential search first sets an initial small bound, doubles it until it overshoots the target or the sequence ends (establishing a range of known size roughly proportional to the target's true index), and only then runs a standard binary search confined to that final range.

questions.prompt: Match each search variant to the condition under which it is the right tool.

right.text: Array is sorted but has been cyclically shifted by an unknown offset
Sequence is sorted but its length is unknown or unbounded
Array is sorted and keys are (expected to be) uniformly distributed

questions.explanation: Rotated-array search exploits the single-break structure of a cyclic shift; exponential search handles unknown or unbounded lengths by doubling a bound before binary searching within it; and interpolation search exploits an assumption of uniform key distribution to estimate probe positions, which is exactly the assumption that fails on skewed data.

lessons.label: Quickselect: Finding the k-th Element Without Sorting

sections.heading: Hoare's 1961 FIND: partition, then recurse into only one side
sections.body: In 1961, Tony Hoare -- who also invented quicksort -- published Algorithm 65, FIND, in the same July 1961 issue of CACM as Algorithms 63 (Partition) and 64 (Quicksort), describing what is now called quickselect. The insight is that finding the k-th smallest element does not require the array to be fully sorted; it only requires locating the one boundary at rank k. The algorithm partitions the array exactly as quicksort does: pick a pivot, rearrange the array so everything less than the pivot comes before it and everything greater comes after, and the pivot lands at its final sorted position p. If p equals k, you are done -- the pivot IS the k-th element. If k < p, the k-th smallest must lie in the left partition, so recurse ONLY into [lo, p). If k > p, recurse only into (p, hi]. The crucial difference from quicksort is that quicksort recurses into BOTH sides after every partition, while quickselect recurses into exactly ONE side, discarding the other entirely -- it never needs to know the internal order of the elements it throws away, only that they are all correctly on the wrong side of the pivot for the purposes of rank k.

sections.heading: Deriving the expected Theta(n) cost
sections.body: Because each partition step costs O(current range size) and quickselect discards roughly half the remaining range on average (assuming reasonably balanced pivot choices, e.g. random pivot selection), the expected total work follows the geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + ... which sums to at most 2n, i.e. Theta(n) -- linear in the ORIGINAL array size, not n log n. A more precise classical analysis (Knuth; Grubel-Rosler) gives an expected comparison count of approximately 2*(h(alpha)+1)*n for finding the alpha*n-th smallest among n elements, where h(alpha) = -alpha*ln(alpha) - (1-alpha)*ln(1-alpha) is the binary entropy function; this is highest near the median (alpha = 1/2, h(1/2) = ln 2, giving about 2*(ln2+1)*n ~ 3.39n) and lowest (approaching 2n) when k is near either end. This Theta(n) expected bound is the headline result of the whole lesson: finding the median of an unsorted array costs Theta(n) in expectation, which is STRICTLY LESS than the Theta(n log n) required to sort the array and then read off the middle element -- selection is a genuinely easier problem than sorting, and quickselect is the proof by construction.

sections.heading: The catch: Theta(n^2) under adversarial or unlucky pivots
sections.body: Quickselect's Theta(n) bound is an EXPECTED cost, not a worst-case guarantee, and it inherits the same Achilles' heel as quicksort: if the pivot is chosen poorly and consistently lands near the minimum or maximum of the current range (for example, always picking the first element as pivot on an already-sorted or adversarially-constructed array), each partition step discards only a constant number of elements instead of a constant fraction. That degrades the recursion to n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1, which is Theta(n^2) -- quadratic, no better than a naive nested-loop selection. Mitigations mirror quicksort's: randomizing the pivot choice makes the adversarial worst case require an adversary who can predict the random number generator, and choosing the pivot via a more careful (though costlier) sub-procedure -- exactly the motivation for the median-of-medians technique -- eliminates the worst case entirely at the price of a larger constant factor, a tradeoff explored in the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: Find the 3rd smallest element (k=3, 1-indexed) in [9, 3, 7, 1, 8, 2, 5]. Pick pivot = 5 (say, the last element). Partition: elements less than 5 go left, greater go right: [3, 1, 2] | 5 | [9, 7, 8]. The pivot 5 lands at index 3 (1-indexed rank 4, since 3 elements are smaller than it). Since k=3 < rank 4, recurse into the left partition [3, 1, 2] looking for the 3rd smallest overall, which is now the 3rd smallest of this length-3 subarray, i.e. its maximum. Partition [3, 1, 2] with pivot = 2: [1] | 2 | [3]. Pivot 2 has rank 2 within this subarray; since we want rank 3 and 3 > 2, recurse into the right partition [3], which has exactly one element at the target rank -- answer: 3. Partitioning a range of size n against a pivot costs roughly n-1 comparisons, so total work across the shrinking ranges (size 7, then 3, then 1) came to roughly 6 + 2 + 0 = 8 comparisons, never touching the right partition [9,7,8] from the first split at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will likely ask why quickselect is faster than "just sort and index" -- the precise answer is that quickselect achieves Theta(n) expected time by discarding one whole side after each partition, never recursing into both, whereas sorting necessarily does Theta(n log n) work to establish a total order it doesn't need. A sharper follow-up asks about the worst case, and citing Theta(n^2) under adversarial pivot choice (not just "it can be slow") shows you know the algorithm's actual failure mode, not just its happy path. Naming Hoare, 1961, and CACM Algorithm 65 signals you know this is a specific, dated, citable result rather than folklore.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between quickselect and quicksort's partitioning approach?

options.text: Quickselect uses a different partitioning scheme entirely
Quickselect recurses into only ONE side of the partition (the side containing rank k), while quicksort recurses into both
Quickselect never uses a pivot
Quickselect sorts the array first and then selects

explanations.a: Quickselect uses the same partitioning step as quicksort; the difference is in what happens after partitioning, not the partition itself.
explanations.b: Correct -- after partitioning, quickselect determines which side contains rank k and recurses only into that side, discarding the other side's internal order entirely.
explanations.c: Quickselect partitions around a pivot exactly as quicksort does; it very much uses a pivot.
explanations.d: The entire point of quickselect is to AVOID full sorting; it partitions repeatedly but never sorts the whole array.

questions.prompt: Who published the quickselect algorithm (as "FIND," CACM Algorithm 65), and when?

options.text: Donald Knuth, 1968
Tony Hoare, 1961
Robert Tarjan, 1973
Jon Bentley, 1986

explanations.a: Knuth analyzed and refined selection algorithms in his later work but did not originate FIND.
explanations.b: Correct -- Tony Hoare, who also invented quicksort, published FIND as CACM Algorithm 65 in 1961, in the same issue as quicksort itself.
explanations.c: Tarjan is one of the five authors of the 1973 median-of-medians (BFPRT) paper, a different, later algorithm covered in the next lesson.
explanations.d: Bentley's relevant contributions (discussed elsewhere in this unit) are to binary search pedagogy and exponential search, not to quickselect's origin.

questions.prompt: Why is quickselect's expected Theta(n) time considered a meaningfully different result from sorting-then-indexing?

options.text: It isn't different -- both approaches cost the same asymptotically
Theta(n) is strictly less than the Theta(n log n) required to sort, showing selection is an easier problem than full sorting
Sorting is actually faster than quickselect in all cases
Quickselect only works on already-sorted arrays

explanations.a: They are asymptotically different: Theta(n) versus Theta(n log n) is a real complexity-class gap for large n.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the headline result: finding a single rank statistic costs Theta(n) in expectation, strictly cheaper than the Theta(n log n) needed to establish a total order via sorting.
explanations.c: For large n, Theta(n) expected quickselect beats Theta(n log n) sorting; sorting is not faster asymptotically.
explanations.d: Quickselect operates on arbitrary unsorted arrays; that is the entire premise of the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one round of quickselect searching for the k-th smallest element.

items.text: Choose a pivot from the current range
Partition the range so elements less than the pivot precede it and greater elements follow
Compare the pivot's final position p to k
Recurse into only the one side that must contain rank k (or stop if p equals k)

questions.explanation: Each round picks a pivot, partitions around it exactly as quicksort would, compares the pivot's resulting rank to the target k, and then recurses into only the single side known to contain rank k -- or stops immediately if the pivot itself is at rank k.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to quickselect's resulting time complexity.

left.text: Random or well-balanced pivot choices on average
Pivot consistently near the min/max of the current range (e.g., adversarial input with a fixed pivot rule)
Sorting the whole array first, then indexing to find rank k

right.text: Expected Theta(n)
Theta(n^2) worst case
Theta(n log n)

questions.explanation: Well-balanced pivots give quickselect its expected Theta(n) bound via the n + n/2 + n/4 + ... series; consistently poor pivot choices degrade it to the quadratic Theta(n^2) worst case, the same failure mode as quicksort; and sorting the entire array first costs Theta(n log n) regardless of how well-balanced the sort's pivots are, since sorting must establish a total order that selection does not need.

lessons.label: Median of Medians (BFPRT 1973): Guaranteed Linear Selection

sections.heading: The groups-of-five pivot-selection scheme
sections.body: Quickselect's Theta(n^2) worst case comes entirely from bad pivot choices, so in 1973 Manuel Blum, Robert Floyd, Vaughan Pratt, Ronald Rivest, and Robert Tarjan -- five authors whose initials give the algorithm its common name, BFPRT, published as "Time Bounds for Selection" -- devised a way to choose a provably GOOD pivot in linear time, guaranteeing worst-case linear selection rather than merely expected linear selection. The scheme: split the n elements into groups of 5 (the last group may have fewer), sort each group of 5 with a fixed, tiny sorting network (a handful of comparisons, O(1) work per group), take each group's median (the 3rd of 5), collect all ceil(n/5) group medians into a new array, and recursively find the MEDIAN OF THAT ARRAY OF MEDIANS using the same BFPRT algorithm. That recursively-computed median-of-medians is then used as the pivot for a standard partition step, exactly as in quickselect, and the algorithm recurses into whichever side contains the target rank -- but now with a mathematical guarantee about how much of the array that pivot discards.

sections.heading: Why the pivot provably discards at least 3n/10 elements
sections.body: The guarantee comes from counting an ordering relationship. At least half of the ceil(n/5) group medians are <= the median-of-medians (by definition of being its median), and for each such group median, at least 2 more elements in its group of 5 are also <= it (since the median of 5 sorted elements has 2 elements below it in its own group). So at least half of ceil(n/5) groups times 3 elements each (the median itself plus its 2 smaller group-mates) are <= the pivot -- roughly (n/5)/2 * 3 = 3n/10 elements are guaranteed <= the pivot, and by the symmetric argument, at least 3n/10 elements are guaranteed >= the pivot. That means whichever side the recursion discards, it discards AT LEAST 3n/10 of the elements, so the surviving side has AT MOST 7n/10 elements. This produces the recurrence T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n): T(n/5) for recursively finding the median of medians, T(7n/10) for the worst-case recursive selection call on the remaining side, and O(n) for the grouping, group-sorting, and partitioning work. Because 1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10 < 1, this recurrence solves to T(n) = O(n) -- guaranteed worst-case linear time, with no dependence on luck or randomization.

sections.heading: Why groups of 5, not 3 -- and the practical verdict
sections.body: The choice of group size 5 is not arbitrary: it is the smallest odd group size for which the recurrence's fractions sum to strictly less than 1. With groups of 3, the same counting argument gives roughly half of n/3 groups (n/6 groups) contributing 2 elements each (the median plus 1 smaller group-mate) <= the pivot, guaranteeing at least (n/6)*2 = n/3 elements discarded, leaving up to n - n/3 = 2n/3 on the recursive side, and the recurrence becomes T(n) <= T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n) -- and since 1/3 + 2/3 = 1 exactly, this is the borderline case whose recurrence does NOT collapse to O(n); it solves to O(n log n) instead, no better than sorting. Groups of 5 (or 7, or any larger odd size) push the fractions below 1 and recover linear time, with 5 chosen because it is the smallest such size and therefore has the best constant factor among the family. That constant factor, however, is still large in absolute terms: median-of-medians carries a substantially larger constant factor than randomized quickselect -- reported overheads range from roughly 10% to several times slower depending on implementation quality -- which is why it is rarely used standalone. Because of this, BFPRT rarely runs alone in production code; it ships as the guaranteed-linear FALLBACK inside introselect (the selection analogue of introsort), invoked only when quickselect's recursion depth exceeds a threshold suggesting adversarial or unlucky input. Median-of-medians is the cleanest textbook case of "provably better, practically worse": it eliminates quickselect's Theta(n^2) worst case entirely, at the cost of being the slower choice on nearly every typical input.

lessons.workedExample: Take n = 25 elements. Split into 5 groups of 5 and sort each internally (cheap, fixed-size sorts). Collect the 5 group medians into a new array and recursively find ITS median (the median of 5 numbers, found directly by sorting since 5 is small) -- call it M. By the counting argument, at least 3 groups have their median <= M (roughly half of 5 groups, rounded), and each contributes its median plus its 2 smaller members, so at least 3*3 = 9 of the 25 elements are guaranteed <= M -- consistent with the 3n/10 = 7.5 guarantee (floor to 7, with the actual count often higher). Partitioning the full 25-element array around M as pivot is guaranteed to leave at most about 25 - 9 = 16 elements on one side (close to the 7n/10 = 17.5 bound), so recursing into that side, in the worst case, operates on a provably shrinking fraction of the original array every round, guaranteeing termination in O(n) total work rather than risking the Theta(n^2) blowup an adversarial quickselect pivot could cause on this same input.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will almost certainly ask you to justify the 3n/10 discard guarantee rather than just quote it, and the correct path counts elements group by group: half the groups have medians <= the pivot, and each such group contributes 3 elements (not just the median) below or equal to the pivot. A sharper follow-up asks why groups of 3 fail -- the answer must show the recurrence's fractions summing to exactly 1 (1/3 + 2/3 = 1), the borderline case that gives O(n log n) rather than O(n), not just "3 is too small." Finally, a judge testing whether you understand the algorithm's REAL-WORLD role (rather than treating it as a pure theory curiosity) will want to hear that it ships only as introselect's fallback, because its larger practical constant factor makes it a poor default despite its superior worst-case guarantee.

questions.prompt: Who are the five authors credited in the 1973 BFPRT median-of-medians paper, "Time Bounds for Selection"?

options.text: Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest, and Tarjan
Bentley, Floyd, Prim, Robbins, and Turing
Boyer, Fisher, Post, Ritchie, and Thompson
Bloch, Feynman, Papert, Ross, and Tanenbaum

explanations.a: Correct -- Manuel Blum, Robert Floyd, Vaughan Pratt, Ronald Rivest, and Robert Tarjan published this 1973 paper, giving the algorithm its BFPRT nickname.
explanations.b: This mixes in unrelated names (Prim, Robbins, Turing) not part of the actual author list.
explanations.c: This list of names is unrelated to the BFPRT paper's actual authors.
explanations.d: This list of names is unrelated to the BFPRT paper's actual authors.

questions.prompt: In the median-of-medians algorithm, what guarantee does using the median of ceil(n/5) group-medians (each group sorted internally) provide about the chosen pivot?

options.text: It guarantees the pivot is exactly the true median of the whole array
It guarantees at least 3n/10 elements are <= the pivot and at least 3n/10 are >= the pivot
It guarantees the pivot is always one of the smallest 5 elements
It guarantees the partition step can be skipped entirely

explanations.a: The median of medians is a good APPROXIMATE pivot, not necessarily the exact true median of the whole array.
explanations.b: Correct -- roughly half of the ceil(n/5) groups have medians <= the overall median-of-medians, and each such group contributes 3 elements (its median plus 2 smaller group-mates) that are <= the pivot, yielding the 3n/10 guarantee on both sides.
explanations.c: There is no such guarantee about absolute rank position among the smallest elements; the guarantee is about the FRACTION of elements on each side of the pivot.
explanations.d: Partitioning around the chosen pivot still happens exactly as in quickselect; the group-of-5 scheme only changes how the pivot itself is chosen.

questions.prompt: Why does the median-of-medians technique use groups of 5 rather than groups of 3?

options.text: Groups of 3 are computationally harder to sort than groups of 5
With groups of 3, the resulting recurrence's fractions sum to exactly 1 (1/3 + 2/3 = 1), so it no longer solves to O(n) and collapses to O(n log n) instead
Groups of 5 are required by definition of the median operation
Groups of 3 would make the algorithm use more memory

explanations.a: Sorting cost is not the issue -- sorting a fixed group of 3 or 5 elements is trivially cheap either way; the issue is the resulting recurrence's asymptotic behavior.
explanations.b: Correct -- with groups of 3, the recurrence T(n) <= T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n) has fractions summing to exactly 1, the borderline case, so it no longer collapses to linear time and instead solves to O(n log n), no better than sorting.
explanations.c: The median operation works on any group size; there is no definitional requirement for size 5 specifically.
explanations.d: Memory usage scales similarly regardless of group size; the deciding factor is the resulting time-recurrence, not space.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the median-of-medians (BFPRT) algorithm for selecting the k-th smallest element.

items.text: Split the n elements into groups of 5 and sort each group internally
Take the median of each group of 5 and collect all group medians into a new array
Recursively find the median of that array of group medians
Use that median-of-medians as the pivot to partition the full array
Recurse into whichever side contains rank k

questions.explanation: The algorithm groups and sorts small chunks, extracts each chunk's median, recursively finds the median of those medians to get a provably good pivot, partitions the full array around that pivot, and finally recurses into only the side known to contain the target rank -- with the guarantee that at least 3n/10 elements are discarded at every level.

questions.prompt: Match each selection algorithm or technique to its defining time-complexity characteristic.

right.text: Expected Theta(n), but Theta(n^2) worst case under bad pivots
Guaranteed worst-case O(n), but with a substantially larger constant factor in practice than quickselect
Uses quickselect by default, falling back to median-of-medians only when recursion depth signals a bad pivot pattern

questions.explanation: Randomized quickselect is fast in expectation but retains a quadratic worst case; median-of-medians eliminates that worst case entirely at a steep practical constant-factor cost; and introselect combines both, defaulting to quickselect's speed while using median-of-medians as a guaranteed-linear safety net only when needed.

units.label: Measuring Sorts and Interpreting the Evidence

lessons.label: Instrumenting a Sort: Choosing a Metric That Means Something

sections.heading: Wall-clock time is the wrong first metric
sections.body: Wall-clock time is what everyone wants to report, and it is the worst thing to measure first. It depends on CPU frequency scaling, background processes, cache state left over from the previous run, JIT warm-up, and even ambient temperature throttling — none of which have anything to do with the algorithm. The fix used by serious algorithm studies is to instrument the algorithm itself: wrap the comparator so every call to it increments a counter, and wrap the swap or move operation the same way. Done correctly, this produces a metric that is deterministic — run the same input twice and you get the exact same count, on any machine, in any language. That determinism is what makes the number scientifically useful: it isolates the algorithm's structure from the hardware it happened to run on.

sections.heading: The counts are also a correctness check
sections.body: Comparison counting has a second job: verifying your implementation. The average-case comparison counts for the classic comparison sorts are known analytically. Quicksort with a good pivot rule averages about 2·ln(2)·n·log2(n), roughly 1.39·n·log2(n) comparisons. Mergesort's merge step needs at most n·log2(n) − n + 1 comparisons because each merge of two sorted runs never re-compares an already-placed element. Heapsort needs roughly 2·n·log2(n) comparisons — building the heap is O(n), but each of the n extract-max operations sifts down through about log2(n) levels, and each level costs up to two comparisons. If you instrument your own implementations and run them on large random arrays, the measured counts should land close to these formulas. If your quicksort is instead reporting counts that scale like n² even on random input, that is not an interesting research finding — it is a bug, most likely a bad pivot choice or a partition that isn't actually splitting the array.

sections.heading: Where counts and wall-clock time disagree
sections.body: Once your counts check out, the real finding shows up when you also record wall-clock time and compare the two. Heapsort's comparison count, at roughly 2·n·log2(n), is only about 44% higher than quicksort's roughly 1.39·n·log2(n) — comfortably the same O(n·log n) neighborhood. But timed side by side on large arrays, heapsort is commonly 2 to 3 times SLOWER in wall-clock terms, not 44% slower. Comparison counting alone cannot explain a gap that large — it under-predicts heapsort's real cost. That mismatch is not an error in your instrumentation; it is real, and it is the reason a rigorous sorting study reports both metrics rather than picking one. The gap itself becomes the interesting question, and it points toward memory-access behavior as the missing variable — the subject of a later lesson in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A student instruments quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort with global counters wrapped around every comparator call, then sorts a random array of n = 10,000 integers. Predicted quicksort comparisons: 1.39 × 10,000 × log2(10,000) ≈ 1.39 × 10,000 × 13.29 ≈ 184,700. Measured: 190,300 — close enough (the gap is real overhead from median-of-three pivot sampling) to confirm the implementation is sound. Heapsort's predicted count, 2 × 10,000 × 13.29 ≈ 265,800, is only 44% above quicksort's. But timing the same runs shows quicksort finishing in 4 ms and heapsort in 10 ms — a 2.5x gap the comparison counts alone never predicted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has run benchmarks before will ask why you didn't just time the sorts and call it a day. The answer — wall-clock time is hardware-noisy and non-reproducible, while a wrapped comparator count is deterministic and doubles as a correctness check against known formulas — shows you understand measurement, not just algorithms. A sharper judge will then ask why you kept BOTH metrics instead of just the clean one. Being able to explain that comparison counts and wall-clock time can legitimately disagree, and that the disagreement itself is data, separates a student who ran a benchmark from one who understood what the benchmark was measuring.

questions.prompt: Why wrap the comparator and swap/move calls with counters instead of relying on wall-clock time as your primary metric?

options.text: Wall-clock time is illegal to report in a science-fair study
Wrapped counts are deterministic and hardware-independent, reproducing exactly on any run or machine
Counting comparisons always runs faster than timing the algorithm
Wall-clock time cannot be measured in most programming languages

explanations.a: There is no such rule; wall-clock time is a legitimate metric, just a noisy one to lead with.
explanations.b: Correct — the same input produces the exact same comparator/swap counts every time, isolating algorithmic structure from CPU state, scheduling, and thermal throttling.
explanations.c: Counting adds overhead to every comparison; it is not chosen for speed, but for reproducibility.
explanations.d: Wall-clock timers are available in essentially every language; that is not the issue.

questions.prompt: A student's instrumented quicksort reports a comparison count that scales like n^2 even on large random-input arrays. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Quicksort's true average case is actually O(n^2), contradicting the textbook
A bug in the implementation, most likely a poor pivot choice or a partition that fails to split the array
The counter itself is broken and double-counting every comparison
The random-number generator produced a sorted array by chance

explanations.a: Quicksort's well-established average case is O(n log n), about 1.39 n log2 n comparisons with a reasonable pivot rule; n^2 scaling on random data is not a new discovery.
explanations.b: Correct — n^2 scaling on random input is the signature of a partition that isn't dividing the array roughly in half, e.g. always picking a bad pivot or an off-by-one that leaves one side nearly empty.
explanations.c: A double-counting bug would roughly double the count, not change its growth rate from n log n to n^2.
explanations.d: One unlucky random array wouldn't reliably reproduce n^2 scaling across repeated trials with fresh random arrays.

questions.prompt: Order these three algorithms by their approximate average-case comparison-count coefficient on random input, from smallest to largest.

items.text: Mergesort (~n log2 n − n)
Quicksort (~1.39 n log2 n)
Heapsort (~2 n log2 n)

questions.explanation: Mergesort's merge step never re-compares placed elements, giving the smallest constant (~1.0, actually slightly under, since it's n log2 n minus n). Quicksort with a good pivot averages about 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.39 times n log2 n. Heapsort's repeated sift-downs push its constant to roughly 2, the largest of the three despite all three being O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Match each sort to the mechanism that produces its average-case comparison-count formula.

right.text: Recursive partitioning around a pivot, averaged over random pivot rank
Merging two sorted runs never re-examines an already-placed element
Each of n extract-max calls sifts down through ~log2 n levels, up to two comparisons per level

questions.explanation: Quicksort's constant comes from averaging partition cost over all possible pivot ranks, yielding 2 ln 2. Mergesort's efficiency comes from the merge step's one-pass, no-re-comparison structure. Heapsort's larger constant comes from every sift-down potentially costing two comparisons (comparing both children, then comparing the winner to the parent) at each of roughly log2 n levels, n times over.

lessons.label: The Crossover Point: Finding Your Own Insertion-Sort Cutoff

sections.heading: Why a worse asymptotic class can still win
sections.body: Insertion sort's average-case cost is about n²/4 comparisons and moves — quadratic, strictly worse than n log n for large n. But asymptotic notation hides the constant factor, and for small n the constant is what decides the race. Insertion sort is a tight, branch-predictable inner loop over contiguous memory with no recursive calls, no partition bookkeeping, and no function-call overhead; it fits entirely in L1 cache for small arrays and the branch predictor learns its pattern almost perfectly on nearly-in-place data. A recursive n-log-n sort pays for every one of its recursive calls: stack frame setup, partition-index bookkeeping, pivot selection. Below some size n*, insertion sort's small constant beats n log n's larger constant even though n log n's growth rate is asymptotically superior — the crossover point is exactly where n²/4 (small constant) overtakes c·n·log n (large constant).

sections.heading: What production libraries actually hardcode
sections.body: Because this tradeoff is real, virtually every serious sort implementation falls back to insertion sort below a hardcoded cutoff rather than recursing all the way down. Bentley and McIlroy's 1993 paper "Engineering a Sort Function" set the cutoff for their widely-copied C library qsort at 7 elements. Java's java.util.DualPivotQuicksort (used by Arrays.sort on primitives since Java 7) sets its INSERTION_SORT_THRESHOLD constant to 47. Tim Peters's Timsort, used by Python's list.sort and adopted by Java's Collections.sort for objects, computes a "minrun" between 32 and 64 and treats runs shorter than that floor with a variant of insertion sort — his design notes in listsort.txt describe 32 as sitting in a deliberately chosen "sweet range." Orson Peters's pattern-defeating quicksort (pdqsort) hardcodes its insertion_sort_threshold at 24. These numbers span a factor of nearly 7x from smallest to largest — not because the tradeoff differs, but because each was tuned empirically on different hardware, compilers, and decades.

sections.heading: Finding the crossover on your own machine
sections.body: Because the cutoff is empirical, not theoretical, it is a genuine experiment: for a sweep of small n (say 2 through 100), generate a matched random input, time your instrumented insertion sort and your instrumented n-log-n sort on identical copies, repeat several trials per size, and locate the n where the two timing curves cross. If your measured crossover is, say, n = 23 rather than Bentley and McIlroy's 7, that is not an error — it is an artifact of running on a CPU with a larger L1 cache, a more accurate branch predictor, and a more aggressively optimizing compiler than 1990s hardware, plus whatever function-call overhead your specific language runtime imposes. Reporting a number that differs from the textbook, together with a specific, testable explanation for why, is a stronger result than simply reproducing an old citation.
