questions.explanation: d[v] timestamps give the preorder in which vertices are first reached; f[v] timestamps give the postorder in which their subtrees close, whose reverse is a topological order; and the explicit-stack rewrite of DFS removes the dependency on the call stack's limited depth, avoiding overflow on deep paths.

lessons.label: Edge Classification and Cycle Detection

sections.heading: Four kinds of edges relative to the DFS tree
sections.body: When DFS runs on a directed graph, every edge (u, v) it examines falls into exactly one of four categories relative to the DFS forest it builds. A TREE edge is one DFS actually uses to discover a new vertex — it becomes part of the DFS tree itself. A BACK edge points from a vertex u to one of its own ANCESTORS in the DFS tree (v is still 'in progress,' i.e., discovered but not yet finished, when u examines it) — back edges are the signature of a cycle. A FORWARD edge points from u to a DESCENDANT v that has already been fully finished by the time u reaches it, forming a shortcut down the tree. A CROSS edge connects two vertices with no ancestor-descendant relationship at all — often between different subtrees, or between different DFS trees in the forest entirely. Using the discovery/finish timestamps from the previous lesson, these are distinguished exactly by vertex COLOR at the moment edge (u, v) is examined: WHITE (v undiscovered) means a tree edge, GRAY (v discovered but not finished — i.e., v is an active ancestor on the current recursion path) means a back edge, and BLACK (v already finished) means either a forward or cross edge, disambiguated by comparing discovery times.

sections.heading: Cycle detection in a directed graph: back edges, not plain visited sets
sections.body: The clean theorem is: a directed graph contains a cycle IF AND ONLY IF a DFS over it finds at least one back edge. The forward direction is immediate — a back edge from u to ancestor v means the tree path v-to-u plus the single edge u-to-v forms a cycle. The reverse direction follows because any cycle, once DFS starts inside it, must eventually re-enter some vertex still on the current recursion stack. Implementing this correctly REQUIRES three colors (white/gray/black), not the two-state 'visited or not' set every BFS-based approach uses. The single most common bug in student cycle-detection code is using a plain boolean visited array: with only two states, a CROSS edge to an already-finished (black) vertex looks identical to a BACK edge to a currently-active (gray) ancestor, because both targets read as 'visited' — this produces false positives, incorrectly reporting a cycle where none exists, in any directed graph with cross edges (which appear constantly, e.g., whenever two independent branches both point to a shared downstream vertex). The white/gray/black scheme fixes this by tracking not just whether a vertex has been seen, but whether it is currently ON THE ACTIVE CALL STACK (gray) versus fully closed off (black).

sections.heading: Undirected graphs: the parent-skip rule, and union-find as an alternative
sections.body: Undirected graphs need a different rule, because every tree edge (u, v) is trivially traversed 'backward' as (v, u) the instant DFS looks at v's own adjacency list — without care, this immediate skip-back would be misreported as a cycle on every single edge. The fix is the PARENT-SKIP RULE: when DFS at vertex v examines an edge back to parent[v], it simply ignores that one specific edge (it is the edge that brought DFS here in the first place), and only reports a cycle if it finds a visited neighbor that is NOT its immediate parent. Formally, undirected DFS has no forward or cross edges at all — only tree and back edges — because any edge connecting two 'unrelated' vertices in an undirected graph would have been explored from whichever endpoint DFS reached first, making it a back edge (or tree edge) by construction. A completely different, non-DFS way to detect cycles while BUILDING an undirected graph edge-by-edge is UNION-FIND (disjoint-set union): process edges one at a time, and before adding edge (u, v), check whether u and v are already in the same set (component) — if so, adding this edge would close a cycle, so reject or flag it; otherwise, union the two sets. This is exactly the technique inside Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm, which needs to reject any edge that would create a cycle while greedily adding edges in increasing weight order, and with path compression and union by rank it runs in nearly O(m alpha(n)) time, where alpha is the extremely slow-growing inverse Ackermann function.

lessons.workedExample: A build system models file dependencies as a directed graph (edge A to B means 'A depends on B, so B must build first') and needs to detect circular dependencies. Running white/gray/black DFS from each unbuilt file: suppose file X depends on Y, Y depends on Z, and Z depends back on X. DFS enters X (gray), enters Y (gray), enters Z (gray), and Z's edge back to X finds X still GRAY (on the active path, not yet finished) — this is a back edge, correctly flagged as a cycle: X needs Y needs Z needs X, an unbuildable dependency loop. Contrast this with a non-cyclic case where both Y and Z separately depend on a shared utility file U: DFS reaches U from Y first (finishing it, turning it BLACK), and when Z later examines its edge to U, U is BLACK, not gray — correctly classified as a cross edge, not a cycle, even though a naive plain-visited-set check would have flagged U as 'already visited' and risked a false cycle report if it didn't distinguish colors.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the highest-yield probes a judge can make, because the visited-set-vs-three-color bug is subtle enough that many working programmers get it wrong on a first attempt, yet the underlying reason (cross edges to finished vertices look identical to back edges to active ancestors under a boolean scheme) is a clean, explainable insight. A judge may also test whether you know cycle detection differs between directed and undirected graphs — conflating the two (e.g., applying the parent-skip rule to a directed graph, or forgetting it in an undirected one) is a common tell that the concept was memorized rather than understood, and mentioning union-find's role inside Kruskal's algorithm shows you can connect this lesson to the wider algorithms landscape.

questions.prompt: Match each DFS edge type to its defining relationship to the DFS tree, for a directed graph.

right.text: Discovers a previously white (unvisited) vertex
Points to a gray ancestor still active on the recursion path
Points to an already-finished (black) descendant, shortcutting down the tree
Connects two vertices with no ancestor-descendant relationship

questions.explanation: Tree edges discover new (white) vertices; back edges point to gray ancestors still on the active DFS path and signal a cycle; forward edges point to already-finished (black) descendants; and cross edges connect vertices with no ancestor-descendant relationship, often across different subtrees or DFS trees.

questions.prompt: Why does using a plain two-state visited/unvisited array (instead of white/gray/black) cause false-positive cycle detection in directed graphs?

options.text: Because a boolean array can only store up to 2 billion entries
Because it cannot distinguish a cross edge to an already-finished vertex from a back edge to a currently-active ancestor — both read as simply 'visited'
Because boolean arrays are slower than color-coded arrays
Because undirected graphs require exactly two states while directed graphs require exactly three

explanations.a: Array size limits are irrelevant here; the problem is a lack of information per entry, not capacity.
explanations.b: Correct — a boolean scheme can't tell 'currently on the active recursion path' (gray, meaning a real back edge/cycle) apart from 'fully done and off the path' (black, meaning a harmless cross edge), so cross edges get misreported as cycles.
explanations.c: This is not a performance issue; both approaches run in similar time. The bug is one of correctness, not speed.
explanations.d: The three-color scheme is used for directed-graph cycle detection specifically; undirected graphs use the parent-skip rule with a simpler visited check, but that's a different mechanism, not evidence for this option's claim.

questions.prompt: In undirected-graph cycle detection via DFS, why does DFS at vertex v ignore the edge back to parent[v]?

options.text: Because parent edges are always tree edges and can be skipped for efficiency only

Because that edge is the very same edge that discovered v, and every undirected tree edge trivially appears 'backward' when scanned from the child, so skipping it (and only it) avoids reporting every tree edge as a false cycle
Because undirected graphs never contain real cycles
Because parent pointers are only used for path reconstruction, not cycle detection

explanations.a: This isn't merely an efficiency optimization — skipping it is required for CORRECTNESS, since without the skip every tree edge would be misreported as a cycle.
explanations.b: Correct — in an undirected adjacency list, the edge (u,v) that discovers v also appears as (v,u) in v's own list; the parent-skip rule ignores exactly this one specific occurrence so only genuinely different back edges trigger a cycle report.
explanations.c: Undirected graphs certainly can contain cycles; the parent-skip rule exists precisely to detect real ones while not falsely flagging the discovering edge itself.
explanations.d: Parent pointers serve both purposes; using them to skip the discovering edge during cycle checks is a legitimate and necessary use, not a misuse.

questions.prompt: What alternative to DFS is used inside Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm to detect whether adding an edge would create a cycle?

options.text: Union-find (disjoint-set union), checking whether the edge's two endpoints are already in the same set
A second, independent BFS run after each edge is added
Recomputing all discovery/finish timestamps from scratch after each edge
Sorting vertices by degree before adding any edges

explanations.a: Correct — union-find lets Kruskal's algorithm check, in near-constant amortized time per edge, whether two endpoints are already connected, rejecting any edge that would close a cycle while building the minimum spanning tree.
explanations.b: Re-running a full BFS after every single edge would be far too slow for Kruskal's algorithm, which processes up to m edges one at a time.
explanations.c: DFS timestamps are not the mechanism Kruskal's algorithm uses at all; it relies on union-find specifically because edges arrive one at a time, in weight order, not via a single traversal.
explanations.d: Degree sorting has no role in cycle detection; Kruskal's algorithm sorts EDGES by weight, not vertices by degree.

lessons.label: Connected Components, Bipartite Testing, and Flood Fill

sections.heading: Labeling components with repeated traversal
sections.body: A connected component is a maximal set of vertices where every pair is joined by some path. Finding ALL components of an undirected graph — not just the one reachable from a single start vertex — only requires one small addition to plain BFS or DFS: loop over every vertex in the graph, and whenever the loop reaches a vertex that hasn't been visited yet, that vertex is the start of a brand-new component, so increment a component counter, assign that counter as the vertex's label, and run a full BFS or DFS from it, labeling every vertex it reaches with the same counter. Because each vertex is only ever the SEED of one traversal (once labeled, it is skipped by the outer loop) and each traversal itself still costs O(size of that component), the total work across the whole graph remains O(n + m), the same bound as a single traversal — the outer loop adds only O(n) extra vertex-checks, not a new order of growth.

sections.heading: 2-coloring during traversal: testing bipartiteness
sections.body: A graph is BIPARTITE if its vertices can be split into two groups such that every edge connects a vertex in one group to a vertex in the other — equivalently, it can be properly colored with exactly 2 colors so that no edge joins two same-colored vertices. This can be tested with a single BFS or DFS pass: color the start vertex color 0, and whenever the traversal moves across an edge to an unvisited neighbor, assign it the OPPOSITE color of the vertex it came from. The graph fails to be bipartite exactly when the traversal finds an edge connecting two ALREADY-colored vertices that share the same color — and when that happens, the two tree paths from their nearest common ancestor down to each endpoint, plus that one offending edge, together form an ODD-length cycle, which can be extracted and returned as a certificate proving non-bipartiteness (a graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycle, a theorem traceable to Dénes Kőnig's foundational 1936 graph theory text). This 2-coloring approach costs the same O(n + m) as any single BFS/DFS pass, run once per component.

sections.heading: Where this shows up: islands, pixels, and dependency reachability
sections.body: Component labeling and its flood-fill special case are not academic exercises — they are the direct algorithmic basis of several everyday tools. ISLAND / REGION COUNTING on a 2D grid (a classic interview and competitive-programming problem: count the number of connected groups of 'land' cells surrounded by 'water') is exactly connected-component labeling where each grid cell is a vertex and adjacency is the 4 (or 8) neighboring cells. IMAGE SEGMENTATION in basic computer vision starts from the same idea: flood-fill from a seed pixel outward through neighboring pixels of similar color or intensity, labeling one connected 'blob' at a time — this is literally how the paint-bucket tool in image editors decides which pixels to recolor. And in software engineering, REACHABILITY IN A DEPENDENCY NETWORK — 'which modules are reachable from this one, or which modules would break if I removed this shared library' — is answered by treating the dependency graph as a directed graph and running BFS/DFS from the node in question, with the visited set at the end of the traversal being exactly the answer to 'everything reachable.'

lessons.workedExample: A photo-editing app's paint-bucket tool is clicked on a pixel with color C in a 2D image. The flood-fill algorithm treats the image as an implicit grid graph (each pixel a vertex, 4-directional adjacency) and runs BFS starting from the clicked pixel: enqueue it, and repeatedly dequeue a pixel, check its 4 neighbors, and enqueue any unvisited neighbor whose color also equals C, recoloring it to the new fill color as it's enqueued. Pixels whose color differs from C act as an implicit 'wall' — their edges are simply never followed, since they fail the color-match test that stands in for the visited check. The traversal naturally stops at the boundary of the connected same-colored region, which is exactly the blob the user intended to fill, without ever needing to pre-compute region boundaries explicitly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating this topic will often ask you to state the WHY behind the bipartite odd-cycle characterization rather than just the coloring procedure, since 'no odd cycle' is the deeper mathematical fact the 2-coloring test is built to detect, and being able to explain what the failing edge actually witnesses (a specific odd cycle, not just 'not bipartite') shows genuine understanding of the certificate concept, not memorized pseudocode. A judge may also test whether you can name at least two real applications beyond a textbook maze, since that demonstrates you understand component labeling as a general reachability tool rather than a single fixed algorithm tied to one problem shape.

questions.prompt: Why does labeling all connected components of a graph by repeated BFS/DFS still cost only O(n + m) total, rather than O(n) times the cost of a single traversal?

options.text: Because only the largest component is actually traversed
Because each vertex is the seed of at most one traversal, and every vertex and edge is still visited only once overall, no matter how many components exist
Because components smaller than log(n) vertices are skipped for efficiency
Because the graph is first compressed into a single component before traversal begins

explanations.a: All components must be found and labeled for a correct component count, not just the largest one.
explanations.b: Correct — the outer loop only starts a new traversal from vertices not yet labeled, so across all components combined, every vertex and edge is still processed exactly once, preserving the O(n + m) bound.
explanations.c: No such skipping happens or would be correct; every component, regardless of size, must be found and labeled.
explanations.d: No compression step exists; each component is discovered and labeled by its own separate traversal from an unvisited seed vertex.

questions.prompt: When a 2-coloring bipartiteness test finds an edge connecting two vertices that already share the same color, what does this signify?

options.text: The graph has too many edges to be bipartite by definition
The two tree paths to their common ancestor, plus that edge, form an odd-length cycle, certifying the graph is not bipartite
The traversal must restart from a different source vertex
The graph is disconnected

explanations.a: Edge count alone never determines bipartiteness; a dense graph can still be bipartite (e.g., a complete bipartite graph) and a sparse one can fail (e.g., a single triangle).
explanations.b: Correct — a bipartite graph has no odd cycle, so finding two same-colored, adjacent vertices exposes a concrete odd cycle through their nearest common ancestor, which serves as a certificate of non-bipartiteness.
explanations.c: Restarting from another vertex would not change the underlying structural conflict; the same-color edge is a genuine witness of non-bipartiteness, not an artifact of the chosen start.
explanations.d: This scenario can occur within a single connected component; disconnection is a separate property unrelated to this specific failure signal.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world application to the traversal concept it relies on.

left.text: Answering 'what breaks if this module is removed' in a dependency graph

right.text: Connected-component labeling over grid-cell adjacency
Flood-fill BFS/DFS seeded from one pixel, bounded by a color-match test
Reachability via BFS/DFS traversal from the node in question over a directed graph

questions.explanation: Island counting is component labeling with grid-cell adjacency; paint-bucket fill is flood-fill BFS/DFS seeded at one pixel and bounded by matching color; and dependency-impact analysis is reachability via a directed BFS/DFS traversal, with the final visited set answering the reachability question.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the component-labeling algorithm as it processes the outer loop over all vertices.

items.text: Iterate to the next vertex in the outer loop
Check whether the vertex is already labeled/visited
If unvisited, increment the component counter and assign it as the new label
Run a full BFS or DFS from that vertex, labeling every vertex it reaches with the same counter

questions.explanation: The outer loop visits vertices in order; each is checked for a label; an unlabeled vertex starts a new component with a fresh counter value; and a full traversal from it then labels the entire reachable set with that same value before the outer loop continues.

lessons.label: BFS vs. DFS: Which to Reach For, and Why

sections.heading: Both are O(n + m) — the real discriminator is memory
sections.body: BFS and DFS have identical asymptotic time complexity, O(n + m), so time is almost never the reason to pick one over the other. The reason that actually matters in practice is MEMORY. DFS's space usage is bounded by the depth of the recursion (or explicit stack), which is at most O(n) but is typically much smaller — proportional to how deep a single path goes, O(depth). BFS's space usage is bounded by the size of its FRONTIER — the queue — which in a graph or search tree with branching factor b can grow like b^d at search depth d, i.e., exponentially in the search depth d (with the branching factor b as the base of the exponent). This is why BFS over a large state-space search tree (like a puzzle solver or move-generation tree in a game) can exhaust memory long before it exhausts time: a chess-like game tree with branching factor 30 at depth 10 has a frontier on the order of 30^10, which is computationally intractable to hold in a queue, whereas DFS over the exact same tree only ever holds 10 stack frames at once, no matter how wide the branching factor is.

sections.heading: Iterative deepening: DFS's memory with BFS's optimality
sections.body: The natural question is whether you can keep BFS's guarantee of finding the shallowest (optimal) solution first, without paying its exponential memory cost. ITERATIVE DEEPENING DFS (IDDFS) is exactly this compromise: run a depth-limited DFS with limit 0, then if no solution is found, discard everything and rerun depth-limited DFS with limit 1, then 2, and so on, increasing the limit by one each round until a solution is found at the shallowest possible depth. This looks wasteful — earlier, shallower levels get re-explored on every iteration — but because the number of nodes at the deepest level of a tree with branching factor b dominates the sum of all shallower levels combined (the ratio approaches b/(b-1) as the search deepens, for any fixed branching factor b, a constant that shrinks toward 1 as b itself grows), the total re-exploration overhead is only a small constant factor, while memory drops all the way down to DFS's O(depth). This technique, formalized by Richard Korf in a widely cited 1985 paper, is the standard approach in memory-constrained optimal search (used, for instance, in early solvers for the 15-puzzle and in optimal Rubik's Cube solvers), and is the textbook answer to 'how do I get BFS's shortest-path guarantee without BFS's memory blowup.'

sections.heading: Matching the tool to the job
sections.body: Beyond the memory trade-off, BFS and DFS are simply built for different OUTPUTS. Reach for BFS whenever the question is about FEWEST HOPS or LEVEL STRUCTURE: shortest unweighted path, distance from a source, 'find the nearest X,' or anything organized by ring-distance from a starting point. Reach for DFS whenever the question is about STRUCTURAL properties of the whole graph that depend on finish order or recursive nesting: topological sort of a DAG (reverse postorder, from Lesson 3's finish timestamps), strongly connected components (Tarjan's and Kosaraju's algorithms both build directly on DFS finish order), bridges and articulation points (found via DFS's discovery-time and low-link values), and cycle detection via back edges (Lesson 4). A canonical real-world case study that uses BOTH, deliberately, is a WEB CRAWLER: a crawler exploring links from a seed page often uses BFS-like frontier management — visiting pages roughly by increasing 'click distance' from the seed, which naturally spreads coverage broadly across many different sites before drilling deep into any one of them, avoiding the trap of DFS-style crawling, which could follow one site's internal links arbitrarily deep and never surface to sample the rest of the web at all.

lessons.workedExample: A puzzle-solving program needs the minimum number of moves to reach a goal state from a start state, where each state can branch into up to 4 next states. Plain BFS would guarantee the minimum-move solution but its frontier could reach roughly 4^d states at depth d — at d=15 that's over a billion states, infeasible to queue. Plain DFS would use trivial memory (just 15 stack frames at depth 15) but has no guarantee of finding the SHORTEST solution first; it might tunnel 200 moves deep down one branch before ever finding a 15-move solution elsewhere. Iterative deepening DFS resolves this: it runs depth-limited DFS with limit 0, 1, 2, ... up to 15, and the limit-15 run is guaranteed to find a solution if the limit-15 depth-bounded search space contains one, using only O(15) memory at any instant, at the cost of having briefly re-explored the shallower limits 0 through 14 first.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this topic is really testing whether you understand that 'both are O(n+m)' is NOT the end of the comparison — a naive answer stops at time complexity and misses that memory, not time, is what actually breaks BFS in wide search trees. Bringing up iterative deepening unprompted, and being able to explain WHY the repeated shallow re-exploration is only a constant-factor overhead rather than a real inefficiency, signals a deeper grasp of the trade-off than reciting 'BFS finds shortest paths, DFS uses less memory' as two disconnected facts. A judge may also ask you to justify a real system's traversal choice (like a crawler's breadth-first frontier), which tests whether you can connect the abstract trade-off to an engineering decision.

questions.prompt: Both BFS and DFS run in O(n + m) time. What is the primary practical reason to prefer one over the other in a wide search tree?

options.text: BFS is always faster in wall-clock time because it uses a queue
Memory: BFS's frontier can grow exponentially with branching factor, while DFS's memory use is bounded by search depth
DFS cannot be implemented iteratively, only recursively
BFS cannot be used on directed graphs

explanations.a: Both have the same asymptotic time bound; the queue vs. stack choice does not by itself make one algorithm faster.
explanations.b: Correct — BFS's queue can hold on the order of b^d states at search depth d with branching factor b, while DFS never holds more than O(depth) states at once, making memory the real discriminator.
explanations.c: DFS has both recursive and iterative (explicit-stack) implementations, as covered in an earlier lesson; this option is simply false.
explanations.d: BFS works fine on directed graphs; graph directionality does not restrict which traversal algorithm applies.

questions.prompt: What does iterative deepening DFS (IDDFS) achieve, and at what cost?

options.text: It achieves DFS's memory profile while guaranteeing BFS's shallowest-solution-first property, at the cost of re-exploring shallower depth limits on each iteration
It achieves BFS's memory profile while guaranteeing DFS's speed, at no additional cost
It eliminates the need for a visited set entirely
It guarantees finding the deepest possible solution first

explanations.a: Correct — IDDFS reruns depth-limited DFS with an increasing limit each round, keeping memory at O(depth) like DFS while still finding the shallowest solution first like BFS, paying only a small constant-factor overhead for re-exploring earlier limits.
explanations.b: This reverses the trade-off; IDDFS is specifically designed to AVOID BFS's memory profile, not adopt it.
explanations.c: IDDFS still needs to track visited/explored states within each depth-limited run to behave correctly; it does not remove this requirement.
explanations.d: IDDFS is built to find the SHALLOWEST solution first, which is the opposite of prioritizing the deepest one.

questions.prompt: Match each task to the traversal it is naturally suited for.

left.text: Finding the fewest-hop path from a source
Producing a topological order of a DAG
Finding strongly connected components or bridges

right.text: BFS, using its layer/frontier structure
DFS, using reverse finish order
DFS, using discovery time and low-link values

questions.explanation: Fewest-hop shortest paths are exactly what BFS's layer structure computes; topological sort is the reverse of DFS postorder (finish time) on a DAG; and strongly connected components and bridges are found using DFS's discovery times combined with low-link values, as in Tarjan's and related algorithms.

questions.prompt: Why does a web crawler commonly use BFS-like frontier management rather than pure DFS when exploring links from a seed page?

options.text: Because BFS uses less memory than DFS for this task

Because BFS-like exploration by increasing click-distance naturally spreads coverage broadly across many sites, avoiding DFS's risk of tunneling arbitrarily deep into one site before sampling the rest
Because DFS cannot follow hyperlinks between different domains
Because BFS guarantees finding every page on the internet in finite time

explanations.a: This is backwards for this scenario — BFS's frontier actually costs MORE memory than DFS in general; the crawler's reason for preferring BFS-like exploration is coverage breadth, not memory savings.
explanations.b: Correct — expanding by increasing click-distance from the seed page ensures the crawler samples broadly across many different sites early on, rather than risking a DFS-style crawl that could follow one site's internal links indefinitely deep.
explanations.c: DFS can follow cross-domain hyperlinks just as easily as BFS; this option describes a limitation that doesn't exist.
explanations.d: No traversal strategy guarantees crawling the entire internet in finite time, given the web's effectively unbounded and constantly changing size.

lessons.label: The Relaxation Framework: One Idea Behind Every SSSP Algorithm

sections.heading: Two arrays and one operation
sections.body: Every single-source shortest path (SSSP) algorithm you will meet — Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, the DAG relaxation order, even the inner loop of A* — is built from exactly the same two arrays and one operation. dist[v] holds the best upper bound found SO FAR on the true shortest-path distance from the source s to vertex v, initialized to dist[s] = 0 and dist[v] = infinity for every other v. prev[v] (also called pi[v] or parent[v]) records which vertex immediately precedes v on the best path found so far, initialized to undefined. The single operation, RELAX(u, v, w), tests one edge (u, v) with weight w(u, v): if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v], then dist[v] is updated to dist[u] + w(u, v) and prev[v] is set to u. That is the entire mechanism. Relaxation can only ever decrease a dist[] value or leave it alone — it never makes an estimate worse — which is why dist[] is a monotonically non-increasing sequence of upper bounds that eventually locks onto the truth.

sections.heading: Why every prefix of a shortest path is itself a shortest path
sections.body: The correctness of every relaxation-based algorithm rests on one structural fact called optimal substructure: if P is a shortest path from s to v that passes through some vertex u, then the portion of P from s to u is ALSO a shortest path from s to u. The proof is a one-line contradiction — if a shorter s-to-u path existed, splicing it onto the remainder of P would produce an s-to-v path shorter than P, contradicting that P was shortest. This is what licenses building shortest paths incrementally out of relaxations on individual edges rather than having to evaluate whole paths at once: because optimal sub-paths are optimal in isolation, a correct algorithm never needs to "look ahead" past the edge it is currently relaxing, only guarantee it processes edges in an order (or repeats them enough times) that every edge on the true shortest path eventually gets relaxed in the right sequence. Different algorithms differ ONLY in what order they choose to visit edges — Dijkstra visits them in increasing distance order via a priority queue, Bellman-Ford just relaxes all m edges repeatedly for n-1 rounds, and DAG relaxation uses topological order. The relaxation step itself never changes.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the path, not just the number
sections.body: dist[v] alone answers "how far," but prev[v] answers "which way," and the two together let you reconstruct the actual route. Once the algorithm terminates, walk backward from the destination t: output t, move to prev[t], output that, move to prev[prev[t]], and so on until you reach the source s, then reverse the collected list. This walk takes O(path length) time and touches nothing but the prev[] array — no re-running of the algorithm is needed. Because each vertex has exactly one prev[] pointer at any time, the union of all prev[] edges (once dist[] is final) forms a shortest-path tree rooted at s: a single tree that simultaneously encodes the shortest path from s to EVERY reachable vertex, not just one destination. That tree structure is also what tells you an algorithm is finished: correctness is precisely the claim that once termination is reached, dist[v] equals the true shortest-path weight and prev[v] traces a genuine shortest path, for every v — not an approximation, and not just for the specific case that happened to be tested.

lessons.workedExample: Consider vertices s, a, b with edges s->a (weight 4), s->b (weight 1), and b->a (weight 1). Initialize dist[s]=0, dist[a]=dist[b]=infinity, prev[a]=prev[b]=undefined. Relax edge s->a first: dist[0]+4=4 < infinity, so dist[a]=4, prev[a]=s. Relax edge s->b: dist[0]+1=1 < infinity, so dist[b]=1, prev[b]=s. Now relax b->a: dist[b]+1 = 1+1 = 2, and 2 < 4, so dist[a] improves to 2 and prev[a] is overwritten from s to b. Reconstructing the path to a: start at a, follow prev[a]=b, follow prev[b]=s, reverse to get s -> b -> a with total weight 2 — cheaper than the direct edge s->a of weight 4, exactly because relaxation was allowed to revise an earlier, suboptimal estimate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen shortest-path projects before has almost certainly seen a student who can recite "Dijkstra uses a priority queue" without being able to say what a priority queue update actually computes. Asking the student to state the relaxation condition from memory (dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v]) and explain why optimal substructure is what makes incremental, edge-at-a-time updates valid — rather than requiring the algorithm to compare whole paths — separates a student who understands the shared mechanism from one who has memorized five unrelated algorithm names. It also sets up every later question about why a specific algorithm's edge-visiting order is or is not safe.

questions.prompt: What does the RELAX(u, v, w) operation do?

options.text: It removes edge (u, v) from the graph if it is not on the shortest path
If dist[u] + w(u,v) is less than the current dist[v], it updates dist[v] and sets prev[v] = u
It recomputes dist[] for every vertex in the graph from scratch
It swaps dist[u] and dist[v] to keep the array sorted

explanations.a: Relaxation never deletes edges; it only updates distance estimates using an edge's weight.
explanations.b: Correct — relaxation checks whether routing through u gives a strictly shorter path to v than the current best known, and if so records both the new distance and the new predecessor.
explanations.c: Relaxation is a local, single-edge check, not a global recomputation.
explanations.d: There is no array sorting involved in a single relaxation step; that is a queue-implementation detail, not what relaxation does.

questions.prompt: Why is optimal substructure (every prefix of a shortest path is itself a shortest path) essential to relaxation-based algorithms?

options.text: It lets algorithms build shortest paths incrementally, edge by edge, without evaluating whole candidate paths
It guarantees every graph has a unique shortest path between any two vertices
It means edge weights must all be equal
It is only needed for graphs with negative edges

explanations.a: Correct — because a sub-path of a shortest path is guaranteed optimal, an algorithm can relax edges one at a time and trust that locally optimal decisions compose into a globally optimal path.
explanations.b: Optimal substructure says nothing about uniqueness; multiple shortest paths of equal length can exist.
explanations.c: Optimal substructure holds regardless of whether weights are equal or vary.
explanations.d: Optimal substructure is a general property used by every relaxation algorithm, including those restricted to nonnegative weights like Dijkstra's.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of reconstructing a shortest path from s to t in the correct order, assuming dist[] and prev[] are already final.

items.text: Start at vertex t and add it to a list
Repeatedly move to prev[current] and add that vertex to the list
Stop once the source vertex s is reached
Reverse the collected list to get the path from s to t

questions.explanation: Path reconstruction walks backward from the destination using prev[] pointers until the source is hit, collecting vertices in reverse order, then reverses the list once at the end to present the path from source to destination.

questions.prompt: Match each array or operation to its role in the relaxation framework.

right.text: The best distance estimate found so far from the source to v
The immediate predecessor of v on the current best path
The single update rule that can improve dist[v] using edge (u, v)

questions.explanation: dist[] holds the running upper bound on shortest-path distance, prev[] holds the pointer needed to reconstruct the path, and RELAX is the atomic operation that updates both when a shorter route is discovered.

lessons.label: Dijkstra's Algorithm: The Greedy Frontier and Its Priority Queue

sections.heading: Extract-min and the settled set
sections.body: Edsger Dijkstra devised the algorithm in 1956 (published in 1959) while thinking about the shortest route between two Dutch cities, and it works by maintaining a set S of vertices whose shortest distance is already known to be final, called "settled," and repeatedly growing S by one vertex at a time. On each round the algorithm calls EXTRACT-MIN on a priority queue keyed by dist[] to pull out the unsettled vertex u with the smallest current dist[u], adds u to S, and relaxes every outgoing edge from u. The central invariant is: whenever a vertex is extracted as the minimum among all unsettled vertices, its dist[] value is already final and will never improve again. That invariant is what makes the algorithm greedy rather than exhaustive — it never revisits a settled vertex — and the whole correctness proof of Dijkstra's algorithm is a proof that this invariant holds, which depends critically on all edge weights being nonnegative (covered in the next lesson).

sections.heading: Why the invariant holds: a proof sketch
sections.body: Suppose for contradiction that u is extracted with dist[u] not yet optimal. Then the true shortest path to u must leave the settled set S at some point, crossing an edge (x, y) where x is in S but y is not, before eventually reaching u. Because x is settled, dist[x] is already correct, and RELAX has already been applied to edge (x,y), so dist[y] <= dist[x] + w(x,y) equals the length of the true shortest path's prefix up to y. Since all remaining edge weights from y to u are nonnegative, the true shortest path to u is at least as long as dist[y]. But u was chosen as the vertex with the SMALLEST dist[] among all unsettled vertices, so dist[u] <= dist[y] <= true shortest distance to u, forcing dist[u] to equal the true distance — contradiction resolved, and the invariant confirmed. Every step of this argument uses w(x,y) >= 0; drop that assumption and the inequality dist[y] <= true distance to y can fail.

sections.heading: Complexity is entirely about the queue
sections.body: Dijkstra's algorithm's own logic never changes; its running time is set entirely by what data structure implements the priority queue, over n vertices and m edges. With a plain array scanned linearly for the minimum, EXTRACT-MIN costs O(n) and runs n times, plus O(1) per DECREASE-KEY, giving O(n^2) total — and for DENSE graphs (m close to n^2) this is still the best known asymptotic bound in practice, because the O(m) term that other structures pay is not a discount there. With a binary heap, EXTRACT-MIN costs O(log n) and DECREASE-KEY costs O(log n), giving O((n + m) log n). Michael Fredman and Robert Tarjan's 1984 Fibonacci heap (published 1987 in JACM) achieves O(1) amortized DECREASE-KEY and O(log n) amortized EXTRACT-MIN, giving the asymptotically best known bound of O(m + n log n) — but its large constant factors and complex bookkeeping mean pairing heaps or even binary heaps routinely beat it in real measured running time, a textbook example of asymptotic optimality losing to practical constants.

lessons.workedExample: On a graph with source s and vertices a, b, c, t connected by nonnegative edges, Dijkstra's queue starts with dist[s]=0 and everything else infinity, so s is extracted first (round 1) and its edges relaxed, say setting dist[a]=2 and dist[b]=5. Round 2 extracts a (smallest remaining key, 2), settles it, and relaxes a's edges, perhaps lowering dist[b] to 4 via a->b. Round 3 extracts b at key 4 — note it never gets re-extracted after being lowered, the queue simply reflects the newest key — settles it, and relaxes b->t giving dist[t]=6. Round 4 extracts t at 6 and the algorithm halts once all reachable vertices are settled. At every extraction the vertex pulled out has a final, correct distance; nothing extracted early is ever revisited, which is exactly the settled-set invariant in action.
lessons.judgeFraming: A common surface-level answer is "Dijkstra uses a priority queue so it's fast." A judge probing depth will ask what specific invariant justifies never revisiting a settled vertex, and will expect the student to connect that invariant to the nonnegative-weight assumption rather than treating it as an arbitrary rule. A second common probe is complexity: naming O((n+m) log n) without knowing which queue produces it, or without knowing that the theoretically superior Fibonacci heap often loses in practice due to constant factors, signals memorized rather than understood complexity analysis.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a vertex to be "settled" in Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.text: It has been added to the graph as a new node
Its dist[] value is guaranteed final and will never be improved again
All of its outgoing edges have negative weight
It has been removed from the graph entirely

explanations.a: Settling is not about graph construction; it's a property assigned to vertices during the algorithm's execution.
explanations.b: Correct — once extracted as the current minimum, a vertex's distance is proven optimal and the algorithm never revisits it.
explanations.c: Settling has nothing to do with the sign of a vertex's outgoing edge weights.
explanations.d: Settled vertices remain in the graph; they are simply marked as finalized in the distance computation, not deleted.

questions.prompt: Which priority-queue implementation is generally the best asymptotic choice for Dijkstra's algorithm on a DENSE graph (m close to n^2)?

options.text: A Fibonacci heap, since it is always asymptotically optimal
A simple array scanned for the minimum, giving O(n^2) with no benefit from a heap's O(m) term
A binary heap, because O((n+m) log n) is always smaller than O(n^2)
No priority queue is used when the graph is dense

explanations.a: Fibonacci heaps give O(m + n log n), which reduces to the same O(n^2) order as the array approach when m is close to n^2 -- so a Fibonacci heap does not asymptotically beat the array here, meaning "always optimal" overstates its advantage on dense graphs; the array wins in practice mainly on constant-factor/simplicity grounds, not asymptotics.
explanations.b: Correct — on dense graphs the O(m) term dominates any heap-based bound, so a plain O(n^2) array-based approach matches or beats heap-based options while being much simpler.
explanations.c: On dense graphs, O((n+m) log n) grows like n^2 log n, which is larger than O(n^2), so the binary heap is not the better choice here.
explanations.d: A priority queue (or an equivalent structure) is always used conceptually; on dense graphs it is just implemented as a simple array rather than a heap.

questions.prompt: Order these events for the vertex u that is extracted at some round of Dijkstra's algorithm.

items.text: u is chosen as the unsettled vertex with the smallest dist[] value
u is added to the settled set S
Every outgoing edge from u is relaxed
dist[u] is guaranteed never to change again

questions.explanation: Dijkstra extracts the minimum-key unsettled vertex, marks it settled, relaxes its outgoing edges to possibly improve neighbors' distances, and by the algorithm's core invariant its own distance is now permanently fixed.

questions.prompt: Match each priority-queue implementation to the total running time it gives Dijkstra's algorithm.

right.text: O((n + m) log n)
O(m + n log n)

questions.explanation: A simple array gives O(n) per extract-min for n extractions, O(n^2) total. A binary heap gives O(log n) per extract-min and per decrease-key, O((n+m) log n) total. Fredman and Tarjan's 1984 Fibonacci heap gives O(1) amortized decrease-key and O(log n) amortized extract-min, O(m + n log n) total — the asymptotically best known, though rarely fastest in practice.

lessons.label: Why Dijkstra Breaks on Negative Edges

sections.heading: A concrete counterexample
sections.body: Take four vertices s, a, b, t with edges s->a weight 2, s->b weight 3, a->t weight 100, and b->a weight -10. Run Dijkstra: dist[s]=0 is extracted first, relaxing s->a to dist[a]=2 and s->b to dist[b]=3. The next extraction pulls the smallest unsettled key, which is a at 2, so a is SETTLED and its edge a->t is relaxed to dist[t]=102. But b has not been processed yet — when b is extracted next at key 3 and its edge b->a is relaxed, dist[a] would improve to dist[b] + (-10) = 3 - 10 = -7, far below the 2 that was already locked in. Dijkstra's algorithm, however, never revisits a settled vertex, so dist[a] stays wrongly frozen at 2 and the true shortest distance to a (-7, via s->b->a) is never found. This is not a rare edge case; it is the generic failure mode any time a negative edge leads INTO a vertex that was settled too early because its apparent distance looked small.

sections.heading: The exact spot the greedy proof breaks
sections.body: The correctness proof of Dijkstra's algorithm (covered in the previous lesson) hinges on one inequality: for the vertex y where the true shortest path to u first leaves the settled set, dist[y] <= true distance to u, because all edge weights from y onward are assumed nonnegative. That single "nonnegative" assumption is where negative weights break the proof — once an edge can be negative, a path that looks longer partway through (has already accumulated more weight than a settled vertex's dist[]) can still end up SHORTER overall, because a later negative edge subtracts enough to win. Dijkstra's greedy extraction order fundamentally assumes weight only accumulates, never that a longer prefix can lead to a shorter total; negative edges violate that assumption directly, which is why the fix is not a small patch to Dijkstra but a structurally different algorithm — Bellman-Ford — that tolerates revisiting a vertex's distance downward as many times as needed.

sections.heading: Negative edges vs. negative cycles, and the constant-shift myth
sections.body: Negative EDGES and negative CYCLES are different problems. A graph with negative edges but no negative cycle still has a well-defined shortest path for every pair of reachable vertices; Bellman-Ford computes it correctly. A negative CYCLE (a cycle whose total weight sums below zero) means there is NO shortest path at all for any vertex reachable from that cycle, because you could loop around it arbitrarily many times to make the path arbitrarily cheap — shortest-path distance is then undefined (formally, -infinity). A frequently repeated but wrong fix is: "just add a large constant c to every edge weight to make them all nonnegative, then run Dijkstra." This fails because shifting every edge by +c changes different paths by different total amounts depending on how many edges they use — a path with 5 edges gains 5c while a path with 2 edges gains only 2c, so a path that was truly shortest before the shift can become artificially more expensive than a longer, previously-worse path after the shift. Constant shifting only preserves the ranking of paths that use the SAME number of edges; it does not preserve shortest-path structure in general. (Johnson's algorithm, covered later in this unit, achieves a correct reweighting, but it needs vertex-specific potentials derived from Bellman-Ford, not one global constant.)

lessons.workedExample: Suppose two paths from s to t exist: path P1 uses 2 edges summing to weight 10, and path P2 uses 5 edges summing to weight 9 (so P2 is truly shorter by 1). Add a constant c=100 to every edge to force nonnegativity. P1's new total is 10 + 2*100 = 210. P2's new total is 9 + 5*100 = 509. After the shift, P1 (210) looks dramatically shorter than P2 (509), even though P2 was the true shortest path before shifting. Running Dijkstra on the shifted graph would confidently return the WRONG path. This demonstrates concretely why "just add a constant" fails: the shift penalizes paths in proportion to their edge count, not their true weight, so it silently reorders which path looks best whenever paths being compared use different numbers of edges — which is the common case in any real graph.
lessons.judgeFraming: The single most valuable thing a judge can hear here is a specific counterexample constructed live, with numbers, rather than the vague claim "Dijkstra doesn't work with negative weights." A judge will often follow up by testing whether the student actually understands WHY — tying the failure to the exact inequality in the greedy proof that assumes nonnegative weights — rather than treating it as a memorized rule. The negative-edge-versus-negative-cycle distinction and the constant-shift myth are both classic places where students who only skimmed a summary get caught, since both require reasoning about specific path structures rather than reciting a fact.

questions.prompt: In the counterexample with s->a (2), s->b (3), a->t (100), b->a (-10), what goes wrong?

options.text: Dijkstra settles a at distance 2 before discovering the shorter route s->b->a of distance -7, and never revises it
Dijkstra crashes because it cannot process negative numbers at all
Dijkstra correctly finds dist[a] = -7 but reports the wrong predecessor
The graph has a negative cycle, so no shortest path exists

explanations.a: Correct — a is settled too early at distance 2 because Dijkstra's queue extraction order never anticipates that a later negative edge could produce a much shorter total.
explanations.b: Dijkstra does not crash on negative weights; it runs to completion but produces an incorrect distance, which is the more dangerous failure mode.
explanations.c: Dijkstra never even computes -7 for dist[a] in this run; it stays frozen at 2 because a was already settled.
explanations.d: There is no cycle in this graph at all (s, a, b, t with the given directed edges), so negative-cycle behavior does not apply here.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a graph with negative edges (but no negative cycle) and a graph with a negative cycle?

options.text: There is no difference; both make shortest paths undefined
Negative edges alone still allow well-defined shortest paths; a negative cycle makes shortest-path distance undefined for vertices reachable from it
Negative cycles are only a problem for undirected graphs
Negative edges require more memory than negative cycles

explanations.a: There is a real difference: Bellman-Ford computes correct finite shortest paths when negative edges exist but no negative cycle is present.
explanations.b: Correct — without a negative cycle, every shortest path is still finite and well-defined; a negative cycle lets you loop indefinitely to drive the path weight to negative infinity, so no finite shortest path exists.
explanations.c: Negative cycles cause the same undefined-distance problem in directed graphs, which is the typical context for this discussion; the issue is not specific to undirected graphs.
explanations.d: This is a distinction about mathematical well-definedness of the answer, not about memory usage.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a constant c to every edge weight fail to fix negative weights for Dijkstra?

options.text: It changes paths with different edge counts by different total amounts, which can reorder which path is truly shortest
Adding a constant is illegal in graph theory
It works perfectly and is the standard technique used in practice
It only fails for undirected graphs

explanations.a: Correct — a path using k edges gains k*c in total weight, so paths with different edge counts are shifted by different amounts, which can make a previously-shortest path look longer than a previously-longer path.
explanations.b: There is nothing illegal about the arithmetic; the technique is simply mathematically unsound for preserving shortest-path order.
explanations.c: The standard correct technique is Johnson's algorithm's vertex-specific potential reweighting, not a single global constant shift.
explanations.d: The flaw is about edge-count-dependent distortion and applies regardless of whether the graph is directed or undirected.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to its correct shortest-path behavior.

left.text: Some negative edges, no negative cycle
A negative cycle reachable from the source

right.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is correct and efficient
Bellman-Ford is correct; Dijkstra is not
Shortest-path distance is undefined (effectively negative infinity)

questions.explanation: Dijkstra requires nonnegative weights to be correct. Negative edges without a negative cycle still yield well-defined finite shortest paths, which Bellman-Ford correctly computes. A negative cycle allows unbounded looping to reduce path weight arbitrarily, so no finite shortest path exists for vertices reachable from it.

lessons.label: Bellman-Ford: Paying O(nm) to Buy Negative Weights

sections.heading: n-1 rounds, m edges each
sections.body: Bellman-Ford, developed by Richard Bellman (1958) and Lester Ford Jr. (1956) independently, gives up Dijkstra's clever ordering entirely and instead relaxes EVERY edge in the graph, in any fixed order, for n-1 full rounds, where n is the number of vertices. The key fact licensing exactly n-1 rounds is that any simple shortest path (one that does not repeat a vertex) can contain at most n-1 edges, since a simple path on n vertices visits at most n vertices and therefore has at most n-1 edges between them. After round k, the algorithm is guaranteed to have found the correct shortest distance for every vertex whose true shortest path uses k or fewer edges; after n-1 full rounds, every simple shortest path — regardless of how many edges it needed — has been captured. Each round costs O(m) to relax every edge once, so the total running time is O(nm): worse than any of Dijkstra's queue variants, but the price paid for tolerating negative edge weights, since Bellman-Ford's proof never needs the nonnegative-weight assumption that Dijkstra's greedy argument requires.

sections.heading: Detecting and tracing a negative cycle
sections.body: Because Bellman-Ford relies on the fact that a simple shortest path needs no more than n-1 edges, running ONE additional, n-th round after the guaranteed n-1 have completed gives a direct negative-cycle detector: if any edge (u, v) can still be relaxed in that n-th round (dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v] still holds), then some vertex's distance has not stabilized after enough rounds to cover every simple path, which can only happen if the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source. To actually TRACE the cycle rather than just detect its existence, follow prev[] pointers backward starting from the vertex v that still relaxed in round n: because a cycle must exist somewhere in that backward walk, continuing for n more steps guarantees landing back inside the cycle, at which point the repeated vertex marks the cycle's boundary and the prev[] chain between its two occurrences is the cycle itself.

sections.heading: The SPFA optimization and its adversarial worst case, and where the O(nm) cost pays off
sections.body: The Shortest Path Faster Algorithm (SPFA), described by Fanding Duan in 1994, is a common practical speedup: instead of blindly relaxing all m edges every round, maintain a queue of vertices whose dist[] value just improved, and only re-relax edges leaving those vertices. On typical sparse, non-adversarial graphs SPFA often runs close to O(m) in practice, but its worst case is still O(nm) — and specific adversarial graph constructions (chains of vertices designed so each relaxation triggers a cascade of re-insertions) force it to hit that worst case, so SPFA is a practical heuristic, not an asymptotic improvement, and competitive programmers have learned to avoid relying on it in adversarial settings. Where Bellman-Ford earns its O(nm) cost: detecting arbitrage in currency exchange graphs (take the negative log of exchange rates; a negative cycle means a sequence of trades that returns more money than you started with — this is a real technique used in quantitative finance), solving systems of difference constraints (each constraint x_j - x_i <= c_ij becomes an edge i->j of weight c_ij, and a feasible solution exists exactly when the constraint graph has no negative cycle), and distance-vector routing protocols like RIP (Routing Information Protocol), where each router only knows its neighbors' costs and Bellman-Ford's edge-relaxation structure maps directly onto rounds of routers exchanging distance updates with only local information.

lessons.workedExample: A trader has exchange rates USD->EUR at 0.90, EUR->GBP at 0.85, and GBP->USD at 1.35. Convert each rate r to a graph edge weight -log(r): -log(0.90) = 0.105, -log(0.85) = 0.163, -log(1.35) = -0.300. Summing the cycle USD->EUR->GBP->USD gives 0.105 + 0.163 - 0.300 = -0.032, a NEGATIVE total, meaning the cycle is a negative cycle in the reweighted graph. Translating back: multiplying the original rates gives 0.90 * 0.85 * 1.35 = 1.033, meaning trading $1 through this three-currency loop returns $1.033 — a genuine arbitrage opportunity. Bellman-Ford's negative-cycle detection, run on the -log-transformed exchange-rate graph, is exactly the mechanism real trading systems use to flag this kind of loop automatically across dozens of currencies at once.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge assessing depth will want to know not just that Bellman-Ford is "the negative-weight version of Dijkstra" but why exactly n-1 rounds suffice (tied to the maximum number of edges in a simple path) and how the algorithm can be extended, with one more round, into a negative-cycle detector — a capability Dijkstra fundamentally cannot offer. Asking for a real application (currency arbitrage, RIP routing, difference constraints) checks whether the O(nm) cost is understood as a deliberate trade bought for a real capability, rather than simply "the slow one."

questions.prompt: Why does Bellman-Ford run for exactly n-1 rounds of relaxing all edges?

options.text: Because n-1 is an arbitrary safety margin with no structural justification
Because any simple shortest path on n vertices has at most n-1 edges, so n-1 rounds guarantee every such path is fully relaxed
Because the priority queue can only hold n-1 items
Because negative edges require one round per negative weight in the graph

explanations.a: The n-1 bound is a direct structural consequence of what a simple path on n vertices can contain, not an arbitrary choice.
explanations.b: Correct — a simple path visits at most n vertices and therefore has at most n-1 edges, and each round guarantees paths of one more edge are correctly relaxed.
explanations.c: Bellman-Ford does not use a priority queue at all; that is a Dijkstra-specific detail.
explanations.d: The round count depends on path length in edges, not on how many edges happen to be negative.

questions.prompt: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle reachable from the source?

options.text: By checking if any dist[] value is negative after n-1 rounds
By running one additional (n-th) round and checking if any edge can still be relaxed
By counting the total number of edges in the graph
Negative cycles cannot be detected by Bellman-Ford at all

explanations.a: A negative dist[] value by itself is perfectly valid and expected when negative edges (without a cycle) exist; it is not the detection signal.
explanations.b: Correct — if an n-th round still finds an edge that can improve dist[], some vertex's distance never stabilized, which is only possible if a negative cycle is reachable from the source.
explanations.c: Simply counting edges reveals nothing about weight structure or cycles.
explanations.d: Bellman-Ford's n-th-round test is precisely how negative-cycle detection is implemented; it is one of the algorithm's signature capabilities.

questions.prompt: What is the tradeoff of the SPFA (Shortest Path Faster Algorithm) optimization?

options.text: It reduces the asymptotic worst-case bound to O(m log n) in all cases
It often runs faster in practice on typical graphs but still has an O(nm) worst case under adversarial inputs
It only works on graphs with all positive edge weights
It eliminates the need for negative-cycle detection entirely

explanations.a: SPFA's worst-case bound remains O(nm); it does not achieve a better asymptotic guarantee.
explanations.b: Correct — by only re-relaxing edges from vertices whose distance recently improved, SPFA is often fast in practice, but adversarial graph constructions can still force its O(nm) worst case.
explanations.c: SPFA is specifically an optimization of Bellman-Ford, which is used precisely because it must handle negative edges.
explanations.d: SPFA can still be adapted for negative-cycle detection using similar round-counting logic; it is a speed optimization, not a feature removal.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world use case to the Bellman-Ford capability it depends on.

right.text: Negative-cycle detection on a -log(rate)-weighted exchange graph
No negative cycle in the constraint graph means a feasible variable assignment exists
Rounds of relaxation matching rounds of routers exchanging only local neighbor-cost information

questions.explanation: Arbitrage detection reweights exchange rates by -log and looks for a negative cycle; difference-constraint systems map each constraint to a weighted edge and require an absence of negative cycles for feasibility; RIP's distributed, neighbor-only updates mirror Bellman-Ford's edge-relaxation rounds rather than Dijkstra's global priority-queue view.

lessons.label: DAG Shortest — and Longest — Paths in O(n + m)

sections.heading: One pass, no priority queue, negative weights allowed
sections.body: On a directed acyclic graph (DAG), shortest paths can be computed in a single linear pass with no priority queue at all: first compute a topological ordering of the vertices (an ordering where every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one in the sequence, computable in O(n + m) via depth-first search or Kahn's algorithm), then process vertices in that order and relax every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once. Because the graph has no cycles, once a vertex u is processed in topological order, every edge that could possibly improve dist[u] has ALREADY been relaxed — there is no possibility that a later vertex feeds back into u, since a cycle would be required for that. This means dist[u] is guaranteed final the moment u is reached in the topological pass, which is a strictly stronger and cheaper guarantee than Dijkstra's settled-vertex invariant, and critically it holds regardless of edge sign: negative weights are completely fine on a DAG, because the entire correctness argument that failed for Dijkstra (weight can decrease along a path) never gets a chance to bite, since there is no cycle to create the kind of ordering ambiguity that negative edges exploit. Total cost: O(n + m) for the topological sort plus O(n + m) for the relaxation pass, so O(n + m) overall — asymptotically the cheapest of every shortest-path algorithm in this unit.

sections.heading: Longest path: NP-hard in general, linear on a DAG
sections.body: Finding the longest simple path in a general graph is NP-hard — it is closely related to the Hamiltonian path problem, since a graph has a Hamiltonian path if and only if its longest simple path visits every vertex, and no polynomial-time algorithm is known (or, under the widely believed P != NP conjecture, exists) for solving it on general graphs. On a DAG, however, the identical topological-order trick that solves shortest paths ALSO solves longest paths, in the same O(n + m) time, by one of two equivalent tricks: either negate every edge weight and run the DAG shortest-path relaxation looking for the minimum (which is now the most negative, i.e., the original maximum), or run the exact same topological relaxation pass but flip the relaxation inequality to keep the LARGER accumulated value instead of the smaller one. This is a striking asymmetry worth sitting with: the presence or absence of cycles alone is what separates a problem believed to require exponential time from one solvable in linear time, using the very same algorithmic skeleton.

sections.heading: The critical-path method and PERT scheduling
sections.body: The practical payoff of DAG longest paths is the critical-path method (CPM), developed by Morgan Walker of DuPont and James Kelley of Remington Rand in 1957, and the closely related Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT), developed by the U.S. Navy around the same time for the Polaris missile program. Model a project as a DAG where vertices are tasks, edges represent "task A must finish before task B starts," and edge weights are task durations; the LONGEST path from the project's start to its end is the critical path — the minimum possible time the entire project can take, because every task on that path is on the tightest possible dependency chain, and delaying any task on it delays the whole project. Tasks NOT on the critical path have "slack": room to be delayed without affecting the overall completion date, and that slack is computed directly as the difference between a task's earliest possible start (a DAG shortest-path-style forward pass) and its latest allowable start (a DAG longest-path-style backward pass) — the same O(n + m) machinery run twice, forward and backward, is literally how modern project-management and build systems (like the critical path shown in Microsoft Project, or dependency graphs in build tools like Bazel) compute what to prioritize.

lessons.workedExample: A small build system has tasks A (2 minutes), B (3 minutes), C (1 minute), and D (2 minutes), with dependencies A->C, B->C, and C->D (C cannot start until both A and B finish; D cannot start until C finishes). Topologically order them as A, B, C, D. Processing in this order for longest path: dist[A]=2, dist[B]=3 (both are sources, start at their own duration), dist[C] = max(dist[A], dist[B]) + duration(C) = max(2,3) + 1 = 4, dist[D] = dist[C] + duration(D) = 4 + 2 = 6. The critical path is B->C->D at total 6 minutes — meaning the whole build takes at minimum 6 minutes, and task A (finishing at minute 2, while C cannot start until minute 3 because it waits on B) has 1 minute of slack: A could take up to 3 minutes total without delaying the build at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots that DAG relaxation tolerates negative weights, unlike Dijkstra, will likely ask WHY — the correct answer ties directly back to the absence of cycles removing the specific failure mode from the negative-edges lesson, not a separate unrelated fact. The sharper follow-up is the NP-hard-versus-linear asymmetry for longest paths: a judge testing real understanding will ask what specifically about DAGs makes an NP-hard problem become linear, and the answer (topological order eliminates the combinatorial explosion of choosing which cycle-avoiding path to take, because there are no cycles to avoid) is where genuine insight, not memorized vocabulary, shows.

questions.prompt: Why does DAG shortest-path relaxation tolerate negative edge weights when Dijkstra's algorithm cannot?

options.text: DAGs never have negative edges by definition
Processing vertices in topological order guarantees all edges into a vertex are relaxed before it is finalized, with no cycle to create the ordering ambiguity that breaks Dijkstra's proof
DAG algorithms use a priority queue that automatically corrects for negative weights
Negative weights are simply converted to positive weights before the pass begins

explanations.a: DAGs are perfectly compatible with negative edge weights; "acyclic" restricts cycles, not edge signs.
explanations.b: Correct — topological order ensures a vertex is only processed after every possible predecessor has already relaxed its edges, so there is no possibility of a later, cheaper path arriving after a vertex was finalized.
explanations.c: DAG shortest paths use no priority queue at all; that is a Dijkstra-specific structure.
explanations.d: Weights are used as-is, sign and all; no conversion happens in the standard DAG relaxation algorithm.

questions.prompt: What is true about the longest simple path problem on a general (possibly cyclic) graph versus on a DAG?

options.text: It is NP-hard on general graphs but solvable in O(n + m) on a DAG
It is solvable in polynomial time on both
It is NP-hard on both general graphs and DAGs
It is undecidable on general graphs

explanations.a: Correct — the general longest-simple-path problem is NP-hard (related to Hamiltonian path), while on a DAG the same topological relaxation technique used for shortest paths solves it in linear time.
explanations.b: The general-graph version is NP-hard, not polynomial, under the standard assumption that P != NP.
explanations.c: On a DAG the problem is efficiently solvable in O(n + m); it is only the general-graph version that is NP-hard.
explanations.d: The problem is NP-hard, not undecidable; it is solvable given enough time, just not believed solvable in polynomial time.

questions.prompt: In the critical-path method (CPM), what does the critical path represent?

options.text: The shortest possible path through the fewest tasks
The longest path through the task-dependency DAG, representing the minimum time the whole project can take
A path that can be skipped without affecting the schedule
The path with the most slack

explanations.a: The critical path is the LONGEST dependency chain, not the shortest or fewest-task one.
explanations.b: Correct — the critical path is the longest path through the DAG of task dependencies, and it sets the minimum possible completion time because every task on it is a hard bottleneck.
explanations.c: The critical path cannot be skipped or delayed without delaying the entire project; that is precisely why it is called critical.
explanations.d: Tasks on the critical path have zero slack by definition; slack belongs to tasks NOT on the critical path.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing shortest (or longest) paths on a DAG.

items.text: Compute a topological ordering of all vertices
Initialize dist[source] = 0 and all others to infinity (or negative infinity for longest path)
Process vertices in topological order, relaxing each vertex's outgoing edges
Read off final dist[] values, each guaranteed correct with no further updates possible

questions.explanation: DAG shortest/longest paths first establish a topological order, initialize distance estimates, then perform a single relaxation pass following that order, after which every distance is final because no cycle can ever cause a later update to an already-processed vertex.

lessons.label: All-Pairs Shortest Paths: Floyd-Warshall and Johnson's

sections.heading: Floyd-Warshall: dynamic programming over allowed intermediates
sections.body: The algorithm carries two names because two people found it at once: Robert Floyd published "Algorithm 97: Shortest Path" in Communications of the ACM in June 1962, and in that same year Stephen Warshall independently published "A Theorem on Boolean Matrices" in the Journal of the ACM, giving the transitive-closure version of the same idea. Neither built on the other — they were simultaneous, independent discoveries, and Bernard Roy had in fact published the transitive-closure result three years earlier (1959, "Transitivite et connexite"), though his paper went largely unnoticed at the time. The algorithm solves ALL-PAIRS shortest paths (every vertex to every other vertex) in O(n^3) using dynamic programming over a single, elegant state variable: for each pair (i, j), let dist_k[i][j] be the shortest path from i to j using ONLY intermediate vertices numbered 1 through k. The recurrence is dist_k[i][j] = min(dist_{k-1}[i][j], dist_{k-1}[i][k] + dist_{k-1}[k][j]) — either the best path avoiding vertex k entirely is still best, or routing through k as an intermediate stop is better. Crucially, k must be the OUTERMOST of the three nested loops (k, then i, then j), because dist_k[i][j] depends on dist_{k-1} values that must already be fully finalized for ALL pairs before vertex k is used as an intermediate for ANY pair; looping i or j outermost would use dist_k values before they were correctly computed, silently corrupting the answer. The entire algorithm operates on the graph's adjacency MATRIX directly — no adjacency list, no priority queue, just three nested loops over an n-by-n array — which makes it exceptionally simple to implement and highly cache-friendly, a genuine practical advantage on modern hardware despite its O(n^3) asymptotic cost.

sections.heading: Negative-cycle detection on the diagonal, and Warshall's boolean twin
sections.body: Floyd-Warshall detects negative cycles for free as a side effect: after the full computation, if any diagonal entry dist[i][i] is negative, that means there is a path from i back to itself with negative total weight — a negative cycle passing through i — since in a well-behaved graph dist[i][i] should always be exactly 0 (the trivial path of staying put). Warshall's 1962 algorithm, discovered independently of Floyd's numeric version in the same year, solves the BOOLEAN twin of this problem — transitive closure — using the identical triple-nested-loop structure but with reachable[i][j] = reachable[i][j] OR (reachable[i][k] AND reachable[k][j]) in place of the min/plus recurrence: it answers "is j reachable from i at all" rather than "what is the shortest distance." That the two results appeared in the same year without either author knowing of the other is not a coincidence so much as a sign that the underlying idea is forced: the two algorithms are frequently taught together precisely because the loop structure is the same idea applied to two different semirings (min-plus versus or-and), and the name Roy-Floyd-Warshall is sometimes used to credit all three independent discoverers.

sections.heading: Johnson's algorithm: reweight once, then n Dijkstras
sections.body: Donald Johnson published his algorithm in 1977 specifically to beat Floyd-Warshall on SPARSE graphs. The key trick is computing a correct reweighting (unlike the broken constant-shift idea from an earlier lesson) using a single Bellman-Ford run from a new, artificial source vertex connected to every real vertex by a zero-weight edge, which produces a potential h(v) for every vertex v; each real edge (u, v) is then reweighted to w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) - h(v), a transformation that Johnson proved always produces NONNEGATIVE weights (when no negative cycle exists) while PRESERVING which path is shortest between any fixed pair of vertices, because the h(u) - h(v) telescopes to a constant depending only on the endpoints, not on the path taken between them — this is exactly the correct version of the constant-shift idea, using per-vertex potentials instead of one global constant. With all weights now nonnegative, Johnson's algorithm runs Dijkstra's algorithm once from EVERY vertex (n runs total) on the reweighted graph, then converts each result back to true distances by inverting the shift. Total cost: O(nm) for the initial Bellman-Ford plus O(n) calls to Dijkstra at O(m + n log n) each with a Fibonacci heap (a binary heap instead gives O((n+m) log n) per call, for a larger total of O(n(n+m) log n)), giving O(nm + n^2 log n) overall with the Fibonacci-heap implementation — for a SPARSE graph where m is close to n, this beats Floyd-Warshall's O(n^3) decisively, which is precisely why Johnson's algorithm exists as a separate, sparse-graph-specialized alternative rather than Floyd-Warshall being used universally.

lessons.workedExample: Consider vertices 1, 2, 3 with dist_0 (direct edges only) giving dist[1][3]=10, dist[1][2]=3, dist[2][3]=4, and all diagonal entries 0. At k=1, no improvement uses vertex 1 as an intermediate here. At k=2, check dist[1][3] against dist[1][2] + dist[2][3] = 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than the current 10, so dist[1][3] updates to 7 and this reflects the path 1->2->3 discovered by allowing vertex 2 as an intermediate stop. At k=3, no further improvement is found. The final dist[1][3]=7 is only reached because k=2 was processed as the OUTER loop value before dist[1][3] was checked; if the loops were ordered with i or j outermost instead, the algorithm might read the stale dist_0[1][3]=10 in a context expecting the already-updated dist_2 value, producing a wrong or inconsistent answer for some pair depending on iteration order.
lessons.judgeFraming: A very common but shallow answer is "Floyd-Warshall is three nested loops with O(n^3)." A judge testing depth will ask specifically why k must be the outermost loop, since getting the loop order wrong is a real, easy-to-make bug that silently produces wrong answers instead of crashing — understanding WHY the ordering matters demonstrates real grasp of the DP formulation, not just memorized pseudocode. The Johnson's-algorithm comparison is the second natural probe: a judge may ask when you would ever choose Johnson's over Floyd-Warshall, and the correct answer (sparse graphs, where O(nm + n^2 log n) beats O(n^3)) shows the student can reason about asymptotic tradeoffs rather than treating one algorithm as universally superior.

questions.prompt: In Floyd-Warshall's triple-nested loop, why must the intermediate-vertex variable k be the OUTERMOST loop?

options.text: It is just a stylistic convention with no effect on correctness
dist_k[i][j] depends on dist_{k-1} values for ALL pairs being already finalized before k is used as an intermediate for any pair
Outer loops are always faster than inner loops in every language
It ensures the algorithm runs in O(n^2) instead of O(n^3)

explanations.a: The loop order is not stylistic; swapping it can produce incorrect results because the DP recurrence's dependency structure is violated.
explanations.b: Correct — every dist_k[i][j] computation needs dist_{k-1}[i][k] and dist_{k-1}[k][j] to already reflect the correct value across ALL pairs, which is only guaranteed if k has fully completed its outer-loop iteration before i and j vary.
explanations.c: Loop ordering does not change per-language execution speed by itself; the issue here is correctness, not raw performance.
