explanations.d: The loop order does not change the asymptotic complexity; it remains O(n^3) regardless, but only the correct ordering gives a correct answer.

questions.prompt: How does Floyd-Warshall detect a negative cycle after running to completion?

options.text: By checking if the total sum of all matrix entries is negative
By checking if any diagonal entry dist[i][i] is negative
Floyd-Warshall cannot detect negative cycles at all
By counting the number of negative edges in the original graph

explanations.a: A summed total gives no reliable signal; individual diagonal entries are the correct test.
explanations.b: Correct — dist[i][i] should be exactly 0 in a well-behaved graph; a negative value means a path exists from i back to itself with negative total weight, i.e., a negative cycle through i.
explanations.c: Floyd-Warshall detects negative cycles naturally, as a direct side effect of its normal computation, with no extra pass required.
explanations.d: The count of negative edges says nothing about whether they form a cycle; the diagonal check is the direct, correct signal.

questions.prompt: What does Johnson's algorithm's reweighting achieve that a single global constant shift cannot?

options.text: It produces nonnegative weights while preserving which path is shortest, using per-vertex potentials so the shift telescopes to a path-independent constant between any two endpoints
It removes all negative edges from the graph entirely before computing anything
It works identically to a global constant shift but is slower
It only works on graphs with no edges at all

explanations.a: Correct — using vertex-specific potentials h(v) derived from Bellman-Ford means the added amount depends only on the two endpoints of a path (via telescoping), not on how many edges the path used, unlike a flat global constant.
explanations.b: Reweighting changes the weights' values, not whether edges exist; the graph's structure is unchanged.
explanations.c: It is fundamentally different from a global shift — that is precisely why it correctly preserves shortest-path order where the constant-shift idea fails.
explanations.d: Johnson's algorithm applies generally to any graph without a negative cycle; it is not restricted to edgeless graphs.

questions.prompt: What is the actual historical relationship between Floyd's and Warshall's 1962 publications?

options.text: Floyd built his shortest-path algorithm directly on Warshall's previously published theorem
They were independent, simultaneous 1962 results — Floyd on shortest paths, Warshall on transitive closure — with Bernard Roy having published the closure version in 1959, largely unnoticed
Warshall extended Floyd's earlier numeric algorithm to the boolean case decades later
Floyd and Warshall co-authored a single 1962 paper describing both versions

explanations.a: There is no dependency: Floyd's CACM paper and Warshall's JACM paper appeared the same year, neither building on the other.
explanations.b: Correct — Floyd published "Algorithm 97: Shortest Path" (CACM, June 1962) and Warshall published "A Theorem on Boolean Matrices" (JACM, 1962) independently in the same year; Roy's 1959 "Transitivite et connexite" had the closure result first but went unnoticed, which is why the algorithm is sometimes called Roy-Floyd-Warshall.
explanations.c: Both papers are from 1962, and Warshall's boolean version did not follow Floyd's by decades.
explanations.d: They never collaborated; the hyphenated name reflects two separate papers, not a joint one.

questions.prompt: Match each algorithm or technique to its role in all-pairs shortest paths.

right.text: O(n^3) DP over allowed intermediate vertices, computing actual shortest distances
Same loop structure applied to boolean reachability instead of distances
Bellman-Ford-based reweighting followed by n runs of Dijkstra, favoring sparse graphs

questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall computes numeric shortest distances via the min-plus DP recurrence; Warshall's independently discovered 1962 algorithm computes only reachability using the analogous or-and recurrence; Johnson's algorithm reweights edges nonnegative via vertex potentials and then runs Dijkstra from every vertex, winning on sparse graphs where O(nm + n^2 log n) beats O(n^3).

lessons.label: A* Search: Dijkstra Plus a Heuristic

sections.heading: f(v) = g(v) + h(v)
sections.body: A* was introduced by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael in a 1968 IEEE paper written at the Stanford Research Institute for robot path planning (for the robot Shakey). It modifies Dijkstra's priority-queue ordering by ranking the frontier not purely on g(v), the actual accumulated distance from the source so far (exactly Dijkstra's dist[v]), but on f(v) = g(v) + h(v), where h(v) is a HEURISTIC estimate of the remaining distance from v to the goal. Instead of blindly exploring outward in every direction like Dijkstra, A* prioritizes vertices that both are cheap to reach AND appear, according to the heuristic, to be headed toward the goal — which is why A* typically explores a dramatically smaller region of the graph than Dijkstra when searching for a single specific destination, while Dijkstra (run to find one destination) explores an expanding ball around the source with no sense of direction at all.

sections.heading: Admissible and consistent heuristics — the two guarantees that keep A* correct
sections.body: A heuristic h is ADMISSIBLE if it never OVERESTIMATES the true remaining distance to the goal: h(v) <= true shortest distance from v to goal, for every v. Admissibility alone guarantees A* finds the optimal path, because an overestimating heuristic could cause the algorithm to deprioritize a vertex that is actually on the true shortest path, mistakenly believing a costlier-looking route was cheaper. A stronger property, CONSISTENCY (also called monotonicity), requires h(u) <= w(u, v) + h(v) for every edge (u, v) — the heuristic estimate can never drop by more than the actual edge weight as you move one step closer. Consistency implies admissibility and additionally guarantees that once A* settles a vertex (analogous to Dijkstra's settled set), its distance never needs revision, which is what allows A* to be implemented with the exact same settled-set machinery as Dijkstra rather than needing to reopen closed nodes. With h identical to the zero function for every vertex, f(v) = g(v) + 0 = g(v), and A* degenerates EXACTLY to Dijkstra's algorithm — Dijkstra is the special case of A* with no heuristic information at all. At the opposite extreme, a PERFECT heuristic (h(v) exactly equal to the true remaining distance) causes A* to expand only the vertices that lie exactly on a shortest path, with zero wasted exploration.

sections.heading: Straight-line distance, inadmissible heuristics, and bidirectional search
sections.body: The canonical heuristic for road-network or grid pathfinding is straight-line (Euclidean) distance to the goal: it is provably admissible because no real road route can ever be shorter than a straight line between two points, and it is usually consistent too under normal metric assumptions. Using an INADMISSIBLE heuristic — one that sometimes overestimates — trades away the optimality guarantee for speed: the search becomes more aggressively greedy toward the goal and explores far fewer vertices, but can return a path that is not truly shortest, which is a deliberate and common engineering tradeoff in time-critical applications like real-time game AI pathfinding, where a near-optimal path found instantly beats a perfect path found too slowly to matter. Bidirectional search is a separate, complementary technique for shrinking the explored region: instead of a single search expanding outward from the source, two simultaneous searches run — one forward from the source, one backward from the goal — and the algorithm terminates once their explored frontiers meet, which for many graphs means each direction only needs to search out to about half the radius, so the combined explored area (two half-radius circles) ends up roughly half the area of one full-radius circle reaching all the way across, and bidirectional search can be combined with A*'s heuristic-guided prioritization for a further reduction in explored vertices.

lessons.workedExample: On a city grid where each block is 1 unit, searching from (0,0) to (4,4) with actual road distance g and straight-line heuristic h = sqrt((4-x)^2 + (4-y)^2): at vertex (2,2), g=4 (two blocks east, two north, Manhattan-style road distance), and h = sqrt(4+4) = 2.83, giving f = 6.83. Now consider (0,4): g=4, h=sqrt(16+0)=4, f=8, clearly worse than (2,2)'s f=6.83. A* extracts the lowest-f vertex from its frontier at each step just like Dijkstra extracts lowest-dist, so (2,2) — which is closer to the straight-line direction of the goal — gets explored before (0,4), even though both have the same g value in a symmetric grid, precisely because h(2,2) correctly estimates it needs less remaining travel than h(0,4) does.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask the direct question "what does A* reduce to if you remove the heuristic?" — and the correct, precise answer is that it becomes exactly Dijkstra's algorithm, not merely "something similar," because f(v) collapses to g(v) with h identical to zero. A second common probe distinguishes admissible from consistent heuristics: many students can define admissible (never overestimates) but cannot explain why the stronger consistency property is what actually lets A* reuse Dijkstra's settled-set machinery without reopening nodes. Being able to state the real cost of an inadmissible heuristic — faster search, but a possibly non-optimal answer — signals an engineering-tradeoffs understanding beyond rote heuristic vocabulary.

questions.prompt: What does A* become if the heuristic function h(v) is identically zero for every vertex?

options.text: It becomes exactly Dijkstra's algorithm, since f(v) = g(v) + 0 = g(v)
It becomes Bellman-Ford, since it can now handle negative weights
It stops working entirely and cannot find any path
It becomes a purely random search with no priority ordering

explanations.a: Correct — with h(v)=0 for all v, ranking by f(v) is identical to ranking by g(v) alone, which is precisely Dijkstra's priority-queue ordering.
explanations.b: A zero heuristic does not change anything about how negative weights are handled; A* still requires the same nonnegative-weight assumption Dijkstra needs unless a different algorithm is substituted.
explanations.c: A* with a zero heuristic still functions correctly; it is simply equivalent to Dijkstra, not broken.
explanations.d: The queue still orders by g(v), which is a meaningful, non-random priority — this is standard Dijkstra behavior, not randomness.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an admissible heuristic and a consistent (monotone) heuristic?

options.text: Admissible means it never overestimates the remaining distance; consistent additionally requires h(u) <= w(u,v) + h(v) along every edge, which lets A* avoid ever reopening a settled vertex
They are exactly the same property with two different names
Admissible heuristics can overestimate; consistent heuristics cannot
Consistency only applies to undirected graphs

explanations.a: Correct — admissibility alone guarantees optimality but may require reopening vertices in some implementations; consistency is the stronger edge-wise condition that guarantees a vertex's cost never needs revision once settled.
explanations.b: They are related but distinct: every consistent heuristic is admissible, but not every admissible heuristic is consistent.
explanations.c: It is admissible heuristics that must NOT overestimate by definition; overestimating would violate admissibility itself.
explanations.d: Consistency is a general property defined over edges and applies regardless of whether the graph is directed or undirected.

questions.prompt: What is the tradeoff of using an inadmissible heuristic (one that sometimes overestimates) in A*?

options.text: It speeds up the search by exploring fewer vertices, but the returned path may not be truly shortest
It has no effect on speed or correctness
It guarantees a faster search AND a still-optimal path
It makes the algorithm equivalent to Bellman-Ford

explanations.a: Correct — an inadmissible heuristic makes the search more aggressively greedy toward the goal, often finding a path much faster, but optimality is no longer guaranteed.
explanations.b: Inadmissible heuristics have a real, deliberate effect: faster exploration at the cost of the optimality guarantee.
explanations.c: Optimality is exactly what is sacrificed; only speed is gained, not both.
explanations.d: Changing the heuristic's admissibility has nothing to do with Bellman-Ford, which is a fundamentally different algorithm for negative-weight graphs.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description in A* search.

right.text: The actual accumulated cost from the source to v so far
The heuristic estimate of remaining cost from v to the goal
Running two simultaneous searches, forward and backward, that terminate when their frontiers meet

questions.explanation: g(v) is the exact known cost so far (identical to Dijkstra's dist[v]), h(v) is the heuristic's estimate of the remaining distance to the goal, and bidirectional search is a separate technique that shrinks the explored region by searching from both endpoints at once and can be combined with A*'s heuristic guidance.

units.label: Spanning Trees, Ordering, and Connectivity Structure

lessons.label: Minimum Spanning Trees and the Cut Property

sections.heading: n-1 edges, no cycles, one component
sections.body: A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph with n vertices is a subgraph that touches every vertex, contains no cycle, and stays connected. Those three constraints force exactly n-1 edges: a connected graph on n vertices needs at least n-1 edges to reach every vertex, and any acyclic connected graph on n vertices has at most n-1 edges (add one more and you close a cycle). A minimum spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree whose edge-weight sum is smallest among all spanning trees. If the graph is disconnected, no spanning tree exists at all, and algorithms instead produce a minimum spanning FOREST, one tree per connected component.

sections.heading: The cut property: the engine behind every MST algorithm
sections.body: A cut is any partition of the vertices into two nonempty sets S and V-S; an edge crosses the cut if it has one endpoint in each. The CUT PROPERTY states: for any cut, if there is a unique lightest edge crossing it, that edge belongs to every MST (and if weights tie, at least one of the lightest crossing edges belongs to some MST). The proof is an exchange argument: suppose an MST T omits the lightest crossing edge e; T must still contain some other edge f crossing the same cut (or S and V-S would be disconnected in T). Swapping f out for e produces a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to T's, contradicting T's minimality if e is strictly lighter. This single fact justifies Prim's algorithm (it repeatedly picks the lightest edge crossing the cut between the growing tree and the rest) and half of Kruskal's correctness proof. The mirror-image CYCLE PROPERTY says the heaviest edge on any cycle belongs to NO MST: if you look at any cycle and its strictly-heaviest edge, removing that edge from any spanning tree containing it and replacing it with a lighter cycle edge crossing the same cut only helps. Kruskal's algorithm leans on this: by processing edges lightest-first and rejecting any edge that would close a cycle, it is exactly discarding the eventual heaviest edge of every cycle it detects.

sections.heading: MST paths are not shortest paths, and uniqueness needs distinct weights
sections.body: A common misconception is that the unique path between two vertices in an MST is also the shortest path between them in the original graph. It is not, and a minimal counterexample makes this concrete (see the worked example): the MST minimizes the TOTAL weight of the tree, not any single pairwise distance, so it can force a long detour between two vertices that had a cheap direct edge, if that edge was not needed to keep the whole tree light. Uniqueness of the MST itself is guaranteed when all edge weights are distinct: with no ties, the cut property's 'unique lightest edge' clause applies to every cut, pinning down one specific tree. When weights can tie, a graph may have several equal-weight MSTs, and different algorithms (or different tie-breaking rules within the same algorithm) can legitimately return different, equally optimal, trees.

lessons.workedExample: Take four vertices A, B, C, D with edges A-B weight 1, B-C weight 1, C-D weight 1, and A-D weight 2 (a 4-cycle, no other edges). The MST drops the heaviest cycle edge, A-D (weight 2), leaving the path A-B-C-D with total weight 3. Now the MST path between A and D is A-B-C-D, cost 3 -- but the ORIGINAL graph has a direct edge A-D of weight 2, which is shorter. The MST is optimal for total tree weight, not for any single-pair distance; an MST-based routing scheme would misroute A-to-D traffic through B and C when a cheaper direct hop exists. This is why MST and shortest-path-tree are different objects built by different algorithms (Prim/Kruskal vs. Dijkstra) even though their pseudocode looks similar.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows graph theory will often ask a student to confirm 'so the MST gives you the shortest way to get from any node to any other node, right?' -- and the expected sophisticated answer is no, with a one-sentence counterexample ready, since the MST optimizes for a single global total, not for pairwise distances. Judges also probe whether the student can state the cut property in their own words and explain WHY it works (the exchange argument), rather than just naming it as jargon, because the cut property is the one idea that unifies Kruskal, Prim, and Boruvka into a single family instead of three unrelated recipes.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 12 vertices. How many edges does every spanning tree of this graph contain?

options.text: It depends on the graph's total edge count

explanations.a: Correct -- a spanning tree on n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges (12-1 = 11), regardless of how many extra edges the original graph has.
explanations.b: 12 edges on 12 vertices would necessarily include a cycle, so it would not be a tree.
explanations.c: 13 edges is even further from tree structure; a tree can never have more edges than vertices minus one.
explanations.d: It does not depend on the graph's edge count -- every spanning tree of every connected graph on n vertices has exactly n-1 edges, always.

questions.prompt: According to the cut property, if a cut has a single edge that is strictly lighter than every other edge crossing it, what can you conclude?

options.text: That edge is in every MST of the graph
That edge is in no MST of the graph
The graph has no MST
That edge must be the single lightest edge in the whole graph

explanations.a: Correct -- the cut property guarantees the unique lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to every MST; an exchange argument shows any MST omitting it can be improved by swapping it in.
explanations.b: That description matches the cycle property's heaviest-edge-on-a-cycle case, not the cut property's lightest-edge-crossing-a-cut case.
explanations.c: The cut property presupposes a connected graph with an MST; it says nothing about MST existence.
explanations.d: The edge only needs to be lightest among edges crossing THIS particular cut, not lightest in the entire graph.

questions.prompt: Under what condition is a graph's MST guaranteed to be unique?

options.text: When all edge weights are distinct
When the graph is a complete graph
When the graph has an even number of vertices
When Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms are both run on it

explanations.a: Correct -- distinct weights mean every cut has a single unambiguous lightest crossing edge, which pins down one specific MST with no tie-breaking choices.
explanations.b: Completeness (every pair of vertices connected) has no bearing on uniqueness; a complete graph with tied weights can still have multiple MSTs.
explanations.c: Vertex count parity is irrelevant to MST uniqueness.
explanations.d: Running two different correct algorithms on the same graph will simply return the same MST if it is unique, or possibly different equally-valid MSTs if weights tie -- running algorithms doesn't create uniqueness.

questions.prompt: Order these facts as they build the exchange argument that proves the cut property.

items.text: Assume MST T omits e, the unique lightest edge crossing some cut
T must contain some other edge f that also crosses that same cut
Swap f out and e in, producing a new spanning tree
The new tree weighs strictly less than T, contradicting T's minimality

questions.explanation: The argument starts by supposing a violation (T omits e), observes T must still bridge the cut via some other edge f, performs the swap, and derives a contradiction because e was strictly lighter than f -- forcing the conclusion that no MST can omit e.

questions.prompt: Match each property to what it guarantees about MST edges.

right.text: The unique lightest edge crossing a cut is in every MST
The unique heaviest edge on a cycle is in no MST
Guarantees the graph has exactly one MST

questions.explanation: The cut property includes the lightest crossing edge (used by Prim); the cycle property excludes the heaviest cycle edge (used by Kruskal's rejection rule); and distinct weights remove all ties, making every cut's and cycle's extreme edge unambiguous, which forces MST uniqueness.

lessons.label: Kruskal's Algorithm: Sort, Scan, and Reject Cycles

sections.heading: The algorithm: a greedy scan over sorted edges
sections.body: Joseph Kruskal published the algorithm in 1956 in 'On the Shortest Spanning Subtree of a Graph and the Traveling Salesman Problem' (Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society). The recipe is short: sort all m edges by weight ascending, then walk the sorted list and add each edge to a growing forest UNLESS it would connect two vertices already in the same component -- in which case adding it would close a cycle, so it is rejected. The algorithm halts once n-1 edges have been accepted (or the list is exhausted, leaving a minimum spanning forest if the graph was disconnected). Correctness follows directly from the cycle property from the previous lesson: because edges are processed lightest-first, any edge Kruskal rejects is, at the moment it is considered, the heaviest edge on the cycle it would create among edges seen so far -- exactly the edge the cycle property says belongs to no MST.

sections.heading: Testing 'same component' efficiently: union-find
sections.body: The naive way to test whether two vertices are already connected -- rerunning a traversal from scratch for every edge -- would cost O(m*n) overall, far too slow. Kruskal's algorithm instead pairs with the union-find (disjoint-set) data structure, which supports FIND(v) (which component is v in) and UNION(u, v) (merge two components) as its only two operations. With two standard optimizations -- union by rank (always attach the smaller tree under the root of the larger, keeping trees shallow) and path compression (every FIND flattens the path it walks, pointing nodes directly at the root) -- a sequence of m union-find operations on n elements costs O(m * alpha(n)) total, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. Alpha(n) grows so slowly that for any n representable in a real computer's memory (fewer than about 2^65536 elements) it is at most 4 or 5, so union-find is treated as amortized near-constant per operation in practice. That said, the full formal amortized analysis (the potential-function argument bounding path compression's cost) is a data-structures topic in its own right -- here we use union-find as a proven component, not something to re-derive.

sections.heading: Total cost, and what shifts the balance
sections.body: Kruskal's total running time is O(m log m) for the sort plus O(m alpha(n)) for the union-find scan; since log m is O(log n) for simple graphs (m is at most n^2, so log m <= 2 log n), the standard statement is O(m log n). The sort dominates in the general case -- comparison sorting m arbitrary real-valued weights cannot beat O(m log m) in the comparison model. Two situations shift this balance. First, if edges arrive PRE-SORTED (e.g., weights were generated in sorted order, or a previous computation already produced a sorted edge list), Kruskal degrades gracefully to O(m alpha(n)), dominated entirely by the union-find scan -- a genuine linear-ish speedup. Second, if weights are small non-negative INTEGERS bounded by a polynomial in n, radix sort or counting sort can sort the edges in O(m) time instead of O(m log m), again leaving union-find as the bottleneck. Both cases matter in practice: sensor networks and grid graphs often have small integer distances, and pipeline stages sometimes hand off already-ordered data.

lessons.workedExample: Consider edges (weight): A-B(1), B-C(4), A-C(3), C-D(2), B-D(5). Sorted ascending: A-B(1), C-D(2), A-C(3), B-C(4), B-D(5). Scan: accept A-B (FIND(A) != FIND(B); components become {A,B}, {C}, {D}); accept C-D (FIND(C) != FIND(D); components become {A,B}, {C,D}); accept A-C (FIND(A) != FIND(C); merges the two components into {A,B,C,D} -- exactly n-1=3 edges accepted, so the algorithm halts immediately). B-C(4) and B-D(5) are never even examined, because the scan already produced a full spanning tree before reaching them in the sorted list. The union-find structure answered three FIND-pair comparisons and performed two UNION merges, never needing a fresh graph traversal to test connectivity; total work here was dominated by sorting five edges, O(5 log 5), a trivial cost at this scale but the same asymptotic shape as the m log m bound that governs a graph with m=1,000,000 edges.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask 'why sort first instead of just scanning edges in graph order?' -- the answer must connect back to the cycle property: sorting guarantees that whenever an edge is rejected, it is provably the heaviest edge on some cycle at that point, which is what makes the greedy choice correct rather than a heuristic. A sharper judge probes whether the student can separate Kruskal's own complexity claim from union-find's: Kruskal is 'correct because of the cycle property, and fast because of union-find,' and conflating the two (e.g., claiming Kruskal itself has amortized-constant behavior) signals a shallow read.

questions.prompt: Why does Kruskal's algorithm sort edges by weight before scanning them?

options.text: So that any rejected edge is guaranteed to be the heaviest edge on the cycle it would form, matching the cycle property
Sorting is required so union-find can be initialized
Sorting reduces the number of vertices in the graph
It is a historical convention with no effect on correctness

explanations.a: Correct -- processing lightest-first means a rejected edge is, at the moment it's considered, the heaviest edge among the cycle it would close, which the cycle property guarantees is safe to exclude from the MST.
explanations.b: Union-find initialization (each vertex its own singleton component) does not depend on edge order at all.
explanations.c: Sorting reorders edges; it never changes vertex count.
explanations.d: Sorting is load-bearing for correctness -- without ascending order, the greedy exclusion argument breaks down and the wrong edges could be rejected.

questions.prompt: What does path compression contribute to union-find's performance?

options.text: It flattens the tree during FIND so future FIND calls on the same elements are faster
It sorts the edge list in place
It merges the two smallest components first
It detects cycles directly without needing FIND

explanations.a: Correct -- path compression repoints every node visited during a FIND directly to the root, so the amortized cost of later FINDs on those nodes drops toward constant.
explanations.b: Path compression is entirely internal to the union-find structure and has nothing to do with edge sorting.
explanations.c: That describes union by rank/size, a separate optimization from path compression.
explanations.d: Cycle detection in Kruskal is done indirectly: FIND(u) == FIND(v) before a UNION signals a cycle; path compression only speeds up FIND, it doesn't perform the check itself.

questions.prompt: If the m edges of a graph are handed to Kruskal's algorithm already sorted by weight, what happens to the overall running time?

options.text: It drops from O(m log n) to O(m alpha(n)), since the union-find scan now dominates
It stays exactly O(m log n) because sorting cost is unavoidable
It increases, since Kruskal must first verify the list is sorted
It becomes O(n^2) regardless of m

explanations.a: Correct -- with sorting no longer needed, only the union-find scan over m edges remains, which is O(m alpha(n)), effectively near-linear.
explanations.b: The whole point of pre-sorted input is that the O(m log m) sorting term disappears from the total.
explanations.c: Verifying sortedness (if done at all) costs only O(m), not enough to change the asymptotic bound, and is not the standard framing of this scenario.
explanations.d: O(n^2) has no relation to this scenario; the improvement is in the m-dependent sorting term, not a blowup in n.

questions.prompt: Order the steps Kruskal's algorithm performs on a graph with m edges and n vertices.

items.text: Sort all m edges by weight ascending
Initialize each vertex as its own union-find singleton
For each edge in sorted order, check if its endpoints are in different components
If they differ, union the components and accept the edge; otherwise reject it
Stop once n-1 edges have been accepted

questions.explanation: Sorting and singleton initialization can happen in either order relative to each other but both must precede the scan; the scan itself checks-then-unions per edge in weight order, and the process halts once a full spanning tree's worth of edges (n-1) has been accepted.

questions.prompt: Match each cost driver in Kruskal's algorithm to the term it contributes to the total running time.

left.text: Sorting m arbitrary real-valued edge weights
Union-find with path compression + union by rank

right.text: O(m log m), the general-case dominant term
O(m alpha(n)), near-linear amortized
Enables O(m) counting/radix sort, removing the log factor

questions.explanation: In the general comparison-sort case, sorting's O(m log m) dominates over union-find's near-linear O(m alpha(n)) scan; when weights are small bounded integers, a linear-time sort removes the log factor entirely, leaving union-find as the bottleneck.

lessons.label: Prim's Algorithm: Grow One Tree from a Seed

sections.heading: One tree, one cut, growing outward
sections.body: Where Kruskal builds a forest that merges into one tree, Prim's algorithm grows a single tree outward from one seed vertex. The algorithm, credited to Vojtech Jarnik (1930), rediscovered by Robert Prim (1957), and again by Edsger Dijkstra (1959), maintains a set S of vertices already in the tree (initially just the seed) and repeatedly adds the lightest edge with exactly one endpoint in S -- i.e., the lightest edge crossing the cut (S, V-S) -- pulling its other endpoint into S. This is a direct, repeated application of the cut property: at every step there is a well-defined cut, and the algorithm always takes its lightest crossing edge, which the cut property guarantees is safe to add. The process repeats n-1 times until S contains every vertex.

sections.heading: Implementation: a priority queue keyed by cut-crossing weight
sections.body: The practical challenge is finding the lightest crossing edge quickly at each step without rescanning every edge. The standard implementation keeps a priority queue over vertices NOT yet in S, keyed by the minimum edge weight connecting that vertex to any vertex currently in S (initialized to infinity, updated as S grows). With a binary heap, each of the n extract-min operations costs O(log n), and each of the m edges can trigger at most one decrease-key/relaxation, also O(log n), giving O(m log n) total -- effectively the same complexity class as Kruskal's O(m log m). With a Fibonacci heap, decrease-key drops to O(1) amortized, improving the bound to O(m + n log n), which matters on dense graphs with large m. On the other end, a simple array-based priority queue (no heap at all -- linear scan for the minimum) gives O(n) per extract-min and O(1) per update, totaling O(n^2). Because O(n^2) has no log factor and no dependence on m, it BEATS the heap version once m approaches n^2, i.e., on dense graphs; the array implementation is the standard choice for dense-graph MST in practice, while the heap version wins on sparse graphs.

sections.heading: Prim vs. Dijkstra: identical skeleton, one changed key
sections.body: Prim's algorithm and Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm are so structurally similar that students routinely fuse them into an incorrect hybrid, so the distinction deserves to be stated precisely. Both maintain a frontier via a priority queue and repeatedly extract the minimum-key vertex, relaxing its neighbors. The ENTIRE difference is the key. Dijkstra keys each candidate vertex v by dist[u] + w(u,v) -- the total path length from the source through the current tree to v -- because Dijkstra answers 'what is the shortest PATH from the source to every vertex.' Prim keys each candidate vertex v by w(u,v) alone -- the single edge's weight, with no accumulated path cost -- because Prim answers 'what is the lightest way to CONNECT v to the tree,' a purely local question. Confusing the two produces a broken algorithm: using Dijkstra's cumulative key inside Prim's tree-growth loop would build a shortest-path tree, not an MST, and as the earlier MST lesson showed, those are provably different objects.

lessons.workedExample: On vertices A,B,C,D with edges A-B(1), A-C(3), B-C(4), C-D(2), B-D(5), start Prim from A. S={A}; frontier keys: B=1 (via A-B), C=3 (via A-C), D=infinity. Extract min: B (key 1), add edge A-B, S={A,B}. Update frontier from B's edges: C's key improves from 3 to min(3, 4)=3 (B-C is weight 4, worse, no change), D's key improves from infinity to 5 (via B-D). Extract min: C (key 3), add edge A-C, S={A,B,C}. Update from C's edges: D's key improves from 5 to 2 (via C-D). Extract min: D (key 2), add edge C-D, S={A,B,C,D}, done. Result MST edges: A-B, A-C, C-D, total weight 1+3+2=6 -- matching Kruskal's result on the same graph shape from the prior lesson once tie-breaking is accounted for, confirming both algorithms converge on an equally optimal tree.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask a student to trace Prim's algorithm by hand on a small graph and state, at each step, WHICH CUT is being exploited -- a student who can only recite 'grab the smallest edge' without naming the (S, V-S) cut has memorized the mechanic without absorbing the cut-property justification. An even sharper judge asks the student to explain, in one sentence, exactly what changes if you swap Prim's key for Dijkstra's cumulative-distance key -- testing whether the student understands that the two algorithms are cosmetically identical but semantically answer different questions (connect vs. reach), a distinction many CS students get wrong on exams.

questions.prompt: At each step, Prim's algorithm adds the lightest edge crossing which set of vertices?

options.text: The cut between the vertices already in the tree and all remaining vertices
The cut between the two endpoints of the heaviest edge in the graph
Any cut chosen at random each iteration
The cut separating even-indexed and odd-indexed vertices

explanations.a: Correct -- Prim maintains a growing set S (the tree so far) and repeatedly takes the lightest edge crossing the cut (S, V-S), which the cut property guarantees is always safe to add.
explanations.b: Prim's cut is defined by tree membership, not by any single heaviest edge.
explanations.c: The cut is not random -- it is deterministically (S, V-S) at every step, tracking exactly which vertices are already connected.
explanations.d: Vertex parity has no role in Prim's algorithm; the cut is defined purely by current tree membership.

questions.prompt: On a dense graph where m is close to n^2, which Prim implementation is typically fastest?

options.text: The array-based priority queue, at O(n^2), since it has no log factor and no dependence on m
The binary heap version, at O(m log n), because heaps are always faster
Neither -- Prim cannot run on dense graphs
The Fibonacci heap version is always slower than both alternatives

explanations.a: Correct -- once m approaches n^2, the heap's O(m log n) term grows past O(n^2), so the simple array implementation (no log factor, no m dependence) wins on dense graphs.
explanations.b: Heaps help specifically when m is small relative to n^2 (sparse graphs); on dense graphs the m log n term makes them slower than the array version.
explanations.c: Prim runs on any connected graph regardless of density; density only affects which implementation is faster.
explanations.d: Fibonacci heaps give the best asymptotic bound, O(m + n log n), and are competitive or best on sparse-to-moderate density graphs; they are not universally slower.

questions.prompt: What is the single difference between Prim's algorithm and Dijkstra's algorithm, given that both use a priority-queue frontier and relax neighbors?

options.text: The priority key: Prim uses raw edge weight w(u,v); Dijkstra uses accumulated path length dist[u] + w(u,v)
Prim works only on directed graphs while Dijkstra requires undirected graphs
Dijkstra requires sorting all edges first; Prim does not
Prim uses union-find internally while Dijkstra does not

explanations.a: Correct -- Prim's key is the single edge's own weight (a local 'cheapest way to connect' question), while Dijkstra's key is the total path cost so far plus the edge weight (a global 'cheapest way to reach' question); everything else in the skeleton is shared.
explanations.b: Both algorithms are typically presented on graphs matching their domain (Prim on undirected weighted graphs for MST, Dijkstra usually on graphs with non-negative weights, directed or undirected); directedness is not the distinguishing factor here.
explanations.c: Neither algorithm pre-sorts all edges; both use a priority queue to extract minimums incrementally, which is a different mechanism from Kruskal's upfront sort.
explanations.d: Neither algorithm uses union-find; that structure is specific to Kruskal's cycle-detection needs.

questions.prompt: Order Prim's steps as it grows the tree from a seed vertex.

items.text: Initialize S with only the seed vertex; set all other keys to infinity
Extract the vertex outside S with the minimum key from the priority queue
Add that vertex and its connecting edge to the tree; move it into S
Relax the keys of its neighbors still outside S
Repeat until every vertex is in S

questions.explanation: Prim seeds S with one vertex, then repeatedly extracts the cheapest way to connect a new vertex, absorbs it into S, updates (relaxes) the frontier keys using the newly added vertex's edges, and loops until all n vertices are inside S.

questions.prompt: Match each Prim implementation choice to its total running time.

right.text: O(m log n)
O(m + n log n)

questions.explanation: A binary heap gives O(log n) extract-min and decrease-key, for O(m log n) total; a Fibonacci heap gives O(1) amortized decrease-key, improving the bound to O(m + n log n); a plain array gives O(n) extract-min but O(1) update, totaling O(n^2), which wins only on dense graphs.

lessons.label: Boruvka's Algorithm and Why MSTs Parallelize

sections.heading: The oldest MST algorithm, built for an electrical grid
sections.body: Otakar Boruvka published his algorithm in 1926 in 'O jistem problemu minimalnim' (On a Certain Minimal Problem), predating Kruskal and Prim by three decades. Boruvka was solving a genuinely applied problem: finding the cheapest way to electrify Moravia (in what is now the Czech Republic) by connecting towns with the least total wire. The algorithm proceeds in rounds rather than a single sequential scan. In each round, EVERY current component simultaneously selects its own cheapest outgoing edge -- the lightest edge with exactly one endpoint inside that component -- and all of these selected edges are added at once (contracting each merged group into a single new component for the next round). Because every component picks its own edge independently and correctly by the cut property (each component's boundary is itself a valid cut), all selections in a round are safe to add simultaneously, even though multiple components might end up selecting the same edge from opposite sides -- that shared edge just gets added once.

sections.heading: Why components at least halve each round
sections.body: The key complexity fact is that the number of components at least HALVES every round. Reasoning: pair up each component with the component on the other end of its chosen cheapest edge. In the worst case, components pair off two-at-a-time (component X picks an edge into Y, and Y might pick a different edge elsewhere, but every component that fires an edge merges into a group of at least 2), so after one round the component count is at most half of what it was. Starting from n components (single vertices), after k rounds at most n / 2^k components remain, so full connectivity (down to 1 component, or one per connected piece of the original graph) is reached in at most O(log n) rounds. Each round costs O(m) to scan all edges and find each component's cheapest outgoing edge (using a shrinking contracted graph), so the total cost is O(m log n) -- the same complexity class as Kruskal and heap-based Prim, arrived at through a completely different structure.

sections.heading: Why this parallelizes, and where it shows up in state-of-the-art MST
sections.body: Boruvka's round structure is why it is the backbone of parallel and distributed MST algorithms: within a single round, every component's cheapest-edge search is INDEPENDENT of every other component's search, so all of them can run concurrently on separate processors (or separate machines, e.g., in MapReduce-style distributed graph processing), with only a synchronization barrier between rounds. Kruskal's algorithm, by contrast, depends on a single globally sorted list processed in strict weight order with a shared union-find structure -- that global ordering is inherently sequential and resists this kind of clean decomposition. One subtlety matters for correctness: when multiple components tie on their cheapest outgoing edge weight, a consistent TIE-BREAKING rule (such as comparing a secondary key like edge or endpoint index) is required to avoid two components each selecting the same edge and accidentally forming a cycle between three or more components in one round. Boruvka's round structure is also the core subroutine inside the Karger-Klein-Tarjan (1995) randomized algorithm, which achieves expected O(m) linear time by interleaving Boruvka rounds (to shrink the graph) with random edge sampling and a linear-time MST-verification step, making it the fastest known MST algorithm in the comparison model.

lessons.workedExample: Consider 6 single-vertex components with edges connecting them so that A's cheapest edge goes to B (weight 1), B's cheapest edge also happens to go to A (weight 1, the same edge), C's cheapest goes to D (weight 2), D's cheapest goes to C (same edge), E's cheapest goes to F (weight 3), F's cheapest goes to E (same edge). Round 1: three edges are selected (A-B, C-D, E-F), each pair contracts into one component, so 6 components become 3 -- exactly half, in a single simultaneous round. Round 2: the three merged super-components (call them {AB}, {CD}, {EF}) each pick their own cheapest outgoing edge to the others, say {AB}-{CD} weight 4 is cheapest for both, and {EF} picks {CD} at weight 5; after contraction, 3 components collapse toward 1. In two rounds the whole graph is spanned, versus Kruskal needing to sort and scan all edges in one global pass.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge with a distributed-systems or high-performance-computing background will likely ask directly: 'why does Boruvka parallelize but Kruskal doesn't?' -- the precise answer is that Boruvka's per-round work is a set of independent per-component searches with no shared mutable state until the synchronization barrier, whereas Kruskal's correctness depends on a single global sort order and a shared union-find structure that edges must be processed against sequentially. A judge may also probe the tie-breaking rule, since it is the one subtlety a student can miss entirely if they've only seen simplified classroom examples where every edge weight happens to be distinct.

questions.prompt: In each round of Boruvka's algorithm, what does every component do?

options.text: Simultaneously select its own single cheapest outgoing edge
Sort all edges in the entire graph before selecting one
Wait for a global priority queue to hand it an edge
Merge with the single largest remaining component only

explanations.a: Correct -- every component independently and simultaneously picks its own cheapest edge crossing its boundary, which is safe by the cut property since each component's boundary is a valid cut.
explanations.b: Boruvka never requires a global sort; each component only needs to know its own cheapest outgoing edge, found by scanning local edges.
explanations.c: There is no shared priority queue; the whole point of Boruvka's structure is that no shared, order-dependent resource is needed within a round.
explanations.d: Components do not target 'the largest' component; each one independently picks whichever edge is locally cheapest, which could lead anywhere.

questions.prompt: Why does the number of components in Boruvka's algorithm halve (at least) every round?

options.text: Because every component fires its own edge, so components pair off into merged groups of at least two
Because the algorithm explicitly deletes half the vertices each round
Because only even-numbered components are allowed to select an edge
It does not halve; it only removes one component per round

explanations.a: Correct -- since every component selects and adds an edge, each ends up merged with at least one other, so the resulting component count is at most half of the previous round's count.
explanations.b: No vertices are deleted; components are contracted (merged), which reduces the component count without discarding any vertex.
explanations.c: There is no parity restriction; every component, regardless of numbering, selects its own cheapest edge every round.
explanations.d: Removing only one component per round would give O(n) rounds, not the O(log n) that makes Boruvka's total cost O(m log n) -- the whole benefit comes from the at-least-halving guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why does Kruskal's algorithm resist the same clean parallelization that Boruvka's enjoys?

options.text: Kruskal depends on a single globally sorted edge list processed sequentially against a shared union-find structure
Kruskal's algorithm is actually easier to parallelize than Boruvka's
Kruskal requires more memory than Boruvka, which is the only barrier
Kruskal cannot run on weighted graphs

explanations.a: Correct -- Kruskal's greedy scan depends on strict global weight order and a shared union-find state updated edge-by-edge, which is inherently sequential, unlike Boruvka's independent per-component rounds.
explanations.b: The reverse is true -- Boruvka is the one whose round structure decomposes into independent concurrent work.
explanations.c: Memory footprint is not the reason; the barrier is the sequential dependency in Kruskal's scan order, not memory usage.
explanations.d: Kruskal is designed specifically for weighted graphs; that is not a limiting factor here.

questions.prompt: Order Boruvka's algorithm as it runs starting from n single-vertex components.

items.text: Each component finds its own cheapest outgoing edge
All selected edges across all components are added simultaneously
Merged groups are contracted into new, larger components
The process repeats on the smaller set of components
After O(log n) rounds, one component (or one per connected piece) remains

questions.explanation: Each round: every component picks its cheapest edge, all picks are added at once, merged components are contracted into single units, and the whole process loops on the shrunken component set until it converges in O(log n) rounds.

questions.prompt: Match each MST-related fact to what it describes.

left.text: The tie-breaking rule in Boruvka's algorithm

right.text: Electrifying Moravia with minimum total wire
Prevents two components from both selecting the same edge and forming an accidental cycle
Randomized algorithm combining Boruvka rounds with sampling for expected O(m) time

questions.explanation: Boruvka's 1926 paper solved an applied electrification-network problem; his algorithm needs a consistent tie-breaking rule when multiple components share a cheapest-edge weight, to avoid a same-round cycle; and Karger-Klein-Tarjan (1995) layers random sampling and verification on top of Boruvka rounds to reach expected linear time, the fastest known MST bound.

lessons.label: Topological Sort: Kahn's Algorithm vs. DFS Finish Times

sections.heading: What a topological order means and when it exists
sections.body: A topological sort of a directed graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge u to v, u appears before v in the ordering. A topological order exists if and only if the graph is a DAG (directed acyclic graph) -- a cycle makes the requirement unsatisfiable, since some vertex on the cycle would need to precede itself transitively. This equivalence is exact and runs both directions: proving a graph is acyclic is equivalent to successfully producing a topological order for it, which is why a topological-sort algorithm doubles as a cycle detector for free. Orders are, in general, NOT unique: any DAG with two vertices that have no path between them (in either direction) admits multiple valid topological orders that differ only in how those independent vertices are interleaved.

sections.heading: Kahn's algorithm: peel off zero-in-degree vertices
sections.body: Arthur B. Kahn published the method in 1962 in 'Topological Sorting of Large Networks' (Communications of the ACM). The algorithm computes the in-degree (count of incoming edges) of every vertex, places all vertices with in-degree zero into a queue, and repeatedly dequeues a vertex, appends it to the output order, and decrements the in-degree of each of its outgoing neighbors -- enqueuing any neighbor whose in-degree drops to zero. This runs in O(n + m): each vertex is enqueued and dequeued once, and each edge is examined exactly once when decrementing. The elegant cycle-detection guarantee falls out immediately: if the queue empties before all n vertices have been output, the LEFTOVER vertices (never reaching in-degree zero) are exactly the vertices that lie on or are only reachable from a cycle -- a graph is acyclic if and only if Kahn's algorithm outputs all n vertices.

sections.heading: The DFS alternative: reverse postorder, and real-world uses
sections.body: The second standard method runs a depth-first search and records each vertex's FINISH TIME -- the moment the DFS call on that vertex returns after all its descendants have been fully explored. Reversing the order of finish times (or equivalently, prepending each vertex to the output the moment it finishes) yields a valid topological order; the intuition is that a vertex finishes only after everything reachable from it has already finished, so it must be placed before all of them in a forward order. This also runs in O(n + m), matching Kahn's bound, and this method extends directly into Kosaraju's SCC algorithm in the next lesson, which reuses exactly this finish-time ordering. Topological sort is not a classroom curiosity: build systems like Make and Bazel use it to determine which targets can compile before others depend on them; university course-scheduling systems use it to sequence prerequisites; spreadsheet engines use it to determine cell RECALCULATION order so a formula is never evaluated before the cells it reads; and package managers (npm, pip, apt) use it to install dependencies before the packages that need them.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a small build graph: compile.o depends on parse.o and lex.o; parse.o depends on lex.o; lex.o depends on nothing. In-degrees: lex.o=0, parse.o=1 (from lex.o), compile.o=2 (from parse.o and lex.o). Kahn's algorithm starts with lex.o in the queue (only zero in-degree vertex). Dequeue lex.o, output it, decrement parse.o to 0 and compile.o to 1; enqueue parse.o. Dequeue parse.o, output it, decrement compile.o to 0; enqueue compile.o. Dequeue compile.o, output it. Final order: lex.o, parse.o, compile.o -- exactly the order a compiler must build these files in. If a bug introduced a cyclic dependency (compile.o requiring parse.o and parse.o requiring compile.o), Kahn's queue would empty with compile.o and parse.o never reaching in-degree zero, immediately flagging the circular build dependency instead of silently producing garbage output.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge is likely to ask what happens when you run a topological-sort algorithm on a graph that turns out to have a cycle -- a student who only knows the happy path will be stuck, while a student who understands the DAG-iff-topological-order-exists equivalence can explain precisely how Kahn's leftover vertices (or DFS's back-edge detection) pinpoint the cyclic region. A judge may also test whether the student wrongly assumes topological order is unique -- a common error -- since recognizing that independent vertices can be freely reordered demonstrates real understanding of what the ordering constraint does and does not pin down.

questions.prompt: A topological order for a directed graph exists if and only if the graph is:

options.text: A DAG (directed acyclic graph)
Fully connected
Weighted with all positive weights
Bipartite

explanations.a: Correct -- a cycle makes a valid linear ordering impossible, since some vertex on it would need to precede itself; this equivalence runs both directions and is exact.
explanations.b: Connectivity is irrelevant; a disconnected DAG (several separate acyclic components) still has a valid topological order.
explanations.c: Edge weights play no role at all in whether a topological order exists; this is purely a question of directed structure and cycles.
explanations.d: Bipartiteness is an unrelated graph property; many bipartite graphs contain cycles and many DAGs are not bipartite.

questions.prompt: In Kahn's algorithm, what does it mean if the output queue empties before all n vertices have been produced?

options.text: The graph contains a cycle, and the leftover vertices are exactly the cyclic part
The graph is simply too large for the algorithm
It means every vertex has in-degree zero
It indicates the graph is undirected

explanations.a: Correct -- vertices that never reach in-degree zero are exactly those on or downstream of a cycle, so an incomplete output is a direct, built-in cycle detector.
explanations.b: Graph size affects running time, not whether the queue empties early; that outcome is a structural signal about cycles, not scale.
explanations.c: If every vertex had in-degree zero, they would all be enqueued immediately and the queue would empty only after producing all n vertices -- the opposite of a stuck, incomplete run.
explanations.d: Kahn's algorithm is defined for directed graphs; an undirected graph is not the input format being discussed here.

questions.prompt: The DFS-based topological sort method orders vertices by:

options.text: Reverse of their DFS finish times
Their DFS discovery (start) times, in forward order
Ascending vertex ID, ignoring the DFS entirely
In-degree, exactly as Kahn's algorithm does

explanations.a: Correct -- a vertex only finishes after everything it can reach has already finished, so reversing (or prepending on finish) the finish-time order produces a valid topological order.
explanations.b: Discovery time alone does not respect edge direction correctly; a vertex can be discovered before a vertex it depends on has finished exploring, so discovery order is not sufficient.
explanations.c: Vertex ID has no bearing on dependency structure; using it would ignore the graph's actual edges.
explanations.d: That describes Kahn's method, which is a distinct O(n+m) algorithm from the DFS finish-time approach.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of Kahn's algorithm as it processes a DAG.

items.text: Compute the in-degree of every vertex
Enqueue all vertices with in-degree zero
Dequeue a vertex and append it to the output order
Decrement the in-degree of each of its outgoing neighbors
Enqueue any neighbor whose in-degree has dropped to zero

questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm first computes in-degrees for all vertices, seeds the queue with zero-in-degree vertices, then repeatedly dequeues, outputs, decrements neighbors, and enqueues any newly zero-in-degree neighbor, continuing until the queue is empty.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world system to how it uses topological sort.

right.text: Determine compile order so dependencies build before dependents
Determine cell recalculation order so a formula never reads a stale value
Install dependency packages before the packages that require them

questions.explanation: Each system models a dependency DAG and uses topological order to guarantee prerequisites are handled before dependents: build targets before consumers, source cells before formulas that read them, and dependency packages before the packages needing them.

lessons.label: Strongly Connected Components: Kosaraju and Tarjan

sections.heading: Mutual reachability and the condensation DAG
sections.body: In a directed graph, two vertices u and v are in the same STRONGLY CONNECTED COMPONENT (SCC) if u can reach v AND v can reach u -- mutual reachability. This relation partitions every directed graph's vertices into disjoint SCCs, each one a maximal set of mutually-reachable vertices. Collapsing each SCC down to a single super-vertex produces the graph's CONDENSATION, and a fundamental structural fact is that the condensation is ALWAYS a DAG, regardless of how tangled the original graph was: if the condensation had a cycle among super-vertices, those super-vertices would be mutually reachable through each other and should have been merged into one larger SCC in the first place, a contradiction. This means every directed graph, no matter how cyclic, decomposes into a DAG-shaped skeleton of strongly-connected clusters -- SCC-finding is the tool that reveals that skeleton, and it feeds directly into topological sort from the previous lesson, since the condensation itself can then be topologically ordered.

sections.heading: Kosaraju's algorithm: two DFS passes
sections.body: Kosaraju's algorithm (attributed to S. Rao Kosaraju in an unpublished 1978 result, later described in print by Micha Sharir in 1981) runs in two depth-first search passes and stays O(n + m). Pass one runs DFS on the original graph G, recording each vertex's finish time (as in the previous lesson's DFS topological sort). Pass two runs DFS on G-REVERSE (every edge flipped), processing vertices in DECREASING order of the finish times recorded in pass one; each DFS tree produced in this second pass is exactly one SCC. The insight behind why this works: the vertex with the latest finish time in G lies in a 'source' SCC of the condensation (or ties for one), and searching from it in the reversed graph can only reach vertices within its own SCC, because escaping to a different SCC in G-reverse would imply a path back in G that should have merged the two SCCs already.

sections.heading: Tarjan's single-pass algorithm, and where SCC shows up
sections.body: Robert Tarjan's 1972 paper 'Depth-First Search and Linear Graph Algorithms' (SIAM Journal on Computing) introduced a different, single-pass SCC algorithm that avoids ever constructing the reversed graph. It tracks two numbers per vertex during one DFS: disc[v] (the order in which v was first discovered) and low[v] (the smallest discovery number reachable from v's subtree via tree edges, plus at most one edge to any vertex still on the explicit stack -- whether that vertex is a DFS-tree ancestor or was reached via a cross edge from an earlier sibling branch). An explicit stack holds vertices currently 'in progress'; whenever a vertex v is found with low[v] == disc[v] (meaning nothing in its subtree can reach further back than v itself), v is the root of a complete SCC, and everything above it on the stack (down to v) is popped off as that SCC. This also runs in O(n + m), matching Kosaraju's bound while touching each edge only once total instead of twice. Both algorithms feed real applications: 2-SAT is solved by building an IMPLICATION GRAPH (each boolean literal a vertex, each clause a pair of implication edges) and observing that a 2-SAT formula is satisfiable if and only if no variable and its negation land in the same SCC (Aspvall, Plass, and Tarjan formalized this in 1979); and web-scale link analysis uses SCC to find the BOW-TIE structure of the web -- Broder et al.'s 2000 study of roughly 200 million AltaVista-crawled pages found a single giant 'core' SCC (about 28% of pages, all mutually reachable via hyperlinks) flanked by an 'IN' component (about 21%, pages that reach the core but aren't reached back) and an 'OUT' component (about 21%, pages reachable from the core but that don't link back), plus smaller tendrils and disconnected pieces.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a directed graph with edges A to B, B to C, C to A (a 3-cycle), plus C to D, D to E, E to D (a 2-cycle downstream). Running Tarjan's algorithm from A: DFS discovers A(disc=0), B(disc=1), C(disc=2); C's edge back to A gives low[C]=0 (A's disc); C also explores D(disc=3), E(disc=4); E's edge back to D gives low[E]=3; back at D, low[D]=min(3,3)=3, and since low[D]==disc[D], {D,E} pops off the stack as one SCC. Back at C, low[C] stays 0 (from the back-edge to A); back at B, low[B]=min(1,0)=0; back at A, low[A]=0==disc[A], so {A,B,C} pops off as the second SCC. Two SCCs found in one pass: {A,B,C} and {D,E}. The condensation is A'BC pointing to D'E, a two-node DAG -- confirming that even though the original graph had two internal cycles, collapsing them yields a strictly acyclic skeleton.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge is likely to ask why the condensation of ANY directed graph is guaranteed to be a DAG -- the crisp answer is a proof by contradiction (a cycle among super-vertices would force those SCCs to merge), and a student who can produce that argument on the spot shows they understand SCC as a structural decomposition, not just an algorithm to run. A judge with a security or networking background may also probe the 2-SAT-via-implication-graph application specifically, since it is a genuinely elegant reduction (a satisfiability question answered by a graph-connectivity check) that rewards a student who read past the pure-graph-theory framing into where SCC actually gets used.

questions.prompt: Why is the condensation of any directed graph always a DAG?

options.text: If super-vertices formed a cycle, they would be mutually reachable and should have been one larger SCC already
Because the original graph must be undirected
Because condensation always removes exactly half the edges
It is not always a DAG; it depends on edge weights

explanations.a: Correct -- a cycle among super-vertices in the condensation would mean those SCCs are mutually reachable through each other, contradicting the assumption that each SCC was already maximal.
explanations.b: SCCs are specifically a directed-graph concept; undirected connected components have no analogous distinction, since reachability is automatically mutual.
explanations.c: Condensation collapses each SCC to one vertex; it doesn't remove a fixed fraction of edges, and that's not why the result is acyclic.
explanations.d: This is a structural guarantee that holds for every directed graph regardless of weights; SCC and condensation don't depend on edge weights at all.

questions.prompt: In Kosaraju's algorithm, the second DFS pass runs on which graph, and in what vertex order?

options.text: The reversed graph, processing vertices in decreasing order of first-pass finish time
The original graph, processing vertices in increasing order of vertex ID
The reversed graph, processing vertices in the order they were discovered in pass one
The original graph again, using breadth-first search instead of depth-first

explanations.a: Correct -- pass two runs on G-reverse, visiting vertices in decreasing order of the finish times recorded during pass one on G, and each resulting DFS tree is exactly one SCC.
explanations.b: Vertex ID order has no role; the algorithm specifically depends on finish-time order to guarantee correctness.
explanations.c: Discovery order (rather than finish order) does not give the same guarantee; the algorithm is defined in terms of finish times specifically.
explanations.d: Kosaraju's second pass uses DFS on the reversed graph, not BFS on the original graph.

questions.prompt: In Tarjan's SCC algorithm, a vertex v is identified as the root of a complete SCC when:

options.text: low[v] equals disc[v]
v has no outgoing edges at all
v is the very first vertex visited by the DFS
The explicit stack becomes completely empty

explanations.a: Correct -- low[v] == disc[v] means nothing in v's subtree can reach back further than v itself, so v is the root of its SCC, and everything above it on the stack down to v is popped as that SCC.
explanations.b: A vertex with no outgoing edges could still have low[v] < disc[v] if it was reached via a path that itself closes a cycle elsewhere -- having no out-edges isn't the defining condition.
explanations.c: Being the first vertex visited overall doesn't determine SCC-root status; that depends on the low-link comparison, which can trigger at any point in the traversal.
explanations.d: The stack empties only after the entire DFS completes across all components; individual SCCs are popped off (partially emptying the stack) throughout the run, not just at the very end.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Kosaraju's two-pass SCC algorithm.

items.text: Run DFS on the original graph G, recording finish times
Build the reversed graph G-reverse
Run DFS on G-reverse, visiting vertices in decreasing finish-time order
Each resulting DFS tree in the second pass is one SCC

questions.explanation: Kosaraju first records finish times via a DFS on G, then constructs G-reverse, then runs a second DFS on G-reverse ordered by decreasing finish time, with each DFS tree from that second pass forming exactly one SCC.

questions.prompt: Match each SCC-related concept or application to its description.

right.text: Single DFS pass using disc/low values and an explicit stack
Formula is satisfiable iff no variable and its negation share an SCC
Found a bow-tie structure: giant core SCC flanked by IN and OUT components

questions.explanation: Tarjan's 1972 SIAM paper introduced the single-pass disc/low-link SCC algorithm; 2-SAT reduces satisfiability to checking no literal and its negation co-occur in an SCC of the implication graph (Aspvall, Plass, Tarjan 1979); and Broder et al.'s AltaVista-scale study found the web's link structure forms a bow-tie with a core SCC plus IN/OUT wings.

lessons.label: Bridges, Articulation Points, and Network Resilience

sections.heading: Two flavors of single point of failure
sections.body: In an undirected graph, a BRIDGE (also called a cut-edge) is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components -- it is the only route between the two sides it connects. An ARTICULATION POINT (also called a cut-vertex) is a vertex whose removal (along with all its incident edges) increases the number of connected components. Both concepts formalize 'single point of failure': a bridge is a fragile LINK, an articulation point is a fragile NODE. John Hopcroft and Robert Tarjan gave the standard linear-time algorithm for finding both in a single DFS pass in their 1973 paper 'Efficient Algorithms for Graph Manipulation' (Communications of the ACM), building on the same disc/low-link machinery Tarjan had used for strongly connected components the year before.

sections.heading: The lowlink test: disc and low, one DFS
sections.body: The algorithm runs one DFS, assigning each vertex v a discovery time disc[v] (the order it was first visited) and a low-link value low[v] (the smallest discovery time reachable from v's DFS subtree, allowed to use at most one back-edge to a proper ancestor, but NOT the tree-edge back to v's own parent). The BRIDGE test: tree edge (u, v), where v is u's child in the DFS tree, is a bridge if and only if low[v] > disc[u] -- meaning nothing in v's subtree can reach back to u or higher, so v's whole subtree depends entirely on that one edge to stay connected to the rest of the graph. The ARTICULATION POINT test is similar but not identical: non-root vertex u is an articulation point if some child v in the DFS tree has low[v] >= disc[u] (note: greater-than-OR-EQUAL, not strict) -- meaning v's subtree cannot escape past u even through a back-edge landing exactly on u itself, so removing u strands that subtree. The ROOT of the DFS tree needs a special-case rule: the root is an articulation point if and only if it has two or more children in the DFS tree, because in that case the root is the only thing connecting those separate subtrees to each other (a non-root can rely on its own parent connection, but the root has no parent to fall back on).

sections.heading: 2-edge-connectivity, 2-vertex-connectivity, and resilient infrastructure
sections.body: A graph with no bridges at all is called 2-EDGE-CONNECTED: every edge failure still leaves the graph connected, because at least two independent paths exist between every pair of vertices. A graph with no articulation points is 2-VERTEX-CONNECTED (biconnected): every single vertex failure still leaves the rest connected. These are exactly the properties infrastructure designers target when they cannot tolerate a single failure taking down the whole system. Power grid engineers check for articulation substations and bridge transmission lines because losing either isolates a whole region rather than degrading gracefully. Network engineers apply the same test to routers and links: an ISP wants no single fiber link (bridge) or no single router (articulation point) whose failure partitions its customer base, which is why backbone topologies are deliberately built with redundant loops rather than pure tree structures. Transit planners use the same lens on subway and rail maps: a single-track bridge segment or a single interchange station that all lines must pass through is a bridge or articulation point in exactly this graph-theoretic sense, and system resilience planning explicitly targets adding a redundant edge or a bypass route to eliminate it.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a graph A-B, B-C, C-A (a triangle), plus a single edge C-D, and D-E, E-F, F-D (another triangle). Running Hopcroft-Tarjan DFS from A: disc[A]=0, disc[B]=1, disc[C]=2; C's back-edge to A gives low[C]=0; back at B, low[B]=min(1,0)=0 (via C); back at A, low[A]=0. Edge C-D: disc[D]=3, and within D's subtree, disc[E]=4, disc[F]=5, F's back-edge to D gives low[F]=3; back at E, low[E]=min(4,3)=3; back at D, low[D]=min(3,3)=3. Check edge C-D: low[D]=3 > disc[C]=2, so C-D IS A BRIDGE -- removing it splits the triangle {A,B,C} from the triangle {D,E,F}. Check vertex C: its child D has low[D]=3 >= disc[C]=2, so C IS AN ARTICULATION POINT -- removing C strands D, E, F from A and B. This matches intuition exactly: the single edge joining two otherwise-solid triangles is the graph's only weak point, both as a link and at its C-side endpoint.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge is likely to test whether a student can state the bridge and articulation-point conditions PRECISELY, since they differ only by a strict-versus-non-strict inequality (low[v] > disc[u] for a bridge vs. low[v] >= disc[u] for an articulation point), and conflating the two is a common, easy-to-catch error. A judge with an infrastructure or public-policy angle may instead ask the student to translate the algorithm into a concrete resilience story -- naming a specific bridge edge or articulation vertex in a power grid, transit map, or network topology and explaining what redundant edge would eliminate it -- which tests whether the student can move from the abstract low-link test to an applied single-point-of-failure argument.

questions.prompt: For a DFS tree edge (u, v) with v as u's child, what is the exact condition for that edge to be a bridge?

options.text: low[v] > disc[u]
low[v] >= disc[u]
disc[v] < disc[u]
low[u] > disc[v]

explanations.a: Correct -- a strict inequality, low[v] > disc[u], means nothing in v's subtree can reach back to u or any of u's ancestors, so the edge (u,v) is the sole connection keeping v's subtree attached.
explanations.b: The non-strict version (>=) is the articulation-point test for a non-root vertex, not the bridge test; using it for bridges would misclassify some non-bridge edges as bridges.
explanations.c: Since v is discovered after u in a DFS tree edge, disc[v] < disc[u] is never true in the first place, and it isn't the relevant comparison regardless.
explanations.d: Low-link and discovery values are compared the other direction (child's low vs. parent's disc); this reversed form doesn't correspond to the actual test.

questions.prompt: Why does the DFS root need a special-case rule for being an articulation point (two or more DFS children), instead of the standard low[v] >= disc[u] test?

options.text: The root has no parent to fall back on, so only having multiple independent child subtrees can strand them from each other
The root's disc value is always undefined
The standard test always returns true for the root, so a special case is needed to override it
Root vertices cannot be articulation points under any circumstances

explanations.a: Correct -- a non-root vertex could rely on its parent connection to stay attached even if a child subtree is 'boxed in'; the root has no such parent, so it's only a cut-vertex if removing it actually separates two or more of its own child subtrees from each other.
explanations.b: The root's disc value is well-defined (typically 0, the first vertex visited); that is not the reason for the special case.
explanations.c: The standard child-based test doesn't inherently always return true for the root; the special case exists because the standard test's logic (relying on a parent connection) doesn't apply to a vertex that has no parent.
explanations.d: Root vertices absolutely can be articulation points -- precisely when they have two or more DFS children, which is exactly what the special-case rule detects.

questions.prompt: A network engineer wants to guarantee that no single router failure can partition the network. Which property should the network's graph have?

options.text: No articulation points (2-vertex-connected)
No bridges (2-edge-connected)
It must be a complete graph
It must be a DAG

explanations.a: Correct -- routers are vertices, so guarding against any single vertex (router) failure partitioning the network means the graph must have no articulation points, i.e., be 2-vertex-connected.
explanations.b: 2-edge-connectivity protects against single LINK failures, not single router (node) failures; it's the wrong property for this specific concern.
explanations.c: Full completeness is far stronger (and far more expensive) than necessary; 2-vertex-connectivity is the minimal sufficient property for single-node-failure resilience.
explanations.d: DAG-ness is a directed-acyclic concept unrelated to resilience against vertex removal in an undirected network topology.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Hopcroft-Tarjan single-DFS bridge and articulation-point algorithm.

items.text: Run one DFS, assigning disc[v] as each vertex is first visited
Compute low[v] as the DFS unwinds, using subtree results and at most one back-edge per vertex
For each tree edge (u,v), test low[v] > disc[u] to flag a bridge
For each non-root u, test whether any child v has low[v] >= disc[u] to flag an articulation point
Apply the special root rule: the root is an articulation point iff it has two or more DFS children

questions.explanation: The algorithm assigns discovery times during the DFS descent, computes low-link values as the recursion unwinds back up each subtree, applies the strict bridge test and the non-strict non-root articulation-point test using those values, and finally applies the special two-or-more-children rule specifically for the root.

questions.prompt: Match each resilience concept to its infrastructure-planning meaning.

right.text: No bridges: every single link failure leaves the network connected
No articulation points: every single node failure leaves the network connected
Introduced the linear-time single-DFS lowlink algorithm for both bridges and articulation points

questions.explanation: 2-edge-connectivity guards against any single edge (link) failure; 2-vertex-connectivity guards against any single vertex (node) failure; and Hopcroft and Tarjan's 1973 paper gave the O(n+m) single-DFS algorithm that tests both properties using disc and low-link values.

lessons.label: Cost Is a Function of Two Variables, Not One

sections.heading: Why 'input size' is not a single number for graphs
sections.body: For an array algorithm, plotting runtime against a single x-axis (n, the array length) is honest, because n determines everything. Graphs do not work that way. A graph has TWO independent size parameters: n vertices and m edges, and m can range from n-1 (a tree, the sparsest connected case) all the way to roughly n^2/2 (a dense graph). Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap runs in O((n+m) log n); an array-based version with no heap runs in O(n^2). Comparing these two bounds on a single 'input size' axis is meaningless unless you also say how m scales with n, because the two formulas cross depending on that relationship. A paper or benchmark that reports 'runtime vs. number of vertices' without stating the edge density is not wrong so much as underspecified: two different readers could each generate graphs that make either algorithm look like the clear winner.

sections.heading: The fix: fix one dimension while sweeping the other
sections.body: Rigorous graph-algorithm evaluation, as formalized in the influential experimental study by Boris Cherkassky, Andrew Goldberg, and Tomasz Radzik ('Shortest Paths Algorithms: Theory and Experimental Evaluation', 1996), controls for this explicitly by using generator families with a STATED density rule.
