This same density-controlled experimental tradition was later extended by the 9th DIMACS Implementation Challenge on shortest paths, a separate effort held roughly a decade later in 2005-2006 (co-organized by Goldberg, among others). Two disciplined sweep strategies exist. First, hold m/n fixed (say, m/n = 4, an average degree of 8 for an undirected graph, or an average out-degree of 4 if arcs are directed) while n grows — this asks 'how does the algorithm scale with problem size at constant sparsity,' which is the realistic regime for road networks and most real graphs. Second, hold n fixed and sweep density from sparse (m ≈ n) to dense (m ≈ n^2), which asks 'at a fixed vertex count, where does the crossover between algorithms happen.' Never sweep n while letting m float implicitly (e.g., by generating a fixed-probability random graph, where m grows quadratically with n without anyone stating so).

sections.heading: Reading normalized figures
sections.body: Because raw wall-clock time conflates n, m, and constant factors, well-designed figures normalize: time-per-edge (total time / m) exposes whether an algorithm's per-edge relaxation cost is actually constant, which is what an O(m log n) bound predicts; time-per-vertex (total time / n) is the natural normalization for algorithms whose dominant cost is extract-min calls, one per vertex. When you see a graph-algorithm figure, the first thing to check is the caption or methods section: does it state m/n or the density rule? If not, treat any claimed asymptotic trend with real skepticism, because the same raw numbers could be re-plotted to look linear, quadratic, or log-linear depending on an unstated edge-growth assumption.

lessons.workedExample: A student benchmarks Dijkstra's algorithm (binary heap) against Floyd-Warshall and plots both against n from 100 to 1000, using randomly generated graphs where each pair of vertices is connected with fixed probability p = 0.5. They see Dijkstra pull ahead and conclude 'Dijkstra beats Floyd-Warshall at scale.' But p = 0.5 fixed means m grows as roughly 0.25*n^2 — the graphs get DENSER, not just bigger, as n increases, since average degree scales with n. Once the student instead holds m/n fixed at, say, 3 while sweeping n (an average degree of 6 for an undirected graph, m ≈ 3n), the comparison becomes a fair test of how each algorithm scales with vertex count alone, and matches what a reader would expect from the two algorithms' actual O((n+m) log n) versus O(n^3) bounds.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read even one systems-benchmarking paper will ask, within the first question, 'what's the edge density in your test graphs, and did it change across your x-axis?' A team that cannot answer, or that generated graphs with a fixed edge probability without noticing that this silently increases average degree as n grows, has produced a chart that looks rigorous but tests an uncontrolled variable. Naming the m/n ratio and stating which dimension was held fixed is the single fastest way to signal that your benchmark design was deliberate rather than accidental.

questions.prompt: A benchmark generates random graphs where each pair of vertices is connected independently with fixed probability p = 0.3, then sweeps n from 50 to 500. What happens to average degree across this sweep?

options.text: It stays constant, since p is fixed
It grows roughly linearly with n, since expected average degree is p(n-1)
It shrinks toward zero as n grows
It is undefined without knowing m directly

explanations.a: Fixing p does not fix degree — expected average degree is p times the number of other vertices, which grows with n.
explanations.b: Correct. Expected average degree of a vertex in this model is p(n-1), so holding p fixed while n grows makes the graph steadily denser, not merely bigger.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: degree grows, it does not shrink, as n increases at fixed p.
explanations.d: Average degree is fully determined once p and n are fixed: it is p(n-1), so it is not undefined.

questions.prompt: Why is 'runtime vs. number of vertices' alone an underspecified x-axis for comparing graph algorithms?

options.text: Because vertices are never the real bottleneck in any graph algorithm
Because runtime for most graph algorithms depends on both n and m, and the same n can pair with wildly different m
Because vertex counts cannot be measured precisely in real datasets
Because only edge count matters, so vertex count is irrelevant

explanations.a: Vertices matter directly too — e.g. extract-min calls scale with n — so this overstates the case.
explanations.b: Correct. Bounds like O((n+m) log n) depend on both variables, and without stating how m scales with n the same vertex count could represent a sparse tree or a near-complete graph.
explanations.c: Vertex counts are trivially exact in any generated or real graph; measurement precision is not the issue.
explanations.d: Vertex count does matter — for example the log n factor and the n extract-min operations both depend on it — so it is not irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Match each normalization or control strategy to what it is designed to reveal or hold fixed.

left.text: Holding m/n fixed while sweeping n
Holding n fixed while sweeping density

right.text: Tests whether per-edge relaxation cost is roughly constant, as an O(m log n) bound predicts
Isolates how the algorithm scales with problem size at constant sparsity
Reveals where a crossover between two algorithms' asymptotic bounds occurs

questions.explanation: Time-per-edge checks whether cost really is linear in m; holding m/n fixed while growing n asks the realistic 'scale up at constant sparsity' question; holding n fixed while sweeping density from sparse to dense is how you locate the point where a sparse-optimized algorithm loses to a dense-optimized one.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in designing a rigorous graph-algorithm density-controlled benchmark, from first decision to last.

items.text: Decide which dimension to hold fixed: average degree (m/n) or vertex count n
Choose a graph generator family whose density rule matches that decision
Sweep the other dimension across a wide enough range to distinguish asymptotic trends
Report results normalized (e.g. time-per-edge or time-per-vertex) alongside raw wall-clock time

questions.explanation: You must first decide the controlled variable, then pick a generator that actually respects that control, then sweep the free variable across a range wide enough to reveal a trend, and only then normalize and report — normalizing raw numbers that were never density-controlled in the first place does not fix the underlying design flaw.

lessons.label: The Benchmark Chooses the Winner

sections.heading: Random graph families are not interchangeable
sections.body: The two dominant synthetic random-graph models produce structurally different graphs, and an algorithm's ranking can flip depending on which one you test against. Erdos and Renyi's original 1959 paper introduced the G(n,M) model, chosen uniformly at random among all graphs on n vertices with exactly M edges; the closely related G(n,p) model, where each pair of vertices is connected independently with fixed probability p, was introduced independently the same year by Edgar Gilbert. The two are asymptotically similar, and 'the Erdos-Renyi model' is often used informally to refer to either, but it is Gilbert's construction that fixes p. It produces a Poisson-like degree distribution — most vertices have degree close to the mean, with no extreme outliers. The Barabasi-Albert model, introduced by Albert-Laszlo Barabasi and Reka Albert in their 1999 Science paper 'Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks', instead grows the graph one vertex at a time, attaching each new vertex preferentially to existing high-degree vertices ('rich get richer'). This produces a power-law degree distribution with a small number of extremely high-degree hub vertices. An algorithm that exploits hub structure (e.g., landmark-based shortest-path heuristics) looks brilliant on Barabasi-Albert graphs and unremarkable on Erdos-Renyi graphs of matching n and m — the benchmark family itself decided the outcome before the algorithm ran.

sections.heading: Real datasets: SNAP, DIMACS, and OpenStreetMap
sections.body: Beyond synthetic generators, three real-world sources anchor most published graph-algorithm evaluations. The Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP), maintained by Jure Leskovec's group, distributes dozens of real social, web, and citation graphs with published statistics, letting researchers test on structure no synthetic model fully captures. The DIMACS Implementation Challenges (a recurring NSF-funded series) devoted their 9th installment in 2005-2006 specifically to shortest paths, distributing continental road networks — including a USA road network with roughly 24 million vertices and 58 million edges — precisely because prior shortest-path papers had over-relied on random graphs that don't resemble real routing problems. OpenStreetMap extracts serve the same purpose today, providing free, continuously updated real road topology at any regional scale.

sections.heading: Why road networks are a distinct benchmark regime
sections.body: Road networks are close to planar (they can be drawn in the plane with few edge crossings, since roads mostly don't tunnel under or fly over each other) and have average degree around 2.5-2.7 with a maximum degree rarely above 6-10 — nothing like a hub-and-spoke Barabasi-Albert graph and nothing like a dense Erdos-Renyi graph either. This near-planarity is exactly what techniques like contraction hierarchies (Robert Geisberger, Peter Sanders, Dominik Schultes, and Daniel Delling, 2008) exploit: they precompute a hierarchy of 'important' shortcut edges that only pays off because real road networks have a genuine hierarchical structure (highways connecting regions, local streets within them). Run contraction hierarchies on a uniform random graph and the speedup mostly evaporates, because random graphs have no such hierarchy to exploit. This is precisely why route-planning papers report benchmarks on continental-scale road data (the DIMACS USA and Europe networks are the de facto standard) rather than on synthetic random graphs: the whole point of the algorithm is to exploit structure that only real road networks have.

lessons.workedExample: A team implements a landmark-based A* variant (ALT: A*, Landmarks, Triangle inequality) and benchmarks it only against Erdos-Renyi random graphs, finding a modest 20% speedup over plain Dijkstra. Discouraged, they almost discard the approach. But when they instead test on a DIMACS-style road network extract (near-planar, average degree ~2.6, hierarchical highway structure), the same algorithm's speedup jumps to 5-10x, because landmark-based lower bounds are far tighter on graphs with real geometric and hierarchical structure than on random graphs where no such structure exists to exploit. The lesson: reporting only one benchmark family without disclosing it can make a genuinely good algorithm look mediocre, or a mediocre one look great — the choice of test graph is itself an experimental variable that must be reported and justified, not left implicit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the DIMACS road-network history will immediately ask 'did you test only on random graphs, or also on something with real topology?' A team that benchmarked exclusively on Erdos-Renyi graphs and claims a general speedup result is making a claim their evidence doesn't support — the result may be an artifact of that one graph family's structure. Naming which generator or dataset you used, and explaining why its structure is or isn't representative of your target application (routing, social networks, the web graph), is exactly the kind of methodological transparency a rigorous judge rewards.

questions.prompt: Why does a landmark-based shortest-path heuristic tend to show a much larger speedup on a Barabasi-Albert graph than on an Erdos-Renyi graph of the same n and m?

options.text: Barabasi-Albert graphs are always smaller in practice, so runtimes are naturally faster
Barabasi-Albert graphs have hub vertices of very high degree the heuristic can exploit, which Erdos-Renyi graphs lack
Erdos-Renyi graphs are always disconnected, so shortest paths cannot be computed
Landmark heuristics only function correctly on graphs generated by preferential attachment

explanations.a: Graph size here is controlled to be equal (matching n and m); the difference is structural, not about scale.
explanations.b: Correct. Barabasi-Albert's preferential attachment produces a power-law degree distribution with hub vertices, and structure-exploiting heuristics benefit far more from that concentrated structure than from the more uniform Erdos-Renyi degree distribution.
explanations.c: Erdos-Renyi graphs are typically connected once p is above the well-known connectivity threshold; disconnection is not the relevant issue here.
explanations.d: Landmark heuristics function on any graph; they simply perform better when there is exploitable structure, which is more pronounced in Barabasi-Albert graphs.

questions.prompt: Approximately what is the m/n ratio (edges per vertex) typical of real road networks, as used in DIMACS-style benchmarks?

options.text: About 2.5-2.7, with maximum degree rarely above 10
About 50, since intersections often have many connecting roads
Equal to n, since road networks are effectively complete graphs
It varies so unpredictably that no representative figure exists

explanations.a: Correct. Road networks are near-planar with most intersections having only a handful of connecting roads, giving low average degree and a low, bounded maximum degree.
explanations.b: This wildly overstates real intersection connectivity; almost no real intersection has anywhere near 50 connecting roads.
explanations.c: Road networks are extremely sparse, essentially the opposite of a complete graph.
explanations.d: This is a well-documented, fairly consistent structural property across real road networks, not an unpredictable one.

questions.prompt: Match each graph source or model to its defining origin or characteristic.

right.text: 1959 model connecting each vertex pair independently with fixed probability p, giving a Poisson-like degree distribution
1999 preferential-attachment model producing a power-law, hub-dominated degree distribution
2005-2006 challenge that distributed continental road networks, including a ~24 million vertex USA network, for shortest-path evaluation
Stanford repository of real social, web, and citation graphs maintained by Jure Leskovec's group

questions.explanation: Erdos-Renyi (1959) gives a Poisson-like degree distribution from independent edge inclusion; Barabasi-Albert (1999) gives a power-law distribution via preferential attachment; the 9th DIMACS Implementation Challenge (2005-2006) focused on shortest paths and distributed continental road data; SNAP is Jure Leskovec's real-world graph repository.

questions.prompt: Order these benchmark sources from most abstract/synthetic to most application-specific/real.

items.text: Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p)
Barabasi-Albert preferential-attachment graph
SNAP real social/web/citation graph
DIMACS/OpenStreetMap continental road network

questions.explanation: Erdos-Renyi graphs are the most structurally generic (uniform random edges); Barabasi-Albert graphs add one specific real-world-inspired mechanism (preferential attachment) but remain synthetic; SNAP graphs are real but drawn from social/web domains with less rigid geometric structure; road networks are the most application-specific, near-planar, and hierarchically structured of the four.

lessons.label: Validating an Asymptotic Claim Against Your Own Timings

sections.heading: Reading a slope off a log-log plot
sections.body: If measured runtime T scales as T = c * n^k for some constant c and exponent k, then taking logarithms gives log(T) = k * log(n) + log(c) — a straight line on a log-log plot whose SLOPE is exactly k, the asymptotic exponent. This is the standard empirical way to validate a claimed complexity bound: generate a graph family with a fixed density rule (say, average degree held constant at m/n = 4, per the earlier lesson on controlling for two variables), measure wall-clock time at several values of n spanning at least two or three orders of magnitude, plot log(T) against log(n), and fit a line. A slope near 2 is consistent with O(n^2) behavior (e.g., an array-based Dijkstra that scans all n vertices to find the minimum, n times over). A slope near 1 with a visible slow upward bend at large n is consistent with O(n log n) or O(m log n) behavior — the log n factor is a much weaker growth term than a polynomial one, so on a log-log plot it appears as a nearly-straight line with slope 1 that curves ever so slightly upward as n grows, rather than a clean straight line.

sections.heading: The honest complication: crossovers are data, not error
sections.body: A well-known and easily misread phenomenon in shortest-path benchmarking, documented empirically in Cherkassky, Goldberg, and Radzik's 1996 experimental evaluation of shortest-path algorithms, is that a simple array-based O(n^2) Dijkstra implementation (no heap: scan all unsettled vertices for the minimum each of n times) can outrun a binary-heap-based O((n+m) log n) implementation on DENSE graphs, and continue to win until n grows quite large. The reason is constant factors: each binary-heap operation involves sift-up/sift-down comparisons with non-sequential, index-jumping memory accesses and a mild cache-locality penalty, while the array scan is a tight, cache-friendly linear loop. On a dense graph (m close to n^2), the heap version does many more log n-factor operations with high per-operation overhead, while the array version's 'wasteful' O(n^2) scan is simple enough for the hardware to execute very fast. If a student's own timing data shows the array version winning at n = 500 but losing at n = 5000, that crossover is not a bug or a measurement error to be explained away — it is exactly the point where the asymptotically inferior algorithm's smaller constant factor stops compensating for its worse growth rate, and reporting the crossover n honestly is more informative than picking one algorithm and hiding the range where it loses.

sections.heading: Confounders to control before trusting any slope
sections.body: Three sources of noise can corrupt a slope estimate before density is even considered. First, JIT/warm-up effects: languages with just-in-time compilation (Java's JVM, JavaScript's V8) run interpreted or unoptimized machine code for the first several thousand iterations, so the very first timed runs at small n can be artificially slow — always discard an initial warm-up period and average over repeated runs. Second, allocation overhead: if the benchmark allocates a fresh adjacency list or priority queue on every trial, garbage-collection pauses can inject timing noise unrelated to the algorithm itself; reusing pre-allocated structures across trials isolates the algorithm's true cost. Third, memory layout: an adjacency MATRIX (n^2 array) has excellent cache locality but wastes memory on sparse graphs, while an adjacency LIST has better asymptotic memory use but worse cache locality due to pointer-chasing; comparing two algorithms implemented with different underlying graph representations conflates the representation's cache behavior with the algorithm's actual asymptotic behavior, and any slope you fit is contaminated by that confound.

lessons.workedExample: A student times their binary-heap Dijkstra on graphs with average degree fixed at 6, for n = 200, 800, 3200, and 12800 (each a 4x jump). They measure T = 1.2ms, 5.9ms, 28ms, and 135ms. Computing log2 of the time ratios: 5.9/1.2 ≈ 4.9, 28/5.9 ≈ 4.7, 135/28 ≈ 4.8 — each 4x increase in n produces roughly a 4.8x increase in time, and log2(4.8)/log2(4) ≈ 1.13, giving an effective exponent near 1.13, consistent with O(n log n)-ish growth (a bit more than linear, less than quadratic) rather than the O(n^2) they had worried about after seeing a naive early implementation lag. They then re-run the same sweep after switching the first 30 iterations to warm-up-only (discarded) runs, confirming the exponent estimate doesn't shift — ruling out JIT warm-up as a confound before writing up the result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge trained to smell hand-waved complexity claims will ask for the actual numbers behind any stated big-O, and specifically whether the student controlled for warm-up, allocation, and graph representation before fitting a slope. A team that reports 'we confirmed O(n log n) scaling' with only two data points, or without discarding early JIT-warm-up runs, has not actually validated anything — they've fit a line through noise. A team that instead shows a log-log plot across two or three orders of magnitude of n, states the fitted slope, and explains a crossover in their own data rather than hiding it, demonstrates they understand that measured performance is an experiment with confounders, not a formula to be looked up.

questions.prompt: On a log-log plot of measured runtime vs. n, what slope would you expect to see for an algorithm with true asymptotic complexity O(n^2)?

options.text: A slope of approximately 2
A slope of approximately 1
A slope of approximately 0.5
The slope cannot be predicted from the complexity class

explanations.a: Correct. If T = c*n^2, then log(T) = 2*log(n) + log(c), so the log-log slope is exactly the exponent, 2.
explanations.b: A slope of 1 corresponds to roughly linear or n log n growth (with a slight upward bend), not quadratic.
explanations.c: A slope below 1 would correspond to sub-linear growth, which is not what O(n^2) predicts.
explanations.d: The slope is directly predictable: it equals the polynomial exponent k in T = c*n^k, which is exactly why log-log plots are used to validate asymptotic claims.

questions.prompt: A student's timing data shows an array-based O(n^2) Dijkstra beating a binary-heap O((n+m) log n) Dijkstra on dense graphs for n up to about 3000, with the heap version winning beyond that. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The measurement is invalid and should be discarded or re-run until the heap version always wins
The crossover reflects real constant-factor and cache-behavior differences and should be reported as a finding
It proves the O(n^2) bound is actually tighter than O((n+m) log n) for all graphs
It means the heap implementation has a bug, since it should always beat the array version

explanations.a: There is nothing invalid here — this exact crossover is a well-documented empirical phenomenon in shortest-path benchmarking; discarding it would be discarding a real result.
explanations.b: Correct. The array version's simpler, cache-friendly constant factor genuinely outruns the heap version's asymptotically better but higher-overhead operations until n grows large enough for the asymptotic gap to dominate — this crossover is legitimate evidence, not a mistake.
explanations.c: The asymptotic bound still holds in the limit; a small-n crossover due to constants does not overturn the asymptotic comparison, it just shows constants matter before the limit is reached.
explanations.d: A slower-but-simpler algorithm outperforming a faster-asymptotic one at moderate n is an expected, well-documented pattern, not a sign of a bug.

questions.prompt: Match each benchmarking confound to the fix that controls for it.

left.text: JIT/warm-up effects making early runs artificially slow
Allocation and garbage-collection pauses injecting timing noise
Comparing algorithms built on different graph representations (matrix vs. list)

right.text: Discard an initial warm-up period and average over many repeated runs
Reuse pre-allocated data structures across trials instead of allocating fresh ones each time
Use the same underlying representation for both algorithms, or explicitly account for its cache-locality effect

questions.explanation: Warm-up noise is controlled by discarding early iterations; allocation noise is controlled by reusing structures across trials; representation-driven cache differences are controlled by holding the representation constant (or explicitly accounting for it) across the algorithms being compared.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for empirically validating a claimed asymptotic bound against your own timing data.

items.text: Fix a density rule and generate a graph family that respects it across a wide range of n
Run and discard a warm-up period, then time multiple repeated trials at each n
Plot log(time) against log(n) and fit the slope
Compare the fitted slope to the claimed exponent, and report any crossover or deviation honestly

questions.explanation: You must first control density so the comparison is fair, then eliminate warm-up and allocation noise from the raw measurements, then fit the log-log slope, and only then compare that slope to the claimed bound — reporting deviations or crossovers rather than only the cases that match the prediction.

lessons.label: Count Operations, Not Just Seconds

sections.heading: Wall-clock time measures the machine, not the algorithm
sections.body: A second stopwatch reading depends on CPU clock speed, cache hierarchy, compiler optimizations, and what else was running on the machine at the time — none of which is a property of the algorithm itself. The complementary, machine-independent technique is to instrument the algorithm to COUNT its own fundamental operations as it runs: the number of edge relaxations (attempts to improve a distance estimate across an edge), the number of extract-min calls (pulling the next-closest vertex from the priority queue), the number of decrease-key calls (updating a vertex's priority when a shorter path is found), the number of vertices settled (finalized with their shortest-path distance), and for search algorithms, the number of visited-set probes or nodes expanded. These counts are reproducible across any machine, compiler, or language, which makes them the right currency for comparing two ALGORITHMS rather than two IMPLEMENTATIONS.

sections.heading: A* vs. Dijkstra: fewer expansions, provably
sections.body: Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael introduced A* in their 1968 paper 'A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths' (IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics), proving that when the heuristic function h(v) never overestimates the true remaining distance (admissibility), A* is guaranteed to find the optimal path, typically expanding far fewer nodes than uninformed Dijkstra. The stronger claim that A* expands no more nodes than any other algorithm using the same admissible heuristic — its 'optimal efficiency' — was proved later, by Rina Dechter and Judea Pearl in their 1985 paper 'Generalized Best-First Search Strategies and the Optimality of A*'. Counting nodes expanded (vertices removed from the open set and finalized) makes this dramatic and machine-independent: on a road-network shortest path with a straight-line-distance heuristic, A* commonly expands 5-10x fewer nodes than Dijkstra to find the identical optimal path, because the heuristic actively steers the search toward the target instead of exploring uniformly outward in every direction. Reporting 'A* was 3x faster in seconds' is a weaker, machine-entangled claim than reporting 'A* expanded 8x fewer nodes' — the latter survives a change of laptop, language, or compiler.

sections.heading: The Fibonacci-heap paradox
sections.body: Michael Fredman and Robert Tarjan introduced the Fibonacci heap in their 1984 paper (published 1987 in the Journal of the ACM as 'Fibonacci Heaps and Their Uses in Improved Network Optimization Algorithms'), which supports decrease-key in O(1) amortized time versus O(log n) for a binary heap, improving Dijkstra's theoretical bound from O((n+m) log n) to O(m + n log n) — asymptotically superior whenever m is large relative to n. Counting operations confirms this exactly as predicted: a Fibonacci-heap Dijkstra performs genuinely fewer decrease-key operations' worth of comparison work than a binary-heap version on the same graph. And yet, in wall-clock terms, Fibonacci heaps are frequently SLOWER in practice — a well-documented paradox discussed in Cherkassky, Goldberg, and Radzik's 1996 experimental survey, and reinforced by later empirical priority-queue studies such as Larkin, Sen, and Tarjan's 2014 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues', which found simpler structures like pairing heaps and even d-ary binary heaps often beat Fibonacci heaps on real workloads. The cause is that Fibonacci heaps' O(1) amortized bound hides a large constant factor: the data structure requires maintaining a complex forest of trees with lazy consolidation, meaning poor cache locality and heavy pointer-chasing, while the binary heap's array-based layout stays cache-friendly. This is the clearest case where operation counts and wall-clock time DISAGREE, and both are telling the truth about different things — one about algorithmic operation count, the other about hardware-level cost per operation.

lessons.workedExample: A team benchmarks A* against Dijkstra on a 50,000-vertex road network, both instrumented to count nodes expanded (settled) and total edge relaxations. On a machine that happens to be running a slower, older laptop for the A* run and a fast desktop for the Dijkstra run, wall-clock times come out nearly equal — a naive read would say 'no real difference.' But the operation counts tell a different story: A* expanded 4,200 nodes and performed 11,000 edge relaxations, while Dijkstra expanded 41,000 nodes (nearly the whole graph) and performed 98,000 relaxations. Reporting the operation counts alongside the (confounded) wall-clock numbers lets the team correctly claim 'A* explores roughly 10x fewer nodes,' a machine-independent result the misleading timing alone would have hidden.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen the Fibonacci-heap literature will specifically probe whether a team's 'faster' claim is about the algorithm or about the machine it happened to run on. Reporting instrumented operation counts (relaxations, extract-min/decrease-key calls, nodes expanded) alongside wall-clock time shows you understand the difference between an asymptotic, hardware-independent property and a constant-factor, hardware-dependent one — and preempts the sharpest version of that question: 'if Fibonacci heaps have a better asymptotic bound, why do you recommend a binary heap?' Being able to answer 'because operation count favors Fibonacci heaps but wall-clock cost favors binary heaps, and here's why' is exactly the kind of nuance a rigorous judge is listening for.

questions.prompt: Why is 'number of nodes expanded' a better metric than wall-clock seconds for comparing A* to Dijkstra across different machines?

options.text: Because nodes expanded is always a smaller number than seconds, making it easier to report
Because it is a property of the algorithm's behavior on the graph, independent of CPU speed, cache, or language
Because wall-clock time is illegal to report in published research
Because A* always expands more nodes than Dijkstra, so the comparison favors Dijkstra

explanations.a: The comparison has nothing to do with which number happens to be smaller; it's about what the number measures.
explanations.b: Correct. Nodes expanded is a count of algorithmic work that does not depend on which machine, compiler, or language ran the code, unlike wall-clock time.
explanations.c: Wall-clock time is a completely standard and legitimate metric to report; it's just not machine-independent, so it should be paired with operation counts.
explanations.d: This reverses the well-established result: an admissible heuristic guarantees A* expands no more nodes than Dijkstra, typically far fewer.

questions.prompt: The Fibonacci heap gives Dijkstra's algorithm an asymptotic bound of O(m + n log n), better than the binary heap's O((n+m) log n). Why might a Fibonacci-heap-based implementation still run SLOWER in wall-clock time on many real graphs?

options.text: Because the asymptotic bound is actually wrong and has been disproven
Because Fibonacci heaps have a large constant factor from complex tree-forest maintenance and poor cache locality
Because Fibonacci heaps cannot be implemented correctly in most programming languages
Because decrease-key is never actually called during Dijkstra's algorithm

explanations.a: The bound is correct and well-established (Fredman and Tarjan, 1984/1987); the issue is practical constants, not theoretical validity.
explanations.b: Correct. The amortized O(1) decrease-key comes at the cost of a more complex data structure with heavier pointer-chasing and worse cache behavior than a flat binary-heap array, which often dominates in wall-clock terms.
explanations.c: Fibonacci heaps can be and have been implemented in many languages; implementation difficulty is not the source of the practical slowdown.
explanations.d: Decrease-key is called whenever Dijkstra finds a shorter path to a vertex already in the queue, which happens routinely during the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Match each instrumented operation count to what it measures during a shortest-path algorithm's execution.

right.text: Attempts to improve a distance estimate across a single edge
Pulling the currently-closest unsettled vertex from the priority queue
Updating a vertex's queue priority after finding a shorter path to it
Vertices whose shortest-path distance has been finalized

questions.explanation: Edge relaxation is the attempt to improve a distance estimate; extract-min pulls the next-closest vertex; decrease-key updates a vertex's priority; settling a vertex means its shortest-path distance is now final.

questions.prompt: Order these events by when the Fibonacci-heap-vs-binary-heap performance story unfolded historically.

items.text: Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduce A* with its admissibility guarantee (1968)
Fredman and Tarjan introduce the Fibonacci heap and its O(1) amortized decrease-key (1984)
Cherkassky, Goldberg, and Radzik's experimental survey documents Fibonacci heaps often losing in wall-clock terms (1996)
Larkin, Sen, and Tarjan's empirical priority-queue comparison reinforces that simpler heaps often beat Fibonacci heaps in practice (2014)

questions.explanation: A* (1968) predates the Fibonacci heap (1984); the practical wall-clock underperformance of Fibonacci heaps was then documented empirically in 1996 and reinforced by further priority-queue benchmarking in 2014.

lessons.label: Reading and Drawing Graph Figures Honestly

sections.heading: Search-space shape as evidence, not decoration
sections.body: When a shortest-path search is run on a 2D graph (a road network or grid) with roughly Euclidean edge weights, plotting which vertices got settled or expanded produces a shape that is itself a meaningful measurement, not just a pretty picture. Dijkstra's algorithm expands vertices in increasing order of true distance from the start, so its settled region grows as an expanding DISK centered on the start vertex, uninformed about where the target is. A* with an admissible straight-line-distance heuristic expands vertices in increasing order of f(v) = g(v) + h(v) (true distance so far plus estimated remaining distance); since the locus of points where g(v) + h(v) equals a constant is by definition an ELLIPSE with foci at the start and the target, A*'s settled region visibly narrows into an elongated ellipse stretching toward the goal. Bidirectional search, which runs simultaneous searches from both start and target and stops when they meet, produces two roughly disk-shaped lobes that visibly shrink relative to a single expanding disk. These shapes are not mere illustrations: the AREA of the settled region is proportional to the number of vertices expanded, so a smaller, more elongated shape is direct visual evidence of fewer operations, exactly the counts discussed in the operation-counting lesson.

sections.heading: Degree distributions and the over-claimed straight line
sections.body: A common figure in network-science papers plots a graph's degree distribution on log-log axes, and a roughly straight line is frequently presented as proof the network is 'scale-free' (power-law degree distributed, as in Barabasi-Albert-type networks). Aaron Clauset, Cosma Shalizi, and Mark Newman's widely cited 2009 SIAM Review paper 'Power-Law Distributions in Empirical Data' showed this inference is far weaker than commonly assumed: a rough straight line across only one or two decades of data on a log-log plot is consistent with MANY distributions besides a true power law (log-normal, exponential with a heavy tail, etc.), and rigorous power-law claims require a formal statistical test — fitting via maximum likelihood and comparing against alternative distributions with a goodness-of-fit test such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov — not just an eyeballed straight line. Their re-analysis found that many previously published 'scale-free' claims did not survive this stricter test. The lesson for reading any degree-distribution figure: ask how many decades of x-axis the straight-line claim spans, and whether any formal statistical test backs the power-law claim, before accepting 'this network is scale-free' as established.

sections.heading: The hairball problem and preempting a judge's chart-breaking question
sections.body: A node-link diagram (dots for vertices, lines for edges) of a graph with 10^4 or more vertices almost universally degenerates into a 'hairball' — a dense tangle of overlapping edges where no individual structure, cluster, or path is visible, because the number of edge crossings grows much faster than the canvas can display distinctly. This is a well-known limitation discussed throughout the graph-drawing literature: node-link layouts communicate structure well only up to roughly a few hundred vertices; beyond that, alternatives such as adjacency-matrix visualizations with a clustering-aware vertex ordering, or aggregated/coarsened views showing only community-level structure, actually convey information a hairball cannot. When you present ANY graph-algorithm figure, the strongest habit is to anticipate the one question a sharp judge will ask to break it — is your log-log slope based on enough decades of data, does your degree-distribution figure include a statistical test, is your search-space diagram drawn to scale, is your hairball actually communicating anything — and address that weakness in the figure's caption before the judge has to raise it.

lessons.workedExample: A team draws Dijkstra's and A*'s search regions on the same road-network segment, shading every settled vertex. Dijkstra's shading fills a near-circular blob covering the whole visible map; A*'s shading forms a narrow, cigar-shaped ellipse stretching directly from start to target, covering visibly less area. Alongside this, they overlay a full node-link diagram of the underlying 15,000-vertex road graph as a 'context' image — but it renders as an indecipherable black smear. A judge asks what the smear shows; the honest answer is 'nothing legible,' which undercuts the otherwise-strong ellipse-vs-disk comparison. Replacing the hairball with either a zoomed-in sub-region or an aggregated community-level view (fixing the search-space figure's context problem rather than including a chart that adds nothing) is the correct fix.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge with any data-visualization literacy will single out exactly the weakest figure in a poster or slide deck. A hairball node-link diagram invites the immediate question 'what does this actually show me,' and a straight line on a log-log degree-distribution plot invites 'did you test that against a null model, or is this just a good-looking line.' Teams that preempt these questions — labeling axes with decade counts, stating whether a formal power-law test was run, and choosing search-space visuals whose area differences are the actual point being made — demonstrate they understand a chart is a claim that can be checked, not a decoration that fills space.

questions.prompt: On a 2D graph with roughly Euclidean edge weights, why does A* search (using an admissible straight-line-distance heuristic) settle vertices in an elliptical region rather than a circular one like Dijkstra?

options.text: Because A* only works correctly on graphs shaped like ellipses
Because the set of points where g(v) + h(v) equals a constant is, by the geometric definition of an ellipse, an ellipse with foci at the start and target
Because A* explores vertices in a random order, which happens to look elliptical
Because A* ignores the true distance g(v) and only uses the heuristic h(v)

explanations.a: A* works on any graph shape; the ellipse describes the shape of the settled region, not a requirement on the input graph.
explanations.b: Correct. A* expands vertices in order of f(v) = g(v) + h(v); since an ellipse is defined as the set of points whose sum of distances to two foci is constant, the settled region traces an ellipse with foci at the start and target vertices.
explanations.c: A*'s expansion order is deterministic and priority-driven, not random; the elliptical shape emerges directly from the f(v) formula.
explanations.d: A* uses BOTH the true distance so far, g(v), and the estimate, h(v) — using only h(v) would make it greedy best-first search, a different algorithm with no optimality guarantee.

questions.prompt: According to Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman's 2009 analysis, what is the main flaw in claiming a network is 'scale-free' based only on a roughly straight line on a log-log degree-distribution plot?

options.text: Log-log plots cannot display degree distributions at all
A rough straight line over a short range is also consistent with several non-power-law distributions, so a formal statistical test is needed
Power-law distributions never produce straight lines on log-log axes
The claim is correct as stated and their paper confirmed all prior scale-free claims

explanations.a: Log-log plots are a standard and appropriate way to display degree distributions; the issue is over-interpreting them, not their basic validity.
explanations.b: Correct. Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman showed that a rough straight line spanning only one or two decades is also consistent with log-normal and other heavy-tailed distributions, so rigorous claims require maximum-likelihood fitting and a goodness-of-fit test against alternatives.
explanations.c: A true power-law distribution DOES produce a straight line on log-log axes — that part is correct; the flaw is that other distributions can produce similar-looking lines too.
explanations.d: Their re-analysis found the opposite: many previously published scale-free claims did NOT survive the stricter statistical test.

questions.prompt: Match each graph figure or visualization to what it correctly communicates when drawn honestly.

left.text: A*'s settled region with an admissible straight-line heuristic
A raw node-link diagram of 10^4+ vertices

right.text: Uniform outward growth from the start, with no information about the target's location
A narrowed, elongated region stretching toward the target, reflecting fewer vertices expanded
Two smaller shrinking regions meeting near the midpoint between start and target
Essentially no legible structure, since edge crossings overwhelm the canvas at that scale

questions.explanation: Dijkstra's disk reflects uninformed uniform expansion; A*'s ellipse reflects heuristic-guided narrowing toward the target; bidirectional search's two lobes reflect simultaneous shrinking searches meeting in the middle; a hairball of 10^4+ vertices communicates essentially nothing due to edge-crossing overload.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for preempting a judge's chart-breaking question about a degree-distribution figure.

items.text: Plot the degree distribution on log-log axes
Check how many decades of x-axis the apparent straight line spans
Fit the distribution via maximum likelihood and compare against alternative distributions with a goodness-of-fit test
State in the caption whether the power-law claim is statistically supported or only visually suggestive

questions.explanation: You first produce the log-log plot, then assess how much of the range actually supports a straight-line claim, then run the rigorous statistical test Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman prescribe, and only then state honestly in the caption how strong the evidence for 'scale-free' really is.

lessons.label: Euler 1736: The Konigsberg Bridges and the Birth of Graph Theory

sections.heading: A city puzzle that could not be solved by trying harder
sections.body: The Prussian city of Konigsberg (now Kaliningrad) straddled the Pregel River, with two islands connected to the mainland and to each other by seven bridges. A local puzzle asked whether a walker could cross every bridge exactly once and return to the start. Enough failed attempts had piled up that the question reached Leonhard Euler, then at the St. Petersburg Academy, who at first considered it beneath serious mathematics -- geometry had no established techniques for a problem with no distances or angles. He solved it anyway, and presented the result to the Academy on 26 August 1735. Publication lagged badly: the paper appeared only in 1741, as 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis' ('The solution of a problem relating to the geometry of position'). The work is universally cited as 'Euler 1736' for a mundane reason worth knowing -- it ran in volume 8 of the Commentarii academiae scientiarum Petropolitanae, a volume NUMBERED for the year 1736 but not actually printed until 1741. So three different years attach to this one paper: 1735 (presented), 1736 (the volume's nominal year, hence the conventional citation), and 1741 (actually published). None of them is the year Euler did the thinking. The paper's real significance is not the answer to the bridge puzzle -- it is Euler's method. He threw away everything about Konigsberg except which landmasses connected to which by how many bridges, reducing the city to four points (two riverbanks, two islands) and seven connecting lines. That act of stripping a physical layout down to a pattern of connections is the founding move of graph theory.

sections.heading: The parity argument
sections.body: Euler's insight was to look at each landmass and count how many bridges touch it -- its degree. Every time a walker passes through a landmass mid-route, they use one bridge to arrive and a different one to leave, consuming its bridges in pairs. A landmass can be left with one unpaired bridge only if the walk starts or ends there. So a walk that uses every edge exactly once (now called an Eulerian path) can have at most two odd-degree vertices, and if it returns to its start (an Eulerian circuit), zero. In Konigsberg all four landmasses had odd degree (three had degree 3, one had degree 5), so no such walk -- round-trip or not -- could exist. The general theorem, that a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree, is often stated as Euler's, though he proved only the necessity of the condition; the first rigorous proof that even degree everywhere is also sufficient came from Carl Hierholzer, published posthumously in 1873.

sections.heading: From existence to construction: Hierholzer's algorithm
sections.body: Euler's theorem tells you whether a solution exists but not how to build one. Hierholzer's 1873 method does both efficiently: pick a start vertex, walk arbitrarily until you are stuck (which, given even degrees everywhere, can only happen back at the start, closing a sub-circuit), then find any vertex on that sub-circuit with unused edges, splice in another sub-circuit from there, and repeat until no edges remain. Because each edge is used exactly once and the splicing can be organized with a stack in a single pass, the whole procedure runs in O(V + E) time -- linear in the size of the graph. This combination, a clean existence criterion plus a matching linear-time construction, is why the Konigsberg problem is treated as the discipline's origin story rather than a historical curiosity: it demonstrates, in the first paper, that reducing a physical structure to an abstract graph and reasoning about local vertex properties (degree) can decide a global question (does this route exist) that raw enumeration cannot.

lessons.workedExample: Model Konigsberg as four vertices: N (north bank), S (south bank), A (large island), B (small island). The seven bridges give: N-A (x2), N-B (x1), S-A (x2), S-B (x1), A-B (x1). Degree count: N = 3, S = 3, A = 5, B = 3 -- all four odd. Since an Eulerian path allows at most two odd-degree vertices, and here all four are odd, no walk crossing every bridge exactly once can exist, with or without returning to start. If a city planner removed the A-B bridge, A would drop to degree 4 and B would drop to degree 2 (both even), leaving only N and S odd (degree 3 each) -- exactly two, so an Eulerian path (not circuit) would become possible, starting at N or S.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the story will ask the version most students skip: what did Euler actually prove, versus what got attributed to him later? The precise answer -- Euler showed even degree everywhere is NECESSARY for a circuit, but the SUFFICIENCY direction (even degree everywhere guarantees one exists) was rigorously nailed down only by Hierholzer in 1873 -- separates a student who memorized 'Euler's theorem' as a slogan from one who understands that mathematical results accumulate across more than one paper and more than one author. A sharper judge may probe the dates, since the conventional label 'Euler 1736' matches none of the events: Euler presented on 26 August 1735, and the paper was printed in 1741 in a journal volume merely NUMBERED 1736. Being able to say which year denotes what -- and that a citation year can be an artifact of a publisher's backlog rather than a fact about the science -- is the kind of precision that reads as genuine familiarity with the source rather than with a textbook summary of it.

questions.prompt: Why was a round-trip crossing every Konigsberg bridge exactly once impossible?

options.text: The bridges were too far apart to walk in one day
All four landmasses had odd degree, but a closed walk requires every vertex to have even degree
The river was too wide to cross on foot
There were more bridges than landmasses

explanations.a: Physical distance is irrelevant to Euler's argument -- he deliberately discarded geometry and kept only the connection pattern.
explanations.b: Correct -- every visit to a landmass pairs up an incoming and outgoing bridge, so a closed walk needs even degree everywhere; Konigsberg's four landmasses were all odd (three had degree 3, one had degree 5).
explanations.c: Bridge width and river width play no role; the argument is purely about the count of bridges touching each landmass.
explanations.d: The relevant quantity is the degree of each individual vertex, not the raw count of bridges versus landmasses.

questions.prompt: Euler's Konigsberg paper is conventionally cited as 'Euler 1736.' What does that 1736 actually refer to?

options.text: The year Euler presented the solution to the St. Petersburg Academy
The nominal year of the journal volume it appeared in, which was not actually printed until 1741
The year the paper was printed and distributed
The year the Konigsberg bridge puzzle was first posed to the public

explanations.a: Euler presented the result on 26 August 1735, not in 1736.
explanations.b: Correct -- the paper ran in volume 8 of the Commentarii academiae scientiarum Petropolitanae, a volume numbered for 1736 but delayed in press until 1741. The citation year is an artifact of the volume's numbering, matching neither the presentation nor the printing.
explanations.c: Actual publication was in 1741; the journal's backlog put six years between the presentation and the printing.
explanations.d: The puzzle circulated in Konigsberg as local lore well before Euler took it up; 1736 does not mark its origin.

questions.prompt: What did Euler's Konigsberg paper actually establish, precisely?

options.text: That even degree everywhere is necessary for an Eulerian circuit, plus a full proof that it is also sufficient
That even degree everywhere is necessary for an Eulerian circuit; the rigorous sufficiency proof came later, from Hierholzer in 1873
A linear-time algorithm for constructing an Eulerian circuit
That the Konigsberg bridges could be crossed if two more bridges were built

explanations.a: Euler did not supply a rigorous sufficiency proof in the modern sense; that came later.
explanations.b: Correct -- Euler proved the necessary condition (even degree everywhere); Hierholzer supplied the rigorous sufficiency proof and a constructive method in 1873.
explanations.c: The constructive, efficient algorithm is Hierholzer's contribution, not Euler's.
explanations.d: Euler's paper analyzed the existing seven-bridge layout; it did not propose adding bridges.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Euler presents his solution to the St. Petersburg Academy
Euler's paper is published as 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis'
Hierholzer's linear-time construction and sufficiency proof is published (posthumously)

questions.explanation: Euler presented the result on 26 August 1735; the paper was published in 1741 (in the volume numbered 1736, which is why it is cited as 'Euler 1736'); and Hierholzer's construction and sufficiency proof followed more than a century later, in 1873.

questions.prompt: Match each contributor to what they specifically established.

right.text: Proved even degree everywhere is necessary for a closed walk crossing every edge once; reduced the city to an abstract vertex/edge structure
Proved even degree everywhere is also sufficient, and gave a linear-time O(V+E) method to build the circuit

questions.explanation: Euler's contribution was the necessity direction and the abstraction of the city into a graph; Hierholzer closed the gap with the sufficiency proof and a constructive, efficient algorithm.

lessons.label: Dijkstra 1959: Three Pages, Twenty Minutes, and One Precondition

sections.heading: A demo problem for a new machine
sections.body: Edsger Dijkstra worked at the Mathematisch Centrum in Amsterdam in the mid-1950s, where one of his jobs was showing off what the new ARMAC computer could do. He wanted a problem that was simple enough to explain to a non-specialist audience in minutes, yet visibly nontrivial to solve by machine -- and settled on: given a map of Dutch cities, find the shortest road route between two of them. By his own account, he designed the algorithm without sitting at a desk at all: about twenty minutes one morning in 1956, while out shopping in Amsterdam with his fiancee (soon to be his wife), the two of them stopped to rest at a cafe terrace, and the algorithm came to him there, with no pencil or paper. Dijkstra later said the absence of paper was not incidental -- it forced him to avoid any formulation that needed complex notation, which is part of why the resulting method is so short and easy to state.

sections.heading: Three pages, two algorithms
sections.body: The algorithm was not published until three years later: 'A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs' appeared in Numerische Mathematik, volume 1, pages 269-271, in 1959 -- a three-page note, remarkable for containing not one but two results still taught today. The first problem is the shortest path from one node to all others; the second is the minimum spanning tree (rediscovering, independently, an approach close to Jarnik's and Prim's). The published shortest-path method keeps a running tentative-distance estimate for every vertex, repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, and relaxes its outgoing edges. As originally written it scans the whole vertex set at each step to find that minimum, giving O(n^2) time with no priority queue at all -- the heap-based O((V+E) log V) version most courses teach is a later refinement, not what the 1959 paper describes.

sections.heading: The precondition was a design choice, not an oversight
sections.body: The algorithm's correctness rests on every edge weight being nonnegative. This is not a limitation Dijkstra failed to notice -- his greedy step, permanently fixing the shortest known distance to the closest remaining vertex, is only justified because no later edge can ever decrease a distance already deemed final, which requires weights to never subtract from a path length. Introduce even one negative edge and a path through it can undercut a distance already 'closed,' silently producing a wrong answer with no error raised. Because road distances, transit times, and similar real-world weights are naturally nonnegative, the restriction is a reasonable and stated assumption for the target application, not a gap. Later algorithms (Bellman-Ford among them) exist precisely to relax this precondition at the cost of worse asymptotic running time, making Dijkstra's stated assumption the boundary that defines an entire family of alternative algorithms.

lessons.workedExample: A logistics student wants shortest routes from a warehouse (vertex W) across a road network where every road has a nonnegative travel time. Dijkstra's algorithm sets dist(W)=0 and all others to infinity, then repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with smallest tentative distance and relaxes its edges. Suppose one edge is mistakenly encoded as a toll REBATE of -5 minutes (a negative weight) to model a shortcut. The algorithm may already have marked a vertex's distance as final before discovering that rebate edge, so it never revisits that vertex -- the final answer is silently too large, with no crash or warning. The fix is not a code patch to Dijkstra's algorithm; it is recognizing that negative weights violate the algorithm's precondition, and switching to Bellman-Ford, which tolerates negative edges (though not negative cycles) at the cost of O(VE) time instead of near-linear time.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges who know the algorithm will often ask why it fails on negative weights, expecting the student to locate the exact broken step (permanently finalizing a vertex's distance before all edges into it are known) rather than reciting 'it doesn't work with negative numbers' as a memorized fact. A strong answer also resists the temptation to call this a flaw -- it shows the student understands that Dijkstra explicitly built a fast algorithm for a restricted, common case, and that the restriction is what buys the speed.

questions.prompt: What made the original 1959 published shortest-path algorithm O(n^2) rather than the O((V+E) log V) most courses teach today?

options.text: It used a Fibonacci heap, which has slower constant factors
It scanned all unvisited vertices at each step to find the minimum tentative distance, with no priority queue
It only worked on graphs with fewer than 100 vertices
It required recomputing the entire graph from scratch after each edge relaxation

explanations.a: Fibonacci heaps postdate the 1959 paper by decades and were never part of Dijkstra's original description.
explanations.b: Correct -- the 1959 note has no priority queue at all; each step does a linear scan over unvisited vertices for the minimum, giving O(n^2) overall.
explanations.c: There is no vertex-count limitation in the algorithm's design; the complexity bound applies at any size.
explanations.d: Only the single vertex just finalized triggers relaxation of its outgoing edges, not a recomputation of the whole graph.

questions.prompt: Why does a single negative-weight edge break Dijkstra's algorithm's correctness?

options.text: Negative numbers cause integer overflow in the distance array
The algorithm permanently finalizes a vertex's distance once selected, assuming no later edge can shorten it -- an assumption negative weights violate
Negative weights make the graph disconnected
The algorithm cannot represent negative numbers in its data structures

explanations.a: Overflow is a separate implementation concern, not the reason the algorithm's LOGIC breaks.
explanations.b: Correct -- the greedy step assumes the closest unvisited vertex's distance can never later be beaten, which requires all weights to be nonnegative; a negative edge can undercut a 'finalized' distance without the algorithm ever revisiting it.
explanations.c: Negative weights say nothing about connectivity; the graph's structure is unaffected.
explanations.d: Standard numeric types represent negative numbers fine; the failure is algorithmic, not representational.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Dijkstra's shortest-path story.

items.text: Dijkstra designs the algorithm mentally on a cafe terrace in Amsterdam, without pencil or paper
Dijkstra uses the algorithm to demonstrate the ARMAC computer
The algorithm is published in Numerische Mathematik as a three-page note

questions.explanation: Dijkstra conceived the algorithm around 1956 as a demo for ARMAC, then designed it during the cafe episode as part of preparing that demo, and the formal write-up did not appear in print until 1959.

questions.prompt: Match each element of Dijkstra's 1959 note to its correct description.

left.text: 'A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs'

right.text: Numerische Mathematik, vol. 1, pages 269-271 (1959), three pages total
Single-source shortest paths, using nonnegative edge weights
Minimum spanning tree

questions.explanation: The three-page 1959 note covers both the shortest-path problem (nonnegative weights) and the minimum spanning tree problem in a single publication.

lessons.label: Bellman, Ford, and Moore: How Credit Gets Assigned

sections.heading: Four names, one algorithm, no coordination
sections.body: The algorithm taught today as 'Bellman-Ford' -- relax every edge in the graph, repeated V-1 times, tolerating negative weights as long as there is no negative cycle -- was not discovered once. Alfons Shimbel described the core relaxation idea in a 1955 paper on communication networks. Independently, Lester Ford Jr. described essentially the same method in a 1956 RAND Corporation report on network flow. Richard Bellman then published 'On a Routing Problem' in 1958, in the Quarterly of Applied Mathematics, framing the algorithm explicitly as an instance of dynamic programming -- his broader theory of breaking problems into optimal sub-solutions, which he had formalized only a few years earlier. None of the three appears to have known of the others' work at the time of publication; each arrived at nearly the same procedure from a different motivating problem (communication networks, flow routing, and routing-as-dynamic-programming, respectively).

sections.heading: Moore's maze, and why it belongs in the same story
sections.body: Edward F. Moore published 'The Shortest Path Through a Maze' in 1959, developed at Bell Labs in the context of routing calls through telephone switching networks -- literally finding a path through a maze of switches. Moore's algorithm is, in modern terms, breadth-first search: explore the graph in expanding layers outward from the source, guaranteeing that the first time a vertex is reached is via a shortest path, correct for unweighted graphs (or graphs where every edge has equal weight). Because BFS is a special case of the more general relaxation approach when all weights equal 1, and because Moore's paper predates or overlaps the wider adoption of Bellman's and Ford's results, his name is sometimes attached to the family as 'Bellman-Ford-Moore,' though many textbooks drop it and simply teach BFS as a separate, simpler algorithm for the unweighted case.

sections.heading: Why the field settled on a compromise name
sections.body: The name 'Bellman-Ford' itself is a compromise, not a claim about priority: it groups the two names most textbooks encountered first, largely because Bellman's paper reached a wider theoretical-computer-science audience through his dynamic programming framing, while Ford's contribution circulated as an internal RAND report rather than a journal article and so was, for a time, less visible in citations despite plausibly preceding Bellman's publication. Shimbel's 1955 priority is rarely credited at all in casual usage, a common fate for results published in adjacent fields (his was aimed at communication-network engineers, not the emerging algorithms community). This is not an unusual story in the history of algorithms: simultaneous, independent discovery is closer to the norm than the exception when a problem is 'in the air' -- reachable from several different starting motivations at once -- and naming conventions tend to freeze around whichever publication became most citable, not necessarily whichever came first.

lessons.workedExample: A telecommunications engineer in 1955-1959 could have arrived at the same core idea from three different desks: Shimbel modeling signal delay in a communication network, Ford modeling maximum flow along routes for RAND's transportation studies, and Bellman modeling a multi-stage decision problem where the 'stage' happens to be hops along a route. Concretely, all three converge on the same relaxation rule: for every edge (u,v) with weight w, if dist(u) + w < dist(v), update dist(v) to dist(u) + w. Repeating this rule for every edge, V-1 times over, guarantees the shortest distances are found in any graph without a negative cycle, regardless of which of the three motivating problems led there. Moore's telephone-maze problem, since all connections were equal-cost, needed only the special case of that same rule applied via BFS layers rather than full relaxation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'who really invented Bellman-Ford' is testing whether the student reaches for a clean, false answer (one inventor, one date) or can explain that Shimbel (1955), Ford (1956), and Bellman (1958) arrived independently, and that Moore's 1959 BFS solves the unweighted special case from an entirely different application (telephone switching) -- and can explain WHY the textbook name still favors only two of at least four contributors, which is really a question about how citation visibility, not priority, shapes the names algorithms end up with.

questions.prompt: Put these publications in chronological order.

items.text: Shimbel's communication-network paper
Ford's RAND report
Bellman's 'On a Routing Problem'
Moore's 'The Shortest Path Through a Maze'

questions.explanation: Shimbel published in 1955, Ford's RAND report followed in 1956, Bellman's paper appeared in 1958, and Moore's maze paper was published in 1959.

questions.prompt: What framing did Bellman specifically bring to 'On a Routing Problem' that distinguishes his contribution from Ford's or Shimbel's?

options.text: He was the first to allow negative edge weights at all
He framed the routing algorithm explicitly as an instance of dynamic programming
He proved the algorithm ran in O(V+E) time
He restricted the algorithm to trees only

explanations.a: Negative-weight tolerance is a property shared by the relaxation approach generally, not something unique to Bellman's version.
explanations.b: Correct -- Bellman's distinguishing contribution was casting the routing problem within his broader dynamic programming theory, which he had developed only shortly before.
explanations.c: The algorithm's running time is O(VE), not O(V+E), and this was not Bellman's specific claim to fame.
explanations.d: The algorithm works on general weighted graphs (without negative cycles), not merely trees.

questions.prompt: Why is Moore's 1959 algorithm sometimes included in the same lineage as Bellman-Ford, and sometimes taught as a wholly separate algorithm?

options.text: Moore's algorithm is breadth-first search, a special case of the general relaxation idea that applies when all edge weights are equal
Moore's algorithm predates and supersedes both Bellman's and Ford's work entirely
Moore's algorithm was developed for a different data structure (trees, not graphs)
Moore never published his method, so it is only informally associated with the name

explanations.a: Correct -- Moore's method is BFS, which coincides with the general relaxation approach exactly when every edge has equal weight (as in his telephone-maze setting), which is why it is sometimes folded into the family name and sometimes taught on its own.
explanations.b: Moore's paper (1959) follows Bellman's (1958) and Ford's (1956), and solves a more restricted case (unweighted graphs), not a superseding generalization.
explanations.c: Moore's algorithm operates on general graphs (the telephone switching network), not specifically trees.
explanations.d: Moore did publish, in 'The Shortest Path Through a Maze' (1959); it is a documented, not merely informal, contribution.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to the application context that led them to the same core algorithm.

right.text: Communication network delay modeling
Network flow / transportation routing at RAND
Multi-stage decision problems (dynamic programming)
Telephone switching network maze routing at Bell Labs

questions.explanation: Each researcher reached the same relaxation-based shortest-path idea from a distinct motivating application, which is exactly why the discovery happened independently and near-simultaneously rather than through shared collaboration.

lessons.label: The Minimum Spanning Tree, Discovered at Least Five Times

sections.heading: An electrical grid problem in 1920s Moravia
sections.body: The earliest known solution to the minimum spanning tree (MST) problem was not motivated by computer science at all -- computers did not exist yet. Otakar Boruvka, a Czech mathematician, published his algorithm in 1926 while working on the most efficient way to design an electrical power network for Moravia, minimizing total wire length while connecting every town. Boruvka's method works in rounds: every component simultaneously finds its cheapest edge leaving the component and adds it, which can merge many components in parallel each round, giving O(log V) rounds and prefiguring modern parallel and distributed MST algorithms by roughly six decades. Vojtech Jarnik, another Czech mathematician, gave a different vertex-growing approach in 1930 -- start from one vertex and repeatedly attach the cheapest edge connecting the growing tree to a new vertex -- which is exactly the algorithm taught today as 'Prim's algorithm.'

sections.heading: Rediscovery in postwar America
sections.body: The problem resurfaced independently in the United States without apparent knowledge of the Czech work. Joseph Kruskal published his edge-sorting approach in 1956: sort all edges by weight, then add each edge in increasing order unless it would create a cycle, using a union-find structure to test that cheaply. Robert Prim published, in 1957, the same vertex-growing method Jarnik had already described in 1930 -- a rediscovery so complete that the algorithm is now typically credited jointly as 'Prim-Jarnik' in careful historical accounts, though most courses still say only 'Prim's algorithm.' The same year, Loberman and Weinberger independently rediscovered Kruskal's edge-sorting technique, applying it to minimize wire length in digital computer circuitry (reducing capacitance and signal-delay effects from long leads). Dijkstra's three-page 1959 note, alongside its shortest-path result, contributes yet another independent rediscovery of the Jarnik/Prim vertex-growing method, not a new technique. This whole tangled history -- at least five substantially independent discoveries across three decades and two continents -- is documented in Ronald Graham and Pavol Hell's 1985 paper 'On the History of the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem' (Annals of the History of Computing, vol. 7), which traces solutions appearing in Czechoslovakia, France, and Poland going back to the start of the century.

sections.heading: The still-open frontier: is there a deterministic linear-time algorithm?
sections.body: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms both run in roughly O(E log V) time using standard heaps. The question of whether MST can be solved faster stayed open for decades until Karger, Klein, and Tarjan published a randomized algorithm in 1995 achieving expected O(V+E) time -- linear -- by combining a Boruvka-style round with a random edge-sampling step that provably discards most edges as irrelevant to the final tree, then recursing on what remains. That algorithm is randomized: its expected running time is linear, but no deterministic linear-time algorithm was known to match it. Bernard Chazelle closed most of that gap in 2000 with a deterministic algorithm running in O(m alpha(m,n)) time, using a data structure called a soft heap; alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, which grows so slowly that it is less than 5 for any input size that could physically be written down, making Chazelle's bound 'essentially linear' in practice. Whether a truly linear O(V+E) DETERMINISTIC algorithm exists remains an open problem in the field today.

lessons.workedExample: A network engineer designing fiber-optic cable routes between six data centers with known pairwise trenching costs could apply Kruskal's algorithm by sorting all 15 possible connecting edges by cost and adding each in increasing order, skipping any edge that would close a cycle among already-connected centers, using union-find to check that in near-constant time per edge -- stopping once 5 edges have been added (a spanning tree on 6 vertices always has exactly V-1 edges). The same engineer could instead run Prim-Jarnik's algorithm, starting from any one data center and always attaching the cheapest edge that reaches a not-yet-connected center. Both produce a minimum-cost tree, and for this small a graph both run comfortably fast -- the choice between Boruvka-round-based, edge-sorting, and vertex-growing strategies only starts to matter for graphs at the scale where the difference between O(E log V) and the essentially-linear O(m alpha(m,n)) bound is significant.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges familiar with the MST literature often ask which algorithm 'came first,' expecting the honest complication: Boruvka's 1926 electrical-grid solution predates Kruskal (1956) and Prim (1957) by three decades, and Prim's 1957 method duplicates Jarnik's 1930 result almost exactly. A judge probing this wants to see the student resist the tidy textbook story and instead cite Graham and Hell's 1985 survey as the source for that tangled priority, and separately wants to see the student know that the field's current open question is not 'can MST be solved fast' (Karger-Klein-Tarjan's 1995 randomized linear time and Chazelle's 2000 near-linear deterministic bound both answer that) but specifically whether a DETERMINISTIC linear-time algorithm exists.

questions.prompt: Put these MST milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Boruvka's electrical-grid algorithm
Jarnik's vertex-growing algorithm
Kruskal's edge-sorting algorithm
Karger-Klein-Tarjan's randomized linear-time algorithm
Chazelle's deterministic soft-heap algorithm

questions.explanation: Boruvka published in 1926, Jarnik in 1930, Kruskal in 1956 (with Prim's independent rediscovery of Jarnik's approach in 1957), Karger-Klein-Tarjan's randomized linear-time result in 1995, and Chazelle's deterministic near-linear result in 2000.

questions.prompt: What motivated Boruvka's original 1926 MST algorithm?

options.text: Designing an efficient electrical power network for Moravia
Routing telephone calls through a switching network
Sorting large datasets for early computers
Testing planarity of geographic maps

explanations.a: Correct -- Boruvka developed his round-based algorithm while working on minimizing wire length for an electrical grid covering Moravia.
explanations.b: Telephone switching motivated Moore's shortest-path work and Loberman-Weinberger's MST work, not Boruvka's.
explanations.c: Sorting was not the motivating application; computers as we know them did not yet exist in 1926.
explanations.d: Planarity testing is a distinct graph problem (see Hopcroft-Tarjan's later work), unrelated to Boruvka's motivation.

questions.prompt: As of the current state of research, what remains unresolved about MST algorithms?

options.text: Whether any algorithm can solve MST faster than exponential time

Whether a deterministic linear-time O(V+E) algorithm exists, given that randomized linear expected time (Karger-Klein-Tarjan, 1995) and near-linear deterministic time (Chazelle, 2000) are both already known
Whether MST can be solved at all for weighted graphs
Whether Kruskal's algorithm produces a correct tree

explanations.a: MST has been solvable in polynomial time since at least Boruvka's 1926 algorithm; exponential time is far from the actual state of the art.
explanations.b: Correct -- the open frontier is specifically the gap between Chazelle's near-linear O(m alpha(m,n)) deterministic bound and a hypothetical true linear O(V+E) deterministic algorithm, which has not been found or ruled out.
explanations.c: MST for weighted graphs has long-established correct algorithms (Boruvka, Kruskal, Prim, among others).
explanations.d: Kruskal's algorithm's correctness was established decades ago via the cut property; it is not an open question.

questions.prompt: Match each algorithm to its core strategy.

right.text: Every component adds its own cheapest outgoing edge simultaneously, in repeated rounds
Sort all edges by weight; add each in increasing order unless it closes a cycle
Start from one vertex; repeatedly attach the cheapest edge connecting the growing tree to a new vertex

questions.explanation: The three classical strategies are Boruvka's simultaneous round-based merging, Kruskal's global edge-sorting with cycle avoidance, and Prim-Jarnik's single-tree vertex-by-vertex growth.

lessons.label: Hopcroft and Tarjan: The Depth-First Search Revolution

sections.heading: Turning a walk into an instrument
sections.body: Before the early 1970s, depth-first search was understood mainly as a way to visit every vertex of a graph -- a traversal, not a tool for proving structural facts efficiently. Robert Tarjan changed that starting in 1972 by showing that the ORDER in which DFS discovers vertices, recorded as a simple 'discovery time' counter, contains enough information to solve several classically hard-seeming structural problems in linear time. His 1972 paper, 'Depth-First Search and Linear Graph Algorithms,' gives, alongside its SCC algorithm, a result on biconnected components and articulation points (vertices whose removal disconnects the graph): a single depth-first traversal, augmented with one extra number per vertex -- the lowest discovery time reachable via at most one back edge, called the 'lowlink' -- identifies every articulation point and every biconnected component in O(V+E) time, with no need to re-examine the graph a second time from scratch.
