B-trees fix this by making each NODE hold many keys, sized to fill exactly one page, so one page read retrieves an entire level's worth of branching decisions at once.

sections.heading: Branching factor B and height log_B(n)
sections.body: A B-tree's branching factor B (its minimum degree, often stated as the maximum number of children per node) is chosen so a full node's keys and child pointers exactly fill one disk page. With branching factor B, a tree holding n keys has height approximately log_B(n) rather than log2(n). The payoff is dramatic: at B=100 and n=100,000,000 keys, log_100(100,000,000) = 4, since 100^4 = 100,000,000 -- a lookup touches only 4 nodes, and since each node is one page, that is 4 disk reads. A balanced BINARY tree over the same 100 million keys has height around log2(100,000,000), about 27 -- roughly 27 page reads if nodes are scattered, nearly seven times slower for the identical lookup.

sections.heading: Split on overflow, merge or borrow on underflow
sections.body: B-trees stay balanced through structural operations at the NODE level rather than pointer-level rotations. Inserting into a full node causes it to OVERFLOW past its maximum key count; the fix is a SPLIT, in which the node's median key is pushed up into the parent and the remaining keys divide into two new, half-full nodes -- this can cascade upward if the parent is also full, and if it reaches a full root, the tree grows one level taller. Deleting from a node can drop it below the minimum required key count (UNDERFLOW); the fix is either to BORROW a key from an adjacent sibling that has keys to spare (rotating a key through the shared parent), or, if no sibling has spare keys, to MERGE the underflowing node with a sibling, pulling the separating key down from the parent -- which can itself cascade upward and shrink the tree's height by one level.

sections.heading: The B+ tree: linked leaves for sequential range scans
sections.body: Nearly every production database index is not a plain B-tree but a B+ TREE, a variant with two changes. First, all actual data (or row pointers) live only in the LEAF nodes; internal nodes store nothing but routing keys, so more keys fit per internal-node page, shrinking the tree's height further. Second, and more important for real workloads, the leaf nodes are threaded together in a LINKED LIST, left to right in sorted order. A range query like 'all rows where 50 <= key <= 500' descends once to find the starting leaf, then walks the leaf-level linked list forward -- a sequence of adjacent, sequential page reads -- instead of repeating a full root-to-leaf descent for every single matching key. Sequential reads are dramatically faster than scattered random reads on both spinning disks and SSDs, which is exactly why every major relational database's default index structure is a B+ tree.

lessons.workedExample: A database with 100 million rows builds a B+ tree index with branching factor B=100, giving height 4 (log_100(100,000,000) = 4). Finding a single row by key costs 4 page reads: root, then 3 more levels down to the leaf holding (a pointer to) the matching row. Now consider a range query for the 10,000 rows with keys between 50,000 and 60,000: the same 4-page descent locates the first matching leaf, and then the query simply follows the leaf-level linked list forward, reading roughly 10,000 / (keys-per-leaf-page) additional SEQUENTIAL pages -- a handful of fast, adjacent reads -- rather than repeating a 4-level descent 10,000 separate times, which is what a plain B-tree (with no linked leaves) or a binary search tree would effectively force.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating any project that touches a database will likely ask why the index is a B+ tree specifically rather than a red-black tree or a hash map -- the correct answer centers on the disk page cost model (one page read costs the same whether you use 1 key or 1,000 off it) and the linked-leaf range-scan advantage, not a vague 'B-trees are for big data.' Being able to compute an actual height -- log_B(n) with real numbers, not just the formula -- signals you understand branching factor as an engineered constant tied to page size, not an arbitrary parameter.

questions.prompt: Why is branching factor B in a B-tree typically chosen to match the disk or SSD page size (4KB-16KB)?

options.text: So that reading one node costs exactly one page read, maximizing keys examined per expensive disk access
So the tree uses the minimum possible memory
Page size has no relationship to branching factor; B is chosen arbitrarily
To make the tree perfectly balanced in the AVL sense

explanations.a: Correct -- since reading any part of a page costs roughly the same as reading the whole page, packing as many keys as fit into one page per node minimizes the number of expensive page reads per operation.
explanations.b: Minimizing memory is not the goal; minimizing the NUMBER of disk accesses is, even if it means using a full page per node.
explanations.c: The whole design principle of B-trees is precisely this size-matching; it is not arbitrary.
explanations.d: AVL-style balance is a different, in-memory notion; B-trees balance by height log_B(n) driven by page-sized nodes, a distinct goal.

questions.prompt: A B-tree with branching factor B=100 holds 100,000,000 keys. What is its height, and how many disk page reads does one lookup cost?

options.text: Height 4, so 4 page reads
Height 27, so 27 page reads
Height 100, so 100 page reads
Height 1, so 1 page read, since B-trees are always flat

explanations.a: Correct -- log_100(100,000,000) = 4, since 100^4 = 100,000,000, so a lookup touches 4 nodes and thus 4 pages.
explanations.b: 27 is roughly the height a BINARY tree would need for the same 100 million keys (log2(100,000,000) ~ 27), not the B-tree's height.
explanations.c: 100 is the branching factor itself, not the resulting height -- do not confuse the two quantities.
explanations.d: B-trees are shallow but not literally height 1 at this scale; height still grows (slowly) as log_B(n).

questions.prompt: In a B+ tree, why are the leaf nodes linked together left-to-right in a linked list?

options.text: To allow range queries to scan matching keys via fast sequential reads instead of repeating a full root-to-leaf descent per key
To make single-key lookups faster by skipping the tree entirely
Because B+ trees cannot support binary search within a node
It is a historical artifact with no current performance benefit

explanations.a: Correct -- the leaf-level linked list lets a range scan walk forward through sequential, adjacent pages after one initial descent, instead of re-descending the tree for every key in the range.
explanations.b: Single-key lookups still need the initial root-to-leaf descent; the linked list specifically helps RANGE queries, not point lookups.
explanations.c: Nodes still support ordered/binary search internally; the linked list is an additional structure layered on top for range scans.
explanations.d: This is precisely why virtually every production database index is a B+ tree rather than a plain B-tree -- it is a live, load-bearing performance feature.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a B-tree insertion follows when it causes a leaf node to overflow and that overflow cascades to the root.

items.text: Insert the new key into the appropriate leaf, exceeding its maximum key count
Split the overflowing leaf into two half-full nodes, pushing its median key up to the parent
If the parent now also overflows, repeat the split-and-push-up process at the parent's level
If the overflow reaches and splits the root, create a new root one level taller

questions.explanation: Overflow starts at the leaf where the key was inserted, and each split pushes the median key up to the parent; this can cascade level by level, and only grows the tree's height when the split reaches and divides the existing root.

questions.prompt: Match each B-tree or B+ tree term to what it means.

left.text: Where B+ trees store actual data/row pointers
Where a plain B-tree stores data

right.text: Fixed by splitting the node and pushing the median key to the parent
Fixed by borrowing a key from a sibling, or merging with a sibling
Only in leaf nodes, linked left-to-right
In any node, internal or leaf

questions.explanation: Overflow is fixed by splitting; underflow by borrowing from or merging with a sibling. B+ trees confine actual data to linked leaf nodes so internal nodes stay compact and range scans can walk leaves sequentially, unlike a plain B-tree which stores data in any node.

lessons.label: Skip Lists: Randomness Instead of Rotation

sections.heading: Pugh's 1990 structure: express lanes over a linked list
sections.body: William Pugh introduced skip lists in his 1990 Communications of the ACM paper 'Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees.' The core idea starts from a plain sorted singly linked list, where search costs O(n) because every node must be visited in sequence. A skip list adds extra 'express lane' layers above that base list: some nodes also participate in a level-1 list containing only every-other node (roughly), some of THOSE also participate in a level-2 list, and so on. A search starts at the topmost, sparsest level, moves forward as far as possible without overshooting the target, then drops down a level and repeats, funneling toward the target through progressively denser lanes -- similar in spirit to skimming a book's chapter list before flipping to a specific page.

sections.heading: Coin flips instead of balance conditions: p = 1/2
sections.body: The key design decision is how a node's height (how many levels it participates in) gets decided: not by any invariant checked and repaired on every insert, like AVL's balance factor or red-black's coloring rules, but by an independent random coin flip at insertion time. Each new node is promoted from level i to level i+1 with a fixed probability p (commonly taught as p = 1/2): flip a coin, and on heads the node also joins the next level up, then flip again, and so on until a flip comes up tails. This produces a geometric distribution of node heights -- most nodes stay at level 0, a smaller fraction reach level 1, fewer still reach level 2 -- and because the process is memoryless, no rebalancing step, rotation, or recoloring is ever needed. The expected search, insert, and delete cost with this scheme is O(log n).

sections.heading: Pugh's own claim and why RocksDB bet on it
sections.body: Pugh argued explicitly that skip lists match balanced trees' asymptotic performance while being 'significantly simpler to implement' -- there are no rotation cases to enumerate, no color invariants to reason about, just pointer arrays and coin flips. This simplicity has a second, practical payoff: skip lists are far easier to make CONCURRENT than rotation-based trees, because inserting a node into a skip list only requires splicing pointers at each level locally, without the cascading structural rewrites a tree rotation can trigger across a subtree. This is exactly why RocksDB's in-memory write buffer, the memtable, is implemented as a skip list (inherited from its predecessor LevelDB): a memtable must support concurrent inserts from write threads and concurrent iteration for reads/flushes at the same time, and skip lists make lock-free or fine-grained-locked concurrent implementations tractable in a way balanced-tree rotations do not.

sections.heading: The counterargument: probabilistic bounds and cache hostility
sections.body: The trade skip lists make is real, not free. Every complexity bound -- O(log n) search, O(log n) space overhead per node -- is an EXPECTED value over the randomness of the coin flips, not a guarantee. In the worst case, an adversarial (or simply unlucky) run of coin flips could promote every node all the way to the top level, degenerating the structure toward something no better than a linked list; this is vanishingly improbable but, unlike AVL's or red-black's proven worst-case height bounds, it is not RULED OUT, only made unlikely. The second real cost is architectural: skip list traversal is a chain of pointer dereferences scattered across separately allocated nodes at multiple levels, which is hostile to CPU cache behavior -- each hop is a likely cache miss, whereas a B-tree's page-sized nodes and even a compact array-backed structure exploit spatial locality far better on modern hardware.

lessons.workedExample: Building a skip list for keys 3, 6, 7, 9, 12, 17, 19, 21, 25, 26 with p=1/2: suppose during insertion, keys 6, 19, and 25 each happen to win one coin flip (promoted to level 1), and key 19 wins a second flip (promoted to level 2). Searching for 17 starts at level 2, sees only 19 there, and since 19 > 17, drops to level 1 without advancing. At level 1, it sees 6 (already passed), then 19 (still too far), so it drops to level 0 and walks node-by-node: 7, 9, 12, 17 -- found. The express lanes let the search skip past most of the list at the top levels and only pay the O(n)-per-level cost of the base list for the final short stretch, which is exactly how the expected O(log n) bound arises from purely random promotions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge comfortable with balanced trees may ask the pointed question: 'skip lists have no worst-case guarantee -- why would anyone use them in production?' The strong answer names the concurrency argument specifically (rotation-free local pointer splicing versus tree rotations that can touch a whole subtree) and a concrete deployed example like RocksDB's memtable, rather than a vague 'they're simpler.' A judge may also probe whether you understand that the probability parameter p is a tunable trade-off (higher p means more express-lane nodes, faster search, more memory) rather than a fixed law of the structure.

questions.prompt: How does a skip list decide how many levels a newly inserted node participates in?

options.text: By computing the node's exact position and using a deterministic balance formula, like AVL's balance factor
By an independent random process -- repeated coin flips at probability p, promoting the node one level per flip that comes up heads
Every node is placed at every level by default
Levels are assigned by an administrator when the list is created and never change

explanations.a: Skip lists deliberately avoid any deterministic balance computation or invariant-checking step -- that is precisely what distinguishes them from AVL or red-black trees.
explanations.b: Correct -- Pugh's design promotes each node level by level via independent coin flips at probability p, with no rebalancing step required afterward.
explanations.c: Placing every node at every level would make the structure no better than a plain array and waste enormous memory; only a shrinking fraction of nodes reach higher levels.
explanations.d: Level assignment happens per-node, automatically, at insertion time via the random process -- there is no manual or fixed administrative step.

questions.prompt: What is the actual nature of a skip list's O(log n) search bound, as opposed to AVL's O(log n) bound?

options.text: Both are worst-case guarantees that hold for every possible input and coin-flip sequence
Skip list's bound is an EXPECTED value over the randomness of promotions; AVL's bound is a proven worst-case guarantee regardless of randomness
Skip list's bound is a worst-case guarantee, while AVL's is only expected
Neither structure has any provable bound; both are purely empirical

explanations.a: Skip lists have no such worst-case guarantee -- an unlucky sequence of coin flips can (with vanishing but nonzero probability) degrade performance.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the fundamental asymmetry: AVL's height bound (1.44 log2(n+2)) holds for every input deterministically, while skip lists only bound the EXPECTED cost over their internal randomness.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual relationship; AVL is the one with the deterministic worst-case guarantee.
explanations.d: Both have rigorous mathematical bounds -- AVL a deterministic worst-case bound, skip lists an expected-value bound derived from the geometric promotion distribution.

questions.prompt: Why does RocksDB use a skip list for its memtable (in-memory write buffer) rather than a red-black or AVL tree?

options.text: Skip lists use less memory per key than any tree structure
Skip lists' local, rotation-free pointer splicing makes concurrent inserts and reads far easier to implement safely than tree rotations, which can touch a whole subtree
Skip lists guarantee better worst-case height than red-black trees
RocksDB's memtable does not need to support concurrent access, so the choice is arbitrary

explanations.a: Skip lists carry per-node pointer-array overhead for their levels and are not generally more memory-efficient than a tree node.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is Pugh's own argument extended to concurrency: local pointer updates at each level avoid the cascading structural changes rotations can require, which is critical for a memtable serving concurrent writers and readers.
explanations.c: Skip lists have a weaker, probabilistic bound, not a better worst-case guarantee than red-black's proven 2*log2(n+1).
explanations.d: A memtable specifically must support concurrent write threads plus concurrent reads/flushes, which is exactly the scenario the skip list choice is optimized for.

questions.prompt: Why is a skip list traversal generally more hostile to CPU cache performance than, say, a B-tree traversal?

options.text: Skip list nodes at each level are typically separate heap allocations scattered in memory, so each pointer hop is a likely cache miss, unlike a B-tree's page-sized, spatially local nodes
Skip lists require more comparisons per search than B-trees
Skip lists cannot be implemented in languages with garbage collection
CPU caches specifically block probabilistic data structures

explanations.a: Correct -- each skip list hop follows a pointer to a separately allocated node, defeating spatial locality, while a B-tree node packs many keys into one contiguous, page-sized block that the CPU cache handles well.
explanations.b: Comparison count is governed by the O(log n) bound in both cases; the cache issue is about memory LAYOUT, not comparison count.
explanations.c: Skip lists are implemented routinely in garbage-collected languages (Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap is a standard example); this is not a real constraint.
explanations.d: CPU caches have no awareness of a data structure's algorithmic nature; the issue is purely about memory locality of the actual pointers involved.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a skip list search for a target key, from first action to last.

items.text: Start at the topmost, sparsest express-lane level at the head of the list
Advance forward at the current level as far as possible without passing the target key
Drop down one level when no further forward move is safe
Repeat advancing and dropping until reaching level 0 and locating (or ruling out) the target

questions.explanation: Skip list search begins at the top, sparsest level, advances as far as possible without overshooting, drops a level when blocked, and repeats this funnel down to the base level 0 list, where the exact node is found or confirmed absent.

lessons.label: Splay Trees and Self-Adjusting Structures

sections.heading: Sleator and Tarjan's 1985 idea: move what you touch to the root
sections.body: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan introduced splay trees in their 1985 Journal of the ACM paper 'Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees.' A splay tree stores NO extra per-node information at all -- no balance factor, no color bit -- which already sets it apart from AVL and red-black trees. Instead, every single access (search, insert, or delete) ends with a SPLAY operation: the accessed node is repeatedly rotated upward until it becomes the new root of the entire tree. The structure carries no static balance guarantee at any instant; a splay tree can, at any given moment, look exactly like the degenerate linked-list worst case from lesson 1. What Sleator and Tarjan proved instead is a guarantee about SEQUENCES of operations over time.

sections.heading: The three splay moves: zig, zig-zig, zig-zag
sections.body: Splaying a node x up to the root proceeds via one of three moves, chosen by x's position relative to its parent and grandparent, repeated until x is the root. ZIG is the base case: x's parent IS the root, so a single rotation suffices. ZIG-ZIG applies when x and its parent are both left children (or both right children) of their respective parents -- the parent is rotated up first, then x is rotated up, both in the SAME direction. ZIG-ZAG applies when x is a left child and its parent is a right child, or vice versa -- structurally identical to AVL's double rotation, x is rotated up twice in OPPOSITE directions. The zig-zig case, rotating the grandparent before the parent rather than the reverse order, is the specific detail that makes the amortized analysis work; rotating in the naive order would not give the same guarantee.

sections.heading: Amortized O(log n) and the working-set property
sections.body: Using a potential-function argument (an accounting technique that assigns a 'stored credit' to the tree's shape and shows expensive operations are paid for by credit banked during cheap ones), Sleator and Tarjan proved that any sequence of m operations on a splay tree costs O(m log n) total -- an AMORTIZED O(log n) per operation, even though any single operation can cost as much as O(n) in isolation. A sharper consequence is the WORKING-SET property: accessing a key that was accessed t OTHER distinct keys ago costs only O(log t) amortized, not O(log n). This means splay trees adapt automatically to temporal locality -- a small set of hot, recently touched keys becomes cheap to re-access, which is a genuine advantage over AVL or red-black trees, whose cost per lookup is the same O(log n) whether the key was just accessed a moment ago or has been untouched for the whole program's run.

sections.heading: The fatal cost: a read is a write
sections.body: The mechanism that gives splay trees their adaptive advantage is also their most serious practical liability: SPLAYING HAPPENS ON EVERY ACCESS, including a plain search that never inserts or deletes anything. A 'read-only' lookup in a splay tree physically restructures the tree via rotations, moving nodes and rewriting parent/child pointers, exactly like a write. This means splay trees cannot support the classic concurrency pattern of 'many simultaneous readers, no lock needed, because reads do not mutate shared state' that works fine for AVL or red-black trees. Every lookup in a splay tree needs the same EXCLUSIVE WRITE LOCK a genuine insert or delete would need, because it genuinely is a write to the tree's shape. In any concurrent or multi-reader system, this single property can rule splay trees out entirely, regardless of how good their amortized bound or working-set adaptivity looks on paper.

lessons.workedExample: A cache implemented as a splay tree serves lookups for a small set of frequently requested keys (a 'hot set') mixed with occasional one-off lookups for cold keys. After the hot keys have each been accessed once, they cluster near the root because each access splayed them upward -- exactly the working-set property in action, so subsequent hot-key lookups are cheap (small t in the O(log t) bound). But if this cache is queried from ten concurrent reader threads, each lookup call must still take an exclusive lock, because each lookup's splay operation rewrites pointers throughout the path from root to the accessed node -- ten threads issuing pure reads simultaneously will serialize on that lock exactly as if they were all writing, defeating any hoped-for read parallelism.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows amortized analysis may ask you to explain WHY the zig-zig move rotates the grandparent before the parent, rather than the seemingly simpler reverse order -- being able to say that this specific ordering is what the potential-function proof depends on (naive zig-zig ordering does not achieve the same amortized bound) shows you engaged with the actual 1985 argument rather than a diagram. Equally likely: a judge asks whether a splay tree could replace a red-black tree in a multi-reader cache, and the strong answer is no, specifically because every read mutates the tree and therefore needs a write lock -- naming that exact mechanism, not just 'splay trees are slower,' is what a judge is listening for.

questions.prompt: What per-node balance information does a splay tree store, compared to AVL or red-black trees?

options.text: A balance factor, like AVL
A color bit, like red-black
None -- no balance factor, color, or any static invariant is stored at all
Both a balance factor and a color bit, for redundancy

explanations.a: A balance factor is AVL's mechanism; splay trees store no such per-node field.
explanations.b: A color bit is red-black's mechanism; splay trees have no coloring scheme.
explanations.c: Correct -- splay trees carry zero extra per-node state. Their guarantee comes entirely from the splay operation performed on every access, analyzed over time, not from any invariant checked at each node.
explanations.d: Splay trees deliberately avoid ALL such static bookkeeping; that is precisely what makes them structurally simpler, if behaviorally less predictable moment-to-moment.

questions.prompt: What kind of complexity guarantee did Sleator and Tarjan prove for splay tree operations?

options.text: A worst-case O(log n) bound for every individual operation
An amortized O(log n) bound over any sequence of m operations, even though a single operation can cost O(n)
A worst-case O(1) bound for every individual operation
No provable bound at all; splay tree performance is purely empirical

explanations.a: A single splay operation CAN cost O(n) in the worst case; the guarantee is about the total cost over a sequence, not any one operation alone.
explanations.b: Correct -- the potential-function argument shows any m operations cost O(m log n) total, giving an amortized O(log n) per operation despite individual operations sometimes costing more.
explanations.c: O(1) is far too strong a claim; splay trees do not achieve constant-time operations.
explanations.d: Sleator and Tarjan's 1985 paper is precisely a rigorous, proven amortized bound, not an empirical claim.

questions.prompt: What does the working-set property say about accessing a key that was accessed t other distinct keys ago?

options.text: It costs O(log n) regardless of t, identical to every other access
It costs O(log t) amortized, meaning recently accessed keys become cheaper to access again
It costs O(t) exactly, growing linearly with how recently it was touched
The working-set property only applies to the very first access of any key

explanations.a: This is exactly the behavior of AVL or red-black trees, which do NOT adapt to access recency; splay trees are different precisely because of the working-set effect.
explanations.b: Correct -- the working-set property gives an O(log t) amortized cost for a key accessed t distinct keys ago, meaning temporal locality is rewarded automatically.
explanations.c: The bound is logarithmic in t, not linear -- linear would erase any advantage over a plain linked list for hot keys.
explanations.d: The property applies continually to every access based on its recency, not just a special first-access case.

questions.prompt: Why can a splay tree not support multiple concurrent readers without locking, the way a red-black tree can?

options.text: Splay trees use more memory per node, which prevents concurrent access
Every access, including a plain search, splays the accessed node to the root, physically restructuring the tree -- so even a 'read' is a write and needs an exclusive lock
Splay trees are not thread-safe due to a bug in Sleator and Tarjan's original design
Concurrent readers are fine with splay trees; this is a common but incorrect belief

explanations.a: Memory footprint is unrelated to the concurrency problem here; the issue is structural mutation, not size.
explanations.b: Correct -- splaying occurs on every access, so a lookup mutates shared pointer state exactly like an insert or delete would, forcing the same exclusive-lock discipline onto reads.
explanations.c: This is not a bug to be fixed; it is an intrinsic consequence of the splay-on-every-access design itself.
explanations.d: This is backwards -- the inability to support lock-free concurrent reads is one of splay trees' most cited practical limitations.

questions.prompt: Match each splay move to the structural condition that triggers it.

right.text: x's parent is already the root
x and its parent are both left children (or both right children) of their parents
x is a left child while its parent is a right child, or vice versa

questions.explanation: Zig is the single-rotation base case used when the parent is the root. Zig-zig handles the same-side case by rotating the grandparent up before the parent (in that specific order). Zig-zag handles the opposite-side case with two rotations in opposite directions, mirroring AVL's double rotation.

lessons.label: Deletion: The Operation That Breaks Implementations

sections.heading: The three cases of BST delete
sections.body: Deleting a node from a plain BST while preserving the search invariant splits into three cases by how many children the target node has. LEAF (zero children): simply remove it; nothing else changes. ONE CHILD: splice the node out by connecting its parent directly to its single child, exactly like removing a node from a linked list. TWO CHILDREN is the hard case, because you cannot just remove the node without breaking the invariant for both of its subtrees at once. The standard fix, described by Thomas Hibbard in his 1962 paper 'Some Combinatorial Properties of Certain Trees with Applications to Searching and Sorting,' is to find the node's IN-ORDER SUCCESSOR -- the smallest key in its right subtree, reached by walking left as far as possible from the right child -- copy that successor's key into the node being deleted, and then delete the successor node instead, which is guaranteed to have at most one child (it has no left child by definition), reducing it to a case already solved.

sections.heading: The asymmetry Hibbard's rule introduces
sections.body: Hibbard's algorithm always promotes the SUCCESSOR (the right subtree's minimum), never the predecessor (the left subtree's maximum), even though either choice preserves the BST invariant equally well. This asymmetric, one-sided choice, repeated over many deletions, systematically shifts probability mass in the tree's shape: nodes from the right subtree get pulled upward slightly more often than an unbiased rule would. Jeffrey Culberson and J. Ian Munro's analyses in the late 1980s (notably their 1989 and 1990 papers on the behavior of standard deletion algorithms under prolonged updates) showed this bias is not a cosmetic curiosity -- it measurably degrades the tree's expected shape over time, in a way ordinary insert-only analysis never reveals.

sections.heading: The sqrt(n) result: a bug invisible in insert-only tests
sections.body: Culberson and Munro's central finding is that under a long sequence of random insertions PAIRED with Hibbard-style deletions (insert a random key, delete a random key, repeated many times, keeping the tree size roughly constant), the tree's expected height degrades toward Theta(sqrt(n)) -- dramatically worse than the Theta(log n) height a purely-random-insertion BST would have under Devroye's result from lesson 1. This is exactly the kind of failure a student's test suite is likely to miss entirely: a test that only inserts n keys and measures height will see near-optimal O(log n) behavior every time, because the degradation is a property of REPEATED insert/delete CYCLES, not of insertion alone. A plain BST (or even a naively 'balanced' one whose author only verified insert behavior) can look perfectly healthy in benchmarks and still silently rot toward sqrt(n) height in a long-running production system that both adds and removes keys continuously.

sections.heading: Why delete is where implementations and Big-O claims actually fail
sections.body: This same pattern -- delete being harder and more failure-prone than insert -- repeats across every balanced structure in this unit. AVL insert needs at most one rotation, but AVL delete can cascade up to O(log n) rotations (lesson 2). Red-black insert needs at most 2 rotations, but red-black delete needs up to 3, and its case analysis (of the deleted node's sibling and nephews' colors) is famously the part of red-black trees students get wrong even when they have insert working correctly (lesson 3). Culberson and Munro's sqrt(n) result shows the same pattern one level deeper: even the UNDERLYING mechanism used to physically remove a two-child node (successor promotion) carries a hidden, cumulative bias that only manifests over many operations. Any Big-O claim about a tree structure that was validated only against insert-heavy or insert-only test cases should be treated as unverified until it has also been tested against long alternating insert/delete workloads -- which is precisely the scenario real systems (caches, indexes, schedulers) run under continuously.

lessons.workedExample: A student implements a plain BST and a 'balanced' variant, then benchmarks both by inserting 100,000 random keys and measuring height -- both look great, with height near the Devroye-predicted 4.311 ln(100,000) ~ 50 for the plain BST. Satisfied, they deploy it as a session cache that inserts a new key and deletes an old one on every request, running for hours. Because every two-child deletion uses Hibbard's successor-promotion rule, the tree's height slowly drifts upward over the sustained insert/delete cycling, trending toward the Culberson-Munro sqrt(n) regime -- for n=100,000, sqrt(n) is about 316, over six times worse than the height their insert-only benchmark reported, and the student has no test that would have caught it, because their test suite never ran a long delete-heavy workload.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'did you test deletion?' is rarely satisfied by 'yes, I deleted a few nodes and the invariant still held' -- the sharper question is whether the test suite includes a LONG alternating insert/delete workload, since that is the only scenario where Hibbard's successor-bias and the sqrt(n) degradation actually appear. A judge may also ask you to walk through the two-child delete case by hand and explain why the successor (not an arbitrary node) is the only safe replacement -- being able to say it has at most one child, so removing IT reduces to an already-solved case, shows you understand why the algorithm is correct, not just that you copied it.

questions.prompt: When deleting a BST node with two children, why does Hibbard's algorithm specifically use the in-order SUCCESSOR (right subtree's minimum) as the replacement, rather than deleting the node directly?

options.text: The successor is guaranteed to have at most one child, so deleting it instead reduces to an already-solved simpler case
The successor is always a leaf node, making deletion trivial
Deleting the node directly would violate memory safety
The successor is chosen arbitrarily; any node in the tree would work equally well

explanations.a: Correct -- the in-order successor, being the leftmost node of the right subtree, has no left child by definition, so it has at most one child, meaning its removal falls into the already-solved leaf-or-one-child case.
explanations.b: The successor is not always a leaf -- it can have a right child of its own, which is why the reduction relies on the 'at most one child' guarantee, not zero children specifically.
explanations.c: This is not a memory-safety issue; the problem is preserving the BST ordering invariant across both subtrees simultaneously.
explanations.d: The choice is not arbitrary -- copying in a node that isn't between the two subtrees in sorted order would break the BST invariant.

questions.prompt: What did Culberson and Munro's analysis of repeated Hibbard-style delete/insert cycles find about tree height?

options.text: Height stays at the Devroye-optimal Theta(log n), since deletion does not affect the random-BST height bound
Height degrades toward Theta(sqrt(n)) under long alternating insert/delete sequences, due to the successor-only replacement bias
Height degrades to Theta(n), identical to sorted-input insertion
Height improves over time as more deletions occur

explanations.a: Devroye's result applies to insertion-only random BSTs; Culberson and Munro specifically showed delete cycles break that guarantee.
explanations.b: Correct -- always promoting the successor (never the predecessor) introduces a systematic bias that compounds over many delete/insert cycles, degrading expected height to Theta(sqrt(n)).
explanations.c: Theta(n) would match the fully degenerate sorted-insertion case, which is worse than the sqrt(n) degradation Culberson and Munro actually found.
explanations.d: The finding is a DEGRADATION, not an improvement -- height gets measurably worse over sustained insert/delete cycling, not better.

questions.prompt: Why can a test suite that only inserts n random keys and checks height completely miss the Culberson-Munro degradation?

options.text: The degradation is a property of long alternating insert/delete cycles, not of insertion alone, so an insert-only test never exercises the mechanism that causes it
The degradation only happens with negative keys
Insert-only tests always run too fast to observe any height change
There is no way to detect this degradation with any test, ever

explanations.a: Correct -- Hibbard's successor-promotion bias only accumulates across repeated DELETIONS interleaved with insertions; an insert-only benchmark never triggers it, so it looks perfectly healthy.
explanations.b: Key sign is irrelevant; the degradation is about tree shape and deletion mechanics, not the numeric values involved.
explanations.c: Test speed has nothing to do with whether the degradation mechanism is exercised at all.
explanations.d: A test suite that runs a long alternating insert/delete workload and tracks height over time WOULD detect it -- the point is that insert-only testing specifically fails to.

questions.prompt: Order these BST/AVL/red-black delete facts from LEAST rebalancing work required to MOST, per the structures covered in this unit.

items.text: Red-black delete: at most 3 rotations
AVL delete: up to O(log n) rotations, one at potentially every ancestor level
AVL insert: at most 1 rotation (single or double)

questions.explanation: AVL insert needs at most one rotation total, the cheapest case. Red-black delete is bounded at a constant 3 rotations regardless of tree size. AVL delete has no such constant cap -- it can require rebalancing at every ancestor level, up to O(log n) rotations, the most expensive of the three.

questions.prompt: Match each BST delete scenario to how it is resolved.

left.text: Node deletions repeated over many insert/delete cycles

right.text: Remove the node directly; nothing else changes
Connect the node's parent directly to its one child
Copy in the in-order successor's key, then delete the successor node
Expected height can degrade toward Theta(sqrt(n)) due to successor-only bias

questions.explanation: Leaf deletion is trivial removal; one-child deletion splices the parent to the child; two-child deletion copies in the in-order successor's key and deletes the successor node instead. Repeated over many cycles, that successor-only bias is what Culberson and Munro showed drives expected height toward Theta(sqrt(n)).

units.label: Hash Tables: Collisions, Load Factor, and Attack Surface

lessons.label: The Hash Function's Job

sections.heading: Three requirements, not one
sections.body: A hash function h maps an arbitrary key to an integer bucket index in [0, m). To make a hash table fast, h must satisfy three separate properties simultaneously. First, DETERMINISM: h(k) must return the same value every time for the same key within a single process run, or lookups silently fail to find keys they just inserted. Second, UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION: across the actual key population the table will see, outputs should spread roughly evenly across all m buckets, not cluster into a handful of them, because clustering turns O(1) buckets into O(n) linked lists. Third, the AVALANCHE property: flipping a single input bit should flip roughly half of the output bits, with no predictable pattern connecting input structure to output structure. Avalanche matters because real keys are rarely random -- they are sequential IDs, near-duplicate strings, or pointers -- and a hash without avalanche lets that structure leak straight through into bucket collisions.

sections.heading: Standard constructions
sections.body: The DIVISION METHOD computes h(k) = k mod m and is cheap but fragile: choosing m as a power of two makes h(k) equal to the low log2(m) bits of k and nothing else, so if those low bits are non-random -- which they often are -- the whole table degrades. This is why textbooks and production libraries alike push m toward a PRIME number, ideally one not close to a power of two, which mixes more of k's bits into the result. The MULTIPLICATION METHOD instead computes h(k) = floor(m * frac(k*A)) for a carefully chosen irrational constant A (Knuth recommends A close to (sqrt(5)-1)/2, the reciprocal of the golden ratio), and is less sensitive to the choice of m. For strings and variable-length data, production systems use dedicated non-cryptographic hash functions: FNV (Fowler-Noll-Vo, 1991) multiplies by a prime and XORs in each byte in a simple loop, and MurmurHash (Austin Appleby, 2008) mixes blocks with multiply-rotate-multiply-xor steps tuned to pass rigorous avalanche test suites like SMHasher.

sections.heading: The failure mode: structured keys under identity-mod-power-of-two
sections.body: The canonical hash table bug is using an identity or near-identity hash (h(k) = k) combined with a power-of-two table size on keys that are NOT random. Memory pointers on 64-bit systems are typically aligned to 8 or 16 bytes, so their lowest 3-4 bits are always zero -- mod-a-power-of-two on a raw pointer wastes those bits entirely and can collapse an 8-bucket table's effective range down to 1 bucket. Sequential auto-increment database IDs or millisecond timestamps behave similarly: consecutive keys differ only in their low bits, so mod-power-of-two maps long runs of them into the same small set of buckets, while the high bits (which do vary meaningfully across the dataset) are discarded completely. This is exactly why languages that expose hash tables over such keys either force a prime table size or run keys through a multiplicative mixing step before taking the modulus.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a table has m=16 (a power of two) and stores 64-bit pointers that are always 16-byte aligned, so their bottom 4 bits are always 0000. Computing h(p) = p mod 16 reads exactly those 4 always-zero bits, so h(p) = 0 for every single pointer -- all keys land in bucket 0, and the 'hash table' becomes a single linked list with O(n) lookups. Switching to m=17 (prime) forces the modulus to depend on higher-order bits that actually vary between pointers, restoring roughly uniform spread. This is why Java's HashMap XORs a key's hashCode with its own bits shifted right by 16 before taking the modulus -- it is defending against exactly this alignment failure on power-of-two table sizes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has implemented a hash table will ask why you didn't just use h(k) = k as a hash function, since it is trivially fast and deterministic. The strong answer names the specific failure -- aligned pointers or sequential IDs collapsing onto a handful of buckets because only the low bits vary -- rather than a vague 'it might not distribute well.' A judge will also probe whether you understand that uniform distribution is a property of hash-plus-key-population together, not of the hash function in isolation: a hash that is excellent for random strings can still fail catastrophically on a specific structured key set.

questions.prompt: A table uses h(k) = k mod 16 to store 16-byte-aligned pointers. What happens?

options.text: Distribution is uniform because pointers are effectively random addresses
All keys hash to bucket 0, because the low 4 bits of every aligned pointer are always zero
The table throws a runtime error since 16 is a power of two
Half the keys land in bucket 0 and half spread evenly

explanations.a: Pointer VALUES may look random at a glance, but alignment constraints make their lowest bits structurally identical across all keys, which mod-16 exposes.
explanations.b: Correct -- mod 16 reads only the bottom 4 bits, and 16-byte alignment forces those bits to 0000 for every pointer, so every key collides in bucket 0.
explanations.c: Power-of-two table sizes are legal and common; the problem is a silent performance collapse, not an error.
explanations.d: There is no random component here -- the alignment guarantee is absolute, so ALL keys collide, not half.

questions.prompt: What does the 'avalanche' property of a hash function require?

options.text: The function must run in constant time regardless of key length
Flipping one input bit should flip roughly half the output bits, unpredictably
The output must always be smaller than the input
The function must be reversible so the original key can be recovered

explanations.a: That describes a performance property, not avalanche, which is about how output bits respond to input changes.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the formal definition of avalanche behavior, and it is what prevents small, structured differences between keys from producing correlated (and thus collision-prone) hash outputs.
explanations.c: Hash outputs are typically fixed-width regardless of input size; this is not what avalanche describes.
explanations.d: Hash functions are intentionally NOT reversible (many keys map to one output); reversibility is unrelated to avalanche.

questions.prompt: Match each hash construction to its defining mechanism.

right.text: h(k) = k mod m, ideally with m prime
h(k) = floor(m * frac(k*A)) for irrational constant A
Multiply-rotate-multiply-xor block mixing tuned for avalanche

questions.explanation: The division method takes a straight modulus (best with prime m); the multiplication method multiplies by an irrational constant and keeps the fractional part scaled by m; MurmurHash uses explicit multiply-rotate-multiply-xor mixing designed to pass avalanche test suites like SMHasher.

questions.prompt: Order these table sizes by how much of a 64-bit sequential-ID key's variation each one actually uses under mod-m, from LEAST bits used to MOST bits used.

items.text: m = 4 (uses 2 low bits)
m = 16 (uses 4 low bits)
m = 1024 (uses 10 low bits)

questions.explanation: For a power-of-two modulus m = 2^k, h(k) = k mod m depends only on the lowest k bits of the key, so larger powers of two read more low-order bits: m=4 uses 2 bits, m=16 uses 4 bits, m=1024 uses 10 bits.

lessons.label: Collisions Are Guaranteed: The Birthday Bound

sections.heading: Pigeonhole: collisions are forced eventually
sections.body: The pigeonhole principle states that if you place more than m items into m containers, at least one container holds more than one item. Applied to hash tables: once the number of inserted keys n exceeds the number of buckets m, at least one collision is mathematically forced, no matter how good the hash function is. But pigeonhole alone understates the problem -- it only guarantees a collision once n exceeds m. The more surprising and more important result is that collisions become LIKELY far earlier than n = m, while the table is still mostly empty. That earlier, probabilistic collision threshold is described by the birthday paradox, and it is the reason every practical hash table needs a collision-resolution strategy long before it fills up.

sections.heading: The birthday paradox and its generalization
sections.body: The classic birthday paradox asks: in a room of n people, each with a birthday uniformly random among 365 days, how large must n be before there's a better than 50% chance two people share a birthday? The counterintuitive answer is n = 23 -- with only 23 people, the probability of a shared birthday already exceeds 50% (approximately 50.7%), even though 23 is tiny compared to 365. The reason is that the number of PAIRS grows quadratically: 23 people produce C(23,2) = 253 pairs, and each pair has a small but nonzero chance of matching, so the pair-count overwhelms the low per-pair probability. Generalizing to m equally likely 'days' (buckets) instead of 365, the expected number of items inserted before the FIRST collision is approximately sqrt(pi * m / 2). For m = 365 this gives sqrt(pi * 365 / 2) = sqrt(573.6) approximately 23.95, matching the classic result almost exactly. Applied to a hash table with m = 365 buckets, you should expect the first collision after only about 24 insertions -- roughly 6.6% of the table's total capacity.

sections.heading: The design conclusion: every hash table is a collision-resolution strategy
sections.body: The birthday bound generalizes to any table size: the expected number of insertions before a first collision scales as sqrt(m), not as m. A hash table with one million buckets, then, should expect its first collision after only around sqrt(pi * 1,000,000 / 2) approximately 1,253 insertions -- about 0.125% full. This sqrt(m) scaling, rather than a linear-in-m scaling, is the central quantitative fact that separates real hash table engineering from a naive mental model of 'collisions are rare until the table is nearly full.' No choice of hash function -- however uniform, however avalanche-compliant -- changes this asymptotic behavior, because it is a property of the pigeonhole/birthday structure of the problem itself, not of the specific function computing bucket indices. The practical consequence is that every production hash table implementation is, in truth, defined at least as much by its collision-resolution mechanism (chaining, open addressing, and their variants) as by its hash function; a 'collision-free' hash table is not a design that exists at any realistic load.

lessons.workedExample: A programmer builds a hash table with m = 1024 buckets and a perfectly uniform hash function, then is surprised when a collision shows up after inserting only 40 keys (3.9% full). Using the birthday-bound formula, the expected number of insertions before the first collision is sqrt(pi * 1024 / 2) = sqrt(1608.5) approximately 40.1 -- so 40 keys landing a collision is not a bug or a bad hash function, it is exactly the statistically expected outcome. If the programmer instead expected to need m/2 = 512 insertions before any collision (a linear-in-m intuition), they would misdiagnose a correctly functioning uniform hash as broken, and might waste time 'fixing' a hash function that was never the problem.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask a deceptively simple question: 'roughly how full does a hash table get before you see a collision?' A student who answers 'when it's nearly full' or '50% full' reveals they have not internalized the birthday bound and are reasoning from pigeonhole intuition alone. The strong answer cites the sqrt(m) scaling explicitly and can compute an example, showing the birthday paradox is not just a cute probability puzzle but the quantitative justification for why collision resolution is mandatory infrastructure, not an edge-case fallback.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people are needed in a room before there is a better-than-50% chance two share a birthday (365 possible days)?

options.text: 183 (half of 365)
366 (guaranteed by pigeonhole)

explanations.a: This assumes a linear relationship between room size and collision probability; the real scaling is quadratic in the number of pairs, so the true threshold is far smaller.
explanations.b: Correct -- with 23 people, the number of pairs (253) is large enough that the probability of at least one shared birthday exceeds 50%, even though 23 is far below 365.
explanations.c: 365 people would make a shared birthday almost certain, but far fewer people already cross the 50% threshold.
explanations.d: 366 people GUARANTEES a shared birthday by pigeonhole, but the question asks about the much smaller threshold for merely a 50% probability.

questions.prompt: For a hash table with m buckets and a uniform hash function, how does the expected number of insertions before the first collision scale with m?

options.text: Linearly in m (approximately m/2 insertions)
Approximately sqrt(m)
It does not depend on m at all
Approximately log(m)

explanations.a: This is the common but incorrect intuition; the real scaling is much smaller, on the order of the square root of m, not half of m.
explanations.b: Correct -- the expected number of insertions before a first collision is approximately sqrt(pi*m/2), matching the birthday paradox's sqrt(m) scaling.
explanations.c: The bound does depend on m; larger tables push the expected first-collision point later, just not linearly.
explanations.d: Logarithmic scaling would make first collisions occur far too early for large m; sqrt(m) is the correct order of growth.

questions.prompt: Order these reasoning steps that lead from pigeonhole to the design conclusion that every hash table needs collision resolution.

items.text: Pigeonhole: once n exceeds m, a collision is mathematically forced
Birthday paradox: pair count grows quadratically, so collisions become LIKELY when n is only around sqrt(m)
This sqrt(m) scaling holds regardless of how uniform or avalanche-compliant the hash function is
Conclusion: collision resolution is mandatory infrastructure, not a rare edge case

questions.explanation: The reasoning starts from the weak pigeonhole guarantee (collision forced once n > m), sharpens it via the birthday paradox (collisions likely far earlier, around sqrt(m)), notes this holds independent of hash quality, and concludes that collision resolution must be built into every hash table design.

questions.prompt: Match each table size m to its approximate expected number of insertions before the first collision, using sqrt(pi*m/2).

right.text: approximately 24
approximately 1,253
approximately 8.9

questions.explanation: sqrt(pi*365/2) approximately 23.95, sqrt(pi*1000000/2) approximately 1253.3, and sqrt(pi*50/2) approximately 8.86 -- in every case, the expected first collision arrives at roughly sqrt(m), far before the table is anywhere near full.

lessons.label: Chaining vs. Open Addressing

sections.heading: Separate chaining
sections.body: In separate chaining, each bucket holds a linked list (or, in modern implementations like Java 8+'s HashMap, a small balanced tree once a bucket gets long) of every key that hashed to that index. Insertion is O(1): compute h(k) and prepend to that bucket's list. Because buckets can hold an unbounded number of entries, chaining tolerates a load factor alpha = n/m greater than 1 without breaking -- performance degrades gracefully rather than catastrophically. The expected number of probes for a successful search is approximately 1 + alpha/2, and for an unsuccessful search it is approximately 1 + alpha, both derived from the expected chain length under uniform hashing. Deletion is trivial: find the node in its bucket's list and unlink it, an O(1) pointer operation once the node is located, with no side effects on any other key's ability to be found.

sections.heading: Open addressing: probing strategies and their clustering costs
sections.body: Open addressing stores at most one key per slot in the table array itself; on collision, it PROBES a deterministic sequence of alternate slots until it finds an empty one. LINEAR PROBING checks slot (h(k) + i) mod m for i = 0, 1, 2, ... -- it is extremely cache-friendly because probes touch contiguous memory, but it suffers PRIMARY CLUSTERING: once a run of occupied slots forms, any key hashing anywhere into that run extends it, and Knuth's classical analysis (The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 3) gives the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search or insertion as approximately (1 + 1/(1-alpha)^2) / 2, which grows explosively as alpha approaches 1 -- at alpha = 0.9 this is already about 50 probes on average. QUADRATIC PROBING checks (h(k) + c1*i + c2*i^2) mod m, which scatters probes further apart and avoids primary clustering, but introduces SECONDARY CLUSTERING: keys that hash to the same initial slot still follow the identical probe sequence, so they collide with each other at every step. DOUBLE HASHING uses a second hash function to determine the step size itself -- probing (h1(k) + i*h2(k)) mod m -- so two keys sharing an initial slot diverge onto different step sizes and rarely collide with each other twice, largely eliminating both clustering types at the cost of computing a second hash.

sections.heading: The open-addressing deletion trap: tombstones
sections.body: Deletion under open addressing cannot simply empty a slot, because probe sequences rely on the invariant that a run of occupied slots is unbroken -- searches for a later-inserted key that had to probe PAST the deleted slot would stop early at the newly empty slot and incorrectly report the key as absent, even though it is still present further down the probe chain. The standard fix is a TOMBSTONE: a special 'deleted' marker distinct from both 'occupied' and 'empty.' Searches treat a tombstone as 'keep probing past this slot,' while insertions treat it as 'this slot is available for reuse.' The cost is that tombstones accumulate over a mixed insert/delete workload: because searches must still probe past every tombstone, a table with many stale tombstones degrades toward the same O(n) worst case as a nearly-full table, even though many of its slots are logically empty. Production implementations address this by periodically REHASHING the entire table to physically compact it and clear all tombstones once their count crosses a threshold, trading an occasional O(n) compaction pass for consistently fast lookups in between.

lessons.workedExample: A cache implemented with linear probing at alpha = 0.9 experiences a sudden latency spike after a burst of deletions. Investigating, an engineer finds the table's fill ratio (occupied + tombstone slots, divided by m) has crept up over time even though the actual KEY count (alpha excluding tombstones) is well under 0.9 -- deletions replaced occupied slots with tombstones rather than freeing them, and searches must probe past every tombstone exactly as they would past a live key. Using Knuth's formula with the INFLATED effective alpha (counting tombstones as occupied) rather than the true key count explains the observed ~50-probe searches. The fix is a scheduled compaction: rehash all live keys into a fresh table, discarding every tombstone, which resets the effective alpha back down to the true load factor and restores fast lookups.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask 'why not just set the slot to null when you delete a key from an open-addressed table?' -- this tests whether the student understands that open addressing's correctness depends on probe-sequence continuity, not just the mechanics of removing a key. The strong answer explains the broken-search failure mode precisely (a later key becomes unfindable because its probe path is interrupted by a falsely 'empty' slot) and follows through to the tombstone-accumulation cost, showing awareness that the fix itself introduces a new maintenance burden rather than solving the problem for free.

questions.prompt: Why can't a slot in an open-addressed hash table simply be set to 'empty' upon deletion?

options.text: Because empty slots use more memory than tombstoned slots
Because a search for a later-inserted key that probed past this slot would stop early and incorrectly report the key missing
Because the hash function would need to be recomputed for all keys
Because open addressing does not support deletion at all

explanations.a: Memory usage is not the issue; correctness of the probe sequence is.
explanations.b: Correct -- probe sequences assume a run of occupied slots is unbroken, so an empty slot signals 'stop searching,' which would falsely hide any key that had to probe past this position during insertion.
explanations.c: Deletion does not require rehashing every key; only a targeted fix (tombstoning) at the deleted slot is needed.
explanations.d: Open addressing does support deletion, but only correctly when tombstones (not true emptiness) are used.

questions.prompt: Which probing strategy uses a second hash function to determine the step size between probes, largely avoiding both primary and secondary clustering?

options.text: Linear probing
Quadratic probing
Double hashing
Separate chaining

explanations.a: Linear probing uses a fixed step of 1 and is the strategy most prone to primary clustering.
explanations.b: Quadratic probing varies the step by i and i^2 but keys sharing an initial slot still follow an identical sequence (secondary clustering).
explanations.c: Correct -- double hashing computes the step size from a second hash function h2(k), so two keys with the same initial slot diverge onto different probe sequences.
explanations.d: Separate chaining does not use probing at all; it stores multiple keys per bucket via linked lists.

questions.prompt: Match each collision-resolution property to the technique it describes.

right.text: Runs of occupied linear-probe slots grow because any key hashing into the run extends it
Keys sharing an initial slot under quadratic probing always follow the same subsequent probe sequence
Stale deletion markers must still be probed past, degrading lookups even in a logically sparse table

questions.explanation: Primary clustering is linear probing's tendency for occupied runs to self-extend; secondary clustering is quadratic probing's identical-sequence problem for co-located keys; tombstone accumulation is the deletion-driven degradation where stale markers must still be probed past.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the lifecycle of an open-addressed table under a mixed insert/delete workload, from earliest to latest.

items.text: Keys are inserted using a probe sequence (e.g. linear probing)
A key is deleted and its slot is marked with a tombstone rather than emptied
Tombstones accumulate, and search probe lengths grow even though the true key count (alpha) is low
The table is rehashed into a fresh array to physically discard all tombstones

questions.explanation: Keys are first inserted via probing, deletions replace slots with tombstones rather than true emptiness to preserve probe-chain correctness, tombstones accumulate over time and degrade search performance, and periodic rehashing compacts the table to remove them.

lessons.label: Load Factor and Resizing

sections.heading: Load factor as the single space-versus-speed knob
sections.body: The load factor alpha = n/m, the ratio of stored keys n to bucket count m, is the single number that governs the space-versus-speed tradeoff in a hash table. Low alpha means most buckets are empty or hold one key -- fast lookups, but wasted memory. High alpha means buckets are crowded (chaining) or probe sequences are long (open addressing) -- memory is used efficiently, but every operation gets slower. Because this tradeoff is so central, every production hash table implementation picks a concrete threshold at which it triggers a resize, and the specific numbers differ by design philosophy. Java's HashMap resizes (doubles its bucket array) once alpha exceeds 0.75, a value chosen by Java's designers as a balance between space overhead and collision frequency documented directly in the class's own Javadoc. CPython's dict resizes once it is about two-thirds (2/3) full, growing the underlying array by roughly 4x for small tables and 2x for larger ones. Go's built-in map targets an average of about 6.5 entries per 8-slot bucket group before triggering additional bucket allocation, a threshold baked into the runtime's overLoadFactor check in its source.

sections.heading: Why growth must be geometric, not additive
sections.body: When a table resizes, it must allocate a new, larger bucket array and reinsert every existing key into it, since bucket assignment depends on m and changing m invalidates every key's previous bucket index. This reinsertion costs O(current size) work. The critical design decision is HOW MUCH LARGER the new array should be. GEOMETRIC growth -- doubling the table size (or multiplying by any constant factor greater than 1) -- guarantees that resize events become exponentially rarer as the table grows: the table resizes at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ..., so across a sequence of n total insertions, the total copying work summed across ALL resizes is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/4 + n/2, which is bounded above by n (a geometric series sums to less than twice its largest term, and here the largest term is n/2). That means the AVERAGE cost per insert, amortized over the whole sequence, is O(1) -- the total resize work across the entire history is only a small constant multiple of the number of insertions. ADDITIVE growth -- growing by a fixed chunk size c each time the table fills -- is a trap that looks reasonable but is asymptotically much worse: resizes now happen every c insertions, so there are roughly n/c resize events, and each one costs O(current size), which itself grows linearly, up to O(n). Summing O(current size) over n/c evenly-spaced resize points gives total work proportional to n^2/c, meaning n insertions cost O(n^2) overall rather than O(n) -- a quadratic blowup hidden inside what looks like a normal insertion loop.

lessons.workedExample: Consider inserting 1,024 keys into a table that starts at size 1 and doubles each time it fills (geometric growth): resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 512, copying 1+2+4+...+512 = 1023 keys total across all resizes combined -- essentially one extra full copy of the final table, for a total of about 2 * 1024 = 2048 units of work across 1024 inserts, i.e. O(1) amortized per insert. Now compare additive growth by a fixed chunk of 32: the table resizes at sizes 32, 64, 96, ..., 1024, which is 32 resize events, and the i-th resize copies roughly 32i keys, so total copying work is 32*(1+2+...+32) = 32 * 528 = 16,896 units -- over 8 times more total work for the same 1,024 insertions, and this gap widens without bound as n grows, since the additive scheme's total cost scales as n^2/c while the doubling scheme's stays at O(n).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge may ask why a hash table doesn't just grow by a fixed, predictable chunk each time it fills, since that sounds simpler and avoids 'wasting' memory on an aggressive doubling. The strong answer shows the arithmetic: additive growth turns a sequence of n inserts into O(n^2) total work because resize cost grows linearly while resize frequency stays constant, whereas geometric (doubling) growth makes resize events exponentially rarer as the table grows, bounding total copying work to O(n) and giving true amortized O(1) inserts. Being able to name a concrete production threshold (Java's 0.75, Python's 2/3, Go's ~6.5 per bucket) signals the student has looked at real systems, not just textbook asymptotics.

questions.prompt: Why does doubling (geometric growth) give amortized O(1) inserts, while growing by a fixed chunk size gives O(n) per insert over the whole sequence?

options.text: Doubling uses less memory overall, which speeds up every operation
With doubling, total copying work across all resizes is bounded by 2n; with fixed-chunk growth, total copying work grows as n^2/c
Fixed-chunk growth is only slower because it uses a slower memory allocator
There is no real difference; both approaches give the same asymptotic cost

explanations.a: Doubling typically uses MORE memory on average (up to half the array can be unused right after a resize), not less; the speed benefit comes from resize frequency, not memory footprint.
explanations.b: Correct -- doubling makes resize events exponentially rarer as the table grows, so the geometric series of copy costs sums to less than n, while fixed-chunk growth resizes every c insertions at a linearly growing cost, summing to O(n^2/c).
explanations.c: The allocator is not the source of the asymptotic difference; the difference comes from how often resizes happen and how much work each one does.
explanations.d: The asymptotic costs are genuinely different: O(n) total for doubling versus O(n^2) total for fixed-chunk growth.

questions.prompt: At what load factor does CPython's dict trigger a resize?

options.text: Approximately 2/3 full
Approximately 0.75 full, same as Java
Only when completely full (alpha = 1.0)
Approximately 6.5 entries per bucket, same as Go

explanations.a: Correct -- CPython's dict resizes once it is about two-thirds full, a distinct threshold from Java's HashMap.
explanations.b: 0.75 is Java HashMap's threshold, not CPython dict's; the two languages chose different values.
explanations.c: Waiting until alpha = 1.0 would already have severe probe-length degradation under open addressing; CPython resizes earlier, at 2/3.
explanations.d: 6.5 entries per bucket is Go's threshold for its bucketed map design, which is structurally different from CPython's open-addressed dict.

questions.prompt: Match each production hash table implementation to its documented resize threshold.

right.text: Load factor 0.75
About two-thirds (2/3) full
About 6.5 entries per 8-slot bucket group

questions.explanation: Java's HashMap documents a default load factor of 0.75 before doubling; CPython's dict resizes at roughly two-thirds full; Go's runtime map targets an average of about 6.5 entries per 8-slot bucket before growing.

questions.prompt: Order the bucket-array sizes at which a table growing by DOUBLING from size 1 would trigger successive resizes.
questions.explanation: Geometric (doubling) growth produces the size sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., each resize point exactly double the previous one, which is what keeps total copying work bounded to O(n) across the whole insertion sequence.

lessons.label: Amortized O(1) -- What It Does and Doesn't Promise

sections.heading: Aggregate analysis of the doubling sequence
sections.body: Amortized analysis asks not 'how much does the worst single operation cost' but 'how much does a whole SEQUENCE of operations cost, divided by the number of operations.' For a hash table that doubles when full, consider n total insertions starting from an empty table of size 1. Resizes happen when the table holds 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., up to n/2 keys, and each resize copies all currently-held keys into the new array. The total copying work across every resize in the sequence is the geometric sum 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/4 + n/2, which is strictly less than n (a geometric series is bounded by twice its largest term, and here the largest term is n/2). Adding the O(1) cost of each of the n ordinary (non-resizing) insertions, total work across the whole sequence is O(n) + O(n) = O(n). Dividing by n operations gives an AVERAGE of O(1) work per insertion -- this is the precise meaning of 'amortized O(1)': not that every insert is fast, but that the total cost of any sequence of inserts, divided by the sequence length, is bounded by a constant.

sections.heading: The hidden spike: one operation is still O(n)
sections.body: Amortized O(1) is a true and useful guarantee about AVERAGE throughput, but it says nothing about any SINGLE operation's latency. The specific insertion that triggers a resize must still copy every existing key into the new array before it can complete -- that one insertion genuinely costs O(n) wall-clock work, not O(1), and no accounting trick makes it faster in real time. For a batch job or an offline computation, this is a non-issue: the total time across millions of operations is what matters, and amortized analysis correctly predicts it. But for a system with a real-time or p99-latency requirement -- a web server responding to requests, a game server ticking at 60Hz, a trading system -- a single request that happens to trigger a table resize can stall for milliseconds while every other key gets copied, blowing through a latency budget that every other request meets comfortably. This is why amortized O(1) is often called a 'theoretical footnote' by systems engineers when the actual requirement is bounded worst-case latency per operation, not bounded average latency across a sequence.

sections.heading: Incremental (progressive) rehashing as the systems fix
sections.body: The production fix used by both Go's map and Redis's dict is INCREMENTAL (also called progressive or gradual) rehashing: instead of moving every key from the old table to the new one in a single stop-the-world pass, the resize allocates the new, larger array up front but moves only a SMALL, FIXED NUMBER of buckets on each subsequent operation, piggy-backing the migration work onto ordinary inserts, lookups, and deletes. Redis, for example, keeps both the old and new hash tables allocated simultaneously during a rehash and migrates one bucket (or a small fixed batch) per command processed, checking the old table only for keys not yet migrated and the new table otherwise; once every bucket has moved, the old table is freed and the rehash is complete. This changes the cost profile from 'occasional O(n) spike' to 'a small, bounded, CONSTANT extra amount of work added to every single operation during the migration window' -- true bounded worst-case latency per operation, at the cost of added code complexity (every read and write must now check two tables during migration) and a longer overall migration period spread across many operations instead of one.

lessons.workedExample: A real-time multiplayer game server uses a hash table to track connected player sessions, and player counts spike suddenly during a tournament. With naive doubling, the insertion of the player that pushes the table from, say, 65,536 to 65,537 entries triggers a full resize, copying all 65,536 existing entries -- at even 10ns per key copy, that is roughly 655 microseconds of added latency on that ONE player's connect request, which could miss the server's 16ms per-tick budget if it lands late in a frame along with other work. Switching to Redis-style incremental rehashing spreads that same 65,536-key migration across, say, 65,536 subsequent operations at 1 bucket each, adding only a small constant handful of extra work (checking two tables instead of one) to every operation during the migration window, with no single operation ever bearing the full O(n) cost.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read that hash tables are 'O(1) amortized' may assume this settles all performance questions, and a strong student corrects that assumption precisely: amortized O(1) bounds the AVERAGE cost over a sequence, not the cost of any individual operation, and the resize-triggering insert is a genuine O(n) event in real time. The judge will be impressed by a student who can name the specific systems response -- incremental rehashing, as implemented in Go's runtime map and Redis's dict -- and explain that it trades a single large spike for many small additions spread across the migration window, which is the correct engineering tradeoff when p99 latency matters more than total throughput.

questions.prompt: What does 'amortized O(1) insertion' actually guarantee?

options.text: Every single insertion completes in constant time
The total cost of any sequence of n insertions, divided by n, is bounded by a constant, even though some individual insertions cost O(n)
The hash table never needs to resize
Insertions are O(1) only when the load factor is below 0.5

explanations.a: This is the common misreading; amortized analysis explicitly allows some individual operations to be expensive as long as the sequence average is bounded.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the precise definition: the AVERAGE cost per operation across a whole sequence is O(1), while the resize-triggering operation itself is genuinely O(n).
explanations.c: Amortized analysis assumes resizes DO happen periodically; the guarantee is about their total cost being spread thin across the sequence, not about avoiding them.
explanations.d: Amortized O(1) is a statement about a full insertion sequence's average cost, not conditioned on a specific load-factor range.

questions.prompt: Why is naive doubling resize potentially unacceptable for a p99-latency-sensitive system, even though it is amortized O(1)?

options.text: Because doubling uses too much memory in the long run
Because the single insertion that triggers the resize is a real O(n) latency spike, which can blow a strict per-operation latency budget
Because amortized analysis is only a theoretical concept with no bearing on real systems
Because doubling causes incorrect lookups immediately after a resize

explanations.a: Long-run memory usage is a separate concern from latency; the issue here is a timing spike, not memory growth.
explanations.b: Correct -- amortized analysis bounds the average cost, not the worst single operation, and the resize-triggering insert genuinely takes O(n) wall-clock time, which can exceed a strict per-request latency budget.
explanations.c: Amortized analysis is mathematically rigorous and correctly predicts total/average throughput; the issue is that average throughput is the wrong metric for strict per-operation latency guarantees.
explanations.d: A correctly implemented resize preserves lookup correctness; the concern here is purely about the DURATION of the resizing operation, not correctness.

questions.prompt: Match each rehashing strategy to its latency profile.

right.text: One operation pays the full O(n) migration cost as a latency spike
A small, bounded amount of extra work is added to every operation during the migration window

questions.explanation: Naive doubling migrates all keys in one pass triggered by a single insertion, producing one large spike; incremental rehashing (as used by Go and Redis) spreads the same total migration work across many subsequent operations, each paying only a small constant extra cost.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of Redis-style incremental rehashing, from first to last.

items.text: Allocate the new, larger hash table while keeping the old one intact
On each subsequent operation, migrate one bucket (or a small fixed batch) from the old table to the new one
Route reads and writes to check the old table for unmigrated keys and the new table otherwise
Once every bucket has migrated, free the old table and end the rehash

questions.explanation: Incremental rehashing first allocates the new table without discarding the old one, then migrates a small fixed number of buckets on each subsequent operation while checking both tables during the transition, and finally frees the old table once migration completes.

lessons.label: Robin Hood, Cuckoo, and Modern Open Addressing

sections.heading: Robin Hood hashing: steal from the rich, give to the poor
