Fix the environment: same JVM/warm-up state (JIT warm-up alone can distort microbenchmark results by an order of magnitude if untreated, so use a proper benchmarking harness like JMH rather than a naive System.nanoTime() loop), same hardware, same input distribution across runs, and vary exactly ONE independent variable per run — bucket load factor, key count, or the on/off state of path compression, never several at once. For the union-find case specifically, the controlled comparison is: implement find with and without path compression (with union by rank held constant in both arms), then run sequences of union/find operations across a sweep of n, and plot the resulting AMORTIZED cost per operation against n. The signature to look for is a near-flat line for the path-compressed version (consistent with the famous inverse-Ackermann amortized bound) against a visibly growing line for the uncompressed version, and reporting BOTH curves on the same axes is what turns 'path compression helps' into a demonstrated, falsifiable result rather than an assertion.

sections.heading: The log-log plot, and the three questions judges will ask
sections.body: When the claim is about how a data structure's operation cost scales with n, the standard way to present it is a LOG-LOG PLOT: put n on a logarithmic x-axis and measured time (or operation count) on a logarithmic y-axis. On log-log axes, a POLYNOMIAL relationship (cost proportional to n^c) appears as a straight line whose SLOPE is exactly the exponent c — a slope near 1 confirms roughly linear behavior, a slope near 0 confirms roughly constant behavior, and a slowly-but-visibly increasing slope is exactly how you'd empirically distinguish 'amortized near-constant' from 'truly constant.' Three questions belong in every rehearsal for this branch of project, because they are the questions this entire unit exists to prepare you to answer cleanly: 'What is your worst case?' (state it precisely — e.g., a single union-find operation CAN cost O(log n) or worse before amortization kicks in, even though the amortized bound is far better); 'Is that amortized or average-case?' (these are different guarantees — amortized bounds a SEQUENCE of operations no matter the input, average-case assumes a distribution over inputs, and conflating them is the single most common judge-flagged error); and 'Did you test adversarial input?' (a hash table benchmarked only on random keys can hide catastrophic collision behavior that an attacker — or just unlucky real data — would trigger, so a credible experiment includes at least one deliberately adversarial or worst-case input alongside the random-case baseline).

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to empirically locate Java 8 HashMap's treeification threshold. They construct a set of keys engineered (via a custom class with a fixed, colliding hashCode()) to all land in the same bucket, then insert them one at a time into a HashMap with initial capacity forced to at least 64 to satisfy MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY. After each insertion they use reflection to inspect the internal bucket's runtime class, checking whether it is still a linked Node chain or has become a TreeNode structure. The measured transition should occur exactly at the 8th colliding entry, matching TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 in the OpenJDK source. Repeating the experiment while removing entries confirms the reverse transition back to a linked list once the count falls to 6 during a resize, matching UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6 — turning a line in the JDK source code into a directly observed, falsifiable measurement rather than a cited fact.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson exists because judges use exactly these three questions to separate a project that read about a data structure from one that tested it: precisely stating the worst case (not just the common case), correctly distinguishing amortized guarantees from average-case ones, and confirming the experiment included adversarial input rather than only friendly random data. A judge who hears a vague 'it's fast because it's O(1)' without a worst-case caveat, or who hears 'amortized' and 'average' used interchangeably, will immediately probe there — so rehearsing precise, separate answers to all three is the highest-leverage preparation for this entire branch of the fair.

questions.prompt: In Java 8's HashMap, under what exact condition does a bucket's linked list convert (treeify) into a red-black tree?

options.text: Whenever the HashMap contains at least 8 total entries, regardless of table capacity
When a single bucket reaches at least 8 colliding entries AND the table capacity is at least 64
When the table capacity exceeds 64, regardless of any single bucket's load
Only when explicitly requested via a treeify() method call

explanations.a: The threshold is per-BUCKET, not a total-entry count across the whole map; a map could have thousands of entries spread evenly with no bucket ever treeifying.
explanations.b: Correct — both conditions must hold: TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 colliding entries in one bucket, and MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64 for the table overall; below that capacity, the map resizes instead of treeifying.
explanations.c: Capacity alone doesn't trigger treeification; a specific bucket must also be heavily loaded (8+ collisions) for the conversion to happen.
explanations.d: Treeification is automatic and internal to HashMap's implementation; there is no public API to trigger it manually.

questions.prompt: A judge asks whether your union-find speedup claim is 'amortized or average-case.' What is the key distinction you should state?

options.text: They mean the same thing; either term is fine to use interchangeably
Amortized bounds the cost over a SEQUENCE of operations regardless of input; average-case assumes a probability distribution over inputs
Amortized only applies to sorting algorithms, not data structures
Average-case is always a stronger (harder to achieve) guarantee than amortized

explanations.a: Conflating these is exactly the error this question is testing for — they are distinct guarantees with different assumptions.
explanations.b: Correct — an amortized bound holds for ANY sequence of operations, worst-case included, once spread across the sequence; an average-case bound instead assumes inputs are drawn from some distribution (e.g., random keys), which adversarial input can violate.
explanations.c: Amortized analysis applies broadly to data structure operations (e.g., dynamic array resizing, union-find with path compression), not just sorting.
explanations.d: Neither guarantee is universally 'stronger' than the other; they answer different questions and neither implies the other.

questions.prompt: Match each experimental design element to what it protects the result from.

left.text: JIT warm-up / proper benchmarking harness (e.g., JMH)
Varying exactly one independent variable per run
Including adversarial or worst-case input, not just random input

right.text: Distorted timing measurements from an unwarmed or inconsistent runtime
Confounded results where you can't tell which change caused the effect
Hidden catastrophic-case behavior that only shows up on unlucky or attacker-chosen input
Difficulty reading off the scaling exponent directly from a linear-axis plot

questions.explanation: A proper benchmarking harness controls for JIT warm-up distortion; changing one variable at a time avoids confounds; adversarial input testing exposes worst-case behavior random inputs would hide; and log-log axes turn a power-law relationship into a straight line whose slope directly reveals the scaling exponent.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of designing this kind of falsifiable data-structure experiment, from first to last.

items.text: State a specific, falsifiable numeric claim (e.g., an exact threshold or crossover point)
Fix the environment and vary exactly one independent variable
Run the measurement across a sweep of the independent variable, including adversarial input
Plot the results (e.g., log-log) and compare against the predicted theoretical behavior
Rehearse precise answers to worst-case, amortized-vs-average, and adversarial-input questions

questions.explanation: A credible experiment starts from a specific falsifiable claim, locks down controls so only one variable moves, measures across a sweep including adversarial cases, visualizes the result against theoretical predictions, and ends with rehearsed, precise answers to the standard judge questions about worst case, amortized versus average-case guarantees, and adversarial robustness.

units.label: Computability Foundations: What Machines Can and Cannot Do

lessons.label: Decision Problems, Languages, and Encodings

sections.heading: A problem is a set of strings
sections.body: Complexity theory's founding trick is to strip a problem down to a yes/no question and then treat that question as a LANGUAGE: the set of all input strings for which the answer is yes. Take graph 3-colorability. Informally it is 'can this graph's vertices be colored with 3 colors so no edge joins two same-colored vertices?' Formally, fix an alphabet (say binary), fix an encoding scheme <G> that turns any graph G into a finite string over that alphabet, and define 3-COLOR = { <G> : G is a graph that has a proper 3-coloring }. A Turing machine 'solves' 3-colorability by deciding membership in this language — accepting strings that encode 3-colorable graphs and rejecting everything else, including strings that are not valid graph encodings at all. This reframing is what lets wildly different-looking problems (coloring, satisfiability, scheduling) be compared on identical footing: they are all just languages, and 'is this problem hard' becomes 'is this language hard.'

sections.heading: Encodings must be reasonable — and this is where knapsack's trap lives
sections.body: The encoding function <.> is not a free choice. Complexity theory requires a REASONABLE encoding: polynomial-time computable, injective, and — critically — using a SUCCINCT (typically binary) representation of numbers rather than a wasteful one. This matters enormously. Consider the input size of a number n: written in binary it takes about log2(n) bits, but written in UNARY (a run of n tally marks) it takes n symbols. An algorithm that runs in time proportional to n is polynomial in the unary input size but EXPONENTIAL in the binary input size, since n = 2^(log2 n). This exact gap is why the standard dynamic-programming solution to 0/1 knapsack, which runs in O(n·W) time (n items, capacity W), looks polynomial but is only 'pseudo-polynomial': it is polynomial in the numeric VALUE of W, not in the number of bits needed to write W down. Knapsack is accordingly called only WEAKLY NP-hard — it becomes easy if the numbers are written in unary, and hardness results that rely on this gap (versus problems like 3-SAT that stay hard under any reasonable encoding) are called STRONGLY NP-hard. Choice of encoding is therefore not bookkeeping; it is load-bearing for what 'polynomial time' even means.

sections.heading: Decision, search, optimization, and counting are different questions
sections.body: The same underlying problem spawns at least four variants. The DECISION version asks yes/no ('does a 3-coloring exist?'). The SEARCH (function) version asks for a witness ('produce a 3-coloring'). The OPTIMIZATION version asks for the best solution ('find the minimum number of colors'). The COUNTING version asks how many solutions exist ('how many distinct 3-colorings are there?' — this defines the complexity class #P). Theory standardizes on decision problems for two reasons. First, decision problems have the cleanest possible output (accept/reject), which is exactly what a Turing machine's accept/reject states model with no extra apparatus. Second, for a large class of problems the decision version and the search version are essentially equivalent in difficulty via SELF-REDUCIBILITY: if you have a fast decider for 3-COLOR, you can build a fast search algorithm by fixing colors on vertices one at a time and re-querying the decider to check that a solution still exists, recovering a full coloring in polynomially many decider calls. So proving the decision problem is hard (or easy) usually tells you the practical answer for the search problem too, which is why NP-completeness proofs almost always target the decision form even though nobody actually wants a bare yes/no answer in practice.

lessons.workedExample: Consider SUBSET-SUM: given integers a1..an and target T, decide if some subset sums to exactly T. The decision language is SUBSET-SUM = { <a1,...,an,T> : some subset of the ai sums to T }. Its standard DP algorithm runs in O(n·T) time — polynomial in n and in the VALUE T, but T's binary encoding only needs log2(T) bits, so the true input size is n + log2(T) and O(n·T) = O(n·2^(log2 T)) is exponential in that size. This is precisely why SUBSET-SUM (like knapsack) is only weakly NP-hard: rewritten in unary, the same DP becomes genuinely polynomial-time, whereas 3-SAT stays hard no matter how its clauses are written down.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'so what exactly does your algorithm's input size measure?' is probing whether you understand that Big-O claims are meaningless without a stated encoding. A student who can explain, unprompted, why an O(n·W) knapsack algorithm is NOT a polynomial-time algorithm in the complexity-theory sense — because W's bit-length, not its value, is the real input size — demonstrates they understand encodings as a technical commitment, not a formality, and can distinguish weak from strong NP-hardness on sight.

questions.prompt: Why is the 0/1 knapsack DP algorithm, which runs in O(n·W) time, called only 'pseudo-polynomial' rather than truly polynomial-time?

options.text: Because the algorithm uses recursion, and recursive algorithms are never truly polynomial
Because W's binary encoding takes only about log2(W) bits, so O(n·W) is exponential in the actual input size
Because knapsack has no decision version, only an optimization version
Because the DP table requires O(n·W) memory, and memory bounds don't count toward time complexity

explanations.a: Recursion/iteration has nothing to do with it; plenty of truly polynomial algorithms are recursive.
explanations.b: Correct — input size is measured in bits, and W's value is exponential in its own bit-length, so runtime polynomial in W is exponential in the encoded input size.
explanations.c: Knapsack does have a natural decision version ('is there a selection with value >= K and weight <= W?'); that isn't the issue here.
explanations.d: Memory usage is a separate resource from time and isn't why the algorithm is called pseudo-polynomial.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an encoding scheme used in complexity theory to be 'reasonable'?

options.text: It must be polynomial-time computable and represent numbers succinctly (e.g., binary, not unary)
It must use exactly one byte per symbol regardless of alphabet size
It must be human-readable so a judge can verify it by eye
It must avoid encoding negative numbers

explanations.a: Correct — reasonable encodings are efficiently computable and use compact (typically binary) number representations, which is exactly what rules out artificially inflating or deflating input size.
explanations.b: Byte-width has nothing to do with reasonableness; the requirement is about avoiding wasteful blow-ups like unary encoding.
explanations.c: Human readability is irrelevant to the formal definition.
explanations.d: Negative numbers are encodable just fine under standard reasonable schemes; this isn't a real restriction.

questions.prompt: Match each problem variant to what it asks for, using 3-colorability as the running example.

right.text: 'Is this graph 3-colorable?' (yes/no)
'Produce an actual valid 3-coloring'
'How many distinct valid 3-colorings exist?'

questions.explanation: Decision asks yes/no, search asks for a concrete witness solution, and counting asks how many solutions exist (the domain of the class #P) — three distinct questions about the same underlying combinatorial problem.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in reasoning about whether an algorithm for a numeric problem is truly polynomial-time.

items.text: Identify the numeric parameters in the problem (e.g., capacity W)
Determine how those parameters are encoded (binary vs. unary) and their bit-length
Express the algorithm's runtime in terms of the bit-length of the input, not raw numeric values
Classify the algorithm as polynomial-time or only pseudo-polynomial based on that comparison

questions.explanation: You must first spot the numeric parameters, then fix their encoding and bit-length, then re-express runtime in terms of bit-length (the true input size), and only then can you correctly classify the algorithm's complexity.

lessons.label: The Turing Machine as a Model of Computation

sections.heading: The single-tape deterministic machine
sections.body: Alan Turing's 1936 model, from his paper 'On Computable Numbers,' is deliberately austere: an infinite tape divided into cells, each holding one symbol from a finite tape alphabet (including a blank); a read/write head sitting over one cell at a time; a finite set of internal control states, one designated start state and one or more accept/reject states; and a transition function delta(state, symbol) -> (new state, new symbol, direction), where direction is Left or Right. A CONFIGURATION captures the machine's entire situation at one instant: current state, full tape contents, and head position. Computation proceeds by repeatedly consulting delta on the current state and the symbol under the head, writing a new symbol, moving the head one cell, and switching state — one micro-step at a time, nothing more. The machine HALTS when it enters an accept or reject state (or, in some formulations, when delta is undefined for the current state/symbol pair). Despite this minimalism — no random access, no built-in arithmetic, one symbol read or written per step — this model can simulate any algorithm a modern computer can run, given enough tape and time; it just may need far more steps to do it.

sections.heading: Running one by hand: a small example
sections.body: A classic teaching machine decides whether a binary string has an even number of 1s. States q_even (start, accept) and q_odd track the parity seen so far. On reading 0, stay in the same state and move right. On reading 1, flip between q_even and q_odd and move right. On reading blank (end of input), accept if in q_even, reject if in q_odd. Tracing input 1011: start in q_even; read 1, flip to q_odd, move right; read 0, stay q_odd, move right; read 1, flip to q_even, move right; read 1, flip to q_odd, move right; read blank, reject (three 1s is odd). This toy example demonstrates every core mechanic — configurations changing step by step, state as the machine's only 'memory' beyond the tape, and a decision reached only once the machine halts — that scale up, in principle, to deciding any computable language.

sections.heading: Variants, simulation, and why polynomial time is model-independent
sections.body: Several enrichments of the basic model are used constantly in practice: a MULTI-TAPE machine (several independent tapes with independent heads, useful for e.g. copying or merging without re-scanning); a NONDETERMINISTIC machine (delta maps to a SET of possible next moves, and the machine accepts if ANY branch leads to accept — this is the machine that defines the class NP); and the RAM / word-RAM model that real algorithms analysis actually uses, with indexed memory and O(1) arithmetic on machine words. The crucial theorem tying all of these together is SIMULATION WITH ONLY POLYNOMIAL OVERHEAD: any k-tape machine running in time T can be simulated by a single-tape machine in O(T^2) time (each single-tape step must re-scan across the represented multi-tape positions), and any RAM program running in time T can be simulated by a multi-tape Turing machine in time O(T · polylog(T)) or better depending on the exact RAM variant. Because every pair of these models can simulate each other with at most a POLYNOMIAL blow-up, a language decidable in polynomial time on one of them is decidable in polynomial time on ALL of them. This is precisely why the complexity class P is considered a robust, machine-independent notion of 'efficiently solvable' — and why the FINE-GRAINED constant-factor and low-order-term differences between, say, a 2n^2 algorithm and a 5n^2 algorithm belong to ordinary algorithm analysis (the Core), not to this machine-model discussion, where only the coarse polynomial-vs-not distinction survives translation across models.

lessons.workedExample: To simulate a 3-tape Turing machine on a single tape, interleave the three tapes' contents on one tape using extra track symbols (e.g., encode each cell as a triple of symbols, one per virtual tape) and mark each virtual head's position with a special marked symbol. Each single step of the 3-tape machine now requires the single-tape machine to sweep across the ENTIRE used portion of the tape to find all three marked head positions, read the relevant symbols, then sweep back to make the writes and moves. If the multi-tape machine runs for T steps, the used tape region grows to at most O(T) cells, so each simulated step costs O(T) single-tape steps, giving O(T^2) total — a quadratic, not exponential, overhead. This quadratic bound is why nobody worries about 'which model' when classifying a language as being in P: the classification survives the translation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson typically asks 'does it matter which computer you run your algorithm on?' The strong answer names the specific overhead bound (multi-tape to single-tape costs a quadratic slowdown) and explains why a quadratic — as opposed to exponential — overhead is what preserves membership in P across models. A weak answer just asserts 'computers are all equivalent' without being able to say WHY the class P in particular survives translation while exact runtimes do not; being able to draw that line shows real command of the model, not memorized vocabulary.

questions.prompt: A k-tape Turing machine running in time T is simulated by a single-tape machine. What is the standard overhead of this simulation?

options.text: No overhead — the simulation runs in the same time T
A quadratic overhead: the single-tape machine runs in about O(T^2) time
An exponential overhead: the single-tape machine runs in about O(2^T) time
The simulation is impossible in general

explanations.a: Some overhead is unavoidable because a single head must repeatedly re-scan to reach positions that separate heads could access independently.
explanations.b: Correct — each simulated step requires re-scanning the used portion of tape, which grows to O(T), giving O(T^2) total time.
explanations.c: The overhead is polynomial (quadratic), not exponential; this is exactly the fact that makes P model-independent.
explanations.d: The simulation is always possible; single-tape machines can simulate any multi-tape machine, just more slowly.

questions.prompt: Why is the complexity class P considered a robust, machine-independent notion of 'efficiently solvable'?

options.text: Because every reasonable model of computation can simulate every other with at most polynomial overhead, so polynomial-time membership transfers across models
Because P was defined specifically to only apply to the RAM model
Because nondeterministic machines are strictly faster than deterministic ones for every problem
Because Turing machines can access tape cells in O(1) time just like RAM memory

explanations.a: Correct — polynomial-overhead simulations between models mean 'polynomial time' is preserved regardless of which reasonable model you pick.
explanations.b: P is defined and studied across multiple models precisely because it transfers between them, not tied to one.
explanations.c: Whether nondeterminism gives a real speedup for all problems is exactly the open P vs NP question, not an established fact.
explanations.d: Turing machines only ever move one cell at a time from the current head position; this is a key difference from RAM's O(1) indexed access, which is exactly why the simulation overhead exists at all.

questions.prompt: Order the components of a Turing machine's operation from most fundamental/static to most dynamic during a run.

items.text: Finite tape alphabet (fixed for the whole machine)
Transition function delta (fixed rule table)
Current configuration (state + tape contents + head position)
Halting in an accept/reject state

questions.explanation: The alphabet and transition function are fixed once the machine is defined; the configuration changes on every step as the machine runs; halting is the final event that ends the run.

questions.prompt: Match each Turing machine variant to its defining feature.

right.text: Several independent tapes and heads working in parallel
Transition function maps to a set of choices; accepts if any branch accepts
Indexed memory access and O(1) arithmetic on machine words

questions.explanation: Multi-tape machines add parallel tapes for convenience, nondeterministic machines explore multiple computation branches at once and accept if any succeeds (defining NP), and the RAM model is the closer-to-hardware abstraction with constant-time indexed memory and arithmetic used in everyday algorithm analysis.

lessons.label: The Church-Turing Thesis and Its Rivals

sections.heading: Four formalisms converge on one class of functions
sections.body: In 1936, working independently, Alonzo Church published his LAMBDA CALCULUS characterization of 'effectively calculable' functions, and Alan Turing published his A-MACHINES (what we now call Turing machines) as an analysis of what a human 'computer' following a fixed mechanical procedure could do. Emil Post independently proposed his own machine-like formal system that same year, with strikingly similar structure to Turing's. GENERAL RECURSIVE FUNCTIONS came slightly earlier: Kurt Godel had formalized them in his 1934 Princeton lecture notes (transcribed by Kleene and Rosser), building on a suggestion from Jacques Herbrand, and it was Stephen Kleene who published the formal definition in 1936. When these four formalisms were compared, they turned out to define EXACTLY the same set of functions: anything computable by one is computable by all the others, via explicit translation. This convergence, from totally different starting intuitions (algebraic substitution rules, tape-and-head machines, recursive equations, rewriting rules), is the empirical evidence the thesis rests on. Notably, Godel himself was reportedly unconvinced that Church's lambda-definability or his own recursive functions had truly captured 'mechanical procedure' — it was TURING'S machine, with its transparent step-by-step manipulation of symbols by a bounded mind following simple rules, that Godel accepted as the persuasive formalization, and Turing's 1937 paper included a proof that his machines and Church's lambda calculus define the same functions.

sections.heading: A thesis, not a theorem
sections.body: The Church-Turing thesis states: every function that is 'effectively calculable' by any intuitive, informal notion of a step-by-step mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine (equivalently, is general recursive, equivalently, is lambda-definable). This CANNOT be proven as a mathematical theorem, because one side of the equivalence — 'effectively calculable by intuitive means' — is an informal, pre-mathematical notion, not a formal object. What the thesis has going for it instead is overwhelming convergent evidence: every rigorous formalization of 'algorithm' anyone has proposed since 1936 (register machines, cellular automata, most programming languages) has turned out to be equivalent in computational power. No one has ever exhibited an intuitively 'mechanically computable' function that a Turing machine cannot compute. That track record is why the thesis functions as the accepted DEFINITION of computability in the field, even though — unlike, say, the Pythagorean theorem — it is not something derivable from more basic axioms.

sections.heading: Live edges: the extended thesis, quantum computing, and hypercomputation
sections.body: Three modern debates sit at the thesis's boundary. First, the EXTENDED (or polynomial-time) CHURCH-TURING THESIS goes further than the original, claiming any physically realizable computing device can be simulated by a probabilistic Turing machine with at most POLYNOMIAL slowdown — not just that the same functions are computable, but that efficiency classes transfer too. Second, QUANTUM COMPUTING is the most serious challenge to that extended thesis: Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm factors integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer, and factoring is not known to have any classical polynomial-time algorithm, so if factoring is truly classically hard, quantum computers may violate the EXTENDED thesis — but they do NOT violate the original Church-Turing thesis, because a classical machine can still simulate a quantum computer's behavior, just with (believed) exponential slowdown; nothing new becomes computable, only faster. Third, various HYPERCOMPUTATION proposals — Zeno machines that complete infinitely many steps in finite time by halving each step's duration, closed-timelike-curve computers that exploit hypothetical general-relativistic time loops, and real-valued analog computers that use infinite-precision continuous quantities as if they were exact — have been proposed as devices that could compute the classically uncomputable (like the halting problem). None of these is accepted as a genuine refutation of the thesis, because each smuggles in a physically unrealized idealization (infinite precision, unbounded acceleration, or exotic untested spacetime structure) rather than describing a mechanical procedure a real, physically buildable device could carry out — and the thesis has only ever claimed to characterize computation by realizable mechanical means.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose someone hands you a lambda-calculus term that lambda-reduces to a normal form representing 'true' for exactly the natural numbers n such that a given Diophantine equation has a solution below n, and asks whether a Turing machine could decide the same set. Because Church proved lambda-definability and Turing computability coincide (and Turing's 1937 paper gave the explicit translation), the answer is immediate: yes, mechanically translate the lambda term into an equivalent Turing machine, with no loss of computational power in either direction. This is the everyday payoff of the 1936 convergence — results proven in one formalism (often lambda calculus, because it is convenient for functional-programming-style arguments) transfer automatically to Turing machines and vice versa, which is why theoretical computer scientists freely switch models mid-proof without re-justifying equivalence every time.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will ask 'can you prove the Church-Turing thesis?' The correct answer is no — and being able to say clearly why (one side of the equivalence is an informal, intuitive notion, not a formal mathematical object) distinguishes a student who understands the epistemic status of the thesis from one who has only memorized 'Turing and Church agreed on computability.' An even sharper follow-up, 'does quantum computing break it?', separates students who conflate the original thesis with the EXTENDED (polynomial-time) thesis from those who can correctly say quantum computers threaten only the efficiency claim, not the original computability claim.

questions.prompt: Why can the Church-Turing thesis not be formally proven as a theorem?

options.text: Because no one has ever checked whether Church's and Turing's formalisms agree

Because it equates a formal notion (Turing computability) with an informal, intuitive notion ('effectively calculable by mechanical means'), and the informal side cannot serve as a rigorous mathematical object
Because Turing machines cannot simulate the lambda calculus
Because it has already been disproven by quantum computers

explanations.a: This has been checked extensively and repeatedly; the formalisms provably agree with each other, but that's a different question from proving the thesis itself.
explanations.b: Correct — the thesis bridges a rigorous formal class with an informal intuitive one, and no proof can connect a formal object to an inherently informal one.
explanations.c: Turing machines and the lambda calculus have been proven equivalent to each other since Turing's 1937 paper; that equivalence is a genuine theorem, distinct from the thesis itself.
explanations.d: Quantum computers challenge at most the EXTENDED (polynomial-time) thesis about efficiency, not the original thesis about which functions are computable at all.

questions.prompt: Why does Shor's algorithm not refute the ORIGINAL Church-Turing thesis, even though it threatens the extended (polynomial-time) version?

options.text: Because a classical Turing machine can still simulate a quantum computer's behavior (just with believed exponential slowdown), so no new function becomes computable — only faster
Because factoring is not actually a hard classical problem
Because quantum computers are not physically realizable devices
Because Shor's algorithm does not run on a quantum Turing machine

explanations.a: Correct — the original thesis only claims about which functions are computable at all, and classical simulation (however slow) preserves that; only the polynomial-time EXTENSION of the thesis is threatened.
explanations.b: Whether classical polynomial-time factoring exists is unknown, but that's not why the original thesis survives; the survival comes from classical simulability regardless of speed.
explanations.c: Quantum computers are physically realizable (small ones have been built); that isn't the reasoning that saves the original thesis.
explanations.d: Quantum Turing machines are a standard formal model for quantum computation and are themselves simulable classically; the model choice isn't the point here.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of the Church-Turing thesis.

items.text: Church publishes lambda-calculus characterization of effective calculability (1936)
Turing publishes the a-machine model in 'On Computable Numbers' (1936)
Turing proves lambda-definability and Turing computability coincide (1937)
Shor publishes his polynomial-time quantum factoring algorithm (1994)

questions.explanation: Church's lambda calculus and Turing's a-machines both appeared in 1936; Turing then proved the two formalisms equivalent in 1937; decades later, Shor's 1994 algorithm raised the modern challenge to the polynomial-time extension of the thesis.

questions.prompt: Match each hypercomputation proposal to the physically unrealized idealization it relies on.

right.text: Unbounded acceleration: each successive step takes half the time of the last, completing infinitely many steps in finite time
Exotic, untested general-relativistic spacetime structure permitting travel into the past
Infinite-precision continuous quantities manipulated as if exactly representable

questions.explanation: Each hypercomputation proposal is rejected as a genuine refutation of the thesis because it depends on a physically unrealized idealization rather than a mechanical procedure any buildable device could actually carry out.

lessons.label: Universality: Code as Data

sections.heading: Godel-numbering: turning a machine's description into data it can be fed
sections.body: Turing's single deepest structural insight is that a Turing machine's own DESCRIPTION — its states, alphabet, and transition table — can be encoded as a finite string, exactly the same kind of object the machine operates on. Fix a scheme that assigns every machine M a unique string encoding <M>, essentially a Godel number (named for the numbering trick Kurt Godel used in his 1931 incompleteness proofs, where formulas and proofs are encoded as numbers so a system can 'talk about' its own syntax). Once machine descriptions are strings, you can build a single fixed machine U — the UNIVERSAL TURING MACHINE — that takes a string of the form <M, w> (a machine's encoding paired with an input) and simulates M running on w: reading <M>'s transition table to figure out what M would do at each step, and applying those moves to a working copy of w. Turing described this construction in his original 1936 paper as the 'universal computing machine.' The philosophical payoff is enormous: a SINGLE fixed piece of hardware (or fixed program) can execute ANY other machine's behavior, provided that machine's description is handed to it as input — the machine's behavior is no longer wired into the hardware, it is DATA loaded at run time.

sections.heading: From Turing's paper to your laptop: the stored-program computer
sections.body: This 'code as data' idea is not just theoretical elegance — it is the literal architecture of every modern computer. John von Neumann's 1945 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' proposed the STORED-PROGRAM architecture: instructions and data live in the SAME memory, addressed and manipulated the same way, rather than programs being wired into the machine via physical plugboards and switches (as on ENIAC, the EDVAC's immediate predecessor). This is exactly the Universal Turing Machine's design principle realized in hardware: your computer is a fixed piece of silicon (playing the role of U) that executes whatever program (playing the role of <M>) is loaded into its memory alongside the data that program will process. Loading a new app doesn't require rewiring the computer; it requires writing new bits into memory that the fixed CPU will interpret as instructions. Every time you install software rather than buy new hardware, you are relying on the same insight Turing formalized in 1936 and von Neumann architected in 1945.

sections.heading: How small can a universal machine be? Wolfram's prize and the Smith controversy
sections.body: A natural follow-up question: what is the SIMPLEST possible universal Turing machine — fewest states times symbols? Researchers built progressively smaller universal machines through the late 20th century (Marvin Minsky, Yurii Rogozhin, and others produced small universal machines with various state/symbol counts). In his 2002 book 'A New Kind of Science,' Stephen Wolfram conjectured that a particular extremely simple 2-state, 3-symbol machine he had studied was universal, and in May 2007 the Wolfram Science group offered a $25,000 prize for a proof or disproof. In October 2007, Alex Smith, then an undergraduate electronics and computing student at the University of Birmingham, submitted a 40-page proof that the machine IS universal, and the prize was awarded. But the result immediately drew controversy, and the crux is worth stating precisely. Smith's construction does not start the machine on the conventional all-blank tape. It starts it on an infinite, non-blank background that is deliberately NON-PERIODIC (non-repetitive) — and the non-periodicity is not an incidental detail, it is load-bearing. Smith's own proof notes that a merely repetitive background would not do the job: the process generating it 'is clearly not universal,' in analogy to the Thue-Morse sequence. So the background must be non-repetitive enough to carry an unbounded computation, yet still simple enough that constructing it is not itself doing the universal work — Smith builds it by a recursive doubling procedure whose limit supplies the initial condition. That balancing act is exactly what critics attacked. Vaughan Pratt publicly challenged the proof, arguing that similar liberties would let a linear bounded automaton count as universal, contradicting a known non-universality result (Smith replied that his construction restarts automatically, with no external intervention). Because the machine requires an infinite non-periodic initial configuration and never halts, the result is usually filed as 'weakly universal' rather than universal in the standard sense: the objection is that some of the computational work is smuggled into the non-standard starting condition rather than living in the machine itself. The episode is a live illustration that even a seemingly crisp yes/no mathematical question ('is this machine universal?') can hinge on a definitional choice the prize's rules left unresolved.

lessons.workedExample: To build intuition for U(<M>, w), imagine M is the simple even-parity checker from the previous lesson, with its two states and transition rules. Encoding <M> means writing down, as a string, a full table: for each (state, symbol) pair, the resulting (new state, new symbol, direction). U's job, given <M> and an input w like '1011', is to maintain a working copy of w on part of its tape, keep a marker for M's 'current state' as data on another part of the tape, and on each round: look up the current (state, symbol) pair in the encoded table <M>, find the matching rule, and apply the write/move/state-change to the working tape — exactly the way an interpreter reads bytecode instructions and executes them one at a time rather than compiling them into fixed circuitry beforehand. This is precisely why universal machines are also called the theoretical ancestor of interpreters.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does it actually mean for code to be data?' is testing whether a student can connect Turing's abstract Godel-numbering trick to something concrete: the stored-program architecture that makes installing software possible without rewiring hardware. A stronger follow-up — 'is smaller always better for a universal machine, and does smaller ever stop counting as universal?' — invites the Wolfram-prize controversy. A student who can explain that Smith's proof was disputed specifically because of its NON-STANDARD initial tape — infinite, non-blank, and non-periodic, since a merely periodic background provably would not yield universality — shows they understand that universality claims carry real technical fine print, not just a headline result. The sharpest version of that answer names the tension: the background must be non-repetitive enough to support unbounded computation, but simple enough that building it isn't itself the universal computation.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a Universal Turing Machine U to take input <M, w>?

options.text: U is a different physical machine built new for every M
U is one fixed machine that reads an encoding of M's transition table as data and simulates M's behavior on w
U only works if M happens to be universal itself
U converts w into a different alphabet before running M directly on the hardware

explanations.a: This is exactly what universality avoids — one FIXED U handles arbitrarily many different M's without being rebuilt.
explanations.b: Correct — U treats M's description as ordinary input data and interprets it step by step to reproduce M's behavior on w.
explanations.c: U can simulate any machine M, universal or not; M does not need any special property beyond being a valid Turing machine description.
explanations.d: There's no alphabet conversion trick; U directly reads the encoded transition table and applies it to a working copy of w.

questions.prompt: What was the central objection critics raised against Alex Smith's 2007 proof that Wolfram's 2-state, 3-symbol machine is universal?

options.text: The proof had no formal write-up at all

The machine only achieves universality when started on an infinite, non-blank, non-periodic initial tape rather than the conventional all-blank tape, which critics argued smuggles work into the starting condition rather than the machine itself
The machine was later shown not to halt on any input
Wolfram had already proven the opposite result years earlier

explanations.a: Smith submitted a detailed 40-page proof; the dispute was about its validity and definitional scope, not its existence.
explanations.b: Correct — the objection (raised by Vaughan Pratt) centers on the non-standard initial condition. The background must be non-periodic: Smith's proof itself notes a merely repetitive background would not give universality, so the tape is built by a recursive doubling procedure. That the starting condition has to be that carefully structured is precisely why the result is usually called only 'weakly universal.'
explanations.c: The machine indeed never halts under Smith's construction, but that alone isn't the crux — the dispute is about what counts as a fair starting condition for claiming universality.
explanations.d: No prior proof of the opposite existed; this was an open question Wolfram posed a prize for in 2007.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the history of 'code as data' and universal machines.

items.text: Godel encodes formulas and proofs as numbers in his incompleteness proofs (1931)
Turing describes the universal computing machine in 'On Computable Numbers' (1936)
Von Neumann's EDVAC draft proposes the stored-program architecture (1945)
Wolfram offers a prize for resolving universality of the 2-state, 3-symbol machine (2007)

questions.explanation: Godel's 1931 numbering trick predates and inspires the general idea of encoding descriptions as data; Turing applied this to build the universal machine in 1936; von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC draft realized the idea in physical computer architecture; the Wolfram prize and its 2007 resolution came much later as a question about minimal universal machines.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to their specific contribution to the 'code as data' story.

right.text: Pioneered encoding formulas/proofs as numbers, inspiring Godel-numbering of machine descriptions
Proposed the stored-program architecture where instructions and data share memory
Submitted the disputed 2007 proof that a 2-state, 3-symbol machine is universal

questions.explanation: Godel's 1931 numbering scheme is the conceptual ancestor of Godel-numbering machine descriptions; von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC draft turned 'code as data' into real computer architecture; Alex Smith's 2007 proof (and its subsequent controversy) is the modern minimal-universal-machine chapter of the story.

lessons.label: Diagonalization: Why Most Problems Are Uncomputable

sections.heading: Cantor's 1891 diagonal argument
sections.body: Georg Cantor's 1891 diagonal argument shows that no list can ever contain every infinite binary sequence, even though there are infinitely many rows to work with. Suppose, for contradiction, someone claims to have listed ALL infinite binary sequences as rows s1, s2, s3, ... Construct a new sequence d by looking at the diagonal: d's n-th bit is defined to be the OPPOSITE of the n-th bit of sn. By construction, d differs from s1 in position 1, from s2 in position 2, from s3 in position 3, and so on — d differs from EVERY sequence on the list in at least one position, so d cannot equal any si, yet d is itself a valid infinite binary sequence. This contradicts the assumption that the list was complete. The conclusion: the set of infinite binary sequences cannot be placed in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers — it is UNCOUNTABLE, a strictly larger infinity than the countable infinity of the naturals, which Cantor and later set theorists denote aleph-null. This single argument, originally about numbers, becomes the exact mathematical engine behind proving most computational problems have no algorithm at all.

sections.heading: Counting programs: only aleph-null of them
sections.body: A Turing machine's complete description — its states, alphabet, and transition table — is, after encoding, just a finite string of symbols from a finite alphabet. The set of ALL finite strings over a finite alphabet is COUNTABLE: you can enumerate every string of length 0, then every string of length 1, then length 2, and so on, and every individual string appears at some finite position in that enumeration. So the set of all possible Turing machine descriptions — equivalently, the set of all possible programs, in any programming language, since program text is also just a finite string — is countable: there are exactly aleph-null of them, one for each natural number in the enumeration. This holds no matter how generously you define 'program': whether you allow arbitrarily long code, arbitrarily many variable names, or arbitrarily deep nesting, the KEY constraint is that each individual program must be a FINITE string, and the set of finite strings over any finite (or countable) alphabet is always countable.

sections.heading: Counting languages: uncountably many, so almost none are computable
sections.body: Now count the LANGUAGES over a fixed alphabet like {0,1} — recall from Lesson 1 that every decision problem IS a language, a subset of all possible strings. The set of all finite binary strings is countably infinite (aleph-null strings). But the set of all SUBSETS of a countably infinite set — by Cantor's theorem, a generalization of the diagonal argument — has size 2 raised to aleph-null, which Cantor proved is STRICTLY LARGER than aleph-null itself (this is essentially the same diagonalization: assume you've listed all subsets, build a new subset that diagonally differs from each one, contradiction). So there are 2^aleph-null possible languages over {0,1}, but only aleph-null possible Turing machines to decide them. Since a strictly larger infinity cannot be covered by a strictly smaller one, the vast majority of languages — 'almost all' of them, in a precise cardinality sense — have NO Turing machine that decides them. Crucially, this counting argument is purely existential: it proves uncomputable languages must exist without exhibiting even one specific example, which is exactly why the next lesson is needed to name and prove undecidable a single concrete, famous problem (the halting problem) rather than resting on this abstract cardinality mismatch alone.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose you tried to 'cheat' the counting argument by allowing programs to be infinitely long, hoping to get 2^aleph-null many programs to match the 2^aleph-null many languages. This fails: a Turing machine's transition table must be finite for the machine to be a well-defined finite object you can write down, encode, and hand to a universal machine — an 'infinite program' isn't a Turing machine at all under the standard definition, and even generous formalizations (allowing unbounded but always-finite length) still only produce a countable set, because the union of countably many finite-length classes (all length-1 strings, all length-2 strings, all length-3 strings, ...) is still countable. The mismatch between countably many finite programs and uncountably many languages is fundamental, not a technicality that a cleverer encoding scheme could dodge.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'so if the halting problem is undecidable, is it some rare exception?' is testing whether a student understands the cardinality argument BEHIND named undecidable problems. The strong answer flips the framing: undecidability isn't rare, computability is — countably many programs can never cover uncountably many languages, so almost every language is uncomputable, and the famous named examples like the halting problem are just the ones we can point to and prove explicitly, not the exhaustive list of what's uncomputable.

questions.prompt: In Cantor's diagonal argument, why must the constructed sequence d differ from every sequence si on the assumed complete list?

options.text: Because d's n-th bit is defined as the opposite of sn's n-th bit, so d and sn differ in at least position n for every n
Because d is chosen to be the all-zero sequence, which cannot appear on any list
Because the list only contains finite sequences, and d is infinite
Because d is defined recursively, and no computable sequence can be listed

explanations.a: Correct — flipping the n-th bit relative to sn guarantees a difference at position n specifically, for every n, so d cannot coincide with any single row.
explanations.b: d is NOT simply the all-zero sequence; it is built by flipping each si's diagonal bit, which is what forces the difference from every row.
explanations.c: The list is assumed to contain infinite binary sequences already; the mismatch is about countability, not finiteness of the sequences.
explanations.d: This mixes up the diagonal argument for cardinality with computability arguments; the diagonal construction here is purely about set sizes, no notion of computability is involved yet.

questions.prompt: Why is the set of all possible Turing machine descriptions countable (size aleph-null)?

options.text: Because every Turing machine description is a finite string over a finite alphabet, and the set of all finite strings over a finite alphabet can be enumerated by increasing length
Because there are only finitely many Turing machines in total
Because Turing machines can only decide finite languages
Because the halting problem limits how many machines can exist

explanations.a: Correct — enumerating all strings of length 0, then 1, then 2, etc. lists every finite string exactly once, giving a countable set of possible machine descriptions.
explanations.b: There are infinitely many Turing machines (you can always add more states); the claim is that this infinity is countable, not that it's finite.
explanations.c: Turing machines can decide infinite languages (e.g., 'all even-length strings'); this isn't why the set of descriptions is countable.
explanations.d: The halting problem's undecidability is a separate later result and doesn't bound how many machine descriptions exist.

questions.prompt: What does the counting/cardinality argument in this lesson actually prove?

options.text: That uncomputable languages must exist, without identifying any specific one
That the halting problem specifically is undecidable
That every language over {0,1} is uncomputable
That P does not equal NP

explanations.a: Correct — this is a purely existential, non-constructive argument: since there are more languages than programs, most languages have no deciding program, but no single uncomputable language is named or exhibited yet.
explanations.b: Proving the halting problem specifically undecidable requires the explicit diagonalization construction of the next lesson, not just a cardinality mismatch.
explanations.c: Countably many languages ARE computable (e.g., the empty language, or 'all strings' are trivially decidable); only 'almost all' in the cardinality sense are uncomputable, not literally every language.
explanations.d: P vs NP is an unrelated open question about resource-bounded computation, not about computability/uncomputability at all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the argument that most languages are uncomputable.

items.text: Observe that every Turing machine description is a finite string, so the set of machines is countable
Observe that languages over {0,1} are subsets of the countably infinite set of finite binary strings
Apply Cantor's theorem: the set of all subsets of a countably infinite set has size 2^aleph-null, strictly greater than aleph-null
Conclude that countably many machines cannot decide uncountably many languages, so almost all languages are undecidable

questions.explanation: The argument first fixes the (countable) size of the machine/program set, then the (uncountable, by Cantor's theorem) size of the language set, and concludes from the strict inequality that most languages cannot be matched to any machine.

lessons.label: The Halting Problem and Rice's Theorem

sections.heading: The Entscheidungsproblem, and what Turing was actually answering
sections.body: Turing's 1936 paper was not written to settle an abstract curiosity about machines for its own sake; it was his answer to David Hilbert's ENTSCHEIDUNGSPROBLEM ('decision problem'), posed in 1928: is there a general mechanical procedure that, given any statement in first-order logic, decides in finitely many steps whether it is provable? Turing showed the answer is no, by first formalizing 'mechanical procedure' as his a-machine, and then proving that a specific, simpler-sounding question about those very machines — does machine M halt on input w? — has no mechanical procedure that answers it either. If the Entscheidungsproblem's underlying logic could decide provability in general, it could in particular decide halting (since halting behavior can be expressed as a logical statement), so an undecidable halting problem forces an undecidable Entscheidungsproblem. Alonzo Church had reached the same negative conclusion about the Entscheidungsproblem independently and almost simultaneously, using the lambda calculus, which is part of why the Church-Turing thesis carries both names.

sections.heading: The proof: assume a decider, build a contradiction
sections.body: The proof is a direct application of the diagonalization idea to programs treated as data. Suppose, for contradiction, a Turing machine H exists that decides HALT = { <M, w> : M halts on input w }, so H(<M,w>) always halts and correctly outputs 'halts' or 'loops.' Build a new machine D that takes a single machine description x as input, runs H on <x, x> (feeding x its OWN description as the input), and then does the OPPOSITE of what H predicts: if H says x halts on x, D deliberately loops forever; if H says x loops on x, D halts. Now ask the diagonal question: what does D do on input <D> — its own description? If D halts on <D>, that means H(<D,D>) must have said 'loops' (since D was built to halt exactly when H predicts looping) — but D DID halt, contradicting H's correctness. If D loops on <D>, that means H(<D,D>) must have said 'halts' — but D did NOT halt, again contradicting H. Either outcome contradicts H being a correct decider, so no such H can exist: the halting problem is UNDECIDABLE. This is structurally identical to Cantor's diagonal argument from the previous lesson, with 'halts on its own description' playing the role of the diagonal flip.

sections.heading: Rice's theorem: almost every question about program BEHAVIOR is undecidable
sections.body: Henry Gordon Rice generalized this dramatically in his 1953 theorem (from his 1951 doctoral thesis): let P be any NONTRIVIAL property of the LANGUAGE a Turing machine recognizes — nontrivial meaning some machines' languages have property P and some don't (trivial properties, true of every machine or false of every machine, are the only exceptions). Then deciding whether an arbitrary machine M's language has property P is UNDECIDABLE. This is not about syntactic properties of the CODE (like 'does this program contain a loop written with a for-keyword,' which can be checked by inspection) — it is specifically about SEMANTIC properties of program BEHAVIOR: does this program ever output 42? Does it accept the empty language? Does it always terminate? Every one of these is undecidable by Rice's theorem, because each is a nontrivial property of the accepted language. The practical fallout is enormous: a perfect compiler optimization that removes all genuinely dead code, a perfect static analyzer that flags exactly the programs with a certain bug, a perfect virus scanner that identifies exactly the programs exhibiting some malicious behavior, and a perfect universal termination-checker are all PROVABLY IMPOSSIBLE in full generality. This is precisely why real-world tools (compilers, linters, antivirus software, termination checkers) are built as CONSERVATIVE APPROXIMATIONS: they either report 'maybe' alongside 'yes'/'no,' or they restrict themselves to a decidable syntactic subclass, or they accept some false positives/negatives — because a tool that is always fast, always terminates, AND is always correct on the fully general question is a mathematical impossibility, not an engineering gap waiting to be closed.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a 'does this student submission have an infinite loop' auto-grader might assume this is just a hard engineering problem to optimize. Rice's theorem says otherwise: 'has an infinite loop on some input' is a nontrivial semantic property of the program's behavior (some programs have this property, some don't), so NO algorithm can decide it correctly for every possible submission. The auto-grader's real options are: run the program with a timeout and treat 'still running after N seconds' as a proxy for looping (a conservative approximation that can misclassify a slow-but-terminating program as an infinite loop), or restrict submissions to a deliberately weaker language (like one without unbounded loops) where termination IS decidable. Recognizing which option you're taking — and that you're taking one BECAUSE the general question is provably undecidable, not because nobody has been clever enough yet — is the entire point of knowing Rice's theorem.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why can't we just build a perfect virus scanner (or perfect dead-code eliminator, or perfect termination checker)?' is testing whether a student can invoke Rice's theorem correctly: naming it as deciding a NONTRIVIAL SEMANTIC property of program behavior, distinguishing that from decidable SYNTACTIC checks, and explaining that real tools are conservative approximations by mathematical necessity, not because engineers haven't tried hard enough. A student who can also trace the halting problem's proof back to Turing's original target — Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem — shows they understand undecidability as an answer to a real historical question, not an isolated puzzle.

questions.prompt: In the halting problem proof, machine D is run on its own description <D>. What causes the contradiction?

options.text: D was built to do the OPPOSITE of whatever H predicts about D itself, so either outcome (halting or looping) falsifies H's prediction
D simply never halts on any input, which contradicts the definition of a Turing machine
H cannot be run on <D,D> because self-reference is syntactically forbidden
The tape runs out of space when D reads its own description

explanations.a: Correct — D is deliberately constructed to invert H's prediction about itself, so whichever way D actually behaves, H's prediction about that exact behavior turns out wrong.
explanations.b: D's behavior on <D> depends on H's prediction; it isn't fixed to always loop, and Turing machines are allowed to loop forever on some inputs regardless.
explanations.c: Self-reference (feeding a machine its own description) is completely legal; <D> is just a finite string like any other, and there's nothing special stopping H from being run on it.
explanations.d: Turing machine tapes are infinite in the standard model; running out of space is not the source of the contradiction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would Rice's theorem classify as undecidable?

options.text: Whether a program's source code contains the literal substring 'for'
Whether a program, when run, will ever print the number 42
Whether a program's source file is under 1000 characters long
Whether a program's source code uses only ASCII characters

explanations.a: This is a purely syntactic check on the text of the program (string search), fully decidable, not a semantic property of behavior.
explanations.b: Correct — 'ever prints 42' is a nontrivial property of the program's actual runtime behavior (some programs do, some don't), exactly what Rice's theorem covers.
explanations.c: File length is a syntactic property checkable by simple inspection, not a behavioral property of what the program computes.
explanations.d: Character encoding is a syntactic property of the source text, trivially decidable, unrelated to program behavior.

questions.prompt: How does the undecidability of the halting problem relate to Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem?

options.text: Turing used the undecidability of halting to prove there is no general mechanical procedure deciding provability in first-order logic, answering Hilbert's question negatively
They are unrelated; Turing addressed the Entscheidungsproblem in a separate, later paper
The Entscheidungsproblem was already proven decidable before Turing's paper
Hilbert's question was about halting machines specifically, not about logical provability

explanations.a: Correct — Turing's 1936 paper used the halting problem's undecidability as the key tool to show no mechanical decision procedure for provability can exist, resolving the Entscheidungsproblem negatively.
explanations.b: They are directly related; the halting-problem construction was the technical heart of the very same 1936 paper that answered the Entscheidungsproblem.
explanations.c: The Entscheidungsproblem was open until Turing's (and independently Church's) 1936 negative results; it was never proven decidable.
explanations.d: Hilbert's question concerned deciding provability of first-order logic statements generally; the halting problem was Turing's tool for answering it, not a restatement of it.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world tool to why Rice's theorem forces it to be a conservative approximation rather than a perfect decider.

left.text: A universal 'does this program terminate' checker

right.text: 'This code path is never reached' is a nontrivial semantic property of behavior
'This program exhibits malicious behavior' is a nontrivial semantic property of behavior
'This program halts on all inputs' is a nontrivial semantic property of behavior

questions.explanation: Each tool's ideal goal is really a nontrivial semantic property of program behavior, which Rice's theorem proves undecidable in general — so each tool must instead use conservative approximations (heuristics, timeouts, restricted languages, or accepting some false positives/negatives).

lessons.label: The Undecidable Landscape: Recognizable, Co-Recognizable, and Reductions

sections.heading: Decidable vs. recognizable vs. co-recognizable
sections.body: A language A is DECIDABLE if some Turing machine always halts, and correctly accepts strings in A while rejecting strings not in A. A language A is RECOGNIZABLE (also called Turing-recognizable or recursively enumerable, RE) if some Turing machine halts and accepts every string in A, but on strings NOT in A it may either reject OR loop forever without ever deciding. This asymmetry matters: a recognizer for A_TM = { <M,w> : M accepts w } can simply simulate M on w and accept if M accepts — but if M never halts on w, the recognizer never finds out and loops forever too, so it cannot reliably REJECT non-members. A language is CO-RECOGNIZABLE if its COMPLEMENT is recognizable. There is a clean and important theorem tying these together: a language A is decidable IF AND ONLY IF both A and its complement are recognizable. The intuition is direct — run a recognizer for A and a recognizer for the complement in parallel, alternating steps; since every string is in exactly one of A or its complement, and each is recognized by ITS machine eventually halting on true members, one of the two parallel simulations is guaranteed to eventually accept, telling you definitively which side the string falls on. A_TM itself is the classic example of a language that is recognizable but NOT decidable, and its complement is therefore not recognizable — it sits in the recognizable-but-not-co-recognizable region of the landscape.

sections.heading: Mapping reductions: the tool for spreading undecidability
sections.body: Rather than reproving a diagonalization argument from scratch for every new problem, undecidability spreads through MAPPING REDUCTIONS. A maps to B (written A <=m B) if there is a computable function f such that for every string x, x is in A if and only if f(x) is in B. The payoff: if A <=m B and A is undecidable, then B must be undecidable too — because a decider for B combined with f would give a decider for A (just compute f(x) and ask the B-decider), contradicting A's undecidability. This is exactly why theorists prove A_TM <=m HALT_TM (encode <M,w> by building a machine that ignores its own input, simulates M on w, and accepts if M accepts — this reduction shows HALT_TM inherits A_TM's undecidability), and why entire families of problems about compilers, formal grammars, and program behavior can be shown undecidable by exhibiting ONE reduction from a known-undecidable problem, rather than a fresh diagonalization every time. Mapping reductions are computability theory's counterpart to the polynomial-time reductions used for NP-completeness — same underlying idea (reduce a known-hard problem to your new problem to inherit its hardness), applied one level up, to computability instead of efficiency.

sections.heading: The famous undecidables, in their historical order
sections.body: Several landmark problems fill out this landscape. Emil Post's CORRESPONDENCE PROBLEM (1946) asks whether, given two lists of strings, some sequence of indices makes concatenating the first list's strings (in that index order) equal to concatenating the second list's strings — deceptively simple to state, provably undecidable, and a workhorse reduction target for undecidability results about grammars and compilers. HILBERT'S TENTH PROBLEM, from Hilbert's famous 1900 list, asked for a general algorithm to determine whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation (a polynomial equation with integer coefficients) has an integer solution; the MRDP theorem (Yuri Matiyasevich, 1970, completing decades of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam, and Julia Robinson) proved no such algorithm exists — the problem is undecidable. WANG TILING, posed by Hao Wang in 1961, asks whether a given finite set of square tiles with colored edges can tile the entire infinite plane with matching edges and no rotation allowed; Robert Berger proved in 1966 that this is undecidable, using an ingeniously constructed aperiodic tile set to simulate Turing machine computations in the tiling itself. And the BUSY BEAVER function BB(n), which asks the maximum number of steps an n-state halting Turing machine can take before halting, is itself uncomputable (an algorithm computing BB would decide halting for machines with up to n states, contradicting Turing's theorem) — yet finite instances can sometimes be pinned down by exhaustive, heroic effort: in July 2024 the collaborative bbchallenge.org project completed a machine-checked (Coq/Rocq) proof that BB(5) = 47,176,870, resolving a value conjectured since Heiner Marxen and Jurgen Buntrock found a candidate 5-state machine achieving it in 1990. BB(6), by contrast, is currently understood to be so astronomically large (involving iterated-exponential and Ackermann-like growth from known machines) that a full proof is considered far beyond any foreseeable computational or mathematical effort.

lessons.workedExample: To show HALT_TM = { <M,w> : M halts on w (accepting or rejecting) } is undecidable via mapping reduction from A_TM = { <M,w> : M accepts w }, define f(<M,w>) to output the description of a new machine M' that, on any input, first runs M on w; if M rejects, M' enters an infinite loop instead of halting; if M accepts, M' halts and accepts. Then <M,w> is in A_TM exactly when M' halts on its own trivial input, i.e., exactly when f(<M,w>) = <M', anything> is in HALT_TM. Since f is computable (it just writes out a new machine description that wraps M with this loop-on-reject behavior) and membership transfers exactly, A_TM <=m HALT_TM. Because A_TM is already known undecidable (via the halting-problem-style diagonalization), HALT_TM inherits undecidability for free — no new diagonalization needed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'do you have to reprove undecidability from scratch for every new problem?' is testing whether a student understands mapping reductions as the actual mechanism for spreading undecidability across the landscape, structurally parallel to how NP-hardness proofs reduce from a known-hard problem instead of reasoning about nondeterministic machines directly each time. A student who can also correctly place BB(5) = 47,176,870 as a 2024 machine-checked result — and explain why BB(6) is currently out of reach given the function's own uncomputability — shows they track the difference between 'undecidable in general' and 'this specific finite instance was pinned down by heroic effort,' a subtlety judges reward.

questions.prompt: What is the key theorem connecting decidability to recognizability?

options.text: A language is decidable if and only if it and its complement are both recognizable
A language is decidable if and only if it is recognizable
Every recognizable language is automatically decidable
A language's complement is always recognizable if the language itself is decidable, but the converse never holds

explanations.a: Correct — running recognizers for A and its complement in parallel, alternating steps, is guaranteed to eventually confirm which side any given string falls on, exactly when both directions are recognizable.
explanations.b: Recognizability alone is weaker than decidability; A_TM is recognizable but not decidable, showing this direction fails.
explanations.c: This is false in general; A_TM is a standard counterexample: recognizable, but not decidable.
explanations.d: The converse DOES hold too (that's the 'if and only if'); if both a language and its complement are recognizable, the language is decidable.

questions.prompt: What does a mapping reduction A <=m B, combined with A being undecidable, let you conclude about B?

options.text: B must also be undecidable
B must be decidable
B and A must have exactly the same alphabet
Nothing can be concluded about B without further information

explanations.a: Correct — if B were decidable, composing its decider with the reduction's computable function f would give a decider for A, contradicting A's undecidability; so B cannot be decidable either.
explanations.b: This has the direction backwards; undecidability of A transfers TO B, not decidability.
explanations.c: Mapping reductions require f to be a computable function between the languages' domains, but nothing requires identical alphabets.
explanations.d: The whole point of A <=m B with A undecidable is that it DOES let you conclude B is undecidable, without any new diagonalization.

questions.prompt: What did the 2024 bbchallenge.org collaborative proof establish?

options.text: That BB(5) = 47,176,870, via a machine-checked proof, ending a decades-long open conjecture
That the Busy Beaver function is computable after all for small n
That BB(6) is exactly computable and equals a specific known value
That the halting problem is decidable for 5-state machines but not 6-state machines

explanations.a: Correct — the bbchallenge.org project completed a Coq/Rocq machine-checked proof in July 2024 that BB(5) = 47,176,870, confirming the value conjectured since a 1990 candidate machine was found.
explanations.b: The Busy Beaver function remains fundamentally uncomputable in general; pinning down BB(5) required deciding halting behavior for a finite, enumerable set of 5-state machines through exhaustive analysis, not a general algorithm for BB.
explanations.c: BB(6) is not resolved; it is believed to be astronomically large and currently considered far beyond reach of a full proof.
explanations.d: This mischaracterizes the result; the halting problem's general undecidability doesn't change with state count, but resolving BB(5) required deciding halting for the finite set of 5-state candidate machines specifically, which is a different, more tractable task than the general problem.

questions.prompt: Match each famous undecidable problem to its source and resolution.

right.text: Posed by Emil Post in 1946; asks if two string lists can be matched by some index sequence
From Hilbert's 1900 list; proven undecidable by the MRDP theorem (Matiyasevich, 1970, completing Davis-Putnam-Robinson)
Posed by Hao Wang in 1961; proven undecidable by Robert Berger in 1966 using an aperiodic tile set

questions.explanation: Each problem has a distinct origin and proof: Post's correspondence problem (1946) is undecidable by direct construction; Hilbert's tenth problem was resolved by the 1970 MRDP theorem completing work begun by Davis, Putnam, and Robinson; Wang tiling's undecidability was proven by Berger in 1966 via an aperiodic tile set encoding Turing machine computation.

units.label: The Classes: P, NP, and the Complexity Zoo

lessons.label: Measuring Cost on a Machine, and Why Polynomial Means Efficient

sections.heading: TIME(f(n)) on a Turing machine
sections.body: To compare algorithms fairly, complexity theory fixes a single reference machine: the Turing machine, a tape, a read/write head, and a finite set of states. TIME(f(n)) is the set of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine that halts within f(n) steps on every input of length n. DTIME(f(n)) is the same thing spelled out explicitly as deterministic; NTIME(f(n)) is its nondeterministic twin, where the machine may branch and a language is accepted if SOME branch accepts within f(n) steps. These definitions look pedantic, but the point is to have one yardstick: a step is one transition of one specific machine model, so 'n^2 steps' means the same thing for every algorithm measured this way, letting P = union over k of DTIME(n^k) be a single well-defined class rather than a vibe.

sections.heading: The Cobham-Edmonds thesis
sections.body: Why single out POLYNOMIAL time as the boundary of 'efficient,' rather than, say, n log n or n^3 exactly? Two 1965 papers made the case independently. Alan Cobham's 'The Intrinsic Computational Difficulty of Functions' argued that polynomial time is the right notion because it is ROBUST: it does not depend on which reasonable machine model you pick. A single-tape Turing machine, a multi-tape one, and a random-access machine all simulate each other with at most a polynomial-time blowup, so 'is this problem solvable in polynomial time' is a machine-independent question, while 'is it solvable in exactly n^2 steps' is not. Jack Edmonds, in 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers' (also 1965) — the paper that gave a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum matching — made a parallel, more practical case: he explicitly asked for a 'good algorithm,' one whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input size, as opposed to an algorithm that merely works but might take steps proportional to the number of ways to check every possibility. Together these are the Cobham-Edmonds thesis: polynomial time is the formal stand-in for 'tractable,' because it is both closed under composition (a polynomial-time subroutine called a polynomial number of times is still polynomial-time overall) and stable across models.

sections.heading: The honest caveats: P is not the same as 'fast'
sections.body: The thesis is a useful convention, not a law of physics, and treating P as a synonym for 'fast in practice' is a real mistake. An algorithm running in n^100 time is polynomial and utterly useless for any n a computer will ever see. Conversely, an algorithm running in 2^(n/1000) time is technically exponential but perfectly fine for n up to a few thousand, since 2^(n/1000) only becomes astronomical once n reaches tens of thousands.
