And some polynomial-time algorithms are 'galactic': they have better asymptotic exponents than anything before them but such enormous constants or crossover points that they are never actually run. The Harvey-van der Hoeven algorithm for multiplying two n-digit integers in O(n log n) time (posted 2019, published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2021) settled a 1971 conjecture of Schonhage and Strassen about the fastest possible multiplication — a landmark theoretical result — yet it only beats simpler methods like Karatsuba's or the Schonhage-Strassen algorithm itself for numbers vastly larger than anything used in practice today. P vs not-P is the right FIRST cut for asking whether a problem is tractable in principle, but constants, exponents, and galactic-algorithm effects are exactly why computer scientists still need finer measures beyond the P/NP line.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a student times three programs on inputs of size n=20: Program A takes roughly 20^100 operations, Program B takes roughly 2^(20/1000) which is about 2^0.02, nearly 1, and Program C takes n^3 = 8000 operations. Classified strictly by the Cobham-Edmonds thesis, A and C are both 'polynomial time' (n^100 and n^3), while B is 'exponential time' in form. Yet in practice B finishes instantly for any realistic n because the exponent is scaled down by 1000, while A is completely unusable even though it is polynomial — n^100 for n=20 is already a number with over 130 digits. This is precisely the caveat the lesson stresses: the P/not-P line answers 'is there SOME polynomial bound as n grows without limit,' not 'will this finish on my machine today.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows complexity theory will often ask a student who name-drops 'P' whether they understand that P is a robustness argument, not a promise of real-world speed. The strong answer cites the Cobham-Edmonds thesis by name, explains that polynomial time is chosen for its closure and model-independence properties (not because every polynomial is fast), and can immediately produce a counterexample like n^100 or a galactic algorithm such as Harvey-van der Hoeven multiplication. A student who conflates 'in P' with 'fast' has memorized a label without understanding why theorists drew the line where they did.

questions.prompt: What is the core justification the Cobham-Edmonds thesis gives for treating polynomial time as the boundary of tractability?

options.text: Polynomial-time algorithms are always fast enough to run on real hardware
Polynomial time is robust across reasonable machine models and closed under composition
Polynomial time was the fastest class provably achievable in 1965
Polynomial time exactly matches human intuition about difficulty

explanations.a: This is the exact misconception the thesis does not claim; n^100 is polynomial but useless in practice.
explanations.b: Correct — Cobham and Edmonds argued polynomial time is machine-independent (reasonable models simulate each other with polynomial overhead) and composes cleanly, which is what makes it a principled dividing line.
explanations.c: The thesis is not about what was provably fastest; it is about which notion of efficiency is stable and well-behaved as a class.
explanations.d: The thesis is a formal, structural argument, not a claim about matching intuition directly.

questions.prompt: Why is the Harvey-van der Hoeven O(n log n) integer multiplication algorithm called a 'galactic algorithm'?

options.text: Because it was developed for satellite communications
Because it runs in exponential time despite its name
Because its asymptotically superior bound only wins over simpler methods for astronomically large inputs
Because it was never proven correct

explanations.a: The 'galactic' label is a complexity-theory term of art unrelated to any aerospace application.
explanations.b: It is polynomial (indeed O(n log n)), not exponential; that is exactly why it settled the Schonhage-Strassen conjecture.
explanations.c: Correct — it is a real, proven, polynomial-time algorithm, but the crossover point where it beats Karatsuba or Schonhage-Strassen in practice requires numbers far larger than any used in real computation.
explanations.d: It was rigorously proven and published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2021; correctness is not the issue.

questions.prompt: Order these growth rates from fastest to slowest for large n: n^3, 2^(n/1000), n^100, log n.

items.text: log n

questions.explanation: For sufficiently large n, 2^(n/1000) grows fastest: it is exponential and eventually overtakes every polynomial no matter how large the fixed exponent, though the crossover point can be very large depending on the scaling constant. Then n^100 (still polynomial but with a huge exponent), then n^3, and finally log n, which grows slowest.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/paper to its contribution to the tractability discussion.

right.text: Argued polynomial time is machine-independent and thus a principled notion of tractability
Coined the request for a 'good algorithm' while giving a polynomial-time matching algorithm
Proved an O(n log n) integer multiplication bound with no practical advantage at realistic sizes

questions.explanation: Cobham's paper made the model-independence argument for polynomial time; Edmonds's 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers' introduced the 'good algorithm' language alongside a polynomial-time matching algorithm; Harvey and van der Hoeven's result is the canonical modern example of a galactic algorithm.

lessons.label: P: What We Can Actually Solve

sections.heading: P is a discovery machine, not an obvious label
sections.body: P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the input size. It is tempting to picture P as 'the easy problems,' as if membership were self-evident from staring at a problem statement. The actual history says otherwise: several problems sat for decades with only exponential-time algorithms known, looking for all the world like they might require brute-force search, until someone found the polynomial-time algorithm that placed them in P. Proving membership in P is frequently a hard mathematical result in its own right, not a formality.

sections.heading: Matching: Edmonds 1965
sections.body: Given a graph, a MATCHING is a set of edges with no shared endpoints; a PERFECT matching covers every vertex. For bipartite graphs, polynomial-time matching algorithms (augmenting-path methods built on Berge's theorem, that a matching is maximum exactly when it admits no augmenting path) were known earlier, but general (non-bipartite) graph matching resisted a polynomial-time solution because the natural augmenting-path idea breaks down on odd-length cycles, called 'blossoms.' Jack Edmonds solved this in his 1965 paper 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers,' introducing the blossom-contraction technique: shrink an odd cycle to a single vertex, search for an augmenting path in the smaller graph, then expand back. This was one of the first problems for which the paper doing the polynomial-time work was ALSO the paper making the case, explicitly, that polynomial time was the right bar for a 'good algorithm' — Edmonds effectively announced the P-vs-not-P question by demonstrating a nontrivial example on the P side.

sections.heading: Linear programming: Khachiyan 1979, Karmarkar 1984
sections.body: Linear programming (LP) — optimizing a linear objective subject to linear inequality constraints — had a famous practical algorithm, Dantzig's simplex method (1947), that works extremely well in practice but was shown to take exponential time in the worst case on certain constructed inputs (Klee-Minty cubes, 1972). Whether LP was actually IN P remained open until 1979, when Leonid Khachiyan adapted the ellipsoid method from convex optimization to prove LP solvable in polynomial time — a landmark theoretical result, even though the ellipsoid method itself is usually too slow in practice to replace simplex. In 1984, Narendra Karmarkar gave an interior-point method that was both polynomial-time AND competitive with simplex in practice, resolving the theory/practice gap. Both results matter for different reasons: Khachiyan settled the P-membership question; Karmarkar showed polynomial time and practical speed are not in tension for LP.

sections.heading: Primality: AKS 2002
sections.body: Determining whether a number n is prime looks, on its face, like it might need trial division up to roughly the square root of n — exponential in the BIT LENGTH of n, since n itself can be exponential in the number of digits used to write it. Efficient randomized primality tests existed by the late 1970s, but a DETERMINISTIC polynomial-time algorithm was open until 2002, when Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal, and Nitin Saxena published 'PRIMES is in P,' giving an unconditional polynomial-time deterministic test based on a generalization of Fermat's little theorem over polynomial rings. Because P is closed under composition — a polynomial-time algorithm calling other polynomial-time algorithms a polynomial number of times remains polynomial-time overall — results like Edmonds's, Khachiyan's, and AKS's don't just place one problem in P; they let anyone chain them into larger polynomial-time algorithms and, symmetrically, let anyone build a polynomial-time REDUCTION from one problem to another without worrying the reduction itself will blow up the running time.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to solve a resource-allocation problem that includes checking whether an intermediate graph has a perfect matching, then optimizing a cost function subject to linear constraints, then verifying that a generated identifier is prime for a hashing step. Because matching (Edmonds 1965), linear programming (Khachiyan 1979), and primality testing (AKS 2002) are each individually in P, and P is closed under composition, the team can chain all three as subroutines and know the whole pipeline still runs in polynomial time overall — without needing to re-derive a combined complexity bound from scratch. If even one of those three subroutines were NOT known to be in P, the team would have no guarantee the pipeline terminates in reasonable time on large inputs.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will not be satisfied by a student reciting 'P is the class of polynomial-time solvable problems' from memory. The real test is whether the student can name at least one problem that was NOT obviously in P and explain what made proving membership hard — the blossom trick for general matching, the ellipsoid method for LP, or the polynomial-ring argument for AKS primality. This shows the student understands P as a set that had to be populated by real mathematical work over decades, and it sets up why 'is X in P' is treated as a serious open question for problems like graph isomorphism rather than assumed one way or the other.

questions.prompt: Order these results by the year they placed a hard-won problem in P.

items.text: Edmonds's blossom algorithm for general graph matching
Khachiyan's ellipsoid method for linear programming
Karmarkar's interior-point method for linear programming
Agrawal-Kayal-Saxena's deterministic primality test

questions.explanation: Edmonds's matching algorithm was 1965, Khachiyan's ellipsoid-method proof that LP is in P was 1979, Karmarkar's practical interior-point method was 1984, and the AKS 'PRIMES is in P' result was 2002.

questions.prompt: Why did general (non-bipartite) graph matching resist a polynomial-time algorithm before Edmonds's 1965 work?

options.text: Because no graph can have a perfect matching
Because the natural augmenting-path approach fails on odd-length cycles ('blossoms')
Because matching is now known to be NP-complete
Because matching requires exponential space, not just exponential time

explanations.a: Many graphs do have perfect matchings; the difficulty is finding one efficiently, not existence in general.
explanations.b: Correct — augmenting-path search, which works cleanly on bipartite graphs, breaks down on odd cycles in general graphs; Edmonds's blossom-contraction technique fixed this.
explanations.c: Matching is in P (Edmonds proved this); it is not NP-complete.
explanations.d: The obstacle was time complexity of the search strategy, not space usage.

questions.prompt: What is the key practical difference between Khachiyan's ellipsoid method (1979) and Karmarkar's interior-point method (1984) for linear programming?

options.text: Only Karmarkar's method is polynomial-time; Khachiyan's is exponential
Khachiyan's method proved polynomial-time solvability but is usually impractical; Karmarkar's is both polynomial-time and practically competitive
Khachiyan's method solves integer programming, while Karmarkar's solves linear programming
There is no meaningful difference; both are identical algorithms

explanations.a: Khachiyan's ellipsoid method IS polynomial-time; that was precisely its historic significance, even though it's slow in practice.
explanations.b: Correct — Khachiyan settled the theoretical question that LP is in P, while Karmarkar's interior-point method later delivered a polynomial-time algorithm that also competes with simplex in real use.
explanations.c: Both address linear programming, not integer programming, which is a harder (NP-hard) problem in general.
explanations.d: They use different techniques (ellipsoid geometry vs. interior-point methods) with different practical performance.

questions.prompt: Match each problem to the property that made proving its membership in P difficult.

right.text: Odd cycles break the standard augmenting-path technique
The known practical algorithm (simplex) has exponential worst-case behavior
The obvious method is exponential in the number's bit length

questions.explanation: Matching needed the blossom-contraction trick to handle odd cycles; LP's simplex method works well in practice but is exponential in the worst case (Klee-Minty cubes), which is why a separate polynomial-time proof was needed; naive primality testing via trial division is exponential in the bit length of the number being tested.

lessons.label: NP Two Ways: Verifiers and Nondeterminism

sections.heading: Definition one: the certificate/verifier view
sections.body: NP can be defined as the class of decision problems for which a YES-answer has a CERTIFICATE (also called a witness) that is polynomial in the length of the input and can be CHECKED by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. For Boolean satisfiability (SAT), the certificate for a satisfiable formula is a satisfying variable assignment; checking it means plugging in the values and evaluating the formula, which takes time linear in the formula's size. For the Hamiltonian-cycle problem, the certificate is the cycle itself — a sequence of vertices — and checking means confirming each consecutive pair is an edge and every vertex appears exactly once, again polynomial-time work. Crucially, this definition says NOTHING about how hard it is to FIND the certificate; it only requires that once you have one, verifying it is fast.

sections.heading: Definition two: nondeterministic Turing machines
sections.body: The second definition returns to the machine model from the previous lesson: NP is the class of languages decided by a NONDETERMINISTIC Turing machine in polynomial time, meaning a machine that, at each step, may branch into multiple possible next configurations, and the input is accepted if AT LEAST ONE branch reaches an accepting state within a polynomial number of steps. The two definitions are provably equivalent: a nondeterministic machine's accepting branch IS a certificate (the sequence of choices it made), and conversely, a verifier can be simulated by a nondeterministic machine that 'guesses' the certificate on one of its branches and then runs the verifier deterministically on it. Neither definition is more fundamental than the other; they are two lenses on the same class, and different proofs find one or the other more convenient.

sections.heading: Two misconceptions to kill outright
sections.body: The name 'NP' stands for 'nondeterministic polynomial time' — it does NOT mean 'not polynomial.' This is arguably the single most common misreading of the term. Every problem in P is also in NP: if a problem can be SOLVED in polynomial time, then trivially it can be VERIFIED in polynomial time (just re-solve it and compare, ignoring the offered certificate). So P is a subset of NP, not disjoint from it, and whether that containment is strict (P is a PROPER subset) is exactly the P vs NP question — nobody knows. The second misconception is thinking NP membership involves 'lucky guessing' as an actual algorithmic strategy; nondeterminism is a mathematical abstraction for 'a certificate exists,' not a claim that real computers can guess correctly. What NP actually captures is the ASYMMETRY between finding and checking: for NP-complete problems, checking a proposed solution is easy even when nobody knows how to efficiently find one.

sections.heading: Why TSP needs a decision phrasing to be in NP
sections.body: The traveling salesperson problem (TSP) is usually first described as an OPTIMIZATION problem: find the shortest tour visiting every city exactly once and returning to the start. But NP, as defined, is a class of DECISION problems — those with yes/no answers. 'What is the minimum tour length?' has no obvious short certificate, because verifying that a number IS the true minimum requires ruling out every shorter tour, which is not obviously polynomial. The fix is to rephrase TSP as a decision problem: 'Is there a tour of length at most k?' Now a certificate is simple — a specific tour — and verifying it means summing its edge weights and comparing to k, both polynomial-time. This decision version of TSP is in NP, and it is NP-complete; the optimization version can then be solved with a polynomial number of calls to the decision version via binary search on k, which is why complexity theory almost always states its problems as decisions even when the underlying interesting question is an optimization.

lessons.workedExample: Consider SAT on a formula with 50 variables. A brute-force solver would need to try up to 2^50 assignments to determine satisfiability — completely infeasible. But suppose someone hands you an assignment, claiming it satisfies the formula. Checking their claim takes one pass through the formula: substitute each variable's value and evaluate each clause, which is linear-time work, regardless of how astronomically hard it might have been to FIND that assignment in the first place. This gap — exponential to find, polynomial to check — is exactly what places SAT in NP under the certificate definition, and it is why NP-completeness proofs typically focus on constructing a valid certificate format and a fast checker rather than trying to describe a fast solver, which for NP-complete problems is not known to exist.
lessons.judgeFraming: The most common judge-trap question is 'so NP problems just can't be solved in polynomial time, right?' A student who has only memorized the acronym will often agree, which is exactly backwards — P is contained in NP. A strong answer states this containment explicitly, explains that NP is about the EXISTENCE of a fast verifier rather than the absence of a fast solver, and can immediately produce the certificate for a concrete NP problem (a satisfying assignment, a Hamiltonian tour) to show the definition is not just word association. A judge probing further into optimization-vs-decision framing (as with TSP) is checking whether the student understands that NP is technically a class of DECISION problems, a distinction many popular explanations skip.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the relationship between P and NP is correct?

options.text: P and NP are disjoint classes with no overlap
P is a subset of NP, and whether it is a PROPER subset is the open P vs NP question
NP stands for 'not polynomial,' meaning NP problems cannot be in P
NP is a subset of P

explanations.a: They are not disjoint — every problem solvable in polynomial time is trivially also verifiable in polynomial time.
explanations.b: Correct — any polynomial-time-solvable problem has a trivial polynomial-time verifier (re-solve and compare), so P is contained in NP; whether NP has MORE than P is unresolved.
explanations.c: NP stands for 'nondeterministic polynomial time,' not 'not polynomial' — this is the single most common misreading of the acronym.
explanations.d: This direction would resolve P vs NP in the negative and is not known to be true (nor believed to be true by most researchers).

questions.prompt: Why must the traveling salesperson problem be phrased as a decision problem ('is there a tour of length at most k?') rather than left as an optimization problem to be shown in NP?

options.text: Because NP only contains problems with numeric answers
Because NP is defined over decision problems, and verifying a claimed MINIMUM requires ruling out all shorter tours, unlike verifying a single tour against a threshold
Because optimization problems are always undecidable
Because TSP's decision version is not NP-complete but the optimization version is

explanations.a: NP membership is not about numeric versus non-numeric answers; it is about yes/no decisions with checkable certificates.
explanations.b: Correct — a proposed tour of length at most k has a fast certificate (the tour itself), while proving a value is the true MINIMUM has no obvious short certificate.
explanations.c: TSP is decidable; the issue is complexity classification, not decidability.
explanations.d: It is the decision version that is proven NP-complete; the phrasing is required precisely because NP is a class of decision problems.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of verifying a certificate for the decision version of TSP ('is there a tour of length at most k?').

items.text: Receive a candidate tour as the certificate
Check the tour visits every city exactly once and returns to the start
Sum the edge weights along the tour
Compare the total to k and accept if it is at most k

questions.explanation: Verification starts with the offered certificate, confirms it is a valid tour structurally, computes its total length, then compares that length against the threshold k — all polynomial-time steps.

questions.prompt: Match each NP problem to its certificate.

right.text: A satisfying assignment of variables
A sequence of vertices visiting each exactly once via valid edges
A specific tour whose total edge weight is at most k

questions.explanation: SAT's certificate is a satisfying assignment; Hamiltonian cycle's certificate is the cycle itself as a vertex sequence; TSP-decision's certificate is a tour whose summed weight can be checked against the threshold k.

lessons.label: co-NP, NP ∩ co-NP, and the Problems That Escaped

sections.heading: Defining co-NP
sections.body: co-NP is the class of decision problems whose NO-instances (not yes-instances) have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. Equivalently, a language L is in co-NP exactly when its complement is in NP. The canonical co-NP problem is TAUTOLOGY: given a Boolean formula, is it true under every possible assignment of its variables? There is no obvious short certificate for 'this formula is a tautology' — you would seemingly need to check all 2^n assignments to be sure. But there IS an obvious short certificate for the complement question 'is this formula NOT a tautology,' namely a single assignment that falsifies it; that puts NOT-TAUTOLOGY in NP and TAUTOLOGY in co-NP. Similarly, UNSAT (is this formula unsatisfiable) is co-NP-complete, mirroring SAT's status as NP-complete.

sections.heading: Why NP is believed unequal to co-NP
sections.body: It is not known whether NP equals co-NP, but most complexity theorists believe they are different, and the belief carries real weight: if NP were shown equal to co-NP, that would force P equal to NP as well is NOT quite the right implication to state carelessly — the precise, provable fact is the contrapositive-flavored one: if P equals NP, then NP equals co-NP (since P is closed under complement, and P=NP would put NP's problems' complements in P and hence in NP). So NP not equal to co-NP would be sufficient to conclude P not equal to NP, making 'NP = co-NP?' a genuine sub-question worth studying in its own right, and a place where researchers look for evidence (such as certain problems resisting placement in NP intersect co-NP) as indirect support for P not equal to NP.

sections.heading: Primality's journey through NP ∩ co-NP
sections.body: Primality testing is the best worked historical example of a problem's status evolving. Showing PRIMES is in co-NP is comparatively easy: a certificate that a number is COMPOSITE is just one of its nontrivial factors, checkable by a single division. Showing PRIMES is in NP is the harder direction, achieved by Vaughan Pratt in 1975, using certificates built from primitive roots and recursive factorizations of n-1 (Pratt certificates) that a verifier can check in polynomial time. That placed PRIMES in NP ∩ co-NP by 1975 — strong evidence, though not proof, that primality testing was not going to turn out to be intractable, since NP ∩ co-NP problems have certificates for BOTH answers and are widely viewed as 'probably not NP-complete.' Efficient RANDOMIZED primality tests followed soon after: Miller's algorithm (1976, correct assuming the Extended Riemann Hypothesis), Rabin's unconditional randomization of it (1980), and the Solovay-Strassen test (1977), which together put primality testing practically within reach and in the randomized class coRP. The deterministic question stayed open until 2002, when Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena's AKS algorithm finally placed PRIMES in P outright — collapsing nearly three decades of 'probably easy, sitting in NP ∩ co-NP' into a proven, unconditional polynomial-time algorithm.

sections.heading: Factoring: still stuck in NP ∩ co-NP, and RSA's bet
sections.body: The INTEGER FACTORIZATION decision problem (does n have a factor less than some bound k) sits in NP ∩ co-NP today by essentially the same certificate logic used for primality — a candidate factor is a certificate either way — yet unlike primality, nobody has found a polynomial-time algorithm for it, deterministic or otherwise, on a classical computer. Crucially, factoring is NOT believed to be NP-complete; being in NP ∩ co-NP is itself considered evidence against NP-completeness, since no NP ∩ co-NP problem is known to be NP-complete and finding one would be a major surprise (it would imply NP = co-NP). This puts factoring in a strange middle zone: apparently harder than problems known to be in P, but almost certainly easier than NP-complete problems like SAT. The RSA cryptosystem's security rests entirely on this middle-zone status — specifically on the AVERAGE-CASE hardness of factoring products of two large random primes, not on any proof of worst-case intractability. Shor's 1994 quantum algorithm factors integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer, which is precisely why RSA is considered broken in a post-quantum world even though no classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm is known.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to argue that n = 91 is NOT prime versus arguing that n = 97 IS prime. For 91, the co-NP-style certificate is trivial: exhibit the factor 7 (91 = 7 x 13), and the verifier just checks 91 divided by 7 equals 13 exactly — one multiplication. For 97, showing primality via a Pratt certificate requires exhibiting a primitive root mod 97 (namely 5) together with the prime factorization of 96 = 2^5 x 3, and recursively certifying those smaller primes, all checkable in time polynomial in the number of digits of 97. This asymmetry — trivial certificate for compositeness, structured-but-still-polynomial certificate for primality — is exactly why PRIMES sat in NP ∩ co-NP for decades before AKS 2002 found a way to skip certificates entirely and decide primality directly in polynomial time.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing depth here will ask why RSA is considered secure if nobody has PROVEN factoring is hard. The precise answer distinguishes worst-case complexity-class membership (factoring sits in NP ∩ co-NP, believed not NP-complete) from average-case cryptographic hardness (no known efficient algorithm for products of two random large primes specifically). A student who says 'factoring is NP-complete so RSA is secure' has it backwards on two counts: factoring is not believed NP-complete, and NP-completeness would say nothing about the specific structured instances RSA actually uses, since NP-hardness is a worst-case notion.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a problem to be in co-NP?

options.text: The problem cannot be solved in polynomial time
Its NO-instances have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time
It is the complement of a problem in P
It requires a nondeterministic verifier rather than a deterministic one

explanations.a: co-NP membership says nothing about solvability speed directly; it is about certificate structure for NO-answers.
explanations.b: Correct — a language is in co-NP when its NO-instances can be certified and verified in polynomial time, equivalently when its complement is in NP.
explanations.c: co-NP is defined relative to NP (complement of an NP language), not relative to P.
explanations.d: Verification in both NP and co-NP is done by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier checking a certificate; nondeterminism is used in the machine-based definition of NP itself, not in the verifier.

questions.prompt: Why is factoring's membership in NP ∩ co-NP considered evidence AGAINST it being NP-complete?

options.text: Because NP ∩ co-NP problems are already proven to be in P
Because no NP ∩ co-NP problem is known to be NP-complete, and one being NP-complete would imply NP = co-NP, which is widely disbelieved
Because factoring has been proven NP-hard already
Because co-NP problems are always solvable by quantum computers

explanations.a: NP ∩ co-NP is not proven equal to P; primality was in NP ∩ co-NP for decades before it was proven to be in P.
explanations.b: Correct — an NP ∩ co-NP problem being NP-complete would force NP = co-NP, a collapse most researchers believe does not happen, so factoring's membership is treated as evidence it is not NP-complete.
explanations.c: Factoring is not known to be NP-hard; this is precisely the open, believed-false direction.
explanations.d: Shor's algorithm gives a specific quantum speedup for factoring, but this is a separate fact from the classical NP ∩ co-NP classification.

questions.prompt: Order these primality-testing milestones chronologically.

items.text: Miller's deterministic test assuming the Extended Riemann Hypothesis (1976)
Pratt shows PRIMES is in NP via primitive-root certificates (1975)
Solovay-Strassen randomized primality test (1977)
Agrawal-Kayal-Saxena show PRIMES is in P (2002)

questions.explanation: Pratt's NP-membership result (1975) came first, followed by Miller's conditional deterministic test (1976), then Solovay-Strassen's randomized test (1977), with AKS resolving the unconditional deterministic question in 2002.

questions.prompt: Match each problem/claim to the correct classification or status.

right.text: co-NP-complete
In P, via an unconditional deterministic algorithm
In NP ∩ co-NP, no known polynomial-time algorithm

questions.explanation: TAUTOLOGY is the canonical co-NP-complete problem; PRIMES was moved into P outright by AKS in 2002; factoring remains in NP ∩ co-NP with no known classical polynomial-time algorithm, which is the basis of RSA's security assumption.

lessons.label: Space, Hierarchies, and the Things We Have Proved

sections.heading: The hierarchy theorems: rare unconditional proofs
sections.body: Almost everything discussed so far in this unit — P vs NP, NP vs co-NP, factoring's difficulty — is CONJECTURE, believed but unproven. The time and space hierarchy theorems are a welcome exception: they are proven, unconditional theorems. Juris Hartmanis and Richard Stearns proved the time hierarchy theorem in their 1965 paper 'On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms,' work recognized with the 1993 ACM Turing Award for establishing the foundations of computational complexity theory. The theorem says that giving a Turing machine sufficiently more time provably lets it decide strictly more languages: DTIME(f(n)) is a proper subset of DTIME(g(n)) whenever g grows enough faster than f (technically, whenever f(n) log f(n) is o(g(n)), among other technical conditions). The proof works by diagonalization, a descendant of the technique Turing used to prove the halting problem undecidable: construct a machine that runs every other machine using at most f(n) steps and deliberately does the opposite of what it does, guaranteeing a language no f(n)-time machine can decide, and then show that same language IS decidable using g(n) time (given a bigger budget, the diagonalizing machine can be run directly).

sections.heading: What the hierarchy theorems buy us
sections.body: Applying the time hierarchy theorem across the polynomial/exponential boundary shows P is a proper subset of EXP (the class of problems solvable in DTIME(2^(n^k)) for some k) — we KNOW, not merely suspect, that some problems solvable in exponential time cannot be solved in polynomial time. This matters enormously as a sanity check: it proves that the entire enterprise of separating complexity classes is not vacuous, since at least some separations (like P proper subset of EXP) are settled facts, even while the specific separation everyone cares about (P vs NP) remains open. The analogous space hierarchy theorem gives L (logarithmic space) as a proper subset of PSPACE (polynomial space), by the same diagonalization logic applied to space instead of time.

sections.heading: The space classes and their containments
sections.body: L is the class of problems decidable using O(log n) space (not counting the read-only input tape) — surprisingly powerful despite the tiny budget, since log n bits can index any position in an n-length input. NL is L's nondeterministic counterpart, containing problems like graph reachability (does a path exist from vertex s to vertex t). PSPACE allows polynomial space with no explicit time bound (though PSPACE-bounded computations can still be simulated in exponential time, since a machine using p(n) space has at most an exponential number of distinct configurations before it must repeat one). EXP allows time 2^(n^k). These fit into a chain of containments that is one of the field's cleanest maps: L subset-or-equal NL subset-or-equal P subset-or-equal NP subset-or-equal PSPACE subset-or-equal EXP. Several of these inclusions are known to be PROPER (L proper subset PSPACE, P proper subset EXP, via the hierarchy theorems) even though the interior separations (is L proper subset P? is NP proper subset PSPACE?) remain open.

sections.heading: Savitch, Immerman-Szelepcsenyi, and PSPACE-completeness
sections.body: Two structural theorems tame the space classes further. Walter Savitch proved in 1970 that NSPACE(f(n)) is contained in DSPACE(f(n)^2) for any space-constructible f(n) — nondeterminism can only quadratically help with space, a far weaker boost than the exponential gap widely believed for TIME. A direct consequence: NPSPACE equals PSPACE, since squaring a polynomial is still a polynomial. Second, Neil Immerman and Robert Szelepcsenyi independently proved in 1987-1988 (sharing the 1995 Godel Prize) that NL equals co-NL — nondeterministic log-space classes are closed under complementation, a genuinely surprising result since the analogous question for NP vs co-NP is wide open and believed to go the other way. Finally, PSPACE has its own complete problems under polynomial-time reductions, meaning the hardest problems in PSPACE: TQBF (true quantified Boolean formula, deciding formulas with alternating 'there exists' and 'for all' quantifiers over Boolean variables) is the canonical PSPACE-complete problem. Generalized two-player games are the classic source of others, because deciding who wins with optimal play naturally unrolls into alternating quantifiers ('there EXISTS a move for me such that for ALL moves you make...') just like TQBF: Stefan Reisch proved generalized Hex PSPACE-complete in 1981, and Gary Flake and Eric Baum proved generalized Rush Hour (n vehicles on an n-by-n grid) PSPACE-complete in 2002.

sections.heading: Go: a game that escapes PSPACE
sections.body: It is tempting to assume every hard board game is PSPACE-complete, but generalized Go is a sharp counterexample worth knowing precisely. Games like Hex end after at most n^2 moves, which caps the game tree's depth at a polynomial and lets a PSPACE machine search it with a polynomial-depth recursion. Go is different: capture and recapture let positions repeat, so play can run exponentially long. J. M. Robson proved in 1983 ('The Complexity of Go,' Proc. IFIP, pages 413-417) that Go on an n-by-n board under the basic (Japanese) ko rule is EXPTIME-COMPLETE — strictly harder than PSPACE-complete, because the hierarchy theorems in this very lesson prove PSPACE is a proper subset of EXP. So Go is a concrete, PROVEN example of a natural problem living above PSPACE. Two caveats keep the claim honest: with no ko rule at all, Go is only known to be PSPACE-hard, not PSPACE-complete; and under the modern superko rule, both the lower and upper bounds of Robson's proof break down, leaving Go's exact class an open problem. This is the lesson in miniature — 'hard game' is not a complexity class, and the precise rule set decides which box a problem lands in.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to show 2-coloring of a graph is NOT solvable using only O(log n) space via a naive claim that it 'feels hard.' A rigorous approach instead uses the actual proved containments: 2-coloring (equivalent to checking bipartiteness) is known to be in NL, and by the chain L subset-or-equal NL subset-or-equal P, that only tells us it is at most as hard as anything in P — it does not resolve whether it is IN L. Contrast this with a problem the student can prove is NOT in P: by the time hierarchy theorem, since P is a proper subset of EXP, there must exist a problem in EXP that is not in P, and one can explicitly construct it via diagonalization (a language that disagrees with every polynomial-time machine on some input). Better still, the student does not need an artificial diagonalization language — generalized Go under the basic ko rule is EXPTIME-complete (Robson 1983), and since P is a proper subset of EXP, that game is provably not in P. This distinction — a PROVEN separation via diagonalization versus a CONJECTURED one like P vs NP — is the core lesson of the hierarchy theorems.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing complexity depth will often ask 'what do we actually KNOW to be true, versus what's just believed?' This is the single best question the hierarchy theorems answer, and a student who can cite Hartmanis-Stearns 1965 and explain that P proper subset EXP is a proven fact (not a conjecture like P vs NP) demonstrates they understand the difference between complexity theory's proven scaffolding and its open conjectures. A follow-up about Savitch's theorem or Immerman-Szelepcsenyi tests whether the student knows space behaves differently from time under nondeterminism — NL = co-NL is proven, while NP = co-NP is disbelieved, which is a genuinely subtle and often-missed asymmetry. A judge who plays board games may ask about game complexity; the student who says 'Hex and Rush Hour are PSPACE-complete, but Go under the basic ko rule is EXPTIME-complete because play can last exponentially long' shows they track the actual results rather than pattern-matching 'hard game' to one class.

questions.prompt: What technique do Hartmanis and Stearns use to prove the time hierarchy theorem?

options.text: Diagonalization, constructing a machine that disagrees with every machine bounded by the smaller time budget
A polynomial-time reduction from SAT
An empirical survey of known algorithms' running times
Randomized sampling over Turing machine configurations

explanations.a: Correct — the proof adapts Turing's diagonalization technique, building a machine that runs every f(n)-time machine and does the opposite, then showing that language is decidable with the larger budget g(n).
explanations.b: Reductions are the tool for NP-completeness proofs, not hierarchy theorems, which are unconditional separations rather than relative-hardness statements.
explanations.c: The hierarchy theorems are proven mathematical results via diagonalization, not empirical observations.
explanations.d: No randomization is involved; the proof is a deterministic diagonalization argument.

questions.prompt: What does Savitch's theorem (1970) establish?

options.text: NSPACE(f(n)) is contained in DSPACE(f(n)^2), so nondeterminism gives at most a quadratic space blowup
P equals NP
NSPACE(f(n)) is contained in DSPACE(2^f(n))
NL is a proper subset of L

explanations.a: Correct — Savitch showed a deterministic machine can simulate a nondeterministic one using only the square of the space, implying PSPACE equals NPSPACE.
explanations.b: Savitch's theorem is about space complexity, not the P vs NP time-complexity question, which remains open.
explanations.c: The blowup Savitch proved is quadratic (squared), not exponential — that gap is precisely why nondeterminism affects space far less dramatically than it is believed to affect time.
explanations.d: Savitch's theorem does not claim this containment direction or strictness; it establishes a simulation bound, not an equality/inequality between L and NL.

questions.prompt: Generalized Hex is PSPACE-complete (Reisch, 1981). What is proved about generalized Go on an n-by-n board under the basic (Japanese) ko rule?

options.text: It is EXPTIME-complete (Robson, 1983) — strictly harder than PSPACE-complete, since PSPACE is a proper subset of EXP
It is PSPACE-complete, exactly like Hex and Rush Hour
It is NP-complete, by reduction from SAT
It is undecidable, like the halting problem

explanations.a: Correct — Robson (1983) proved Go with the basic ko rule EXPTIME-complete. Because ko allows capture and recapture, play can last exponentially many moves, escaping the polynomial-depth game tree that makes games like Hex fit inside PSPACE. The space hierarchy theorem gives PSPACE proper subset EXP, so this is a strictly higher class.
explanations.b: This is the common trap: not every hard board game is PSPACE-complete. Hex (Reisch 1981) and Rush Hour (Flake and Baum 2002) are PSPACE-complete because their play is polynomially bounded, but Go under ko is proved EXPTIME-complete — one level higher.
explanations.c: Go is far above NP. NP-complete problems have polynomial-size certificates; deciding optimal play in a game with exponentially long play does not.
explanations.d: Go on a fixed n-by-n board is perfectly decidable — the position space is finite. It is expensive, not undecidable.

questions.prompt: Match each theorem or result to what it establishes.

right.text: Proves P is a proper subset of EXP and L is a proper subset of PSPACE
Proves PSPACE equals NPSPACE via quadratic space simulation
Proves NL equals co-NL, i.e. nondeterministic log-space is closed under complement
Proves generalized Go under the basic ko rule is EXPTIME-complete

questions.explanation: The hierarchy theorems give proper containments across time and space budgets; Savitch's theorem shows deterministic space can match nondeterministic space up to squaring; Immerman-Szelepcsenyi proves the surprising closure result NL = co-NL, sharing the 1995 Godel Prize; Robson placed generalized Go with the basic ko rule at EXPTIME-complete, above the PSPACE-complete games like Hex.

questions.prompt: Order these classes by their standard containment chain, from smallest to largest.

items.text: L
NL
P
NP
PSPACE
EXP

questions.explanation: The standard containment chain is L subset-or-equal NL subset-or-equal P subset-or-equal NP subset-or-equal PSPACE subset-or-equal EXP; some links (L vs PSPACE, P vs EXP) are proven proper via the hierarchy theorems, while others (P vs NP, NP vs PSPACE) remain open. Hex sits at the PSPACE-complete level; Go under the basic ko rule sits at the EXP end, EXPTIME-complete by Robson's 1983 theorem.

lessons.label: Above NP: The Polynomial Hierarchy, #P, and the Zoo

sections.heading: Building the polynomial hierarchy from alternating quantifiers
sections.body: NP problems have the form 'there EXISTS a certificate such that a polynomial-time checker accepts.' The polynomial hierarchy (PH) generalizes this by allowing certificates to alternate with quantifiers. Sigma-1 is just NP: exists-a-witness problems. Sigma-2 problems have the form 'there EXISTS an x such that for ALL y, a polynomial-time-checkable relation holds' — one exists-quantifier followed by one for-all-quantifier, each ranging over polynomial-length strings. A canonical Sigma-2 problem is MIN-CIRCUIT-EQUIVALENCE-style reasoning: for instance, deciding whether a given Boolean circuit is NOT the smallest circuit computing its function requires 'there exists a smaller circuit such that for all inputs, it agrees with the original' — an exists-for-all structure that appears to need more than a single NP-style certificate. Pi-2 is the dual, with for-all then exists, and co-NP is Pi-1. The hierarchy keeps building — Sigma-3, Pi-3, and so on — with PH defined as the union of all these levels, capturing problems that need a bounded but arbitrary number of quantifier alternations.

sections.heading: Collapse and containment
sections.body: The polynomial hierarchy has a dramatic structural property: if P equals NP, the ENTIRE hierarchy collapses down to P — every level, no matter how many quantifier alternations, turns out equal to P as well. This is because if Sigma-1 (NP) equals its complement class Pi-1, the machinery used to define Sigma-2 (an NP-style quantifier applied to a Pi-1-decidable relation) collapses too, and the collapse cascades upward through every level. This gives P vs NP even more weight than it might otherwise seem to carry: it is not just a question about one class boundary, it is a question about whether an entire infinite-looking tower of increasingly complex quantifier structures secretly flattens to nothing. PH itself is contained in PSPACE, since a polynomial-space machine can straightforwardly evaluate any bounded number of alternating polynomial-length quantifiers by brute-force recursion, reusing space across each quantifier level.

sections.heading: Counting problems: #P and Valiant's permanent result
sections.body: #P (read 'sharp-P' or 'number-P') shifts from DECIDING to COUNTING: instead of asking whether a solution exists, a #P problem asks HOW MANY solutions exist, for a relation checkable in polynomial time. #SAT, for instance, asks how many satisfying assignments a Boolean formula has. Leslie Valiant's 1979 result 'The Complexity of Computing the Permanent' is the class's landmark theorem: he proved that computing the PERMANENT of a 0-1 matrix (a determinant-like sum, but without the alternating sign) is #P-complete — provably as hard as any counting problem in the class. The striking part is the contrast with a closely related DECISION problem: deciding whether a bipartite graph has a PERFECT MATCHING (equivalent to asking whether the permanent of its adjacency matrix is nonzero) is in P, via Edmonds-style algorithms. So checking WHETHER a matching exists is easy, but counting HOW MANY perfect matchings exist is #P-complete — one of the sharpest known examples of decision and counting versions of the 'same' problem living in wildly different complexity worlds.

sections.heading: Toda's theorem and the Complexity Zoo
sections.body: Seinosuke Toda's 1991 theorem, 'PP is as hard as the polynomial-time hierarchy,' proved PH is contained in P^#P — meaning a polynomial-time machine given an oracle that instantly answers any #P counting query can simulate the ENTIRE polynomial hierarchy, every quantifier-alternation level of it. This was startling because #P was defined around a seemingly narrower task (counting) yet turned out powerful enough to swallow all of PH; the result won Toda the 1998 Godel Prize. Results like this are why complexity theory ends up with hundreds of named classes rather than just P, NP, and PSPACE: BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time), RP, ZPP, IP, PH's individual levels, #P, PP, and many more each capture a genuinely different resource or answer-structure. The Complexity Zoo, a reference site cataloguing over 500 named complexity classes, exists precisely because so many distinct combinations of resource bounds (time, space, randomness, counting, alternation, interaction) turn out to matter, though the size of the zoo is also a standing caution: not every named class represents a load-bearing distinction for practical problems, and part of complexity theory's ongoing work is figuring out which of the zoo's many exhibits actually differ from their neighbors.

lessons.workedExample: A student is asked to classify two closely related questions about a bipartite graph: (1) 'Does a perfect matching exist?' and (2) 'How many perfect matchings exist?' Question (1) is a decision problem solvable in polynomial time via Edmonds-style augmenting-path algorithms, so it is in P. Question (2) asks for a count, computable as the permanent of the graph's bipartite adjacency matrix, and by Valiant's 1979 theorem this counting problem is #P-complete — believed to require far more than polynomial time despite the underlying decision problem being easy. The student can use this pair as a concrete illustration that 'is there a solution' and 'how many solutions are there' are not the same difficulty at all, even when they are transformations of literally the same combinatorial object.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who wants to see whether a student has gone beyond the P/NP headline will ask about counting versions of familiar problems, since the matching-vs-permanent gap (easy decision, #P-complete counting) is one of the cleanest 'gotcha' illustrations in the field. A student citing Valiant 1979 by name, and able to explain WHY the permanent's alternating-sign-free structure makes it harder to compute than the determinant (which has fast algorithms via Gaussian elimination), shows genuine command of the material rather than a memorized hierarchy diagram. Bonus depth: connecting Toda's theorem to explain why counting oracles are so powerful ties the whole unit together — decision, counting, and quantifier-alternation all turn out to be tightly linked.

questions.prompt: What happens to the polynomial hierarchy (PH) if P is proven equal to NP?

options.text: Only the first level (NP) is affected; higher levels are unaffected
The entire hierarchy collapses down to P at every level
PH would then be proven strictly larger than PSPACE
Nothing changes, since PH and NP are unrelated classes

explanations.a: The collapse cascades through every level, not just the first — Sigma-2, Pi-2, and beyond all reduce to P as well.
explanations.b: Correct — because each level of PH is built from the class equalling its complement at the level below, a P=NP collapse at the base propagates upward and flattens the entire hierarchy to P.
explanations.c: PH is contained in PSPACE regardless of whether P=NP; a collapse of PH does not push it above PSPACE.
explanations.d: PH is literally built by stacking NP-style quantifiers on top of each other, so it is deeply dependent on NP's structure.

questions.prompt: What did Valiant's 1979 result about the permanent establish, in contrast to bipartite perfect matching?

options.text: Both counting and deciding perfect matchings are in P
Deciding whether a perfect matching exists is in P, but counting the number of perfect matchings (the permanent) is #P-complete
Computing the permanent is undecidable
The permanent can be computed in the same time as the determinant using Gaussian elimination

explanations.a: Only the decision version is known to be in P; the counting version is #P-complete, believed to be much harder.
explanations.b: Correct — Valiant showed computing the permanent (equivalent to counting perfect matchings) is #P-complete, even though the corresponding decision question is solvable in polynomial time.
explanations.c: The permanent is computable, just believed to require more than polynomial time; it is not undecidable.
explanations.d: Unlike the determinant, the permanent lacks the alternating-sign structure that makes Gaussian elimination applicable, which is exactly why it is far harder to compute.

questions.prompt: What did Toda's theorem (1991) prove?

options.text: PH is contained in P^#P — a polynomial-time machine with a #P oracle can simulate the entire polynomial hierarchy
P equals NP
#P is contained in NP
The permanent can be computed in polynomial time

explanations.a: Correct — Toda proved PH subset-or-equal P^#P, showing that access to exact counting answers is powerful enough to simulate every level of the polynomial hierarchy; the result won the 1998 Godel Prize.
explanations.b: Toda's theorem does not resolve P vs NP; it relates PH to a counting-oracle class.
explanations.c: #P is a counting class believed to be much more powerful than NP for these purposes, not contained in it in any established sense relevant here.
explanations.d: Valiant's result shows the opposite — the permanent is #P-complete, believed to need more than polynomial time.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

right.text: Problems of the form 'exists x such that for all y, a poly-time-checkable relation holds'
The class of problems asking how many solutions a poly-time-checkable relation has
A reference cataloguing 500+ named complexity classes, useful as a map but not proof every class is load-bearing

questions.explanation: Sigma-2 problems alternate an exists-quantifier with a for-all-quantifier over polynomial-length strings; #P problems count solutions rather than deciding existence; the Complexity Zoo catalogues the huge and still-growing collection of named classes complexity theorists have found reason to define.

lessons.label: Polynomial-Time Reductions and the Direction Rule

sections.heading: The Karp reduction: a translator, not a solver
sections.body: A polynomial-time many-one reduction, written A ≤p B and formalized by Richard Karp in his 1972 paper "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems," is a function f computable in time polynomial in the size of its input such that for every string x, x is a YES-instance of A if and only if f(x) is a YES-instance of B. The reduction does not solve A itself — it only rewrites an A-question as a B-question of comparable (polynomially bounded) size, then hands the rewritten question to whatever solves B. Karp's paper is the second half of the founding pair of complexity theory, alongside Stephen Cook's 1971 result: Cook showed SAT was hard for all of NP, and Karp showed twenty-one other combinatorial problems — including CLIQUE, VERTEX COVER, HAMILTONIAN CYCLE, and PARTITION — were exactly as hard, by reducing SAT-family problems to each in polynomial time. This is the machinery that turns one hardness proof into a whole web of them.

sections.heading: Two lemmas that make reductions worth building
sections.body: The entire payoff of A ≤p B rests on two small facts. First, the DOWNWARD lemma: if A ≤p B and B ∈ P, then A ∈ P. The argument is mechanical — given an instance x of A, compute f(x) in polynomial time, run B's polynomial-time algorithm on f(x), and return its answer; composing two polynomials in n is still a polynomial in n. Contrapositively, this is the lemma that actually gets used in practice: if A ≤p B and A is believed to be hard (not in P, assuming P ≠ NP), then B cannot be in P either — because if it were, A would be too. Second, TRANSITIVITY: if A ≤p B and B ≤p C, then A ≤p C, because composing two polynomial-time functions f and g yields a function g∘f still computable in polynomial time (a polynomial of a polynomial is a polynomial). Transitivity is what lets a single anchor — SAT — propagate hardness down an entire tree of reductions without redoing a from-scratch argument at every node.

sections.heading: The direction rule: the single most common error
sections.body: To prove a NEW problem X is NP-hard, you must reduce a problem ALREADY KNOWN to be NP-hard TO X — that is, show K ≤p X for some known-hard K, never X ≤p K. Students reflexively reduce the wrong way because it feels more natural to take the unfamiliar new problem and simplify it into the familiar old one. But that direction proves nothing about hardness: if X ≤p K and K ∈ P, it only shows X ∈ P (or is consistent with X being easy) — it says nothing about X being hard. The construction must also run in time polynomial in |x|, the size of the ORIGINAL instance being translated. A map that is correct but takes exponential time to build — for instance, one that unary-encodes a number that was given in binary, or explicitly enumerates all subsets of a set — is not a valid reduction for hardness purposes, even if f is a mathematically well-defined function, because the whole point is bounding the translation cost so hardness transfers cleanly.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a student wants to argue that a scheduling problem X is NP-hard. They know VERTEX COVER is NP-complete. The correct move is to build a function f mapping any graph-and-budget instance (G, k) of VERTEX COVER to a scheduling instance f(G, k) of X, such that G has a vertex cover of size k if and only if f(G, k) is schedulable under X's constraints, and to show f runs in time polynomial in |G| (e.g., linear in the number of vertices and edges, not exponential). If they instead reduce X to VERTEX COVER, they have shown at most that X is no harder than VERTEX COVER — useless for a hardness claim, and exactly backwards from what a hardness proof requires.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen this material before will almost always ask a project to state which direction its reduction runs and why, because getting the direction backwards is the single most common conceptual error in NP-completeness arguments, and it is easy to catch by asking the presenter to say, out loud, 'I reduced known-hard problem K to my problem X' rather than the reverse. A judge may also probe the polynomial-time claim on the construction itself — not just on solving the instance — since a reduction that secretly does exponential work to build f(x) proves nothing.

questions.prompt: To prove a new problem X is NP-hard, which direction of reduction is required?

options.text: Reduce X to a known NP-complete problem K (X ≤p K)
Reduce a known NP-complete problem K to X (K ≤p X)
Either direction works equally well
Reduce X to itself to establish a baseline

explanations.a: This direction only shows X is no harder than K; it says nothing about X being hard, since if K ∈ P this would just place X in P too.
explanations.b: Correct — reducing a KNOWN hard problem K into X shows that solving X efficiently would let you solve K efficiently, transferring K's hardness onto X.
explanations.c: The directions are not interchangeable; only K ≤p X transfers hardness onto X.
explanations.d: A problem trivially reduces to itself, but that establishes nothing about hardness relative to a known problem.

questions.prompt: A reduction f from A to B is proposed, but computing f(x) requires exponential time in |x| (e.g., it unary-encodes a binary number). What is the status of this reduction?

options.text: It is still a valid Karp reduction as long as f(x) is well-defined and the iff condition holds
It is not a valid polynomial-time reduction, so it cannot be used to transfer NP-hardness
It is valid only if B is already known to be in P
It is valid as long as the exponential blow-up happens only once

explanations.a: Well-definedness and the iff condition are necessary but not sufficient — a Karp reduction also requires f to be computable in polynomial time in |x|.
explanations.b: Correct — the polynomial-time bound on constructing f(x) is part of the definition; without it, the reduction cannot transfer hardness (an exponential blow-up could make an easy problem look hard).
explanations.c: The polynomial-time requirement applies to the construction of f regardless of what is known about B.
explanations.d: A single exponential-time construction step still violates the polynomial-time requirement, no matter how many times it happens.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps used to prove A ∈ P from A ≤p B and a known polynomial-time algorithm for B.

items.text: Start with instance x of problem A
Compute f(x), the reduction's output, in polynomial time
Run B's polynomial-time algorithm on f(x)
Return B's answer on f(x) as the answer for x on A

questions.explanation: The downward lemma composes two polynomial-time steps: translate x into f(x) via the reduction, solve f(x) with B's known algorithm, then hand that answer back as the answer for the original instance x, since x ∈ A iff f(x) ∈ B.

questions.prompt: Match each reduction property to what it guarantees.

right.text: A ≤p B and B ≤p C together imply A ≤p C
A ≤p B and B ∈ P together imply A ∈ P
Ensures composing the reduction with a solver stays polynomial overall

questions.explanation: Transitivity lets hardness propagate through chains of reductions without a fresh argument at each link. The downward lemma is the mechanism by which an easiness result for B is inherited by A. The polynomial-time bound on the reduction's construction is what makes both of these compositions actually polynomial rather than blown up by an expensive translation step.

lessons.label: The Cook-Levin Theorem: Why SAT Is Universal

sections.heading: The claim: every NP problem hides inside SAT
sections.body: The Cook-Levin theorem states that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete: every problem in NP reduces to SAT in polynomial time. This is a stronger claim than showing SAT is merely NP-hard for a handful of problems — it says that no matter what NP problem you name, checking one particular kind of formula for satisfiability can simulate solving it. The proof is a single reduction scheme that works for ANY NP problem L at once, by exploiting the definition of NP itself: L ∈ NP means there is a polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that x ∈ L if and only if there exists a certificate y of length at most p(|x|) with V(x, y) accepting. The trick is to encode the entire RUN of V on input x and certificate y as a giant Boolean formula, so that satisfying assignments of the formula correspond exactly to accepting runs.

sections.heading: The tableau: turning a computation into a grid
sections.body: Since V runs in polynomial time t(n), its computation on any input of length n visits at most t(n) configurations (tape contents, head position, state), and each configuration fits in t(n) cells because the tape head cannot travel further than the number of steps taken. This lets you lay out the entire computation as a t(n) × t(n) TABLEAU: row i shows the machine's full configuration at time step i, so the tableau has one row per time step and one column per tape cell. Each cell (i, j) gets Boolean variables encoding which tape symbol and machine state (if any) occupy that position at that time. The formula is built from clause groups: CELL clauses force exactly one symbol/state per cell; START clauses pin row 0 to the actual input x and guessed certificate y; MOVE clauses — the technical heart of the construction — use a 2×3 sliding WINDOW over three cells in row i and the three cells below them in row i+1, with a clause for every combination that is NOT a legal transition of V's transition function, ruling it out; and ACCEPT clauses require an accepting state to appear somewhere in the tableau. A satisfying assignment to this whole formula exists exactly when there is a legal, accepting computation history — i.e., exactly when x ∈ L. The number of variables and clauses is polynomial in t(n), so the whole formula is built in polynomial time, making this a valid Karp reduction from L to SAT for every L in NP simultaneously.

sections.heading: Two discoveries, one behind the Iron Curtain
sections.body: Stephen Cook proved this result in his 1971 paper "The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures," presented at the Third Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC), establishing SAT's universal hardness; the poly-time reduction from SAT (and 3-SAT) to CLIQUE, along with 20 other combinatorial problems, came a year later in Richard Karp's 1972 paper "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems." Independently and almost simultaneously, Soviet mathematician Leonid Levin proved an equivalent theorem in his 1973 paper "Universal Sequential Search Problems," published in the Russian journal Problems of Information Transmission, working from a different formalization (his own notion of enumeration-style search problems) with no access to Cook's work due to Cold War-era isolation between Soviet and Western computer science. Because both researchers independently identified the same phenomenon — a problem so general that all of NP reduces to it — the result and the resulting complexity class are jointly credited as the Cook-Levin theorem, and the class of problems as hard as SAT is called NP-COMPLETE precisely because they are both IN NP and as HARD AS anything in NP (complete for the class under polynomial-time reductions).

lessons.workedExample: Consider an NP problem L with a verifier V that runs in t(n) = 5n steps on inputs of length n. To reduce an instance x of length n to SAT, build a tableau with 5n rows and roughly 5n columns, giving on the order of 25n² cells, each holding a small constant number of Boolean variables for symbol/state. The CELL clauses fix one symbol per cell; the START clauses hard-wire row 0 to read x followed by placeholder variables for the guessed certificate y; the MOVE clauses check every 2×3 window of adjacent cells across two consecutive rows against V's transition rules, forbidding illegal jumps; and the ACCEPT clause requires an accept-state marker somewhere in the grid. The resulting formula has size polynomial in n (roughly quadratic here), and it is satisfiable exactly when some certificate y makes V(x, y) accept — i.e., exactly when x ∈ L.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to see that a student understands WHY the reduction is universal rather than just naming the theorem — specifically, that the tableau encodes an arbitrary verifier's computation history rather than being tailored to one problem, and that the reduction's size stays polynomial in the input because the verifier itself is polynomial-time. A sharp judge may also ask why the theorem carries two names, and the honest answer — Cook's 1971 STOC paper and Levin's independent 1973 paper written in the USSR without access to Western literature — signals real historical depth rather than a memorized one-line fact.

questions.prompt: What does the Cook-Levin theorem establish about SAT?

options.text: SAT can be solved in polynomial time using a clever backtracking algorithm
Every problem in NP can be reduced to SAT in polynomial time, making SAT NP-complete
SAT is undecidable, like the Halting Problem
SAT is NP-hard but not known to be in NP

explanations.a: SAT is not known to be solvable in polynomial time; in fact it is NP-complete, so a polynomial algorithm for it would imply P = NP.
explanations.b: Correct — Cook and Levin independently showed a single reduction scheme maps any NP verifier's computation into a SAT instance, so all of NP reduces to SAT in polynomial time.
explanations.c: SAT is decidable (just exponentially slow in the worst case by known algorithms); it is not in the same undecidable category as the Halting Problem.
explanations.d: SAT is in NP (a satisfying assignment is a poly-time-checkable certificate) as well as being NP-hard, which together is exactly what NP-complete means.

questions.prompt: In the tableau construction, what do the MOVE clauses (built from 2x3 windows) enforce?

options.text: That row 0 correctly encodes the input x and guessed certificate y
That an accepting state appears somewhere in the tableau
That each cell holds exactly one symbol/state
That consecutive rows represent a legal transition of the verifier's transition function

explanations.a: That is the role of the START clauses, which pin the first row to the actual input and certificate.
explanations.b: That is the role of the ACCEPT clauses, which require an accepting configuration to appear somewhere.
explanations.c: That is the role of the CELL clauses, which force exactly one symbol/state per grid position.
explanations.d: Correct — the MOVE clauses forbid every 2x3 window combination that is not a legal transition, so satisfying the formula forces every row to follow legally from the row above.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of the Cook-Levin theorem.

items.text: Cook publishes "The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures" at STOC
Levin independently publishes "Universal Sequential Search Problems" in the USSR
Karp's "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems" extends the result to 21 more problems

questions.explanation: By publication date: Cook's STOC paper appeared in 1971 and established SAT's universal hardness; Karp's "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems," building on Cook's SAT result to show 21 further problems NP-complete, appeared in 1972; Levin's independent paper, developed separately in the USSR under a different formalization, appeared in 1973 in Problems of Information Transmission.

questions.prompt: Match each clause group in the tableau construction to its function.

right.text: Force exactly one symbol/state per grid position
Pin row 0 to the actual input and guessed certificate
Require an accepting configuration to appear in the tableau

questions.explanation: CELL clauses enforce well-formedness of each grid position, START clauses anchor the computation to the real input and a guessed certificate, and ACCEPT clauses require that the simulated run actually reaches acceptance somewhere in the grid; MOVE clauses (a fourth group) separately enforce legal transitions between rows.

lessons.label: 3-SAT, the 2-SAT Boundary, and Schaefer's Dichotomy

sections.heading: From SAT to 3-SAT: the clause-splitting gadget
sections.body: The Cook-Levin tableau reduction produces a SAT formula whose clauses can be arbitrarily long, but almost every downstream reduction in this unit starts from 3-SAT — formulas where every clause has EXACTLY three literals — because a uniform clause shape makes gadget design far cleaner. SAT reduces to 3-SAT in polynomial time using a clause-splitting gadget. A long clause (l1 ∨ l2 ∨ ... ∨ lk) with k > 3 literals is replaced by a chain of k-2 new three-literal clauses linked by k-3 fresh auxiliary variables z1, ..., z(k-3): (l1 ∨ l2 ∨ z1), (¬z1 ∨ l3 ∨ z2), (¬z2 ∨ l4 ∨ z3), ..., (¬z(k-3) ∨ l(k-1) ∨ lk). The chain works because if any original literal li is true, one can set the z's so every link is satisfied (z1 through z(i-2) true, the rest false); conversely if all original literals are false, no setting of the z chain can satisfy every link, since satisfying the first link forces z1 true, which forces the second link to need z2 true, propagating a contradiction down the chain. Short clauses (one or two literals) are padded by repeating a literal or adding a fresh don't-care variable pair to reach exactly three. The whole construction adds a number of new variables and clauses linear in the original formula's size, so it is a valid poly-time reduction.

sections.heading: Falling off the cliff: 2-SAT is easy
sections.body: Drop the clause length from three literals to two and satisfiability becomes solvable in POLYNOMIAL time — in fact linear time — a sharp complexity cliff with no problem of intermediate difficulty sitting between the two clause lengths. Bengt Aspvall, Michael Plass, and Robert Tarjan gave the standard algorithm in their 1979 paper "A Linear-Time Algorithm for Testing the Truth of Certain Quantified Boolean Formulas" (Information Processing Letters): build an IMPLICATION GRAPH with two vertices per variable (one for the literal, one for its negation), and for every clause (a ∨ b), add two directed edges ¬a → b and ¬b → a (each clause is logically equivalent to two implications). The formula is satisfiable if and only if no variable x has x and ¬x in the same STRONGLY CONNECTED COMPONENT of this graph — because being in the same SCC means x implies ¬x and ¬x implies x, a direct contradiction. Finding SCCs (via Tarjan's own 1972 algorithm, or Kosaraju's) takes time linear in the number of vertices and edges, and if the formula is satisfiable, a satisfying assignment falls out of the topological order of the SCCs: set a variable true if its negation's SCC comes later in that order.

sections.heading: Horn-SAT and Schaefer's complete map of the boundary
sections.body: A second island of tractability is HORN-SAT: formulas where every clause has at most one POSITIVE literal (a Horn clause). These are solved in polynomial time by UNIT PROPAGATION — repeatedly finding a clause reduced to a single unassigned literal by the current partial assignment and forcing that literal true (or, for an all-negative clause, checking it isn't already violated), iterating until no more forcing is possible or a contradiction appears; this runs in time linear in the formula's size. What makes this area of complexity theory unusually satisfying is that it is not just a scattered list of easy special cases — Thomas Schaefer's 1978 paper "The Complexity of Satisfiability Problems" (STOC '78) proved a DICHOTOMY THEOREM: for any finite set of allowed Boolean constraint types (a "constraint language"), the resulting generalized satisfiability problem SAT(A) is either solvable in polynomial time or is NP-complete — there is provably nothing in between. Schaefer further gave an exact syntactic criterion (six special closure properties, including being Horn, dual-Horn, bijunctive/2-SAT-like, or affine) that determines which side of the boundary any given constraint language falls on. This is one of the few places in complexity theory where the entire landscape of a problem family is mapped exactly rather than left as a list of open cases.

lessons.workedExample: Take the 5-literal clause (a ∨ b ∨ c ∨ d ∨ e) and split it into 3-CNF using k-3 = 2 fresh variables z1, z2: (a ∨ b ∨ z1), (¬z1 ∨ c ∨ z2), (¬z2 ∨ d ∨ e). If a is true, set z1 = true and z2 = true (or anything downstream), satisfying all three links regardless of b, c, d, e. If a, b, c, d, e are all false, the first link forces z1 = true to be satisfied, which forces the second link to need z2 = true (since ¬z1 is false and c is false), which then forces the third link to need d ∨ e — but both are false, so the chain is unsatisfiable, exactly mirroring the original clause being all-false. Now contrast with a 2-SAT instance (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ y) ∧ (¬y ∨ z) ∧ (¬z): the implication graph (one vertex per literal, no separate true/false nodes) has edges ¬x→y, ¬y→x, x→y, ¬y→¬x, y→z, ¬z→¬y, and the unit clause (¬z) contributes z→¬z. Tracing SCCs here, the cycle y→z→¬z→¬y→x→y puts z and ¬z (along with x, ¬y, y) in the same strongly connected component, so by the rule above the instance is UNSATISFIABLE — matching a direct check: (¬z) forces z=false, (¬y∨z) then forces y=false, (x∨y) then forces x=true, but then (¬x∨y) = false∨false = false, violated. Finding this in linear time via SCCs is exactly why 2-SAT is tractable even though the same check on 3-SAT's larger implication structure is not enough to decide it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this area will want to hear WHY 3-SAT rather than raw SAT is the standard reduction source — the clause-splitting gadget is a clean, teachable example of turning an unbounded-arity problem into a fixed-arity one without changing satisfiability, and it is the template every later gadget reduction in this unit reuses. An even sharper question is why 2-SAT collapses to polynomial time when 3-SAT does not, and the implication-graph/SCC argument (Aspvall-Plass-Tarjan, 1979) is the precise mechanistic answer, not a hand-wave about clause length; naming Schaefer's 1978 dichotomy theorem on top of that shows the student knows this cliff is a proven, complete boundary rather than an unexplained empirical pattern.

questions.prompt: In the clause-splitting gadget reducing SAT to 3-SAT, what role do the fresh auxiliary variables (z1, z2, ...) play?

options.text: They encode the original clause's literals directly, replacing them entirely
They chain adjacent 3-literal clauses together so the chain is satisfiable exactly when some original literal is true
They are decorative and can be removed without changing satisfiability
They force the formula to become unsatisfiable if the clause was originally too long

explanations.a: The auxiliary variables do not replace the original literals; they link the chain of new clauses containing those literals.
explanations.b: Correct — each z can be set to true to satisfy an early link once some original literal is true, propagating satisfiability rightward down the chain; if no original literal is true, the chain forces a contradiction.
explanations.c: The auxiliary variables are essential; removing them would leave clauses that don't have three literals or would break the equivalence to the original clause.
explanations.d: The construction preserves satisfiability in both directions; it does not force unsatisfiability based on clause length.

questions.prompt: In the 2-SAT implication-graph algorithm, a formula is UNSATISFIABLE exactly when...

options.text: The implication graph has more edges than vertices
Some variable x and its negation ¬x lie in the same strongly connected component
The graph is not connected
There exists a clause with only one literal

explanations.a: Edge count relative to vertex count has no bearing on satisfiability in this construction.
explanations.b: Correct — if x and ¬x are mutually reachable (same SCC), then x implies ¬x and ¬x implies x, a direct logical contradiction that makes the formula unsatisfiable.
explanations.c: Disconnection is irrelevant; satisfiability depends only on whether any complementary literal pair shares an SCC.
explanations.d: A unit clause is fine in 2-SAT (it's a clause of length one, still expressible); it does not by itself cause unsatisfiability.

questions.prompt: According to Schaefer's 1978 dichotomy theorem, a generalized Boolean satisfiability problem SAT(A) for a finite constraint language A is...

options.text: Always NP-complete regardless of A
Always solvable in polynomial time
Either in P or NP-complete, with no intermediate difficulty possible
Undecidable for most choices of A

explanations.a: Counterexamples like 2-SAT and Horn-SAT are in P, so it is not always NP-complete.
explanations.b: Counterexamples like 3-SAT and general SAT are NP-complete, so it is not always in P.
