explanations.c: Correct — Schaefer proved every such problem falls exactly into one of these two categories, with an exact syntactic criterion determining which, and nothing in between (ruling out NP-intermediate status for this entire family).
explanations.d: These are all decidable (finite search space per instance); undecidability does not enter into Schaefer's result.

questions.prompt: Match each satisfiability variant to the algorithmic technique that solves it in polynomial time.

right.text: Implication graph + strongly connected components
Unit propagation on clauses with at most one positive literal
Clause-splitting with fresh chain variables

questions.explanation: 2-SAT is solved by building the implication graph and checking that no variable and its negation share a strongly connected component (Aspvall-Plass-Tarjan, 1979, linear time). Horn-SAT is solved by unit propagation, repeatedly forcing literals in clauses reduced to one unassigned literal. Clause-splitting (r3) is a reduction technique, not a polynomial-time SOLVING algorithm, so it is left unmatched.

lessons.label: Karp's Tree, Part 1: Graph Problems

sections.heading: 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET: a triangle per clause
sections.body: The classic first step out of logic and into graphs reduces 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET. Given a 3-CNF formula with m clauses, build a graph with one TRIANGLE of three vertices per clause, each vertex labeled with one of that clause's three literals; triangle edges force at most one vertex per clause into any independent set, since a triangle's vertices are pairwise adjacent. Then add CONFLICT EDGES between every pair of vertices (in different triangles) labeled with complementary literals (x and ¬x). Set the target size k = m, the number of clauses. Correctness runs both ways: if the formula is satisfiable, pick one true literal per clause and select its vertex in each triangle — this gives m vertices, one per triangle so no triangle-edge is violated, and no two selected vertices can be complementary literals (since a satisfying assignment can't have x true in one clause's choice and ¬x true in another's), so no conflict edge is violated either, making it a valid independent set of size m. Conversely, if an independent set of size m exists, since each triangle contributes at most one vertex, it must contribute EXACTLY one vertex per triangle (m triangles, m vertices), and the absence of conflict edges between selected vertices means the literals selected form a consistent assignment — setting each selected literal true satisfies every clause, since every triangle contributed a true literal.

sections.heading: INDEPENDENT SET, CLIQUE, and VERTEX COVER: three faces of one problem
sections.body: These three problems are essentially restatements of each other on the same graph. INDEPENDENT SET on G and CLIQUE on G's COMPLEMENT graph (same vertices, edges exactly reversed) are identical: S is independent in G if and only if S is a clique in the complement, because independence means no edges among S in G, which means all edges among S in the complement. This reduction is trivial and takes time polynomial in the number of vertices/edges (just build the complement). VERTEX COVER connects to INDEPENDENT SET on the SAME graph via complementation of the vertex set rather than the edges: for any graph G = (V, E), a set S ⊆ V is a vertex cover (every edge has at least one endpoint in S) if and only if V∖S is independent. Proof both ways: if S covers every edge, then no edge can have both endpoints in V∖S (since one endpoint would then not be in S, contradicting coverage), so V∖S is independent; conversely if V∖S is independent, no edge has both endpoints outside S, so every edge has at least one endpoint in S, meaning S covers all edges. This gives an immediate reduction: G has a vertex cover of size k if and only if G has an independent set of size |V| - k.

sections.heading: Downstream: SET COVER and DOMINATING SET
sections.body: VERTEX COVER reduces to the more general SET COVER problem (given a universe and a family of subsets, cover the universe with few subsets) by treating each vertex v as a set S_v containing exactly the edges incident to v; a vertex cover of size k in G exists if and only if the universe of edges can be covered by k of the sets S_v, since selecting vertex v to be in the cover is the same as selecting S_v to include all its incident edges, and every edge needs at least one endpoint (hence at least one S_v) selected. VERTEX COVER also reduces to DOMINATING SET (a set D such that every vertex is in D or adjacent to a vertex in D): for each edge {u, v}, add a new helper vertex w adjacent only to u and v. A minimum dominating set of the augmented graph can always be converted, without increasing its size, to one using only original vertices — because an original endpoint dominates every helper vertex on its incident edges, while a helper vertex dominates nothing beyond its own two endpoints, so swapping any helper into the set for one of its endpoints never costs anything and can only help dominate more of the graph. This pushes an optimal solution toward endpoint-vertices, and a dominating set restricted to original vertices is exactly a vertex cover, since every edge's helper must be dominated by one of its two endpoints.

lessons.workedExample: Take the 3-CNF formula (x ∨ y ∨ z) ∧ (¬x ∨ y ∨ ¬z), m = 2 clauses. Build two triangles: triangle 1 with vertices labeled x, y, z; triangle 2 with vertices labeled ¬x, y, ¬z. Add conflict edges: x—¬x (across triangles) and z—¬z (across triangles); note the two y-labeled vertices are NOT connected by a conflict edge since they carry the same literal, not complementary ones. Set k = 2. The assignment x = true, y = false, z = false satisfies both clauses (via x in clause 1, via ¬z in clause 2); correspondingly, pick the x-vertex from triangle 1 and the ¬z-vertex from triangle 2 — these are in different triangles (no triangle edge violated) and are not a complementary pair (no conflict edge violated), giving a valid independent set of size 2. This mirrors the reduction's guarantee: satisfying assignment maps to a size-m independent set, and vice versa.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask a presenter to prove ONE direction of an iff they haven't shown, precisely because students frequently only demonstrate the easy direction (map a solution to a solution) and skip the harder direction (any solution to the target problem must correspond to a solution of the source problem) — for VERTEX COVER/INDEPENDENT SET complementation specifically, a judge might ask 'why can't a smaller-than-claimed independent set still work,' testing whether the size argument (|V| - k) and the both-directions argument were actually understood rather than pattern-matched from a textbook diagram.

questions.prompt: In the reduction from 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET, why are three vertices in each clause's triangle mutually connected by edges?

options.text: To ensure at most one vertex per clause's triangle can be chosen in an independent set
To represent the three possible truth values a literal could take
To make the graph 3-regular for algorithmic convenience
Triangle edges are decorative and don't affect independent set size

explanations.a: Correct — triangle edges are pairwise adjacencies, so an independent set can include at most one vertex from each triangle, mirroring 'at most one literal choice per clause' in the construction.
explanations.b: Literals are Boolean (true/false), not three-valued; the triangle vertices represent the clause's three LITERALS, not truth values.
explanations.c: Regularity is not the goal; the triangle structure specifically enforces the at-most-one-per-clause constraint needed for correctness.
explanations.d: Triangle edges are essential to the reduction's correctness, not decorative — without them, an independent set could take all three literals from one clause.

questions.prompt: For a graph G = (V, E), which statement correctly relates VERTEX COVER and INDEPENDENT SET?

options.text: S is a vertex cover if and only if S is also an independent set
S is a vertex cover if and only if V∖S is an independent set
S is a vertex cover if and only if S is a clique in G
There is no relationship between the two problems

explanations.a: A vertex cover and an independent set are generally disjoint concepts on the same set; a set can rarely be both unless the graph has no edges.
explanations.b: Correct — S covers every edge exactly when no edge has both endpoints in the complement V∖S, which is exactly the condition for V∖S to be independent.
explanations.c: Being a clique means all pairs in S are connected, an unrelated property to covering all of G's edges.
explanations.d: The two problems are tightly linked via this complementation, which is exactly what allows one polynomial-time reduction to connect them.

questions.prompt: Order these problems as they appear in the reduction chain built in this lesson, from the logic source to the most downstream graph/set problem.

items.text: 3-SAT
INDEPENDENT SET
VERTEX COVER
SET COVER

questions.explanation: The chain built here starts at 3-SAT, reduces to INDEPENDENT SET via the triangle-plus-conflict-edge gadget, connects to VERTEX COVER via vertex-set complementation on the same graph, and finally reduces VERTEX COVER to SET COVER by treating each vertex as the set of its incident edges.

questions.prompt: Match each graph-problem pair to the transformation that relates them.

right.text: Take the complement graph (reverse all edges)
Complement the vertex SET within the same graph (S vs V∖S)
Map each vertex to the set of its incident edges

questions.explanation: INDEPENDENT SET and CLIQUE are related by complementing the GRAPH itself (edges become non-edges and vice versa). INDEPENDENT SET and VERTEX COVER are related by complementing the VERTEX SET within the same graph. VERTEX COVER reduces to SET COVER by mapping each vertex to the set of edges it touches, turning covering vertices into covering the edge universe.

lessons.label: Karp's Tree, Part 2: Colorings, Tours, and Numbers

sections.heading: 3-SAT to 3-COLORING: the palette triangle and the OR-gadget
sections.body: Reducing 3-SAT to graph 3-COLORING uses two clever gadgets. First, a PALETTE TRIANGLE of three special vertices True, False, and Base, mutually connected, forces any proper 3-coloring to assign these three vertices three distinct colors — fix these as the canonical colors 1 (True), 2 (False), 3 (Base). For each variable x, create a pair of vertices x and ¬x, each connected to Base (forcing them to use only colors 1 or 2, i.e., True or False) and connected to each other (forcing them to different colors) — so any proper coloring assigns exactly one of x, ¬x the True color and the other the False color, exactly encoding a Boolean assignment. Second, for each clause, an OR-GADGET (a small fixed subgraph, historically built from paired 'OR' components chained together) takes the three literal vertices of a clause as inputs and can be properly colored if and only if at least one of the three is colored True; if all three inputs are colored False, the gadget has no valid extension, so the coloring fails exactly when the clause is unsatisfied. The whole graph is 3-colorable if and only if the formula is satisfiable, and both the palette and every OR-gadget are constant-size per clause/variable, so the total construction is linear in the formula's size.

sections.heading: HAMILTONIAN CYCLE to TSP: weights that force honesty
sections.body: The reduction from HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (does graph G have a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once?) to the TRAVELING SALESMAN PROBLEM (find a tour of all cities with total weight ≤ budget) is one of the shortest gadgets in the whole tree. Given G = (V, E) with n vertices, build a complete weighted graph on the same vertex set: edges that exist in G get weight 1, and every other pair (non-edges of G) gets weight 2. Set the TSP budget to exactly n. If G has a Hamiltonian cycle, that same cycle is a TSP tour using only weight-1 edges, totaling n — meeting the budget. Conversely, if a TSP tour of total weight ≤ n exists, since the tour has exactly n edges and every edge costs at least 1, achieving total weight n forces EVERY edge in the tour to cost exactly 1, meaning every edge used must be a real edge of G — so the tour is a genuine Hamiltonian cycle in G. The gadget's cleverness is entirely in the weight gap (1 versus 2): any use of even one 'fake' edge blows the budget past n, so cost pressure alone forces the tour to stay inside G.

sections.heading: 3-SAT to SUBSET-SUM, PARTITION, and KNAPSACK: numbers as bit-blocks
sections.body: The reduction from 3-SAT to SUBSET-SUM encodes clauses and variables as large decimal (or binary) numbers built from POSITIONAL BIT-BLOCKS, one digit-block per variable and one per clause, engineered with enough headroom between blocks that no carrying between blocks can occur during addition — this no-carry property is what keeps each block's arithmetic acting like an independent Boolean check. Each variable gets two numbers (for its true and false literal appearances) with a 1 in its own variable-block and 1's scattered into the blocks of clauses it satisfies; slack numbers absorb leftover clause-block counts so any clause satisfied by 1, 2, or 3 of its literals still sums correctly. The target sum has 1 in every variable-block (forcing exactly one of the true/false numbers chosen per variable) and a fixed value in every clause-block (satisfiable only if at least one chosen literal hits that clause). SUBSET-SUM reduces to PARTITION (split a multiset into two equal-sum halves) by adding two auxiliary numbers to the set: given SUBSET-SUM instance (S, target t) with m equal to the sum of S, add a_{n+1} = 2m + t and a_{n+2} = 3m - t (both positive for any valid 0 ≤ t ≤ m); a partition of the augmented set into two equal-sum halves exists if and only if some subset of S sums to t, and using two numbers (rather than one) is what keeps both auxiliary values positive while forcing the equal-sum split to line up exactly with a subset summing to t. PARTITION reduces to KNAPSACK by treating each item's value and weight as equal to its number, with capacity set to half the total sum — a knapsack achieving exactly that capacity/value is exactly a PARTITION solution.

lessons.workedExample: Consider using KNAPSACK's standard dynamic-programming algorithm: for n items and capacity W, the DP table has size O(nW) and fills in O(nW) time — this LOOKS polynomial in n and W, but W is an INPUT NUMBER, not the input's bit-length. If W is given in binary using b = log2(W) bits, then W = 2^b, so the runtime O(nW) = O(n · 2^b) is EXPONENTIAL in b, the actual size of the input. This is why the O(nW) algorithm is called PSEUDO-POLYNOMIAL: polynomial in the numeric VALUE of the input but exponential in its bit-length. This distinction is exactly why knapsack admits an FPTAS (a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme, which can get arbitrarily close to optimal by rounding values and running the pseudo-polynomial DP on the rounded, smaller-range instance) while TSP — whose hardness does not come from large numbers but from combinatorial structure baked into strongly NP-hard problems — has no FPTAS unless P = NP.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing depth here will often ask why KNAPSACK'S O(nW) dynamic program isn't a polynomial-time algorithm that would collapse P and NP, and the correct answer — W's binary representation has only log(W) bits, so O(nW) is exponential in the true input size, making the DP pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial — is the single most-tested distinction between strong and weak NP-hardness. A judge may also ask why TSP, unlike KNAPSACK, has no FPTAS: because TSP's hardness is strongly NP-hard (persists even with small numbers, since it comes from graph structure), whereas KNAPSACK's is only weakly NP-hard (numbers, not structure, drive the hardness), which is exactly why an approximation scheme exists for one but not the other.

questions.prompt: In the 3-SAT to 3-COLORING reduction, what does the palette triangle (True, False, Base vertices) accomplish?

options.text: It encodes which clauses are satisfied
It forces three canonical, distinguishable colors that variable-literal pairs can be assigned against
It is only used to check the graph has at least 3 vertices
It represents the OR-gadget's clause-satisfaction logic

explanations.a: Clause satisfaction is checked by the separate OR-gadgets, not the palette triangle.
explanations.b: Correct — the mutually-connected True/False/Base triangle forces a proper coloring to use three distinct colors, giving fixed reference colors that every variable's literal-vertex pair is anchored against.
explanations.c: The triangle's purpose is to fix canonical colors, not to check a minimum vertex count.
explanations.d: The OR-gadget, a separate structure per clause, encodes clause-satisfaction logic; the palette triangle only establishes the reference colors.

questions.prompt: In the HAMILTONIAN CYCLE to TSP reduction, why are non-edges of G given weight 2 instead of some larger number?

options.text: Weight 2 has no special significance; any weight greater than 1 works identically for this argument
Weight 2 makes the total tour weight always exactly 2n
Weight 2 ensures the graph remains planar
Weight 2 is required so the DP runs in pseudo-polynomial time

explanations.a: Correct — the argument only needs any single fake edge to push total cost strictly above the budget n; since a tour has exactly n edges each costing at least 1, using even one edge of weight greater than 1 makes the total exceed n. Weight 2 is the simplest choice that achieves this, but the specific value 2 (versus, say, 5) is not itself essential to the logic.
explanations.b: The tour's actual weight is exactly n when it uses only real edges (weight 1) and would exceed n if any fake edge were used; it is not always 2n.
explanations.c: Planarity is unrelated to this reduction; the constructed graph is complete and generally not planar for n > 4.
explanations.d: The DP/pseudo-polynomial distinction applies to knapsack-family problems' numeric encoding, not to this graph-based TSP reduction's edge weights.

questions.prompt: Why is the O(nW) dynamic-programming algorithm for KNAPSACK called 'pseudo-polynomial' rather than simply 'polynomial'?

options.text: Because it uses recursion, which is inherently non-polynomial
Because W is the numeric capacity value, and its binary encoding has only log(W) bits, making runtime exponential in true input size
Because the algorithm's correctness has never been formally proven
Because n, the number of items, is not actually part of the input

explanations.a: Recursion (or its DP equivalent) is not inherently non-polynomial; many exact-polynomial algorithms use it.
explanations.b: Correct — W appears in binary with only log(W) bits in the actual input, so an O(nW) runtime is exponential in that bit-length, which is exactly the technical definition of pseudo-polynomial.
explanations.c: The DP algorithm's correctness is a standard, well-established proof; that is not the reason for the pseudo-polynomial label.
explanations.d: n, the item count, is very much part of the input; the issue is specifically W's numeric-versus-bit-length gap.

questions.prompt: Order this reduction chain from the logic source to the final numeric problem covered in this lesson.

items.text: 3-SAT
SUBSET-SUM
PARTITION
KNAPSACK

questions.explanation: 3-SAT reduces to SUBSET-SUM via positional no-carry bit-blocks encoding variables and clauses; SUBSET-SUM reduces to PARTITION by adding a balancing number; PARTITION reduces to KNAPSACK by setting each item's value equal to its weight and capacity to half the total sum.

lessons.label: Proving Your Own Problem NP-Complete

sections.heading: The two-step recipe
sections.body: Proving an arbitrary new problem X is NP-complete always takes exactly two steps, and skipping either one leaves the proof incomplete. STEP ONE, membership in NP: name a CERTIFICATE — a compact piece of evidence (an assignment, a subset, a path, a coloring) — and describe a VERIFIER algorithm that checks, in time polynomial in the input size, whether that certificate actually witnesses a YES-instance. This step is usually easy but is not optional: skipping it only proves X is NP-HARD, not NP-COMPLETE, and the two are not the same claim. STEP TWO, NP-hardness: pick a well-chosen problem K already known to be NP-complete, and construct a function f, computable in polynomial time, mapping instances of K to instances of X such that k is a YES-instance of K if and only if f(k) is a YES-instance of X. Crucially, this direction requires proving the iff in BOTH directions — first that a YES-instance of K maps to a YES-instance of X (often the easier half), and second that any YES-instance of X that arises this way forces the original K-instance to also be a YES-instance (the half students most often skip, but the half that actually establishes the reduction is sound rather than merely plausible).

sections.heading: Choosing your source problem
sections.body: The art of a clean reduction proof is picking K wisely, since a bad choice of source makes the gadget construction needlessly painful even when the underlying claim is true. For problems phrased in propositional LOGIC (choosing values, satisfying constraints, boolean formulas), 3-SAT is almost always the right source, since its fixed clause width (exactly three literals) makes gadget-per-clause constructions clean, as seen throughout this unit. For problems phrased over GRAPHS (selecting vertices or edges under adjacency constraints), VERTEX COVER or INDEPENDENT SET are usually the right source, since they are the simplest possible statement of 'pick a small/large set respecting adjacency.' For problems phrased over NUMBERS (partitioning quantities, meeting a numeric budget), SUBSET-SUM is the natural source, since its no-carry positional-block encoding technique generalizes to almost any numeric-partitioning target. For SCHEDULING problems (assigning jobs to machines or time slots under load constraints), 3-PARTITION — a stronger, strongly NP-hard variant of PARTITION that requires splitting a multiset into equal-sized, equal-sum TRIPLETS — is frequently the right source, because its structure (many small numbers, all forced into specific-size groups) maps naturally onto job-to-slot assignment gadgets in a way that plain PARTITION does not.

sections.heading: Three distinctions students routinely blur
sections.body: First, NP-HARD is not the same as NP-COMPLETE: NP-hard means every problem in NP reduces to it, with no requirement that the problem itself be IN NP. The canonical example is the HALTING PROBLEM, which is NP-hard (every NP problem trivially reduces to it, since NP ⊆ decidable ⊆ things the halting problem can help solve, via constructions that encode a poly-time verifier's search as a machine to run) but is NOT in NP, because it is not even decidable, let alone verifiable in polynomial time — so it is NP-hard without being NP-complete. Second, a Karp (many-one) reduction is not the only kind: a COOK or TURING reduction allows the algorithm for X to call an oracle for K many times (polynomially many calls, each getting a full answer back), rather than a single one-shot translation. Turing reductions are strictly more powerful, which is exactly the problem: they blur the boundary between NP and CO-NP, because an algorithm could, for instance, use a SAT oracle to check both satisfiability AND unsatisfiability-related sub-queries, so closure results that hold cleanly for Karp reductions (like NP-completeness itself, standardly defined via Karp reductions) do not automatically transfer if Turing reductions are substituted. Third, SELF-REDUCIBILITY: a decision oracle for SAT (does a satisfying assignment exist at all?) can be turned into an algorithm that PRODUCES an actual satisfying assignment using only n oracle calls for n variables — fix x1 = true, ask the oracle if the resulting simplified formula is still satisfiable; if yes, keep x1 = true, if no, set x1 = false instead; repeat for x2 through xn, and the fixed values form a genuine satisfying assignment. This shows that for self-reducible problems like SAT, deciding and actually constructing a solution are computationally equivalent up to a polynomial-factor overhead.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to prove their custom TEAM-BALANCING problem NP-complete: given a set of students each with a skill score, decide whether they can be split into two teams of equal size with equal total skill. For membership in NP, the certificate is simply the partition itself (which team each student is on), and the verifier checks team sizes and sums in linear time. For NP-hardness, since this is fundamentally a numeric partitioning problem, PARTITION is the natural source: map a PARTITION instance (a multiset of numbers, split into two equal-sum halves) directly onto TEAM-BALANCING by treating each number as a student's skill score, adding dummy students of skill 0 if needed to force the team-SIZE constraint to be satisfiable independent of the sum constraint. The forward direction (PARTITION solution gives a TEAM-BALANCING solution) and reverse direction (any valid team split gives back a valid PARTITION split) both need to be argued explicitly, not just the forward map.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge assessing whether a student actually understands NP-completeness, rather than having memorized the phrase, will ask them to name BOTH the certificate/verifier for the NP-membership half and the specific source problem and gadget for the hardness half — a student who can only do one half has only half a proof. A sharper judge may ask the difference between NP-hard and NP-complete using the Halting Problem example, or ask why Turing reductions are avoided in standard NP-completeness definitions, both of which separate a student with real technical grounding from one repeating a slogan.

questions.prompt: A student shows a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-complete problem K into their new problem X, but never describes a certificate or verifier for X. What have they actually proven?

options.text: That X is NP-complete
That X is NP-hard, but not necessarily NP-complete
That X is in P
Nothing, since the reduction direction must also be reversed

explanations.a: NP-completeness additionally requires showing X is IN NP (has a poly-time-verifiable certificate), which was never shown here.
explanations.b: Correct — a reduction from a known NP-complete problem into X establishes NP-hardness alone; NP-completeness additionally requires proving X ∈ NP.
explanations.c: Nothing here suggests X is in P; NP-hardness, if anything, suggests the opposite is likely (assuming P ≠ NP).
explanations.d: The reduction direction (K into X) is exactly correct for a hardness proof; the issue is a MISSING step (NP membership), not a wrong direction.

questions.prompt: Why is the Halting Problem NP-hard but NOT NP-complete?

options.text: Because it is not hard enough for any NP problem to reduce to it
Because it is undecidable, so it cannot be in NP (which requires poly-time verifiability), even though every NP problem reduces to it
Because NP-hardness and NP-completeness are actually the same thing for this problem
Because no reduction to it has ever been constructed

explanations.a: Every NP problem does reduce to the Halting Problem, satisfying the NP-hardness requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — the Halting Problem is undecidable, so it cannot have a polynomial-time (or even any terminating) verifier, disqualifying it from NP, even though it is NP-hard.
explanations.c: They are distinct properties; the Halting Problem is a textbook case where one holds (NP-hard) and the other does not (NP-complete, which also requires NP membership).
explanations.d: Reductions from NP problems to the Halting Problem can be constructed, which is exactly why it qualifies as NP-hard.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a Cook (Turing) reduction from a Karp (many-one) reduction?

options.text: A Turing reduction allows polynomially many oracle calls to the target problem, while a Karp reduction is a single one-shot translation
A Turing reduction must run in exponential time, while a Karp reduction runs in polynomial time
They are exactly equivalent in power; the names differ only historically
A Karp reduction can query the oracle multiple times, while a Turing reduction can only query once

explanations.a: Correct — a Turing/Cook reduction allows an algorithm to make many (polynomially bounded) calls to an oracle for the target problem, whereas a Karp reduction is restricted to a single translation with one final oracle call.
explanations.b: Both types of reductions used in complexity theory are required to run in polynomial time overall; the distinction is in the number and structure of oracle calls, not the time bound.
explanations.c: They are not equivalent in power; Turing reductions are strictly more general, which is exactly why they muddy distinctions like NP versus co-NP that Karp reductions preserve cleanly.
explanations.d: This has the definitions backwards — it is the Turing reduction that allows multiple oracle calls, not the Karp reduction.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the self-reducibility construction that turns a SAT decision oracle into an algorithm producing an actual satisfying assignment.

items.text: Fix x1 to true and ask the oracle if the simplified formula is still satisfiable
If yes, keep x1 = true; if no, set x1 = false instead, then simplify the formula accordingly
Repeat the fix-and-query process for each remaining variable x2 through xn
Return the fully fixed variable assignment as a genuine satisfying assignment

questions.explanation: Self-reducibility works by fixing one variable at a time, using the oracle to check whether that choice preserves satisfiability, keeping or flipping the choice accordingly, repeating across all n variables, and returning the resulting fully determined assignment — using only n oracle calls total.

questions.prompt: Match each problem type with the source problem recommended in this lesson for building an NP-hardness reduction.

left.text: Scheduling jobs onto machines or time slots

right.text: 3-SAT
VERTEX COVER / INDEPENDENT SET
3-PARTITION

questions.explanation: 3-SAT's fixed clause width makes it the natural source for logic-flavored problems; VERTEX COVER/INDEPENDENT SET are the simplest statements of adjacency-constrained selection for graph problems; 3-PARTITION's forced equal-sized triplet structure maps cleanly onto scheduling/load-balancing gadgets.

units.label: Reading the Evidence: What Hardness Claims Actually Mean

lessons.label: What an NP-Completeness Proof Licenses You to Say

sections.heading: The one thing the theorem actually gives you
sections.body: Proving a problem NP-complete is a reduction argument: you show every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, so it is at least as hard as the hardest problems in the class. Combined with the (unproven but near-universally believed) assumption P is not equal to NP, this licenses exactly one claim: there is no algorithm that solves EVERY instance of the problem in time polynomial in the input size. That is a statement about the WORST CASE, taken over the infinite family of all possible instances, as instance size n grows without bound. It is a statement about an asymptotic growth rate of a function, not about any concrete computation you could run today. Cook's 1971 theorem for SAT and Karp's 1972 paper reducing 21 problems to it are exactly this kind of worst-case, asymptotic claim, and nothing more.

sections.heading: Four things it does not say
sections.body: First, it says nothing about YOUR instance distribution. NP-completeness is a claim about the worst instances among all conceivable ones; the instances your project actually generates (real molecules, real class schedules) may be a vanishingly rare, structured subset that is always easy. Second, it says nothing about a single fixed instance. Complexity is defined over a growing family of instances indexed by n; one specific 40-city TSP instance does not 'have' a complexity class any more than one number 'has' a growth rate. Big-O talk about a single fixed n is a category error. Third, it says nothing about small n. Worst-case hardness is an asymptotic guarantee that appears only as n gets large enough; for n = 20 an exponential algorithm can easily beat a polynomial one because constants and low-order terms dominate before the crossover point. Fourth, it says nothing about approximation quality. Many NP-hard optimization problems have polynomial-time algorithms that are provably close to optimal (a topic covered elsewhere in this Codex); NP-completeness only forecloses EXACT, WORST-CASE, POLYNOMIAL solving, not approximate solving.

sections.heading: The science-fair error, named and fixed
sections.body: The error a judge hears most often is: 'My problem is NP-complete, so nothing can solve it, so my heuristic's results are automatically impressive.' This is wrong on three counts at once. NP-complete problems ARE solved every day, just not in worst-case polynomial time and not for every instance — SAT solvers close millions of industrial instances with millions of variables. The theorem does not forbid your specific instances from being easy, and it does not make your heuristic's performance self-justifying; you still have to measure it against baselines and report failure cases. The correct framing a judge will accept is narrower and more defensible: 'This problem is NP-complete, which tells us to expect worst-case exponential blowup and motivates why we tested empirically rather than assuming a fast exact algorithm exists; here is how our approach actually performed on the instances we tested, including where it struggled.' That sentence uses the theorem as MOTIVATION for an experiment, not as a substitute for one.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a genetic algorithm for the Traveling Salesman Problem and writes: 'TSP is NP-complete, so my genetic algorithm is a major achievement because no algorithm can solve NP-complete problems quickly.' A judge presses: 'Held-Karp gives an exact answer in exponential time — did you compare against it on your smallest instances? And commercial solvers like Concorde solve real TSP instances with tens of thousands of cities exactly. So what does NP-completeness actually forbid here?' The defensible rewrite: 'TSP being NP-complete means no known algorithm guarantees an optimal tour in polynomial time for ALL instances, which is why exact solvers like Concorde still take long on adversarially structured inputs. My genetic algorithm targets the practical regime: it produces tours within roughly 5% of optimal (verified against Held-Karp for n up to 15) in a fraction of the time, on the delivery-route instances I generated.' This reframes the claim from an unfalsifiable appeal to theory into a specific, checkable empirical result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows complexity theory will specifically test whether a student understands that NP-completeness is a worst-case, asymptotic, exact-solving statement — because the single most common misuse at science fairs is treating it as a blanket excuse ('it's NP-complete, so any result I get is impressive by default'). Asking 'does that mean your specific instances are hard?' or 'what about approximation?' immediately exposes whether the claim was understood or just quoted. A student who can name the boundary of the theorem, and voluntarily narrows their own claim to what is defensible, reads as scientifically mature in a way that citing the theorem's name never does.

questions.prompt: A student says: 'My problem is NP-complete, so my heuristic algorithm's good results are automatically scientifically impressive.' What is the core error?

options.text: NP-completeness only concerns worst-case behavior over all instances; it says nothing about whether THIS heuristic performs well on the tested instances, which still requires empirical measurement
NP-complete problems cannot be solved at all, so any heuristic result is fabricated
NP-completeness has been disproven, so the premise is false
There is no error; the statement is a correct use of the theorem

explanations.a: Correct — NP-completeness is a worst-case, asymptotic claim about the nonexistence of a polynomial algorithm for ALL instances (assuming P is not NP); it says nothing about how a specific heuristic performs on specific tested instances, which is an empirical question requiring measurement and comparison to baselines.
explanations.b: False — NP-complete problems are solved constantly in practice; industrial SAT solvers close instances with millions of variables. The theorem forbids a WORST-CASE polynomial guarantee, not all solving.
explanations.c: P vs NP remains an open problem; NP-completeness proofs are rigorous and not in question.
explanations.d: The statement conflates a worst-case theoretical guarantee with an empirical performance claim, which is exactly the error being tested.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is something an NP-completeness proof, together with the assumption P is not NP, actually establishes?

options.text: That every individual instance of size n = 20 will take exponential time to solve
That no polynomial-time algorithm can solve ALL instances of the problem correctly and exactly, as instance size grows without bound
That no polynomial-time approximation algorithm can get close to the optimum
That the problem's real-world instances (e.g., from a specific application domain) are hard

explanations.a: Wrong — complexity classes describe asymptotic growth over a family of instances as n grows, not the runtime on one fixed small instance; small instances are routinely easy for exponential algorithms.
explanations.b: Correct — this is precisely the worst-case, asymptotic, exact-solving claim that NP-completeness plus P not equal to NP establishes.
explanations.c: Wrong — approximation is a separate question; many NP-hard problems have polynomial-time algorithms with provable approximation guarantees.
explanations.d: Wrong — the theorem is about the worst case over ALL conceivable instances, not about any particular real-world distribution, which may be far easier.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to whether an NP-completeness proof (with P not equal to NP) supports it.

left.text: No poly-time algorithm solves every instance
My application's specific instance distribution is hard
A specific 20-node instance will be slow
No poly-time algorithm gets a good approximate answer

right.text: Supported by the theorem
Not supported by the theorem

questions.explanation: Only the worst-case, asymptotic, exact-solving claim is supported. Whether a specific data distribution is hard, whether a small fixed instance is slow, and whether approximation is possible are all separate empirical or theoretical questions the base theorem does not settle.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of turning an NP-completeness fact into a scientifically defensible science-fair claim.

items.text: Note the problem is NP-complete as motivation for why an exact worst-case-fast algorithm is not expected
Compare your algorithm's output against an exact method (e.g., Held-Karp) on small instances
Run your algorithm on the actual instances you care about and record performance, including failures
State the claim narrowly: performance on the tested instance distribution, not a universal claim about all instances

questions.explanation: The theorem is cited first only as motivation for why an experiment is needed, then results are validated against an exact baseline where feasible, then measured broadly including failure cases, and finally the conclusion is scoped to what was actually tested rather than generalized to all instances.

lessons.label: Worst Case Is Not Typical Case: Average-Case Complexity

sections.heading: Levin's 1986 framework: distributional NP
sections.body: Worst-case NP-completeness says nothing about how hard a problem is 'on average' under some distribution of inputs. Leonid Levin formalized this gap in his 1986 paper 'Average Case Complete Problems,' introducing DISTRIBUTIONAL NP (DistNP): pairs of a decision problem together with a probability distribution over its instances (restricted to distributions samplable in polynomial time, so the setup stays meaningful). Levin defined a problem as 'average-case tractable' if it has an algorithm whose running time is polynomial ON AVERAGE with respect to that distribution, and showed a version of a tiling problem is DistNP-COMPLETE: every problem in DistNP reduces to it in a distribution-respecting way. This mirrors Cook-Levin worst-case NP-completeness but is a strictly different, additional theorem — proving a problem NP-complete says nothing about whether it, or any DistNP-complete problem, is average-case hard, and vice versa.

sections.heading: Why average-case hardness is the harder requirement
sections.body: Average-case hardness is a strictly stronger demand than worst-case hardness: a problem can be worst-case exponential yet trivially easy on, say, 99.99% of randomly drawn instances, with all the difficulty concentrated in a vanishing sliver of pathological cases. This matters enormously for cryptography, which needs problems that are hard on the specific distribution of instances an adversary actually encounters (e.g., 'randomly generated keys'), not just hard in some worst case that may never arise. Andrej Bogdanov and Luca Trevisan's result 'On Worst-Case to Average-Case Reductions for NP Problems' (2003 FOCS, journal version 2006) shows a structural barrier: no NON-ADAPTIVE black-box reduction can base average-case hardness of an NP problem on the worst-case hardness of an NP-complete problem, unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses (specifically implying NP is contained in coNP/poly). This is why cryptographers do not simply invoke 'SAT is NP-complete' to justify a cipher — they instead build on separate, direct average-case hardness assumptions (factoring, discrete log, lattice problems) that are conjectured hard on their own terms.

sections.heading: Planted vs. uniform: a concrete illustration
sections.body: The planted clique problem makes the contrast vivid. In a uniformly random Erdos-Renyi graph G(n, 1/2), the largest clique is typically only about 2 log2(n) vertices, and FINDING even that largest clique is believed hard, but there is no interesting 'yes/no' distinction to exploit for cryptography. In the PLANTED clique model, a clique of size k noticeably larger than 2 log2(n) (e.g., k around sqrt(n)) is planted into an otherwise random graph, and the question becomes distinguishing 'planted' from 'pure random.' For k greater than roughly sqrt(n), simple spectral algorithms recover the planted clique in polynomial time; for k smaller than sqrt(n), no polynomial algorithm is known despite extensive effort, and this specific average-case gap (not general NP-completeness) is what modern cryptographic and statistical hardness constructions rely on. Planted random SAT instances behave similarly: planting a satisfying assignment and adding random clauses consistent with it produces instances that are satisfiable by construction but can range from trivially easy (few clauses) to solver-defeating (many clauses, camouflaging the plant), showing that 'has a satisfying assignment' and 'is hard to find it' are separate, tunable properties, not automatic consequences of NP-completeness.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a student claims: 'Since 3-SAT is NP-complete, any encryption scheme built on random 3-SAT instances would be as secure as the hardest cryptographic problems.' To test this, generate 10,000 UNIFORM random 3-SAT instances at a clause-to-variable ratio well below the satisfiability threshold (say alpha = 2) and time a solver on each — nearly all resolve in milliseconds via simple unit propagation, because sparse random instances are typically under-constrained and easy, regardless of the class's worst-case hardness. Now generate PLANTED instances: fix a hidden satisfying assignment, then add random clauses consistent with it at a much higher ratio. Time the same solver. The planted instances near the phase boundary take orders of magnitude longer, illustrating that the same nominal problem (3-SAT) can be worst-case NP-complete yet average-case trivial under one distribution and average-case hard-ish under another — exactly the gap Levin's framework and the Bogdanov-Trevisan barrier are built to describe, and exactly why 'NP-complete' alone cannot certify a distribution is safe to encrypt on.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a cryptography-adjacent or heuristic-solver project will ask 'hard for whom, on what distribution?' because the single most common overreach is treating worst-case NP-completeness as if it implied average-case hardness on the project's own generated data. A student who can name Levin's DistNP framework, explain that average-case hardness is a distinct and STRONGER claim, and cite the planted-vs-uniform distinction with concrete numbers (2 log2 n vs sqrt(n) clique thresholds) demonstrates they understand why real cryptographic hardness assumptions are never just 'X is NP-complete' — a distinction that separates genuine depth from a superficial theory citation.

questions.prompt: What did Leonid Levin's 1986 paper 'Average Case Complete Problems' introduce?

options.text: A proof that P equals NP under average-case assumptions
The framework of distributional NP (DistNP) and a DistNP-complete tiling problem, an average-case analogue of Cook-Levin completeness
The first NP-completeness proof, predating Cook and Karp
A proof that all NP-complete problems are automatically average-case hard

explanations.a: Levin's paper does not touch P vs NP; it defines an entirely separate axis of hardness (average-case, under samplable distributions).
explanations.b: Correct — Levin formalized DistNP (problem + polynomial-time-samplable distribution pairs) and proved a tiling problem DistNP-complete, mirroring worst-case NP-completeness but for the average-case setting.
explanations.c: Cook (1971) and Karp (1972) established worst-case NP-completeness over a decade before Levin's 1986 average-case paper; Levin's own worst-case NP-completeness work was contemporaneous with Cook's, but the 1986 paper is specifically about the average-case framework.
explanations.d: This is exactly the false inference the lesson corrects — NP-completeness and DistNP-completeness are logically independent properties.

questions.prompt: Why can't cryptography simply be built on the fact that a problem like SAT is NP-complete?

options.text: Because SAT has since been shown to be in P

Because NP-completeness is a worst-case guarantee, but cryptography needs average-case hardness on the actual distribution of keys/instances used, and Bogdanov-Trevisan show black-box worst-case-to-average-case reductions face a structural barrier for NP
Because SAT instances are always trivially easy in practice
Because NP-completeness only applies to decision problems, not encryption

explanations.a: SAT is still believed NP-complete and not known to be in P; this option is factually false.
explanations.b: Correct — an adversary faces instances drawn from a specific, typically 'nice' distribution, not the adversarial worst case, and Bogdanov-Trevisan (2003/2006) show non-adaptive worst-case-to-average-case reductions for NP-complete problems would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, so cryptography instead relies on standalone average-case hardness assumptions.
explanations.c: Some SAT instances are easy, but this is not the reason cryptography avoids basing security on generic NP-completeness; the real reason is the worst-case/average-case mismatch.
explanations.d: The decision-problem framing is not the obstacle; the worst-case-vs-average-case distinction is.

questions.prompt: Match each clique-size regime in the planted clique model (graph size n) to its known algorithmic status.

left.text: Largest clique in a uniformly random G(n,1/2) graph
Planted clique of size roughly sqrt(n) or larger
Planted clique of size well below sqrt(n)

right.text: Approximately 2 log2(n) vertices
Recoverable in polynomial time (e.g., spectral methods)
No polynomial-time recovery algorithm is known

questions.explanation: A uniformly random graph's largest clique is about 2 log2(n) vertices. A planted clique of size around sqrt(n) or larger can be recovered in polynomial time via spectral or greedy methods, but for planted cliques smaller than roughly sqrt(n), no efficient recovery algorithm is known, and this specific gap is the basis of several average-case hardness assumptions.

questions.prompt: Order these random 3-SAT construction/testing steps from least to most likely to produce a hard instance for a solver, based on the lesson's contrast between sparse uniform, dense uniform-near-threshold, and camouflaged planted instances.

items.text: Uniform random 3-SAT at clause-to-variable ratio well below the satisfiability threshold
Planted satisfying assignment with few added random clauses
Planted satisfying assignment with clauses added up near the phase-transition density

questions.explanation: Sparse uniform instances are typically resolved almost instantly by unit propagation. Adding a small number of clauses around a planted assignment leaves the instance nearly as easy. Pushing the planted instance's clause density up toward the phase transition camouflages the plant among many constraints and can make it dramatically harder to find or verify, illustrating that difficulty is a tunable property of the distribution, not a fixed consequence of the underlying NP-complete problem.

lessons.label: Phase Transitions: The Easy-Hard-Easy Curve

sections.heading: Discovering the curve: Cheeseman, Kanefsky, Taylor and Mitchell, Selman, Levesque
sections.body: Peter Cheeseman, Bob Kanefsky, and William Taylor's 1991 IJCAI paper 'Where the Really Hard Problems Are' proposed that many NP-complete problems have an 'order parameter' — a single tunable statistic of the instance-generation process — such that as the parameter crosses a critical value, the population of instances undergoes a sharp transition from almost-all-solvable to almost-all-unsolvable, and the hardest instances for search algorithms cluster right at that crossover. David Mitchell, Bart Selman, and Hector Levesque's 1992 AAAI paper 'Hard and Easy Distributions of SAT Problems' made this concrete for random k-SAT: for random 3-SAT with n variables and m clauses, define the ratio alpha = m / n (clauses per variable). They showed empirically that below a critical alpha, generated formulas are almost always satisfiable AND easy to satisfy (a solver finds an assignment fast); above the critical alpha, formulas are almost always unsatisfiable AND easy to refute (a solver quickly derives a contradiction); and runtime for complete solvers like DPLL spikes sharply in a narrow band around the crossover, producing the canonical 'easy-hard-easy' curve when solver time is plotted against alpha.

sections.heading: Where the crossover sits
sections.body: For random 3-SAT the crossover is empirically near alpha is approximately 4.2 to 4.3, commonly cited as alpha is approximately 4.267 from statistical-physics cavity-method estimates, with Mitchell-Selman-Levesque's original empirical crossover measurements closer to 4.2 to 4.25 for the instance sizes they tested. The two numbers are not in conflict: 4.267 is a large-n theoretical/heuristic estimate from physics methods, while empirical experiments on finite, computationally tractable n see a slightly shifted, finite-size value that drifts toward the asymptotic estimate as n grows. The key qualitative fact — a sharp threshold exists and solver difficulty peaks there — is what the science-fair-relevant literature actually established first, well before the exact number was pinned down.

sections.heading: The theory catches up: Friedgut, then Ding-Sly-Sun
sections.body: The empirical curve raised a precise mathematical question: does a SHARP threshold (a single critical alpha such that satisfiability probability jumps from near 1 to near 0 in a vanishing window as n grows) actually exist, or could the transition stay smeared out forever? Ehud Friedgut answered this in 1999 ('Sharp thresholds of graph properties, and the k-SAT problem'), proving that random k-SAT does have a sharp threshold sequence — but his proof did not pin down what constant the threshold converges to, or even prove it converges to a single fixed constant rather than depending weakly on n. That harder question — the exact limiting value of the threshold — was resolved by Jian Ding, Allan Sly, and Nike Sun in their 2015 STOC paper 'Proof of the Satisfiability Conjecture for Large k,' which established the precise threshold formula for all sufficiently large k, matching the one-step replica symmetry breaking (1RSB) prediction from statistical physics developed by Marc Mezard, Giorgio Parisi, and Riccardo Zecchina ('Analytic and Algorithmic Solution of Random Satisfiability Problems,' Science 297(5582):812-815, 2002). So the timeline is: 1991 to 1992 empirical discovery of the curve, 1999 proof that a sharp threshold exists (location unresolved), 2015 proof of the exact location for large k — nearly 25 years from observation to a rigorous pinned-down constant.

lessons.workedExample: A student generates random 3-SAT instances at n = 100 variables, sweeping alpha from 2.0 to 6.0 in steps of 0.2, running a DPLL-style solver at each ratio and plotting median solver runtime (log scale) against alpha. At alpha = 2.0 the curve sits near-instant (under-constrained, almost every formula is satisfiable and easy). At alpha = 6.0 it is also near-instant (over-constrained, almost every formula is unsatisfiable and the solver finds a short refutation fast). Between alpha = 4.0 and alpha = 4.5 the runtime spikes by one to two orders of magnitude, and the fraction of satisfiable formulas measured empirically crosses 50% right in that band — reproducing, at small scale, exactly the curve Mitchell, Selman, and Levesque reported in 1992. Reporting the crossover alpha alongside the theoretical alpha of approximately 4.267 (noting the finite-size gap) turns a qualitative plot into a quantitatively anchored result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen the easy-hard-easy curve before will ask two things: can you reproduce it (not just describe it), and do you know that its EXISTENCE as a sharp threshold and its EXACT LOCATION are two historically separate results (Friedgut 1999 versus Ding-Sly-Sun 2015)? Conflating 'a threshold exists' with 'we know exactly where it is' is a common error, and a student who keeps the two claims straight — and who reports their own measured crossover honestly next to the theoretical constant rather than just asserting 4.267 as if it were self-evidently reproduced — demonstrates they understand phase transitions as an empirical-then-theoretical research arc, not a factoid.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the study of the random 3-SAT phase transition chronologically.

items.text: Cheeseman, Kanefsky, Taylor propose the 'order parameter' / phase-transition framing for NP-complete problems (1991)
Mitchell, Selman, Levesque empirically identify the easy-hard-easy crossover in random 3-SAT (1992)
Friedgut proves a sharp threshold exists for random k-SAT, without locating it (1999)
Ding, Sly, Sun prove the exact threshold formula for all sufficiently large k (2015)

questions.explanation: The order-parameter framing (1991) preceded the specific 3-SAT crossover discovery (1992), which preceded the proof that a sharp threshold exists at all (1999), which preceded the proof of its exact asymptotic location for large k (2015).

questions.prompt: What exactly did Friedgut's 1999 result establish, and what did it leave open?

options.text: It established the exact numeric value of the 3-SAT threshold, alpha is approximately 4.267
It established that a sharp threshold sequence exists for random k-SAT, but left open (for general k) the exact constant the threshold converges to
It disproved the existence of any sharp threshold, showing the transition is always smeared out
It proved P equals NP by analyzing the threshold

explanations.a: That is the later, distinct achievement: Ding, Sly, and Sun (2015) proved the exact threshold location for sufficiently large k, matching the 1RSB statistical-physics prediction; Friedgut's 1999 result did not pin down the number.
explanations.b: Correct — Friedgut proved random k-SAT has a sharp threshold (satisfiability probability jumps from near 1 to near 0 in a vanishing window), a strong qualitative/existence result, but did not identify or prove convergence to one universal constant.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: Friedgut proved sharpness (existence), not its absence.
explanations.d: Phase-transition results in random SAT are orthogonal to the P vs NP question; they concern typical-case behavior of random instances, not worst-case complexity classes.

questions.prompt: In the random 3-SAT easy-hard-easy curve, what happens to solver difficulty as the clause-to-variable ratio alpha moves far above the critical threshold (e.g., alpha = 8)?

options.text: Difficulty keeps increasing without bound, since more clauses always means harder instances
Formulas become almost always unsatisfiable, and this becomes easy to detect quickly, so difficulty drops again — the second 'easy' region
The formulas become satisfiable again
Solver runtime becomes undefined because the problem stops being NP-complete

explanations.a: This contradicts the observed curve — difficulty peaks near the threshold and then DROPS on the over-constrained side, it does not keep climbing indefinitely.
explanations.b: Correct — well above threshold, formulas are almost always unsatisfiable and heavily over-constrained, so a solver typically finds a short contradiction quickly, making this region easy again, completing the 'easy-hard-easy' shape.
explanations.c: Increasing alpha adds more constraints, driving satisfiability probability toward zero, not back toward satisfiable.
explanations.d: Random 3-SAT remains NP-complete as a problem class at every alpha; what changes is the TYPICAL difficulty of randomly generated instances under this specific distribution, not the worst-case classification.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or research team to their specific contribution to the phase-transition story.

right.text: Proposed the general order-parameter / phase-transition framing for NP-complete problem families
Empirically identified the easy-hard-easy crossover specifically for random 3-SAT
Proved a sharp threshold sequence exists for random k-SAT
Proved the exact threshold formula for sufficiently large k

questions.explanation: Cheeseman, Kanefsky, and Taylor (1991) proposed the general order-parameter framing; Mitchell, Selman, and Levesque (1992) found the specific 3-SAT crossover empirically; Friedgut (1999) proved sharp thresholds exist; Ding, Sly, and Sun (2015) proved the exact large-k threshold formula.

lessons.label: Heavy Tails, Restarts, and Runtime Distributions

sections.heading: The discovery: runtime is not normally distributed, it's heavy-tailed
sections.body: Carla Gomes, Bart Selman, Nuno Crato, and Henry Kautz ran the same backtracking SAT and CSP solver, with different random variable/value-ordering tie-breaking, thousands of times on the SAME instance, and plotted the distribution of solving time across those runs. Instead of clustering around a mean the way a normal or exponential distribution would, the distributions had HEAVY, Pareto-like tails: most runs finished quickly, but a nontrivial fraction took vastly longer, and the tail did not decay fast enough for the distribution to have a finite mean in the limiting model that fit the data. This was reported across several papers, notably Gomes, Selman, and Kautz's 1998 AAAI paper 'Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization' and Gomes, Selman, Crato, and Kautz's fuller 2000 Journal of Automated Reasoning paper 'Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in Satisfiability and Constraint Satisfaction Problems.' The mechanism: a backtracking solver makes an early branching decision; if that decision is 'unlucky' (leads deep into a barren subtree before the solver can detect and backtrack out of it), the single run can be catastrophically slower than a typical run, and these rare catastrophic branches are common enough and severe enough to dominate the tail.

sections.heading: Why 'average runtime' becomes a meaningless statistic
sections.body: If the underlying runtime distribution has infinite or near-infinite variance (and in the most extreme observed cases, an effectively infinite mean under the best-fitting heavy-tailed model), then reporting 'the average runtime over 100 runs' is statistically unstable: running the experiment again with a different random seed can produce a wildly different sample mean, because one unlucky outlier run can dwarf the sum of all the others combined. This directly undercuts a common science-fair reporting habit — averaging a handful of trials and presenting the mean plus/minus a standard deviation as if the distribution were well-behaved. For heavy-tailed search processes, the median, or better, the full empirical distribution (or a survival/cactus-style plot, covered in the companion lesson on benchmark charts), is the honest statistic; the arithmetic mean of a small number of runs is close to uninformative.

sections.heading: The fix: rapid randomized restarts and Luby's universal schedule
sections.body: Gomes and Selman's practical response was RAPID RANDOMIZED RESTARTS: rather than letting one unlucky run continue indefinitely down a bad branch, periodically abandon the current run and restart the solver from scratch with a fresh random tie-breaking sequence, cutting off the run at a cutoff time before restarting. This exploits the heavy tail directly — since most runs are fast, restarting frequently means you are usually sampling from the FAST part of the distribution instead of getting stuck waiting out one slow run to completion. The remaining question is what cutoff schedule to use, since the optimal fixed cutoff depends on the (generally unknown) underlying distribution. Michael Luby, Alistair Sinclair, and David Zuckerman answered this in their 1993 paper 'Optimal Speedup of Las Vegas Algorithms': a UNIVERSAL restart sequence, run lengths 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (each 'round' doubles the previous round's final length before repeating the shorter lengths), achieves expected total runtime within a LOGARITHMIC factor of the best possible FIXED cutoff strategy — even without knowing the true runtime distribution in advance. This is why essentially every modern complete SAT solver (MiniSat, Glucose, CaDiCaL, and their descendants) restarts frequently, using either the Luby schedule or a closely related geometric/adaptive variant, rather than running a single uninterrupted search to completion.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs a DPLL-style backtracking SAT solver on the SAME hard random 3-SAT instance 500 times, randomizing only the tie-breaking rule for variable selection, and records each run's time-to-solution. Instead of a bell curve, the histogram shows a sharp peak near a fast solve time with a long right tail; a handful of runs take 50 to 100 times longer than the median. Computing the sample mean across the 500 runs is dominated by 3 or 4 outlier runs — dropping just those changes the reported average by an order of magnitude, demonstrating the mean's instability. The student then re-implements the solver with Luby-schedule restarts (cutoffs 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, ... in whatever base unit, e.g., thousands of branching decisions) and reruns the same 500-trial experiment: total time-to-solution collapses toward the FAST end of the original distribution, and the run-to-run variance shrinks dramatically, empirically reproducing the Gomes-Selman-Kautz restart benefit and the Luby et al. logarithmic-competitiveness guarantee.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots 'average runtime over N trials, mean plus/minus standard deviation' in a search-algorithm project will ask whether the runtime distribution was checked for heavy tails before treating the mean as meaningful — because for backtracking search, it very often is not. A student who instead reports the median or a survival curve, and who explains WHY restarts help (exploiting a heavy tail rather than just 'trying again for luck'), and who can name the Luby schedule's specific guarantee (log-factor-competitive with the unknown-optimal fixed cutoff, no distributional knowledge required), demonstrates they understand solver behavior at the level practitioners actually engineer to, not just at the level of running an experiment once and reporting one number.

questions.prompt: What did Gomes, Selman, Crato, and Kautz find about the runtime of a backtracking solver run repeatedly on the SAME instance with different random tie-breaking?

options.text: Runtime clustered tightly around a mean, following a normal distribution
Runtime followed a heavy-tailed, Pareto-like distribution, where a small fraction of runs took catastrophically longer than typical, undermining the arithmetic mean as a stable summary statistic
Runtime was identical across all runs, since the instance itself, not the tie-breaking, determines difficulty
Runtime decreased monotonically with each successive run due to caching

explanations.a: This is the opposite of the finding — a normal distribution would make the sample mean a stable, informative statistic, which is exactly what the heavy-tailed finding rules out.
explanations.b: Correct — Gomes, Selman, Crato, and Kautz (1998 to 2000) found heavy-tailed / Pareto-like runtime distributions across repeated randomized runs on single hard instances, meaning rare catastrophic branches dominate the tail and the sample mean is unstable.
explanations.c: Runtime varied substantially precisely because of the randomized tie-breaking — that variability is the entire finding.
explanations.d: There is no caching mechanism implied here; each run is an independent randomized search, and no such monotonic decrease was reported.

questions.prompt: Why does a heavy-tailed runtime distribution make 'average runtime over a handful of trials' an unreliable statistic to report?

options.text: Because the mean is always mathematically undefined for any distribution with a tail
Because one or a few extreme outlier runs can dominate the sum, making the sample mean highly sensitive to which few outliers happened to occur, and unstable across repeated experiments
Because backtracking solvers are deterministic, so repeated trials are redundant
Because heavy tails only occur in continuous, not discrete, runtime measurements

explanations.a: Not all heavy-tailed distributions have literally undefined means, but the ones fitted to this data have such extreme tails that the empirical mean over a small sample is dominated by rare events and behaves as if it were unstable/near-infinite.
explanations.b: Correct — with a heavy tail, a small number of catastrophically slow runs can outweigh all the fast runs combined, so the sample mean swings wildly depending on which outliers appeared in a given small batch of trials.
explanations.c: The solver here is randomized via tie-breaking, so repeated trials are not redundant — they are exactly what reveals the heavy tail.
explanations.d: Heavy-tailed distributions and their instability apply equally to discrete measurements like a count of backtracks or branching decisions.

questions.prompt: Order the first six run-length values in Luby, Sinclair, and Zuckerman's universal restart schedule.

items.text: term 1: 1
term 2: 1
term 3: 2
term 4: 1
term 5: 1
term 6: 2

questions.explanation: The Luby sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, ... — each completed 'round' (1,1,2), (1,1,2,4), (1,1,2,4,8), ... repeats the prior round's pattern and appends the next power of two, and the first six terms are 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

left.text: Luby et al.'s universal restart schedule

right.text: A distribution where rare, extremely slow runs dominate the tail, making the sample mean unstable
Periodically abandoning and re-running a randomized solver from scratch to avoid getting stuck on one unlucky branch
A specific cutoff-length sequence (1,1,2,1,1,2,4,...) proven competitive within a log factor of the best fixed cutoff, without needing to know the runtime distribution

questions.explanation: Heavy-tailed distributions are the empirical phenomenon Gomes, Selman, Crato, and Kautz documented; rapid randomized restarts are the general practical remedy; and the Luby schedule is the specific, provably near-optimal restart-length sequence from Luby, Sinclair, and Zuckerman (1993) that requires no prior knowledge of the distribution.

lessons.label: Reading Solver Benchmark Charts

sections.heading: Cactus plots: cumulative solved-instances curves
sections.body: The dominant chart at the annual SAT Competition is the CACTUS PLOT (also called a survival plot): instances are sorted independently for each solver by that solver's own solving time, then plotted with the number of instances solved so far on the x-axis and cumulative time (usually log-scaled) on the y-axis. Because each solver's instances are sorted by ITS OWN time (not a shared fixed ordering), the resulting curve directly shows, for any x, how much total time that solver needed to solve its x fastest instances. A curve that stays LOW and FLAT longer, then rises steeply only near the far right, indicates a solver that is robust — it solves most instances quickly and only struggles on a small residual set. A curve that rises early and steadily indicates a solver that is consistently mediocre or that has fewer very-fast instances. Comparing two solvers' cactus plots side by side answers 'which solver solves more instances within any time budget T,' which is exactly the metric the SAT Competition uses to rank solvers, because it does not require every solver to be run on identically-ordered instances.

sections.heading: Scatter plots and the diagonal timeout border
sections.body: A complementary chart is the pairwise SCATTER PLOT: each point is one benchmark instance, with solver A's runtime on the x-axis and solver B's runtime on the y-axis, both typically log-scaled. Points below the diagonal line y = x mean solver B was faster on that instance; points above mean solver A was faster. Because every benchmark run has a TIMEOUT (a hard cutoff, e.g., 5000 seconds), instances that neither solver finished pile up as a horizontal and vertical band of points pinned exactly AT the timeout value along the top border and right border of the plot — this is a visual signature of censored data, not a real measured runtime, and a reader who mistakes a wall of points sitting exactly at 5000 seconds for genuine solving times will badly misjudge relative solver speed.

sections.heading: Virtual Best Solver and the honesty problem: censoring and PAR-2
sections.body: The VIRTUAL BEST SOLVER (VBS) is not a real solver at all — it is a hypothetical baseline constructed after the fact by taking, for every instance in the benchmark, the minimum runtime achieved by ANY solver in the portfolio on that instance. Plotting the VBS cactus curve alongside real solvers' curves shows the theoretical ceiling a perfect portfolio-selection oracle could achieve, and the GAP between the best real solver and the VBS quantifies how much room is left for algorithm-selection techniques. The deeper statistical issue underlying all of this is that a timeout is a RIGHT-CENSORED observation: the true solving time is known only to be GREATER than the timeout, not equal to it. If a report simply averages runtime over the instances a solver managed to solve and silently drops (or worse, ignores) the unsolved ones, a weak solver that times out on all the hardest instances looks artificially fast, because its reported average excludes exactly the cases that would have dragged it down. PAR-2 scoring (Penalized Average Runtime, factor 2) fixes this: every solved instance counts at its actual runtime, but every unsolved (timed-out) instance is counted as TWICE the timeout value, and the resulting penalized average is computed over ALL instances, solved or not. This is the official scoring metric of the SAT Competition precisely because it prevents a solver from gaming its score by cherry-picking which instances to report.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two SAT solvers, A and B, on a 200-instance benchmark with a 5000-second timeout. Solver A solves 180 instances with a mean time of 40 seconds over those 180 (ignoring the 20 timeouts) and reports 'Solver A averages 40 seconds per instance, much faster than Solver B.' Solver B solves all 200 instances with a mean time of 90 seconds. Naively, A looks faster. But computing PAR-2 tells a different story: A's score is (180 x 40 + 20 x 2 x 5000) / 200 = (7200 + 200000) / 200 = 1036 seconds per instance, while B's PAR-2 score is 90 x 200 / 200 = 90 seconds per instance (since B has zero timeouts). Under the honest, censoring-aware PAR-2 metric, B is over 11 times better than A, the reverse of the naive solved-only comparison — because A's 20 silent timeouts were exactly the instances hiding its true weakness.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who works with benchmarks will immediately ask 'did you include the instances your algorithm failed to solve, or only the ones it solved?' because averaging over solved-only instances is the single most common way a benchmarking result is quietly inflated. A student who reports PAR-2 (or an equivalent censoring-aware score), who shows a cactus plot rather than a single mean, and who can correctly read a timeout-pinned scatter-plot border as censored (not real) data demonstrates they understand that benchmark charts encode a specific statistical convention for handling failure, not just a plotting style choice.

questions.prompt: In a SAT Competition-style cactus plot, what do the x-axis and y-axis represent?

options.text: x = instance ID number (fixed order shared across solvers); y = memory used
x = number of instances solved so far (each solver's own instances sorted by that solver's time); y = cumulative time to solve them, usually log-scaled
x = clause-to-variable ratio; y = probability of satisfiability
x = number of variables; y = number of clauses

explanations.a: Cactus plots do not use a fixed shared instance ordering across solvers, and they plot time, not memory.
explanations.b: Correct — each solver's own solved instances are independently sorted by that solver's runtime, then plotted as cumulative count solved (x) versus cumulative time (y), letting different solvers be compared without needing a shared instance ordering.
explanations.c: That describes a phase-transition plot (covered in the phase-transitions lesson), not a cactus/survival plot.
explanations.d: That would describe an instance-size scatter, not the standard cactus plot used for solver comparison.

questions.prompt: In a pairwise runtime scatter plot with a fixed timeout, what does a cluster of points sitting exactly at the timeout value along the top and right borders represent?

options.text: Instances both solvers solved unusually quickly
A plotting error that should be removed from the data
Right-censored data — instances where the true solving time is unknown beyond 'greater than the timeout,' not a real measured runtime equal to the timeout
Instances where the two solvers produced different (contradictory) answers

explanations.a: Points at the timeout border represent the SLOWEST outcomes (failures to solve within the budget), not fast ones.
explanations.b: This is real, meaningful data about solver failure, not an artifact to discard; removing it would hide exactly the information PAR-2 scoring is designed to capture.
explanations.c: Correct — the timeout is a right-censoring bound: the solver did not finish, so all that is known is the true time exceeds the timeout, and plotting it AT the timeout value visually flags this censoring.
explanations.d: Timeouts reflect failure to reach a conclusion in the time budget, not disagreement between solvers' answers on solved instances.

questions.prompt: Why does PAR-2 scoring count each unsolved (timed-out) instance as twice the timeout value, rather than simply excluding it from the average?

options.text: Because excluding timeouts from the average lets a solver that times out on the hardest instances look artificially fast, since exactly the cases that would lower its apparent performance are dropped
Because doubling makes the arithmetic simpler to compute by hand
Because the SAT Competition requires all scores to be even numbers
Because timeouts always take exactly twice as long as the timeout limit in reality

explanations.a: Correct — averaging over solved-only instances silently removes the failures, inflating a weak solver's apparent speed; PAR-2 penalizes every timeout so the score reflects performance across the WHOLE benchmark, not a cherry-picked solved subset.
explanations.b: The factor of 2 is a deliberate penalty design choice, not a computational convenience.
explanations.c: There is no such parity requirement; PAR-2 scores are real-valued averages.
explanations.d: The true time for a timed-out instance is unknown (only known to exceed the timeout); doubling is a scoring penalty convention, not a claim about the actual elapsed time.

questions.prompt: Match each benchmarking concept to its correct role.

right.text: Shows cumulative solved-instance count versus cumulative time for one solver, revealing robustness versus speed
A hypothetical portfolio baseline taking the minimum runtime any solver achieved per instance, showing the ceiling for algorithm selection
A single censoring-aware number penalizing every unsolved instance at twice the timeout, preventing solved-only averages from hiding failures

questions.explanation: Cactus plots visualize one solver's cumulative solving profile; the Virtual Best Solver is an oracle baseline built from per-instance minimums across a portfolio; PAR-2 is the official penalized scoring convention that folds timeouts into a single honest number.

lessons.label: Fitting Growth Curves to Solver Data — Honestly

sections.heading: The hazard: two very different functions can look alike over a short range
sections.body: The Core curriculum teaches that plotting log(runtime) against n turns an exponential function 2^(cn) into a straight line (since log(2^(cn)) = cn log 2, linear in n), while plotting log(runtime) against log(n) turns a polynomial n^k into a straight line (since log(n^k) = k log(n), linear in log n). This is the correct diagnostic in principle, but it hides a specific empirical trap: any real experiment can only measure n over a narrow window, typically one to two orders of magnitude (say n = 50 to n = 500, or n = 10^3 to n = 10^5), because runtime grows too fast to push much further.
