A CSPRNG, by contrast, must satisfy a much stronger property: even an adversary who has seen many previous outputs must be computationally unable to predict the next one or recover the seed. Operating systems expose this distinction directly: on Linux, /dev/urandom (and the newer getrandom() syscall) is the standard interface for a CSPRNG seeded from genuine hardware entropy sources (interrupt timing, thermal noise, etc.), and it is what security-sensitive code (key generation, nonces, session tokens) must use -- never a statistical PRNG like Mersenne Twister, whose internal state can in fact be fully reconstructed from a few hundred consecutive outputs, a known practical attack against naive uses of it in security contexts.

lessons.workedExample: A research team benchmarks randomized quicksort by running it 10,000 times, seeding Python's Mersenne-Twister-based random module with the fixed integer 42 for every run so that the SAME sequence of pivot choices is reproduced exactly when a colleague reruns the benchmark script later to verify the reported average comparison count -- reproducibility working exactly as intended. Separately, a different team builds a web service that uses the same fixed-seed approach to generate session tokens for user logins. Because Mersenne Twister's entire internal state (624 32-bit words) can be reconstructed from about 624 consecutive observed outputs, and because the seed here is fixed and guessable, an attacker who observes a handful of issued tokens can predict every future token -- the reproducibility that made the benchmark trustworthy is exactly what makes the token generator broken; the fix is to seed session-token generation from /dev/urandom (a CSPRNG) instead, never from a fixed or guessable seed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read about McIlroy's adversary (Lesson 2) may ask the pointed follow-up: 'if the pivot randomness comes from a seeded PRNG, couldn't a real adversary just recover the seed and defeat randomized quicksort after all?' The strong answer distinguishes the threat models precisely: for algorithmic worst-case avoidance, a statistical PRNG with a properly unpredictable (not fixed, not clock-guessable) seed is sufficient, because the adversary in that model cannot observe the coins as they are generated; but for genuinely security-critical randomness (keys, tokens, nonces) the bar is categorically higher and only a CSPRNG drawing from OS entropy (e.g. /dev/urandom) is acceptable, because there the adversary is explicitly modeled as able to observe outputs and try to predict future ones.

questions.prompt: Why is a fixed, recorded PRNG seed simultaneously good for scientific reproducibility and dangerous for security?

options.text: It isn't actually useful for either purpose; fixed seeds are a bad practice in all contexts

A fixed seed deterministically reproduces the exact same output sequence, which lets researchers rerun experiments identically, but also lets an adversary who learns or guesses the seed reconstruct every future 'random' choice
Fixed seeds only affect running time, not correctness or security
Security systems require fixed seeds by design, so this is not actually a tradeoff

explanations.a: Fixed seeds are genuinely valuable for reproducible science; the issue is not that they're universally bad practice but that the same property is a serious liability in security contexts.
explanations.b: Correct -- determinism from a fixed seed is exactly what enables bit-for-bit reproducible experiments, and exactly what lets an adversary who recovers the seed predict all subsequent output, defeating any protection the randomness was meant to provide.
explanations.c: The seed determines the entire output SEQUENCE, which affects both which values are produced (correctness of subsequent random choices) and, in security contexts, predictability -- not merely running time.
explanations.d: Security-sensitive systems should specifically AVOID fixed or guessable seeds and instead draw from a CSPRNG seeded with genuine entropy, which is the opposite of what this option claims.

questions.prompt: What is the key property that distinguishes a cryptographically secure PRNG (CSPRNG) from a statistical PRNG like Mersenne Twister?

options.text: A CSPRNG produces truly infinite output while a statistical PRNG eventually repeats immediately
A CSPRNG must remain unpredictable even to an adversary who has observed many previous outputs, while a statistical PRNG only needs to pass statistical uniformity tests
A CSPRNG is always slower and therefore never used in practice
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable

explanations.a: Both types of PRNG have finite periods (e.g. Mersenne Twister's is 2^19937 - 1, extremely long but still finite); infinite output is not the distinguishing property.
explanations.b: Correct -- a CSPRNG's defining requirement is computational unpredictability against an adversary who has seen prior outputs, a much stronger property than merely passing statistical randomness tests, which is all a statistical PRNG needs to satisfy.
explanations.c: CSPRNGs are used constantly in practice for security-critical purposes (e.g. /dev/urandom-backed key and token generation); the tradeoff is about security guarantees, not simply about speed.
explanations.d: The terms describe categorically different guarantees, as shown by the fact that Mersenne Twister's state can be fully reconstructed from observed outputs, which is precisely the attack a CSPRNG is designed to resist.

questions.prompt: Match each PRNG or randomness source to its correct description.

right.text: Published by Matsumoto and Nishimura in 1998; period of 2^19937 - 1, historically the default in Python and many other languages
George Marsaglia's 2003 family using only shift and XOR operations for speed
Melissa O'Neill's 2014 design applying a permutation to a linear congruential generator's output; small state, strong statistical quality
OS-level CSPRNG interface seeded from hardware entropy sources, used for security-critical randomness

questions.explanation: Mersenne Twister (1998) is the long-period, historically ubiquitous statistical PRNG; xorshift (2003) trades some statistical quality for raw speed; PCG (2014) combines small state with strong statistical properties via output permutation; and /dev/urandom is the OS-provided CSPRNG interface appropriate for security-critical randomness, not any of the statistical generators.

questions.prompt: Order the steps describing how an attacker exploits a predictable PRNG seed used for security-sensitive randomness.

items.text: A system seeds its PRNG from a guessable source (e.g. the system clock at startup)
The attacker observes one or more outputs (e.g. issued session tokens) generated by the PRNG
The attacker recovers or reconstructs the seed or internal state from the observed outputs and known algorithm
The attacker predicts all future 'random' outputs, defeating the intended protection

questions.explanation: The attack begins with a predictable or guessable seed, proceeds through the attacker observing enough generated outputs to reconstruct the generator's internal state, and ends with the attacker able to predict every subsequent output -- which is exactly why security-critical randomness must instead come from a CSPRNG such as /dev/urandom, seeded from genuine hardware entropy.

lessons.label: Approximation: Trading Exactness for Time

sections.heading: A second axis besides speed: how close is the answer?
sections.body: Every algorithm studied elsewhere in this Codex track is judged on a single axis: how much time (and space) it takes to produce the EXACT, provably correct answer. For a large and important class of problems -- many of them NP-hard, where exact solutions are believed to require exponential time in the worst case -- insisting on exactness is simply not affordable at real-world scale. An APPROXIMATION ALGORITHM accepts a second axis of measurement, SOLUTION QUALITY, in exchange: it runs in polynomial (often much faster) time and returns an answer that is PROVABLY close to optimal, where 'close' is quantified by an explicit, guaranteed number rather than a hope. This is the pivot point of the whole branch: once solution quality becomes something you can measure and prove a bound on, it becomes a legitimate design target in its own right, exactly the way running time always has been -- and it is the axis on which the metaheuristics half of this branch (simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and the like) will ultimately be judged.

sections.heading: Approximation ratio and the (1+epsilon) guarantee
sections.body: The standard way to quantify closeness is the APPROXIMATION RATIO. For a minimization problem, an algorithm is a rho-approximation if, for every instance, the algorithm's output cost is at most rho times the true optimal cost (rho >= 1; rho = 1 would mean exact). For a maximization problem the inequality flips: the algorithm's output is at least (1/rho) times optimal. A particularly important and common form is the (1+epsilon)-APPROXIMATION, where epsilon is a small positive number the user can dial: the algorithm guarantees an answer within a factor of (1+epsilon) of optimal (so epsilon = 0.1 means 'provably no more than 10% worse than the best possible answer'), and critically, many such algorithms let epsilon shrink toward 0 at the cost of increased running time -- a PTAS (polynomial-time approximation scheme) formalizes exactly this tradeoff, giving a family of algorithms, one for each epsilon, each polynomial in the input size for that fixed epsilon. This turns 'how good is good enough' into a dial the algorithm designer and the user can explicitly negotiate, rather than an all-or-nothing choice between exact-but-slow and fast-but-unquantified.

sections.heading: Approximation algorithm versus heuristic: the line that matters
sections.body: It is essential to keep separate two things that are often conflated in casual usage: an APPROXIMATION ALGORITHM comes with a PROVEN mathematical bound (a rho or a (1+epsilon)) that holds for every possible input, no exceptions -- the guarantee is a theorem. A HEURISTIC, by contrast, is a strategy that tends to work well in practice, is often fast, and is frequently the method of actual choice for hard problems -- but carries NO proven worst-case quality guarantee at all; it could in principle perform arbitrarily badly on some (possibly rare, possibly adversarial) input, and there is no theorem forbidding that. Simulated annealing and genetic algorithms, central topics of this branch's later units, are heuristics in exactly this sense: they are typically excellent in practice and are analyzed empirically and probabilistically, but they do not carry a blanket proven approximation ratio the way, say, the classic 2-approximation for vertex cover does. Recognizing which category a given method falls into -- provable bound versus empirically good but unguaranteed -- is the single most important classification skill for the remainder of this branch, because it determines what kind of claim you are allowed to make about a solution's quality.

lessons.workedExample: The classic vertex cover approximation algorithm repeatedly picks any remaining uncovered edge and adds BOTH its endpoints to the cover, removing all edges those two vertices touch, and repeats until no edges remain. This produces a valid vertex cover in linear time, and a short proof shows its size is never more than 2 times the true minimum vertex cover -- a proven 2-approximation, true for every graph, no exceptions. Contrast this with a different algorithm for the same problem: 'greedily pick the vertex touching the most remaining edges, remove it, repeat.' This greedy-by-degree method is often observed to perform very well in practice and frequently beats the 2-approximation's output size on typical graphs -- and it does have a proven worst-case ratio, just a weaker one: O(log n) (specifically H(Delta), the Delta-th harmonic number for max degree Delta), the same greedy-analysis bound used for Set Cover, of which Vertex Cover is a special case. So the contrast here is between two different proven approximation ratios (constant-factor 2 versus O(log n)), not between a guarantee and no guarantee at all -- a genuinely unguaranteed heuristic would be something like a local-search or simulated-annealing method with no known worst-case bound. A quality claim about the first algorithm ('at most 2x optimal, provably, always') is a fundamentally different kind of statement than a quality claim about the second ('usually quite good, based on practice').
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson will often present a method that 'works great on the test cases we tried' and ask whether that constitutes an approximation guarantee -- the correct, precise answer is no: good empirical performance on observed instances is exactly what a heuristic offers, and it is categorically different from a PROVEN approximation ratio that a theorem guarantees holds on every instance, including ones never tested. Being able to state a method's approximation ratio precisely (e.g. '2-approximation' or '(1+epsilon)-approximation with running time depending on epsilon') and to explain in one sentence why that differs from 'usually works well in practice' is exactly the distinction that separates a superficial grasp of this branch from a rigorous one, and it sets up the standard this branch's later metaheuristics content will be measured against.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an algorithm to be a '(1+epsilon)-approximation' for a minimization problem?

options.text: It runs in exactly (1+epsilon) times the optimal algorithm's running time
It is guaranteed, for every possible instance, to output a solution whose cost is at most (1+epsilon) times the true optimal cost
It finds the exact optimal solution but only epsilon percent of the time
It is a heuristic that performs well on most inputs but has no formal guarantee

explanations.a: The (1+epsilon) factor describes solution QUALITY relative to optimal cost, not a running-time multiplier relative to some other algorithm.
explanations.b: Correct -- a (1+epsilon)-approximation is a proven bound: the algorithm's output cost is at most (1+epsilon) times the optimal cost, and this holds for every instance, not merely typical or observed ones.
explanations.c: The guarantee is about solution quality on every run, not about the frequency of finding the exact optimum; a (1+epsilon)-approximation with epsilon > 0 may never find the exact optimum yet still satisfy its guarantee every time.
explanations.d: This is precisely the opposite of what distinguishes an approximation algorithm from a heuristic -- the (1+epsilon) label specifically denotes a PROVEN worst-case guarantee, which a heuristic by definition lacks.

questions.prompt: What is the essential difference between an approximation algorithm and a heuristic?

options.text: Heuristics are always slower than approximation algorithms

An approximation algorithm carries a proven mathematical bound on solution quality that holds for every input, while a heuristic has no such proven worst-case guarantee, even if it performs well in practice
Approximation algorithms only apply to maximization problems, while heuristics only apply to minimization problems
There is no meaningful difference; the terms are used interchangeably in the literature

explanations.a: Speed is not the distinguishing factor; heuristics are often chosen precisely because they are fast, sometimes faster than a proven approximation algorithm for the same problem.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the core classification skill the lesson establishes: a proven ratio (theorem-backed, true for every instance) versus empirically good but formally unguaranteed performance.
explanations.c: Both approximation algorithms and heuristics can be applied to either minimization or maximization problems; the problem type is unrelated to this distinction.
explanations.d: The terms describe categorically different kinds of claims about solution quality and should not be treated as interchangeable, even though both may be applied to the same hard problem.

questions.prompt: Match each approximation-related term to its correct definition.

right.text: A bound such that the algorithm's cost is at most rho times optimal (minimization) on every instance
A family of polynomial-time algorithms, one for each epsilon, trading a smaller epsilon for more running time
A strategy that performs well in practice but carries no proven worst-case quality guarantee
The measured dimension of how close an output is to optimal, alongside running time

questions.explanation: The approximation ratio rho is the proven worst-case multiplicative bound on output cost versus optimal; a PTAS is a family of algorithms indexed by epsilon trading quality for time; a heuristic performs well empirically but lacks a proven bound; and solution quality is the second measured axis this whole lesson establishes alongside running time.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that justify accepting an approximation algorithm instead of demanding an exact solution for an NP-hard problem.

items.text: Recognize the problem is NP-hard, so an exact polynomial-time algorithm is not believed to exist
Design or select an algorithm with a proven approximation ratio rho (or a (1+epsilon) guarantee)
Run the algorithm in polynomial time to obtain a solution
Cite the proven bound to state precisely how far the output can be from optimal, for every possible instance

questions.explanation: The reasoning starts from recognizing the problem's hardness (making exactness infeasible at scale), proceeds to selecting an algorithm with an explicit proven quality bound, runs it efficiently, and concludes by citing that proven bound to make a precise, defensible claim about solution quality -- the defining structure of an approximation algorithm as opposed to an unguaranteed heuristic.

lessons.label: Counting with Indicator Random Variables

sections.heading: The technique: turn a hard count into a sum of 0/1 variables
sections.body: Many randomized-algorithm analyses need E[X] for a random variable X that counts something complicated -- comparisons made, collisions occurring, cells touched. Rather than reasoning about X directly, decompose it into simple indicator random variables X_1, ..., X_m, each equal to 1 if some elementary event happens and 0 otherwise, so X = sum of the X_k. Linearity of expectation then gives E[X] = sum of E[X_k], and each E[X_k] is just P(X_k = 1), a single-event probability. The crucial fact that makes this so powerful is that linearity of expectation holds unconditionally: E[sum X_k] = sum E[X_k] regardless of whether the X_k are independent. You do not need to understand how the events interact with each other -- you only need each individual probability. This is what lets you analyze quicksort's comparisons, hashing collisions, and matching problems with the same two-line argument each time.

sections.heading: Setting it up for randomized quicksort's comparison count
sections.body: Take an input array of n distinct elements and let z_1 < z_2 < ... < z_n denote them in sorted order (their ranks). Randomized quicksort picks a pivot uniformly at random at each recursive call. Define X_ij = 1 if z_i and z_j are EVER directly compared to each other during the entire execution, 0 otherwise; the total comparison count is C = sum over all pairs i<j of X_ij. Key structural fact: z_i and z_j are compared if and only if, among the set S_ij = {z_i, z_i+1, ..., z_j} (the j-i+1 elements with rank between i and j inclusive), the FIRST element of S_ij ever chosen as a pivot is z_i or z_j itself -- if any strictly-between element is chosen first, it separates z_i and z_j into different partitions and they are never compared afterward. Since the algorithm's pivot choices are uniform and independent of rank, each of the j-i+1 elements in S_ij is equally likely to be the first one picked as a pivot, so P(X_ij = 1) = 2 / (j - i + 1).

sections.heading: Summing the pairs: 2n ln n and the 39% overhead
sections.body: By linearity of expectation, E[C] = sum_{i<j} 2/(j-i+1). Grouping by the gap k = j - i (which ranges 1 to n-1, with n-k pairs at each gap), E[C] = sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (n-k) * 2/(k+1). Evaluating this double sum gives the closed form E[C] = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n, where H_n is the n-th harmonic number, and asymptotically E[C] ~ 2n ln n. Converting to log base 2 (since ln n = ln2 * log2 n), 2n ln n = 2 ln2 * n log2 n ~ 1.39 n log2 n. Compare this to the information-theoretic lower bound for ANY comparison-based sort: log2(n!) ~ n log2 n - n/ln2, i.e. roughly n log2 n comparisons is optimal. Randomized quicksort's ~1.39 n log2 n is therefore about 39% more comparisons than the theoretical optimum -- a modest, fixed constant-factor tax paid in exchange for never needing to inspect the input distribution or guard against an adversarial ordering.

lessons.workedExample: Take n = 4 elements ranked 1,2,3,4. Adjacent ranks are always compared (gap 1: P = 2/2 = 1), so pairs (1,2), (2,3), (3,4) each contribute probability 1. Gap-2 pairs (1,3) and (2,4) each have P = 2/3. The gap-3 pair (1,4) has P = 2/4 = 0.5. Summing: 1+1+1 + 2/3+2/3 + 0.5 = 3 + 1.333 + 0.5 = 4.833. Checking against the closed form 2(n+1)H_n - 4n with n=4, H_4 = 1 + 0.5 + 0.333 + 0.25 = 2.0833: 2(5)(2.0833) - 16 = 20.833 - 16 = 4.833. The two computations agree exactly, confirming the pairwise-indicator method is not an approximation -- it recovers the exact expected comparison count for any finite n.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why do you get to add up probabilities from events that clearly aren't independent -- whether z_1 and z_2 are compared surely affects whether z_2 and z_3 are' is testing whether you understand that linearity of expectation is unconditional. The correct answer distinguishes E[sum] = sum E[] (always true) from claims about the SUM's variance or distribution (which would require independence). A student who can also produce the 2/(j-i+1) probability from the 'first pivot among the enclosing set' argument, and connect the final 2n ln n to the n log2 n lower bound as a concrete 39% overhead, demonstrates they derived the result rather than memorized it.

questions.prompt: In the quicksort comparison analysis, what does the event X_ij = 1 represent?

options.text: The i-th and j-th smallest elements happen to be equal in value
The i-th and j-th smallest elements are directly compared to each other at some point during the run
The i-th smallest element is chosen as the very first pivot of the whole algorithm
The i-th and j-th elements are swapped during a partition step

explanations.a: X_ij is about comparison events during execution, not about value equality between distinct-ranked elements.
explanations.b: Correct -- X_ij is defined as the indicator that z_i and z_j are ever directly compared, and the total comparison count is the sum of all such indicators over pairs.
explanations.c: This describes a specific pivot event, not the pairwise comparison event the analysis is built around.
explanations.d: Quicksort's partition step does data movement, but X_ij tracks comparisons, not swaps.

questions.prompt: Why is P(X_ij = 1) exactly 2/(j-i+1)?

options.text: Because among the j-i+1 elements with rank between i and j inclusive, z_i and z_j are compared iff one of them (2 of the j-i+1) is the first of that set chosen as a pivot, and each is equally likely to be first
Because every partitioning step performs exactly 2 comparisons on average, independent of i and j
Because random pivoting makes every pair of elements compared with the same fixed probability 2/n
Because quicksort always compares an element to exactly 2 others before discarding it

explanations.a: Correct -- if any strictly-between element becomes a pivot first, z_i and z_j land in different partitions and are never compared; only if z_i or z_j itself is the first of the enclosing set to be chosen as pivot do they get compared, giving 2 favorable outcomes out of j-i+1 equally-likely 'first pivot' candidates.
explanations.b: There is no fixed '2 comparisons per step' rule; the count depends on how the recursion actually splits.
explanations.c: The probability explicitly depends on the gap j-i+1, not a constant 2/n.
explanations.d: This misdescribes the mechanism; the probability comes from a first-pivot-among-a-set argument, not a per-element comparison cap.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the randomized-quicksort comparison analysis in the order they are actually carried out.

items.text: Define X_ij as the indicator that z_i and z_j are ever compared
Argue P(X_ij = 1) = 2/(j-i+1) via the 'first pivot among the enclosing set' argument
Apply linearity of expectation to sum E[X_ij] over all pairs i<j
Evaluate the double sum asymptotically to get E[C] ~ 2n ln n
Convert to ~1.39 n log2 n and compare against the n log2 n comparison-sort lower bound

questions.explanation: The derivation first defines the indicator variables, then computes each one's probability, then invokes linearity of expectation to turn the sum of indicators into a sum of probabilities, then evaluates that sum asymptotically, and finally interprets the resulting constant against the known optimum.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity from the analysis to what it represents.

right.text: Probability that ranks i and j are ever compared
Expected number of comparisons in randomized quicksort (leading order)
Information-theoretic lower bound on comparisons for any comparison-based sort
Approximate ratio of quicksort's expected comparisons to the optimal bound

questions.explanation: 2/(j-i+1) is the per-pair comparison probability; summing it over all pairs gives the leading-order expected comparison count 2n ln n; the comparison-sort lower bound is log2(n!) ~ n log2 n; and 2n ln n rewritten in log2 units is ~1.39 n log2 n, about 39% above optimal.

lessons.label: Expected Time vs Worst Case vs Average Case

sections.heading: Three different claims that get casually swapped
sections.body: WORST CASE is a statement about every possible input of size n: the running time is at most f(n) no matter which input the adversary hands you, with no probability involved at all. AVERAGE CASE is a statement about a DETERMINISTIC algorithm's running time in expectation over an ASSUMED distribution on inputs -- commonly 'assume every permutation of n distinct keys is equally likely.' That assumption is doing all the work, and it is an assumption about the DATA, which the algorithm's designer does not control and cannot verify at runtime. EXPECTED TIME is a statement about a RANDOMIZED algorithm's running time in expectation over the algorithm's OWN internal coin flips, for a single FIXED, arbitrary, even adversarially chosen input. This is the crucial asymmetry: average-case analysis needs the world to cooperate; expected-time analysis needs only the algorithm's own random number generator to behave, and that holds no matter what input arrives.

sections.heading: When the average-case assumption breaks on real data: algorithmic complexity attacks
sections.body: Hash tables are the textbook example. A fixed hash function gives O(1) expected lookup 'on average' only if keys behave like a random sample with respect to that function -- but an adversary who can choose which keys get inserted (e.g. an attacker submitting HTTP form field names or JSON keys to a server) can pick keys that all hash to the same bucket. Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach's 2003 USENIX Security paper, 'Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks,' formalized this: a fixed, public hash function turns 'average-case O(1)' into 'worst-case O(n) per operation, O(n^2) total' whenever the attacker controls the keys. The threat was not hypothetical: in December 2011, Alexander Klink and Julian Walde presented 'Efficient Denial of Service Attacks on Web Application Platforms' at the Chaos Communication Congress (28C3), showing that a few kilobytes of crafted POST data could pin PHP, Java, and other runtimes' default hash tables at 100% CPU for hours -- the assumed distribution (roughly random keys) that the average-case claim depended on simply did not hold for attacker-supplied data.

sections.heading: Why expected time survives where average case failed
sections.body: The fix illustrates the distinction precisely: instead of a single fixed public hash function, choose the hash function's parameters RANDOMLY at process start from a universal family (the framework Larry Carter and Mark Wegman introduced in 1979). Now, for ANY fixed set of keys the adversary commits to in advance -- including a set specifically crafted to collide under some particular hash function -- the EXPECTATION is taken over the algorithm's own private coin flip (which hash function got chosen), a coin flip the adversary cannot predict in advance. That is an expected-time guarantee of O(1), and it holds for every input, not just 'typical' ones. CPython made hash randomization the default starting in version 3.3 (2012) via PYTHONHASHSEED. That original randomized hash was later shown vulnerable to seed-recovery by its own designers' adversaries, and CPython 3.4 (2014, PEP 456) switched to Aumasson and Bernstein's SipHash keyed hash function (2012) as the fix. The lesson generalizes far beyond hashing: whenever you can move the randomness from an assumption about the data into a coin flip the algorithm itself controls, a fragile average-case claim becomes a robust expected-time guarantee.

lessons.workedExample: Java's original String.hashCode() is a fixed polynomial hash with multiplier 31, published in the language spec. An attacker who wants to attack a Java servlet's parameter hash table can precompute, offline, thousands of distinct strings that all hash to the same 32-bit value under that exact fixed formula -- this is a solved, publishable construction, not a probabilistic long shot. Submitting them as form field names forces every one into the same bucket, turning n insertions into an O(n^2) chain-building operation. If the same servlet instead seeded a universal hash family with a random 64-bit key generated fresh at JVM startup, the attacker's precomputed collision set (built for one specific hash function) would almost certainly not collide under the actual runtime instance's randomly-chosen function -- the expected O(n) total insertion time now holds regardless of which strings the attacker picks, because the coin flip the guarantee relies on is private to the process.
lessons.judgeFraming: A rigorous judge will ask you to name a case where a textbook average-case claim demonstrably fails on real data, and to explain in mechanism terms (not just 'attackers are mean') why it fails -- the answer must locate the failure precisely in the assumed input distribution being violated. The follow-up question probes whether you understand the fix: judges want to hear that randomizing the ALGORITHM's own behavior (not merely hoping the data is nice) is what converts the claim into one that survives adversarial or simply atypical real-world data, and that this is a general principle applicable well beyond hash tables.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an 'average case' running-time claim and an 'expected time' claim?

options.text: Average case takes expectation over an assumed input distribution for a deterministic algorithm; expected time takes expectation over a randomized algorithm's own coin flips for a fixed input
They are the same claim, just stated with different words
Average case is always faster than expected time by definition
Expected time only applies to sorting algorithms, while average case applies to all algorithms

explanations.a: Correct -- average case bakes in an assumption about the DATA (e.g. uniform random permutations) that real inputs may violate, while expected time only assumes the ALGORITHM's own randomness behaves, which holds for any fixed input including adversarial ones.
explanations.b: They are frequently conflated but are logically distinct claims with different failure modes, as the hash-flooding example shows.
explanations.c: Neither is inherently faster; they differ in what they assume, not in their numeric guarantee.
explanations.d: Both apply broadly across algorithm types; the distinction is about the source of randomness, not the problem domain.

questions.prompt: Why did fixed-hash-function tables' 'average-case O(1)' claim fail against real attacker-supplied data in the 2011 hashDoS incident?

options.text: The hash function itself was computed incorrectly by the runtimes involved
The average-case analysis assumed roughly random keys, but attackers could precompute keys that all collide under the known, fixed hash function, violating that assumption
Hash tables have no average-case guarantee to begin with, so nothing actually broke
The attack exploited a buffer overflow unrelated to hashing

explanations.a: The hash functions were computed correctly; the vulnerability was that they were fixed and public, making deliberate collisions computable in advance.
explanations.b: Correct -- the average-case O(1) claim requires keys to behave like a random sample with respect to the hash function, and a known, fixed function lets an adversary construct keys that violate this by design.
explanations.c: Standard hash tables do carry an average-case guarantee under a random-input assumption; the 2011 demonstrations showed real data (adversarial input) can violate that assumption.
explanations.d: The attack was purely algorithmic, exploiting the assumed-distribution gap in hashing, not a memory-safety bug.

questions.prompt: Match each running-time claim to what it is actually taken over.

right.text: Maximum over every possible input, no probability involved
Expectation over an assumed distribution on inputs, for a fixed deterministic algorithm
Expectation over the algorithm's own internal randomness, for any single fixed input

questions.explanation: Worst case ranges over inputs with no randomness; average case takes expectation over an assumed input distribution for a fixed algorithm; expected time takes expectation over the algorithm's own coin flips, holding for every fixed input including adversarial ones.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the hash-flooding story in chronological order.

items.text: Crosby and Wallach publish 'Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks' (USENIX Security 2003)
Many popular language runtimes continue shipping fixed, public hash functions in their default hash tables
Klink and Walde demonstrate practical hashDoS attacks at 28C3 (December 2011)
Runtimes adopt randomized/keyed hashing, e.g. CPython 3.3's PYTHONHASHSEED and the SipHash keyed hash function (2012)

questions.explanation: The theoretical vulnerability was published in 2003, went largely unaddressed across many runtimes for years, was demonstrated as a practical multi-platform attack at 28C3 in December 2011, and prompted runtimes to adopt randomized keyed hashing shortly after in 2012.

lessons.label: Markov, Chebyshev, and Chernoff

sections.heading: Markov's inequality: only the mean, nothing else
sections.body: Markov's inequality states that for any NONNEGATIVE random variable X, P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a, for any a > 0. It requires nothing about X beyond nonnegativity and a finite mean -- not independence, not a known distribution, not even a finite variance. That generality is also its weakness: it throws away all information about how X is spread around its mean. Take X = sum of n = 100 independent fair coin flips (each 0 or 1), so E[X] = 50. To bound P(X >= 60), Markov gives P(X >= 60) <= 50/60 = 0.833 -- technically true, but so loose it barely says anything (an 83% upper bound on an event that turns out to have true probability around 3%).

sections.heading: Chebyshev's inequality: paying for a variance
sections.body: Chebyshev's inequality uses one more piece of information -- the VARIANCE -- to tighten the bound: P(|X - E[X]| >= t) <= Var(X)/t^2. For the same n=100 fair-coin sum, Var(X) = n p(1-p) = 100 * 0.25 = 25. Setting t = 10 (bounding the two-sided deviation of at least 10 from the mean of 50, which upper-bounds our one-sided event X >= 60), Chebyshev gives P(X >= 60) <= P(|X-50| >= 10) <= 25/100 = 0.25. That is more than 3 times tighter than Markov's 0.833, purchased by requiring the extra assumption that Var(X) is finite and known -- still nothing about independence or the shape of the distribution, just its spread.

sections.heading: Chernoff/Hoeffding: independence buys exponential decay
sections.body: The Chernoff bound, developed from Herman Chernoff's 1952 technique of bounding a moment generating function, and extended by Wassily Hoeffding in 1963 to sums of bounded independent random variables (the Hoeffding bound), requires a genuinely stronger structural assumption: the summands must be INDEPENDENT (or near-independent) and bounded. In exchange, the tail decays EXPONENTIALLY rather than polynomially: Hoeffding's bound gives P(X - E[X] >= t) <= exp(-2t^2/n) for a sum of n independent [0,1]-bounded variables. Plugging in t=10, n=100: exp(-2*100/100) = exp(-2) ~= 0.135, about 1.8x tighter than Chebyshev's 0.25, and over 6x tighter than Markov's 0.833. The true probability (from the exact binomial tail) is about 0.028 -- Chernoff/Hoeffding is the only one of the three that lands in the right order of magnitude, and it is the only one that required independence of the summands to earn that tightness.

lessons.workedExample: Scale the same setup to n=400 independent fair coin flips (E[X]=200) and ask for P(X >= 220), a deviation of t=20. Markov: 200/220 = 0.909. Chebyshev: Var(X) = 400*0.25=100, so bound = 100/400 = 0.25. Hoeffding: exp(-2*20^2/400) = exp(-2*400/400) = exp(-2) = 0.135 -- the identical numeric bound as the n=100, t=10 case. This is not a coincidence: the Hoeffding exponent depends only on the ratio t^2/n, and here 20^2/400 = 10^2/100 = 1. Because a binomial sum's standard deviation itself scales as sqrt(n), holding t proportional to sqrt(n) keeps the exponential bound fixed -- exactly the scaling behavior the Central Limit Theorem predicts for deviations that matter.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask 'why not just always use the Chernoff bound, since it's the tightest?' The correct answer is that tightness is not free: Chernoff/Hoeffding requires independence (or a substitute like negative association) among bounded summands, an assumption Markov and Chebyshev do not need. A strong answer names exactly what each inequality buys with its extra assumption -- Markov needs only a mean, Chebyshev adds a variance, Chernoff adds independence plus boundedness -- and can show, with the shared numeric example, that the bounds tighten in lockstep with the assumptions: 0.833, then 0.25, then 0.135, converging toward the true value of about 0.028.

questions.prompt: What extra piece of information does Chebyshev's inequality require beyond what Markov's inequality needs?

options.text: Independence of the underlying random variables
A finite, known variance
That the variable be bounded between 0 and 1
Nothing extra -- Chebyshev and Markov use identical information

explanations.a: Independence is the extra ingredient Chernoff/Hoeffding needs, not Chebyshev.
explanations.b: Correct -- Chebyshev's inequality is P(|X-E[X]|>=t) <= Var(X)/t^2, which requires knowing the variance, information Markov's inequality does not use at all.
explanations.c: Boundedness is a Chernoff/Hoeffding-style requirement, not something Chebyshev's inequality needs.
explanations.d: They differ specifically in that Chebyshev exploits the variance while Markov uses only the mean, giving Chebyshev a tighter bound.

questions.prompt: What extra structural assumption does the Chernoff/Hoeffding bound require beyond Chebyshev's?

options.text: Nothing more; Chernoff/Hoeffding is just Chebyshev's inequality renamed
That the random variable's mean be exactly zero
That X be a sum of independent (or near-independent) bounded random variables, not merely any variable with a known variance
That n be smaller than 100

explanations.a: The two are distinct: Chebyshev only needs a variance, while Chernoff/Hoeffding needs independence structure to control the moment generating function.
explanations.b: There is no such requirement; the bound concerns deviation from whatever the mean is.
explanations.c: Correct -- Chernoff-style bounds are proved via the moment generating function of a sum of independent (or negatively associated) bounded summands, which is what allows the tail to decay exponentially rather than polynomially.
explanations.d: The bound holds for any n; there is no such size restriction.

questions.prompt: For the n=100 fair-coin-sum example bounding P(X >= 60), order these bounds from loosest to tightest.

items.text: Markov's inequality bound (~0.833)
Chebyshev's inequality bound (~0.25)
Chernoff/Hoeffding bound (~0.135)

questions.explanation: Markov's bound of 0.833 uses only the mean and is loosest; Chebyshev's bound of 0.25 adds variance information and tightens it substantially; Chernoff/Hoeffding's bound of 0.135 adds independence and boundedness and is tightest of the three, though still looser than the true value of about 0.028.

questions.prompt: Match each inequality to the single extra piece of information it exploits beyond the previous one in the hierarchy.

right.text: Only the mean of a nonnegative variable
The mean plus the variance
Independence (or near-independence) of bounded summands, via the moment generating function

questions.explanation: Each successive bound in the hierarchy buys tightness by assuming more structure: Markov needs only a mean, Chebyshev adds a variance, and Chernoff/Hoeffding adds independence of bounded summands to control the full moment generating function, yielding exponential rather than polynomial tail decay.

lessons.label: 'With High Probability' and What It Buys

sections.heading: Defining 'with high probability' (whp)
sections.body: Following the standard definition used in Rajeev Motwani and Prabhakar Raghavan's textbook 'Randomized Algorithms' (1995), an event on inputs of size n happens WITH HIGH PROBABILITY if, for every constant c > 0, its probability is at least 1 - 1/n^c once the algorithm's parameters are tuned for that c -- typically by paying a little more work (e.g. a few extra repetitions or a bigger constant in front of the running time). This is a claim about the entire TAIL of a distribution: not just where the average sits, but how rarely the outcome strays far from what you expect. Crucially, 'expected O(n log n)' is a strictly WEAKER statement than 'O(n log n) with high probability.' Expected time only pins down the mean; by Markov's inequality, an expected time of c*n log n only guarantees P(T >= 100 c n log n) <= 1/100 -- a real but modest guarantee. A whp bound instead controls the probability of ANY large deviation, and that probability shrinks polynomially (or faster) as n grows, which is exactly the property needed to combine many such guarantees together via a union bound.

sections.heading: Why the implication only goes one way
sections.body: A whp bound plus a trivial worst-case cap implies an expected-time bound: if T <= f(n) except with probability at most 1/n^c, and even in the bad case T is at most some polynomial worst case g(n), then E[T] <= f(n) + (1/n^c) g(n), and for c large enough relative to g's degree this extra term is lower-order, recovering E[T] = O(f(n)). But the converse fails. Consider an algorithm that runs in time n log n except with probability exactly 1/n, in which case it takes time n^2 log n. Its expected time is (1 - 1/n)(n log n) + (1/n)(n^2 log n) = (n log n - log n) + n log n = O(n log n) -- a genuinely bounded expectation -- but a 1/n failure probability is not of the form 1/n^c for c > 1, and does not stay small when unioned over the many independent sub-events (recursive calls, parallel processors, repeated queries) a real system needs to survive simultaneously.

sections.heading: Turning an average into an engineering promise: quicksort's recursion depth
sections.body: Apply this to randomized quicksort's recursion depth. Call a partitioning step 'good' if the random pivot lands strictly between the 25th and 75th percentile of the current subarray's ranks -- this happens with probability at least 1/2 for a uniform random pivot, since half of all ranks fall in that middle band. A good split shrinks the subarray to at most 3/4 its size, so after k good splits along any root-to-leaf path in the recursion tree, the remaining size is at most n(3/4)^k, which reaches O(1) once k = Theta(log n). Whether a given step is good is dominated by an independent fair coin flip, so among any window of Theta(log n) consecutive steps along one path, a Chernoff bound on the count of good splits shows the probability of falling short of the Theta(log n) good splits needed is at most n^{-Theta(1)} -- polynomially small for that ONE path. A union bound over all at most n root-to-leaf paths in the recursion tree still leaves total failure probability polynomially small, giving the classical result: randomized quicksort's recursion depth is O(log n) with high probability. That is an engineering-usable promise -- you may safely provision an O(log n) call stack or parallel span -- which 'expected O(n log n) running time' alone never claims, since expectation says nothing about how deep the recursion is ever likely to go.

lessons.workedExample: For n = 1,000,000 elements (log2 n ~= 20), a fixed-first-element pivot rule has WORST-CASE recursion depth n = 1,000,000 on an already-sorted array, regardless of any 'average-case' story about random inputs. Randomized quicksort instead has expected recursion depth around 2 ln n ~= 27.6, and the whp argument goes further: it guarantees depth stays within a constant factor of ln n (the classical constant, from Devroye's 1986 analysis of random BST height, is alpha ~= 4.311, i.e. ~4.311 ln n, so roughly 60 here) except with probability that shrinks polynomially in n. A system that provisions its call stack (or thread pool depth, on a parallel machine) based on the expected depth alone is gambling on the mean; a system that provisions based on the whp bound is buying a guarantee that fails only on a vanishingly small, quantifiable fraction of runs -- the difference between a benchmark number and a service-level promise.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'if the expected time is O(n log n), doesn't that basically mean it's always about that fast?' is probing whether you understand that expectation is silent about the tail. The strong answer produces a concrete counterexample (a rare catastrophic branch that the expectation absorbs without violating an O(n log n) mean) and then explains why whp is different -- it bounds the FAILURE PROBABILITY itself, which is exactly the quantity you need small and controllable when you must combine many probabilistic guarantees at once, as in the union bound over quicksort's recursion tree.

questions.prompt: By the standard definition, an event happens 'with high probability' (whp) on inputs of size n if its probability is at least:

options.text: 1/2, regardless of n
1 - 1/n^c, for every constant c > 0 once parameters are tuned
Exactly equal to the algorithm's expected running time divided by n
1 - 1/log n

explanations.a: A flat 1/2 probability does not shrink as n grows and is not what whp requires.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the standard definition (as in Motwani and Raghavan's textbook): the failure probability is at most 1/n^c for every constant c, once the algorithm is tuned for that c, shrinking polynomially as n grows.
explanations.c: Whp is a probability statement about an event, not a formula derived from expected running time.
explanations.d: 1 - 1/log n shrinks too slowly (only logarithmically) to qualify as the polynomial decay whp requires.

questions.prompt: An algorithm runs in time n log n except with probability 1/n, in which case it takes time n^2 log n, giving expected time O(n log n). What does this example show?

options.text: That expected time and whp time are always equal for any algorithm

That a bound holding 'with high probability' automatically implies a matching bound on expected time, but not the reverse -- an expectation-based claim can hide a failure mode that is too common (here 1/n) to call whp
That whp bounds are weaker than expected-time bounds
That this algorithm cannot exist because expected time must always equal the typical-case time

explanations.a: The example explicitly shows a case where the two diverge -- the expected time is dragged upward by a rare-but-not-rare-enough catastrophic branch.
explanations.b: Correct -- whp (with a worst-case cap) implies a bounded expectation, but the converse fails: this example's expected time genuinely works out to O(n log n) (the (1/n)(n^2 log n) contribution from the bad case is itself only O(n log n)), yet the 1/n failure probability is common enough that it is not of the required 1/n^c (c>1) form, so unioning over many such events (recursive calls, parallel tasks) would not keep failure probability small.
explanations.c: It is the reverse: whp is the strictly stronger claim precisely because it controls the tail, not just the mean.
explanations.d: Such algorithms are common in practice (e.g. randomized algorithms with a rare fallback to a slow deterministic path); nothing about expected time forces typical-case behavior.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the whp argument for randomized quicksort's O(log n) recursion depth in order.

items.text: Define a partitioning step as 'good' if the pivot lands in the middle 50% of ranks
Note a good split shrinks the subarray to at most 3/4 its size, so O(log n) good splits suffice to reach constant size
Apply a Chernoff bound to show that, along one root-to-leaf path, getting too few good splits in a Theta(log n) window has polynomially small probability
Apply a union bound over all at most n root-to-leaf paths in the recursion tree
Conclude the whole recursion tree has depth O(log n) with high probability

questions.explanation: The argument first defines what counts as a good split, then shows how many good splits are needed, then uses a Chernoff bound to show one path is unlikely to lack enough good splits, then extends this across all paths with a union bound, and finally concludes the overall whp depth bound.

questions.prompt: Match each type of running-time statement to what it actually controls.

right.text: Controls only the mean of the running-time distribution; says nothing about how large deviations from it are
Controls the failure probability itself, which shrinks polynomially in n, allowing union bounds over many events
Controls every possible outcome on every input, with no probability involved

questions.explanation: Expected time bounds only the mean; whp bounds the tail/failure probability directly, which is what makes it composable across many simultaneous events via a union bound; worst case is a deterministic, probability-free guarantee over all inputs.

lessons.label: Amplification: Driving Failure Probability to Zero

sections.heading: Karger's contraction algorithm and its telescoping success probability
sections.body: David Karger's 1993 randomized algorithm for the global minimum-cut problem repeatedly picks a uniformly random remaining edge and contracts it -- merging its two endpoints into one supernode and deleting any resulting self-loops -- until exactly 2 supernodes remain; the edges between them form the returned cut. Fix any specific minimum cut C* of size k in the original n-vertex graph. At the moment i supernodes remain, C* is still a valid cut of the current contracted graph, and since the min cut size is k, every supernode has degree at least k, so the current graph has at least ik/2 edges; the chance a uniformly random edge belongs to C* is therefore at most k/(ik/2) = 2/i. The probability the entire run of n-2 contractions never touches C* is the product over i = n down to 3 of (1 - 2/i), which telescopes to (n-2)(n-3)...(1) / [n(n-1)...3] = 2/(n(n-1)) -- exactly 1 over C(n,2). A single run finds any FIXED minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)), small but far from negligible.

sections.heading: Amplifying by repetition and taking the minimum
sections.body: Because the contraction process always returns SOME valid cut of the graph and the true minimum cut is a hard lower bound on cut size, running the algorithm N independent times and keeping the SMALLEST cut found across all runs can only help -- this is a ONE-SIDED error: a run either finds (a) minimum cut or returns something no better than the true answer, never something invalid. The probability that ALL N independent runs miss a specific minimum cut is at most (1 - 2/(n(n-1)))^N <= exp(-2N/(n(n-1))). Choosing N = c * n(n-1)/2 * ln n = O(n^2 log n) for a constant c makes this at most exp(-c ln n) = n^{-c} -- a with-high-probability success guarantee. Each run of the basic contraction procedure takes about O(n^2) time with an adjacency-matrix implementation, so the straightforward amplified algorithm runs in O(n^4 log n) total time; Karger and his co-author Clifford Stein's 1996 recursive refinement ('A New Approach to the Minimum Cut Problem') avoids restarting from scratch on every repetition and brings the total down to O(n^2 log^3 n), by observing that early contractions are safe to share across branches while only the final stretch (where the min cut is most likely to be destroyed) needs to be re-run many times.

sections.heading: When repetition alone is not enough: two-sided error and the median trick
sections.body: Karger's contraction algorithm has one-sided error precisely because there is a cheap, objective verifier -- comparing cut sizes -- that tells you which of several runs to trust; taking the minimum is that verifier. Many Monte Carlo algorithms instead have TWO-SIDED error: a numeric estimator or a decision procedure that is correct with probability only slightly better than 1/2 (say at least 2/3), where errors can push the answer in either direction and there is no cheap way to tell a correct run from an incorrect one just by inspecting its output. For these, the fix is the MEDIAN TRICK (a standard error-reduction lemma appearing in complexity-theory texts such as Sipser's and Arora and Barak's, used for boosting BPP-style algorithms): run k independent copies and output the MEDIAN of the numeric estimates (or the MAJORITY VOTE of the decisions). A Chernoff bound on the number of 'bad' copies among the k independent trials shows the chance that bad copies form a majority -- which is what would corrupt the median or the vote -- decays exponentially in k, so k = O(log(1/delta)) repetitions suffice to push overall failure probability down to any target delta.

lessons.workedExample: For n = 10 vertices, a single contraction run finds a specific minimum cut with probability at least 2/(10*9) = 2/90 ~= 0.0222 (about 2.2%). To drive the failure probability of the min-taking amplification down to 1%, solve (1 - 0.0222)^N <= 0.01: N >= ln(0.01)/ln(0.9778) ~= -4.605 / -0.02247 ~= 205 runs. This matches the O(n^2 log n) formula closely: n(n-1)/2 * ln n = 45 * ln(10) = 45 * 2.303 ~= 103.6, so a constant factor around c=2 in front of that formula reproduces the ~205 runs computed directly -- confirming that 'O(n^2 log n) independent repetitions' is not a hand-wave, it is the exact quantity that makes the telescoping success probability compound into a whp guarantee.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use the median trick for Karger's algorithm too, instead of taking the minimum?' is testing whether you understand the one-sided/two-sided distinction precisely. The correct answer is that you COULD, but it would be needless machinery: contraction's error is one-sided and cheaply verifiable (smaller cut size is always at least as good), so simple min-taking already achieves the amplification the median trick exists to provide for harder, two-sided-error settings where no such cheap verifier is available. A judge probing here wants to see that you can name which structural property (verifiable one-sided error vs. unverifiable two-sided error) determines which amplification tool applies.

questions.prompt: What is the exact probability that a single run of Karger's contraction algorithm finds a specific fixed minimum cut, derived from the telescoping product?

options.text: 1/log n

explanations.a: 1/n does not match the telescoping product of (1 - 2/i) terms for i from n down to 3.
explanations.b: Correct -- the product (n-2)(n-3)...(1) / [n(n-1)...3] telescopes exactly to 2/(n(n-1)), equivalently 1/C(n,2).
explanations.c: A constant 1/2 probability regardless of n contradicts the derivation, which explicitly shrinks as n grows.
explanations.d: The bound is polynomially small in n (order 1/n^2), not logarithmically small.

questions.prompt: Why does simply taking the minimum cut found across many independent Karger runs suffice to amplify success, without needing a median-trick-style vote?

options.text: Because the error is one-sided and cheaply verifiable: every run returns a valid cut, the true minimum is a lower bound, so keeping the smallest result across runs can only help or stay the same, never hurt
Because Karger's algorithm never makes any errors in the first place
Because cut sizes are always equal across all runs, so any run works
Because the median trick only works for sorting algorithms

explanations.a: Correct -- comparing cut sizes is a free, objective verifier of which run's answer to prefer, which is exactly the structure that makes minimum-taking sufficient; two-sided-error settings lack this cheap verifier and need statistical aggregation instead.
explanations.b: The algorithm does make errors (returning a valid but non-minimum cut); amplification exists precisely to reduce the probability of that error.
explanations.c: Cut sizes generally differ across runs; taking the minimum of these differing values is exactly the point.
explanations.d: The median trick is a general Monte Carlo amplification technique for two-sided error, unrelated specifically to sorting.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Karger amplification argument.

items.text: Show a single run finds a fixed minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1))
Run the contraction algorithm N independent times and record the smallest cut found
Bound the probability all N runs miss the minimum cut by (1 - 2/(n(n-1)))^N
Choose N = O(n^2 log n) so this failure probability becomes n^{-c}
Conclude the algorithm finds the minimum cut with high probability

questions.explanation: The argument first establishes the single-run success probability, then defines the repeat-and-take-minimum strategy, then bounds the joint failure probability across all repetitions, then picks a repetition count that drives this bound polynomially small, and finally concludes the whp guarantee.

questions.prompt: Match each amplification scenario to the correct aggregation strategy.

left.text: Karger's contraction algorithm (one-sided error, cheaply verifiable via cut size)
A Monte Carlo numeric estimator with two-sided error and no cheap verifier
A Monte Carlo decision algorithm correct with probability at least 2/3, errors in either direction

right.text: Take the minimum (or best-verified) result across independent runs
Take the median of many independent estimates
Take the majority vote across many independent runs

questions.explanation: One-sided, cheaply-verifiable error (as in Karger's algorithm) is amplified by simply keeping the best verified result; two-sided error without a cheap verifier requires statistical aggregation instead -- the median for numeric estimates, majority vote for binary decisions -- both backed by a Chernoff bound on the number of bad copies among the repetitions.

lessons.label: Randomized Selection, Coupon Collector, and Balls in Bins

sections.heading: Randomized quickselect: expected O(n) via a shrinking recurrence
sections.body: C.A.R. Hoare's 1961 FIND algorithm (now usually called randomized quickselect) finds the k-th smallest element by partitioning around a uniformly random pivot, exactly like quicksort, but recursing into only the ONE side that contains rank k and discarding the other -- there is no need to sort the discarded side at all. Call a pivot 'good' if it lands within the middle 50% of the current subarray's ranks (between the 25th and 75th percentile); a uniformly random pivot is good with probability at least 1/2, and a good pivot guarantees the surviving recursive subproblem has size at most 3n/4. The number of consecutive 'bad' pivots before a good one appears is geometrically distributed with success probability at least 1/2, so its expectation is O(1); amortizing this, the recurrence for expected time solves as E[T(n)] = E[T(3n/4)] + O(n), and summing the resulting geometric series O(n)(1 + 3/4 + (3/4)^2 + ...) = O(n) * 4 gives E[T(n)] = O(n) -- linear expected time to select any order statistic, without ever fully sorting.

sections.heading: The coupon collector problem: n ln n and where it keeps reappearing
sections.body: In the coupon collector problem, each draw picks one of n distinct coupon types uniformly at random with replacement; the question is the expected number of draws until all n types have appeared. Split the process into n phases, where phase i begins once i-1 distinct types have been seen; the probability a draw during phase i yields a NEW type is (n-i+1)/n, so the expected number of draws in phase i is n/(n-i+1). By linearity of expectation, the total expected draws is n * sum_{i=1}^{n} 1/i = n * H_n, the n-th harmonic number, which is approximately n ln n + gamma*n (gamma ~= 0.577, the Euler-Mascheroni constant) -- so n ln n is the leading-order answer. This exact bound recurs across the field: it lower-bounds how many random probes are needed before every bucket of an n-bucket hash table has been touched at least once, it governs how long naive random load-balancing takes to give every one of n servers at least one request, and it is invoked (more informally) in genetic-algorithm theory to argue how many randomly generated individuals a population needs before it is likely to contain every needed building block.

sections.heading: Balls in bins: Theta(log n / log log n), and the power of two choices
sections.body: Throw n balls independently and uniformly into n bins; the MAXIMUM load (the fullest bin) is Theta(log n / log log n) with high probability -- a classical result often credited to Gaston Gonnet's 1981 analysis of hashing ('Expected Length of the Longest Probe Sequence in Hash Code Searching'). Yossi Azar, Andrei Broder, Anna Karlin, and Eli Upfal's 1994 STOC paper 'Balanced Allocations' (journal version, SIAM Journal on Computing, 1999) showed a dramatic improvement: if each ball instead samples d >= 2 bins independently at random and is placed in whichever sampled bin currently has fewer balls, the maximum load drops to Theta(log log n / log d) with high probability -- for the canonical d=2 case, this is Theta(log log n), specifically about (ln ln n)/(ln 2) + O(1). Going from 1 random choice to comparing just 2 changes the growth rate of the worst bin from a fraction of log n down to log log n, an exponential-scale improvement in how balanced the loads become, purchased by a single extra sample and comparison per ball. This 'power of two choices' result is the theoretical basis widely cited behind modern load balancers (e.g. randomized request routing that compares two candidate servers rather than picking one at random or round-robining) and behind refinements like consistent hashing with bounded loads.

lessons.workedExample: For n = 1,000,000 bins and balls: single-random-choice max load scales as log(10^6)/loglog(10^6) = ln(1,000,000)/ln(ln(1,000,000)) = 13.816/ln(13.816) = 13.816/2.625 ~= 5.26, so realistically the fullest bin holds on the order of 5 balls beyond the average of 1. With power-of-two-choices, max load scales as loglog(10^6)/ln(2) = 2.625/0.693 ~= 3.79, on the order of 4 balls. The gap looks modest at n=10^6 because both are small numbers here, but the two bounds have fundamentally different GROWTH RATES as n increases without bound -- Theta(log n/loglog n) keeps growing (however slowly) while Theta(loglog n) grows even slower, so the ratio between them diverges as n gets astronomically large, even though at everyday problem sizes the practical benefit already shows up as a smaller, more predictable worst-case bucket.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson typically asks for the exact recurrence behind quickselect's linear expected time (T(n) = T(3n/4) + O(n), and why 3n/4 specifically -- because a random pivot lands in the middle half with probability at least 1/2), then pivots to asking where else n ln n shows up outside of the literal coupon problem, testing whether the student recognizes it as a reusable coverage-time bound rather than a one-off puzzle. A sharp judge will also ask why comparing just 2 random bins instead of 1 changes the worst-case load's growth rate so drastically -- the answer should name the Azar-Broder-Karlin-Upfal result by its actual mechanism (a bad bin now requires BOTH sampled choices to be bad, compounding recursively), not just cite 'power of two choices' as a slogan.

questions.prompt: In randomized quickselect's recurrence E[T(n)] = E[T(3n/4)] + O(n), why does the recursive subproblem shrink to at most 3n/4 (rather than some other fraction)?

options.text: Because a uniformly random pivot lands in the middle 50% of ranks (between the 25th and 75th percentile) with probability at least 1/2, and any such 'good' pivot leaves at most 3n/4 elements on either side
Because quickselect always partitions the array into exactly two halves of equal size
Because 3/4 is chosen arbitrarily to simplify the algebra, with no connection to pivot placement
Because the discarded side is always exactly n/4 regardless of which pivot is chosen

explanations.a: Correct -- a pivot landing strictly between the 25th and 75th percentile guarantees neither side exceeds 3n/4 elements, and a uniformly random pivot achieves this with probability at least 1/2.
explanations.b: A random pivot does not generally split the array into exact halves; the 3n/4 bound comes from a probabilistic 'good enough' argument, not an equal split guarantee.
explanations.c: The 3/4 factor is derived directly from the middle-50%-of-ranks argument, not chosen for algebraic convenience.
explanations.d: The discarded side's size varies depending on where the random pivot actually lands; 3n/4 is an upper bound for 'good' pivots, not a fixed constant outcome.

questions.prompt: What is the leading-order expected number of draws (with replacement, uniform over n types) needed to collect all n coupon types?

options.text: n ln n (more precisely n * H_n, the n-th harmonic number times n)
log2 n

explanations.a: Correct -- splitting into n phases and using linearity of expectation gives total expected draws n * H_n, which is n ln n + gamma*n + O(1), so n ln n is the leading-order term.
explanations.b: n^2 vastly overstates the expected draws; the correct bound is only a logarithmic factor above n, not a full extra factor of n.
explanations.c: log2 n is far too small; it does not even scale with the number of draws needed in the early, easy phases of collection.
explanations.d: n/2 ignores the increasingly long waits needed to find the last few remaining uncollected types, which is precisely what drives the ln n factor.

questions.prompt: Order these asymptotic growth rates (as functions of n) from SLOWEST-growing to FASTEST-growing as n gets large.

items.text: Theta(log log n) -- power-of-two-choices maximum bin load
Theta(log n / log log n) -- single-random-choice maximum bin load
Theta(log n) -- plain logarithmic growth

questions.explanation: Theta(log log n) grows slowest since it is a logarithm of a logarithm; Theta(log n / log log n) grows faster than loglog n but slower than plain log n because it is log n divided by the slowly-growing loglog n factor; Theta(log n) grows fastest of the three since it has no divisor shrinking it.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its characteristic formula or asymptotic order.

left.text: Coupon collector expected number of draws

right.text: T(n) = T(3n/4) + O(n), solving to E[T(n)] = O(n)
n * H_n ~= n ln n
Theta(log n / log log n)
Theta(log log n)

questions.explanation: Quickselect's recurrence T(n)=T(3n/4)+O(n) solves to linear expected time via a geometric series; the coupon collector's expected draws is n times the n-th harmonic number, approximately n ln n; throwing n balls into n bins with one random choice each gives maximum load Theta(log n/loglog n) (Gonnet, 1981); sampling two bins and picking the emptier one (Azar-Broder-Karlin-Upfal, 1994/1999) drops the maximum load to Theta(loglog n).

questions.prompt: What is the essential mechanism by which the 'power of two choices' improves maximum load from Theta(log n / log log n) to Theta(log log n)?

options.text: Each ball samples 2 independent random bins and goes to the one with fewer balls currently, so a bin only accumulates load if BOTH of a ball's sampled options happened to already be heavily loaded, compounding the improbability recursively
Balls are no longer placed independently; they coordinate globally to avoid any bin exceeding average load
The number of bins is doubled, halving the average load per bin
Each ball is placed in the bin with the fewest total balls across the entire history, computed exactly via a global minimum

explanations.a: Correct -- this is exactly the Azar-Broder-Karlin-Upfal mechanism: since a ball goes to the less-loaded of 2 independently sampled bins, ending up in an already-crowded bin requires BOTH samples to land on crowded bins, which becomes doubly improbable as load grows, driving the recursive bound down to loglog n.
explanations.b: The balls are still placed independently at random; the improvement comes from comparing 2 local samples per ball, not global coordination.
explanations.c: The number of bins is unchanged (n bins, n balls in the classical setup); the improvement is purely from the placement rule, not the bin count.
explanations.d: The algorithm only compares d=2 sampled bins, not the entire global state, which is exactly what keeps it cheap and local while still yielding the improvement.

units.label: Randomized Methods: Primality, Sampling and Hashing

lessons.label: Fermat, Carmichael Numbers, and the Primality Problem

sections.heading: The Fermat test: a fast necessary condition
sections.body: Fermat's Little Theorem says that if n is prime and a is any integer not divisible by n, then a^(n-1) is congruent to 1 mod n. This gives an almost-free primality check: pick a random base a in [2, n-2], compute a^(n-1) mod n by fast modular exponentiation (O(log n) multiplications), and if the result is not 1, n is DEFINITELY composite -- a is called a Fermat witness. The appeal is speed: testing a 300-digit number costs only a few hundred modular squarings, versus trial division which is hopeless at that size. The catch is the converse does not hold: passing the test for one base, or even many bases, is evidence of primality, not proof. A composite n that passes base a is called a Fermat pseudoprime to base a; these exist but are individually rare and avoidable by trying several random bases -- UNLESS n belongs to a much nastier class.

sections.heading: Carmichael numbers: composites that fool every base
sections.body: A Carmichael number is a composite n that satisfies a^(n-1) = 1 mod n for EVERY base a coprime to n -- not most bases, all of them. The smallest is 561 = 3 x 11 x 17, discovered by Robert Carmichael in 1910 (though Alwin Korselt had characterized the property in 1899). Korselt's criterion explains why: n is a Carmichael number if and only if n is squarefree and, for every prime factor p of n, (p-1) divides (n-1). Check 561: 561 - 1 = 560. The factors are 3, 11, 17; and 2 | 560, 10 | 560, 16 | 560 -- all three conditions hold. The next two are 1105 = 5 x 13 x 17 and 1729 = 7 x 13 x 19 (1729 is also the famous Hardy-Ramanujan taxicab number, an unrelated coincidence). For any base coprime to 561, the Fermat test reports 'probably prime' -- it is wrong every single time, for a fixed composite number, regardless of how many random coprime bases you throw at it.

sections.heading: There are infinitely many, and that changes the field
sections.body: For decades it was open whether Carmichael numbers were a finite curiosity or an infinite menace. William Alford, Andrew Granville, and Carl Pomerance settled it in their 1994 Annals of Mathematics paper 'There are Infinitely Many Carmichael Numbers,' proving a lower bound of roughly x^(2/7) Carmichael numbers below any bound x for large x. Combined with the fact that Carmichael numbers are far more numerous than early researchers feared, though still vanishingly rare among all integers (246,683 exist below 10^16, and 1,401,644 below 10^18, per R. Pinch's tabulations), this is the concrete reason the field abandoned pure Fermat testing for anything security-critical: no fixed set of bases, and no amount of Fermat-test repetition, converges to certainty against an adversarially or unluckily chosen composite. This single gap -- a test that can be permanently and silently wrong -- is exactly what motivated the stronger randomized tests (Solovay-Strassen, Miller-Rabin) covered next, which are constructed so that no composite number, Carmichael or otherwise, can fool more than a bounded fraction of possible witnesses.

lessons.workedExample: A student's program flags 561 as 'probably prime' after testing bases 2, 7, and 13, each returning a^560 = 1 mod 561. Suspicious, they factor 561 = 3 x 11 x 17 and apply Korselt's criterion: 560 = 2^4 x 5 x 7; is (3-1)=2 a divisor of 560? Yes. Is (11-1)=10? Yes. Is (17-1)=16? Yes. All three hold, confirming 561 is a genuine Carmichael number -- no choice of coprime base will ever produce a Fermat witness. The lesson: adding more random bases does not fix a Fermat-test failure mode that is structural, not statistical, for this class of composite.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen 'we used the Fermat test to check primality' before will immediately ask what happens on a Carmichael number like 561, because it is the textbook counterexample. A student who can name Korselt's criterion, produce 561 = 3x11x17 from memory, and explain that Alford-Granville-Pomerance proved infinitely many exist (so the failure can't be patched by excluding known bad cases) demonstrates they understand WHY the field moved past Fermat entirely, rather than just having heard the word 'pseudoprime.'

questions.prompt: What makes a Carmichael number different from an ordinary Fermat pseudoprime?

options.text: It is prime, just very large
It fools the Fermat test for every base coprime to it, not just one or a few
It has only one prime factor
It fails the Fermat test for all bases

explanations.a: A Carmichael number is composite by definition -- it just behaves like a prime under the Fermat test.
explanations.b: Correct -- an ordinary pseudoprime fools one particular base; a Carmichael number satisfies a^(n-1)=1 mod n for every base coprime to n, so trying more random bases never catches it.
explanations.c: Carmichael numbers are squarefree with at least three distinct prime factors (per Korselt's criterion), not a single factor.
explanations.d: The opposite is true -- it passes (returns 1) for every coprime base, which is exactly the problem.

questions.prompt: What did Alford, Granville, and Pomerance prove in 1994 that reshaped how the field treats the Fermat test?

options.text: That no Carmichael numbers exist above 10^18
That there are infinitely many Carmichael numbers
That the Fermat test runs in polynomial time
That Miller-Rabin has a 1/2 error rate

explanations.a: The opposite -- Carmichael numbers grow denser than once feared; 246,683 exist below 10^16, and 1,401,644 below 10^18.
explanations.b: Correct -- their Annals of Mathematics paper proved infinitely many Carmichael numbers exist, showing the Fermat test's blind spot can never be eliminated by excluding finitely many known bad cases.
explanations.c: The Fermat test's polynomial runtime was already known well before 1994; that was not their result.
explanations.d: That error bound belongs to Miller-Rabin (covered in the next lesson), not to this 1994 result about Carmichael numbers.

questions.prompt: Match each Carmichael number to its correct prime factorization.
questions.explanation: 561 = 3x11x17 is the smallest Carmichael number; 1105 = 5x13x17 and 1729 = 7x13x19 (also the Hardy-Ramanujan taxicab number) are the next two, all discoverable via Korselt's criterion that each (p-1) must divide (n-1).

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of the primality-testing problem chronologically.

items.text: Korselt states the criterion characterizing what are later named Carmichael numbers (1899)
Carmichael publishes the number 561 and the class is named after him (1910)
Alford, Granville, and Pomerance prove infinitely many Carmichael numbers exist (1994)
Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena publish the deterministic polynomial-time AKS test (2002)

questions.explanation: Korselt's criterion (1899) predates Carmichael's named example 561 (1910); the infinitude proof (Alford-Granville-Pomerance, 1994) came decades later; AKS (2002) is the most recent milestone, giving a deterministic polynomial-time test at last.

lessons.label: Solovay-Strassen and Miller-Rabin

sections.heading: Solovay-Strassen: tightening the test with the Jacobi symbol
sections.body: Published by Robert Solovay and Volker Strassen in 1977, this test strengthens Fermat's check using Euler's criterion: for an odd prime n and any a coprime to n, a^((n-1)/2) = Jacobi(a, n) mod n, where Jacobi(a, n) is the Jacobi symbol (a generalization of the Legendre symbol to composite moduli, computable in O(log n) time via a reciprocity-law recursion without factoring n). The test computes both sides and rejects n as composite if they disagree, or if the result is 0. Crucially, at most half of the bases a in [1, n-1] can satisfy the Euler congruence for a composite n -- this is a theorem, not an empirical observation -- so a single round has error probability at most 1/2. Running k independent rounds with random bases drives the false-positive probability down to at most 2^-k, giving a genuinely tunable confidence level, unlike Fermat's test, which Carmichael numbers can defeat regardless of k.

sections.heading: Miller-Rabin: exploiting square roots of unity
sections.body: Gary Miller proposed a deterministic version in 1976 (correct assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, GRH); Michael Rabin turned it into an unconditional randomized test in 1980. Write n-1 = 2^s * d with d odd. For a random base a, compute x0 = a^d mod n, then repeatedly square: x0, x1=x0^2, ..., x_s. If n is prime, then either x0 = 1, or some x_i = n-1 (i.e., -1 mod n) before reaching x_s -- this follows because the only square roots of 1 mod a prime are +1 and -1. If neither condition holds, n is definitely composite and a is called a witness.
