The key theorem (Rabin 1980, tightened by Monier the same year) is that at most 1/4 of the bases in [1, n-1] can be 'strong liars' for a composite n -- a bound roughly HALF as forgiving as Solovay-Strassen's 1/2, and in practice the empirical failure rate for random composites is far smaller than 1/4, often near 4^-k or better. This is why essentially every production primality check (OpenSSL, GMP, Python's sympy) uses Miller-Rabin, not Solovay-Strassen.

sections.heading: Strong pseudoprimes, GRH determinism, and AKS as the road not taken
sections.body: A composite that survives a Miller-Rabin round for base a is a strong pseudoprime to base a; these are strictly rarer than Fermat or Euler pseudoprimes to the same base, and no composite is a strong pseudoprime to more than 1/4 of all possible bases. Under GRH, testing all bases a up to a constant times (ln n)^2 suffices to prove primality DETERMINISTICALLY (Miller's 1976 result); Bach later showed in 1990 that the constant can be taken to be 2, giving the sharp bound 2(ln n)^2 -- but this is conditional on an unproven conjecture. The unconditional deterministic answer came from Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal, and Nitin Saxena's 2002 AKS algorithm ('PRIMES is in P'), which proves primality in provably polynomial time -- O(log^12 n) in the original 2002 paper, later tightened to O(log^(7.5) n) via subsequent sieve-theory refinements -- using no randomness and no unproven hypotheses. AKS was a landmark theoretical result -- it settled a decades-open question about complexity class membership -- but its polynomial-time exponent makes it dramatically slower in practice than Miller-Rabin at cryptographic sizes, which is why virtually nobody uses AKS in deployed software; randomized testing with a large enough number of rounds gives an error rate lower than the chance of a hardware bit-flip, at a fraction of the cost.

lessons.workedExample: Test n = 221 with Miller-Rabin, base a = 174. First, n-1 = 220 = 2^2 x 55, so s=2, d=55. Compute x0 = 174^55 mod 221 = 47. Since 47 is not 1 and not 220, square it: x1 = 47^2 mod 221 = 220 = n-1. Because we hit n-1 before running out of squarings, base 174 does NOT witness compositeness -- 221 passes this round (it is in fact composite, 221 = 13 x 17, and a different base, e.g. a=137, does expose it: 137^55 mod 221 = 188, then 188^2 mod 221 = 205, neither 1 nor 220, so 137 is a witness). This illustrates the probabilistic core of the method: any single base can be a 'strong liar,' but the 1/4 bound guarantees that across random bases, composites get caught quickly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson wants to see that a student understands error bounds are not marketing language but proven theorems -- Solovay-Strassen's 1/2 versus Miller-Rabin's 1/4 per round is a factual claim with a citation (Rabin 1980, Monier 1980), not folklore. A strong answer also correctly places AKS: judges sometimes ask 'so why don't we just use the deterministic test,' and the right answer is that AKS's polynomial time bound, while a landmark of complexity theory, has a much larger practical exponent, so randomized testing remains the industry standard by a wide margin.

questions.prompt: What is the proven per-round error bound for the Miller-Rabin test on a composite input, and how does it compare to Solovay-Strassen?

options.text: 1/4 for Miller-Rabin, twice as tight as Solovay-Strassen's 1/2
1/2 for both tests, identical bounds
1/4 for Solovay-Strassen, 1/2 for Miller-Rabin
0 for Miller-Rabin -- it never errs

explanations.a: Correct -- Rabin (1980) and Monier (1980) proved at most 1/4 of bases are strong liars for a composite n, versus at most 1/2 for Solovay-Strassen's Euler-liars.
explanations.b: The two tests have different bounds; Miller-Rabin's is strictly tighter (1/4 vs 1/2), which is why it largely replaced Solovay-Strassen in practice.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual bounds -- Solovay-Strassen is the 1/2 test, Miller-Rabin is the 1/4 test.
explanations.d: Miller-Rabin is still probabilistic and unconditional; it can err with probability up to 1/4 per round, though running multiple rounds drives this down exponentially.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does Miller's 1976 version of the test become a DETERMINISTIC primality test?

options.text: If you test only the base a=2
If the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) is assumed and all bases up to 2(ln n)^2 are tested
It is always deterministic regardless of assumptions
If n is odd

explanations.a: Testing a single fixed base never gives a deterministic guarantee -- specific composites can be strong pseudoprimes to base 2.
explanations.b: Correct -- Miller (1976) showed that assuming GRH, testing every base up to a constant times (ln n)^2 suffices to prove primality with certainty, and Bach (1990) pinned that constant down to 2, giving the sharp bound 2(ln n)^2; this is conditional on an unproven conjecture.
explanations.c: Without GRH, Miller-Rabin remains probabilistic; Rabin's 1980 contribution was making it useful UNCONDITIONALLY, but only in a randomized (not deterministic) sense.
explanations.d: Oddness of n is a precondition for the n-1 = 2^s*d decomposition, not the condition that makes the test deterministic.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Miller-Rabin test as actually executed on an input n with base a.

items.text: Write n - 1 = 2^s * d with d odd
Compute x0 = a^d mod n
Repeatedly square to get x1, x2, ..., x_(s-1), checking for a hit of n-1
If x0 is not 1 and no square ever equals n-1, declare n composite (a is a witness)

questions.explanation: The algorithm first decomposes n-1 into 2^s*d, computes the base value a^d mod n, squares repeatedly looking for -1 (n-1) mod n, and only concludes 'composite' if neither the initial value is 1 nor any squaring hits n-1.

questions.prompt: Match each primality-testing approach to its defining property.

right.text: Uses the Jacobi symbol and Euler's criterion; error <= 1/2 per round
Deterministic, unconditional, polynomial time, but slower in practice
Uses the n-1=2^s*d decomposition; error <= 1/4 per round

questions.explanation: Solovay-Strassen relies on the Jacobi symbol / Euler criterion with a 1/2 error bound; Miller-Rabin relies on the 2^s*d decomposition and square-root-of-unity argument with a tighter 1/4 bound; AKS (Agrawal-Kayal-Saxena, 2002) is unconditionally deterministic and polynomial-time but practically slower than either randomized test.

lessons.label: Random Shuffling and Fisher-Yates

sections.heading: The algorithm and why it is provably uniform
sections.body: The Fisher-Yates shuffle (published by Ronald Fisher and Frank Yates in 1938 as a manual card/dice procedure, and turned into the now-standard in-place computer algorithm by Richard Durstenfeld in 1964, with Donald Knuth popularizing it in The Art of Computer Programming) rearranges an array of n elements into a uniformly random permutation in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The procedure: for i from n-1 down to 1, pick a uniformly random index j with 0 <= j <= i (inclusive of i itself), and swap a[i] with a[j]. The proof of uniformity is a clean induction: at step i, the element placed into position i is chosen uniformly from the i+1 remaining unplaced elements, independent of earlier choices, so by induction every one of the n! orderings is reachable via exactly one sequence of choices and each sequence has the same probability product 1/n * 1/(n-1) * ... * 1/1 = 1/n!. This is the exact reason Fisher-Yates is the reference algorithm: it is not merely 'good enough,' it is a bijection between the n! equally likely choice-sequences and the n! permutations.

sections.heading: Bug 1: the off-by-one range error
sections.body: The single most common implementation bug is picking j from the WHOLE array (0 to n-1) at every step instead of restricting it to the shrinking range (0 to i). This 'naive shuffle' still runs in O(n) and still looks random on casual inspection, but it is provably biased: for n elements the n-1 draws produce n^(n-1) equally likely raw outcomes, which cannot divide evenly into n! permutations for n > 2 (a pigeonhole argument -- e.g. for n=3, 3^2=9 outcomes cannot split evenly across 3!=6 permutations). Brute-forcing this n=3 case shows three of the six permutations occur 2/9 of the time and the other three occur 1/9 of the time (3*(2/9) + 3*(1/9) = 1, as a valid distribution must), versus the uniform 1/6 (approximately 16.7%) each should get. (Jeff Atwood's widely cited 2007 'Coding Horror' post 'The Danger of Naivete' analyzes a related but distinct variant that runs a full n-iteration loop with unrestricted range at every step, producing n^n outcomes.) The skew seems small per-permutation but compounds into detectable statistical bias at scale -- exactly the kind of flaw that has shown up in production shuffle code for games and card applications.

sections.heading: Bug 2: modulo bias from rand() % k
sections.body: A second, independent bug appears when generating the random index itself. If a source produces uniform integers in [0, M-1] (e.g., C's rand() with RAND_MAX = 32767, giving M = 32768 possible values) and the code computes rand() % k to get a value in [0, k-1], the result is uniform ONLY if k evenly divides M. When it does not, the low residues get one extra chance. Concretely, for M = 32768 and k = 10: 32768 = 3276*10 + 8, so residues 0 through 7 each occur 3277 times out of 32768 while residues 8 and 9 occur only 3276 times -- a real, measurable, and adversarially detectable skew, not a rounding artifact. The fix is rejection sampling (redraw if the raw value falls in the leftover partial range) or a bias-free method like Java's Random.nextInt(k) or the C++ <random> library's uniform_int_distribution, both of which implement rejection internally so every output index is exactly uniform.

lessons.workedExample: A developer shuffles a 3-card deck [A, B, C] using the buggy 'whole-array' variant: for i from 2 down to 1, choose j uniformly from 0 to 2 (not 0 to i) and swap. Enumerating all 3x3=9 choice pairs (j for i=2, j for i=1) and tracing the resulting permutations shows some final orders appear more often than others -- across all 3^2=9 outcomes, three permutations occur at 2/9 (about 22.2%) and three occur at 1/9 (about 11.1%), instead of the correct uniform 1/6 (about 16.7%) each. A card-counting opponent who sees enough shuffles from this code could statistically detect which orderings are favored -- exactly the failure mode that makes this bug a genuine security issue in gambling and card-game software, not just a cosmetic one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know your shuffle is actually random' is testing whether the student can distinguish 'runs without crashing and looks fine' from 'provably uniform.' The strong answer names Durstenfeld's in-place formulation, states the induction argument for why each of the n! permutations is equally likely, and can immediately diagnose the two classic failure modes -- wrong index range and modulo bias -- with a concrete counting argument (like the n^(n-1) vs n! pigeonhole) rather than a vague 'that could introduce bias.'

questions.prompt: In a correct Fisher-Yates shuffle, when processing index i (counting down from n-1 to 1), from what range should the swap partner j be drawn?

options.text: 0 to n-1, the whole array, every time
0 to i, inclusive, shrinking as i decreases
i to n-1 only
Always i-1

explanations.a: This is exactly the classic bug -- drawing from the whole array every time produces n^(n-1) outcomes that cannot map evenly onto n! permutations, causing measurable bias.
explanations.b: Correct -- restricting j to [0, i] as i shrinks is what makes each step choose uniformly among the still-unplaced elements, giving the clean induction proof of uniformity.
explanations.c: This range excludes already-placed elements from being revisited but is not the standard formulation and does not by itself establish the correct probability structure.
explanations.d: A fixed non-random partner would not shuffle at all; the whole point is a RANDOM j within the correct range.

questions.prompt: For M = 32768 possible raw random values and k = 10 buckets, why does rand() % k introduce bias?

options.text: Because 32768 is not divisible by 10, so residues 0-7 occur 3277 times and residues 8-9 occur only 3276 times
Because modulo operations are inherently non-deterministic
Because rand() itself is not uniform in [0, 32767]
There is no bias as long as k is even

explanations.a: Correct -- 32768 = 3276*10 + 8, so the first 8 residue classes get one extra representative among the 32768 raw values, a small but real and detectable skew.
explanations.b: Modulo is a fully deterministic arithmetic operation; the bias comes from uneven division of the range, not from any non-determinism.
explanations.c: The bias analysis assumes rand() IS uniform over [0, 32767]; the problem is entirely in how the remainder operation maps that uniform range onto k unevenly-sized buckets.
explanations.d: Evenness of k does not prevent bias; what matters is whether k evenly divides M (32768), and most values of k will not.

questions.prompt: Match each shuffle-implementation bug to its correct root cause.

right.text: j drawn from the whole array instead of the shrinking [0,i] range, producing n^(n-1) outcomes that can't map evenly to n! permutations
rand() % k is non-uniform when k does not evenly divide the generator's output range
j drawn uniformly from [0,i] at each step, giving a provable 1/n! probability for every permutation

questions.explanation: The off-by-one bug comes from sampling the wrong index range (whole array vs. shrinking suffix); modulo bias comes from an uneven division between the generator's range and the number of buckets; the correct algorithm's uniformity follows from the induction argument over the shrinking [0,i] range.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the history of the shuffle algorithm.

items.text: Fisher and Yates publish the manual shuffling procedure (1938)
Durstenfeld publishes the efficient in-place computer algorithm (1964)
Knuth popularizes the algorithm in The Art of Computer Programming
Atwood's 'Coding Horror' post analyzes the naive off-by-one shuffle bug (2007)

questions.explanation: Fisher and Yates (1938) described the original manual method; Durstenfeld (1964) gave the O(n) in-place computer version; Knuth's later Art of Computer Programming volumes cemented the standard name and presentation; Atwood's 2007 blog post is a much later, widely cited analysis of the common implementation bug.

lessons.label: Reservoir Sampling over Streams

sections.heading: The problem: sampling when you cannot store the stream
sections.body: Suppose items arrive one at a time -- a server's request log, a sensor feed, a query result too large for memory -- and you want a uniformly random sample of k items, but you do not know the total count n in advance and cannot afford to store all n items to sample from afterward. 'Algorithm R,' attributed to Alan Waterman and popularized in Donald Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming (Volume 2), solves this with a single pass and only O(k) memory: fill a 'reservoir' array with the first k items unconditionally. Then, for each subsequent item i (using 1-indexing, i from k+1 to n), generate a random integer r uniformly in [1, i]; if r <= k, overwrite reservoir slot r with item i, otherwise discard item i entirely. The algorithm never needs to know n ahead of time and never revisits an item once it has passed.

sections.heading: Proving every item lands with probability exactly k/n
sections.body: The elegance of Algorithm R is that this simple local rule produces a globally uniform sample. Item i (for i > k) is included in the reservoir at the moment it arrives with probability exactly k/i (it wins one of the i possible reservoir 'destinations' by drawing r <= k). For item i to survive to the end, it must then avoid eviction by every later item j (j from i+1 to n): each later arrival j replaces a uniformly random one of the k occupied slots with probability k/j, so item i survives that round with probability 1 - k/j * (1/k) = 1 - 1/j = (j-1)/j. Multiplying the survival probabilities across all later arrivals telescopes: the product of (j-1)/j for j from i+1 to n equals i/n (each numerator cancels the previous denominator). So item i's final inclusion probability is (k/i) * (i/n) = k/n -- identical for every item regardless of when it arrived, exactly the uniform k-out-of-n sample the algorithm promises, using only O(k) memory and one pass, with no knowledge of n required in advance.

sections.heading: Weighted reservoir sampling: the A-Res algorithm
sections.body: Algorithm R assumes every stream item is equally likely to be chosen. When items carry weights (e.g., sampling proportional to file size, click count, or importance score), Pavlos Efraimidis and Paul Spirakis's 2006 A-Res algorithm ('Weighted random sampling with a reservoir,' Information Processing Letters, 97(5), 2006) generalizes it: for each item i with weight w_i, draw u_i uniformly from (0,1) and compute a key k_i = u_i^(1/w_i). Maintain the k items with the largest keys seen so far (a min-heap of size k does this in one pass, discarding the smallest key whenever a bigger one arrives). This produces a sample where each item's selection probability is proportional to its weight, still in a single streaming pass with O(k) memory -- the same operational profile as Algorithm R, generalized to non-uniform importance. This is the technique behind sampling a weighted subset of log lines, ad impressions, or sensor readings where some records matter statistically more than others.

lessons.workedExample: A sensor logs one reading per second into a reservoir of size k=2 with no known end time. Readings arrive in order: A, B, C, D. Steps: (1) reservoir = [A, B] after the first two items, unconditionally. (2) Item C arrives as the 3rd item; draw r uniformly in [1,3]. If r=1, C replaces slot 1 (reservoir becomes [C,B]); if r=2, C replaces slot 2 ([A,C]); if r=3, C is discarded ([A,B] unchanged) -- so C is kept with probability 2/3, matching k/i = 2/3. (3) Item D arrives 4th; draw r in [1,4]; D is kept only if r is 1 or 2, i.e. probability 2/4 = 1/2 = k/i. Tracing all branches shows each of A, B, C, D ends up in the final 2-slot reservoir with exactly the same probability, 2/4 = 1/2 -- confirmed by the k/n formula (k=2, n=4) despite A and B having a two-step 'head start' and C and D having only one or zero survival rounds to pass.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this lesson wants the derivation, not just the recipe: can the student explain WHY an item that arrived first (and so has been 'at risk' of eviction the longest) still ends up with the same final probability as an item that just arrived? The strong answer walks through the telescoping product -- (k/i) times the chain of survival probabilities collapsing to i/n -- rather than asserting uniformity as a given. A judge may also probe whether the student knows this generalizes to weighted sampling (A-Res), which shows they understand reservoir sampling as a technique, not a memorized single algorithm.

questions.prompt: In Algorithm R, what is the probability that the i-th arriving item (for i > k) is placed into the reservoir at the moment it arrives?

options.text: k/i
i/n

explanations.a: 1/n is the item's FINAL probability of surviving to the end when k=1, not its probability of being placed at the moment it arrives for general k.
explanations.b: Correct -- a random integer r is drawn in [1,i], and the item is placed only if r falls in the k reservoir slots, giving probability k/i at arrival time.
explanations.c: 1/k would be the chance of landing in one SPECIFIC slot given it is placed at all, not the chance of being placed in the first place.
explanations.d: i/n is not a quantity used in the per-arrival step; the final overall inclusion probability for any item, after all rounds, is k/n, not i/n.

questions.prompt: What is the key mathematical step that shows every item ends up in the reservoir with the SAME final probability, k/n, regardless of arrival order?

options.text: Each item's survival probabilities against later arrivals telescope: the product of (j-1)/j for j from i+1 to n collapses to i/n
Later items are simply ignored once the reservoir is full
The reservoir is re-shuffled after every arrival
Random number generators guarantee uniform output regardless of the algorithm around them

explanations.a: Correct -- multiplying (1 - 1/j) = (j-1)/j across all later arrivals j from i+1 to n telescopes to i/n, which combined with the k/i placement probability gives exactly k/n.
explanations.b: This is false and would break correctness -- later items DO have a chance (k/j) to evict a reservoir occupant even after the reservoir is 'full.'
explanations.c: There is no re-shuffling step in Algorithm R; only a single random slot is chosen for potential replacement per arrival.
explanations.d: A uniform RNG is necessary but not sufficient by itself; it is the specific telescoping structure of the algorithm's replacement probabilities that produces the uniform k/n result.

questions.prompt: Match each reservoir-sampling concept to its correct description.

left.text: Final inclusion probability of any stream item

right.text: Unweighted single-pass reservoir sampling using a uniform random replacement index
Weighted variant using keys u_i^(1/w_i) and a min-heap of size k
k/n, identical for every item regardless of arrival position

questions.explanation: Algorithm R is the classic unweighted one-pass method; A-Res generalizes it to weighted sampling using per-item keys and a min-heap; and the proven final inclusion probability for any item under Algorithm R is uniformly k/n.

questions.prompt: Order the steps Algorithm R performs when the (k+1)-th and later items arrive.

items.text: Fill the reservoir unconditionally with the first k items
For item i > k, draw a random integer r uniformly in [1, i]
If r <= k, overwrite reservoir slot r with item i
If r > k, discard item i and move to the next arrival

questions.explanation: The reservoir is seeded with the first k items, then each later arrival draws a random index over the full range seen so far, is inserted only if that index falls within the reservoir's k slots, and is otherwise dropped.

lessons.label: Universal and Pairwise-Independent Hashing

sections.heading: The 1979 definition: a guarantee over the hash function, not the keys
sections.body: J. Lawrence Carter and Mark Wegman introduced universal hashing in their 1979 paper 'Universal Classes of Hash Functions,' addressing a structural weakness of any single fixed hash function: for any deterministic h, some adversary can always find a set of keys that all collide under h, since h's behavior is fully determined once you know its code. Carter and Wegman's fix was to stop fixing h. A family H of hash functions mapping a universe U to {0, ..., m-1} is called UNIVERSAL if, for any two distinct keys x != y (fixed in advance, before h is chosen), the probability over a uniformly random h drawn from H that h(x) = h(y) is at most 1/m. The critical shift in perspective: the randomness is over the CHOICE OF FUNCTION, drawn fresh (typically at program start) from a family, not over the input keys. An adversary who knows the family H but not the specific random seed cannot force a collision, because they cannot predict which member of H will be used.

sections.heading: A concrete construction: the affine family mod a prime
sections.body: The canonical universal family, given in Carter-Wegman's original paper, works over integer keys: pick a prime p larger than the universe size, then for a in {1, ..., p-1} and b in {0, ..., p-1}, define h_{a,b}(x) = ((a*x + b) mod p) mod m. There are p(p-1) such functions, and choosing a, b uniformly at random at setup time yields a universal family: for any fixed x != y, the number of (a,b) pairs causing a collision is at most p * (ceil(p/m) - 1), which works out to a collision probability of (ceil(p/m)-1)/(p-1), always at most 1/m (since ceil(p/m) <= (p+m-1)/m implies ceil(p/m)-1 <= (p-1)/m) -- a purely algebraic fact about linear functions modulo a prime, provable by noting that as a and b range over their domains, (a*x+b mod p) takes every value in {0,...,p-1} equally often for x != y jointly, so partitioning those p values into m residue classes of size floor(p/m) or ceil(p/m) and bounding colliding ordered pairs within each class yields the stated collision count.

sections.heading: Why this defeats adversarial key choice, and what it buys in practice
sections.body: The practical payoff is a provable bound on expected performance REGARDLESS of what keys are inserted, as long as the seed is kept secret and re-randomized per run. For a hash table with n keys and m buckets under a universal family, the expected length of any chain (the expected number of OTHER keys colliding into the same bucket as a given key) is at most alpha = n/m, so total expected chain length including the key itself is 1 + alpha -- the same O(1) amortized behavior assumed for 'random enough' hashing, now with an actual proof rather than a hope. This matters because a hash table's real-world attacker does not need to know your source code's exact hash constants to exploit a FIXED hash function -- they only need to know the algorithm family (e.g., 'this uses hash function X'), and can precompute a colliding key set offline. Randomizing which member of the family is used per-process (choosing fresh a, b, or an unpredictable seed) closes exactly this hole, which is why this idea underlies both universal hashing's original data-structure motivation and the security property covered in the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: Take p = 11 (prime), m = 3 buckets, and the family h_{a,b}(x) = ((a*x+b) mod 11) mod 3. Fix two distinct keys x=2, y=5. If the random seed happens to be a=1, b=0: h(2) = (2 mod 11) mod 3 = 2, and h(5) = (5 mod 11) mod 3 = 2 -- a collision for this particular seed. But if instead a=3, b=1: h(2) = (7 mod 11) mod 3 = 1, and h(5) = (16 mod 11) mod 3 = 5 mod 3 = 2 -- no collision. Averaging over all valid (a,b) pairs (a in 1..10, b in 0..10, giving 110 total functions), the fraction of seeds for which x=2 and y=5 collide is provably at most 1/3 = 1/m, exactly the universal-hashing guarantee -- no matter which two DISTINCT keys an adversary picks first, the collision chance stays bounded once a random seed is drawn afterward.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing hash-based data structures often ask 'but couldn't someone just pick keys that all collide?' -- this is precisely the question universal hashing answers, and a strong response distinguishes the ORDER of quantifiers: keys are fixed first, then a random function is drawn, so no adversary choosing keys in advance can predict the collision pattern. A student who can state the 1/m bound, sketch the h_{a,b}(x) construction, and explain that the guarantee is over the SEED rather than over an assumed random distribution of keys demonstrates real understanding rather than a memorized buzzword.

questions.prompt: In the definition of a universal hash family, what exactly is the randomness taken over?

options.text: The distribution of the input keys
The choice of hash function h drawn from the family H, with the keys fixed in advance
The order in which keys are inserted
The size of the hash table m

explanations.a: Universal hashing makes no assumption about how keys are distributed; keys can be entirely adversarial and the guarantee still holds.
explanations.b: Correct -- the probability bound Pr[h(x)=h(y)] <= 1/m is taken over a uniformly random choice of h from H, for any FIXED pair of distinct keys x, y chosen before h is selected.
explanations.c: Insertion order affects which chains form but is not the source of randomness in the universality guarantee itself.
explanations.d: m is a fixed parameter (the number of buckets), not a random variable in the definition.

questions.prompt: Why can't an adversary who knows the family H (e.g., h_{a,b}(x) = ((a*x+b) mod p) mod m) defeat a universal hash table the way they could defeat a single fixed hash function?

options.text: Because the family H is kept completely secret and never published
Because the specific (a,b) seed used at runtime is chosen randomly and independently of the keys the adversary picks
Because m is always chosen to be prime
Because universal hash functions never produce collisions

explanations.a: Carter and Wegman's construction is published and public; security does not rely on hiding the family, only the specific random seed instance.
explanations.b: Correct -- the adversary can know the whole family H but still cannot predict which specific member (a,b) will be used, since that is drawn randomly at runtime after (or independent of) the adversary's key choice.
explanations.c: p, not m, is required to be prime in the standard construction; m can be any table size.
explanations.d: Collisions still occur with probability up to 1/m; the guarantee bounds the collision rate, it does not eliminate collisions.

questions.prompt: Match each universal-hashing concept to its correct value or role.

left.text: Expected chain length with load factor alpha=n/m

right.text: Pr[h(x)=h(y)] <= 1/m for fixed x != y over random h
h_{a,b}(x) = ((a*x+b) mod p) mod m, p prime > universe size
1 + alpha

questions.explanation: Universality is defined by the 1/m collision bound over a random h; Carter and Wegman's canonical family uses the affine mod-p-then-mod-m construction; the resulting expected total chain length (including the key itself) under this family is 1+alpha where alpha is the load factor n/m.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps in reasoning about why universal hashing resists adversarial key selection.

items.text: An adversary selects two distinct keys x and y, with full knowledge of the family H
The system independently draws a random seed (a,b), unknown to the adversary
The resulting function h_{a,b} is applied to x and y
The probability of h(x)=h(y), averaged over the random seed, is bounded by 1/m regardless of which x,y the adversary chose

questions.explanation: The order of operations matters for the security argument: keys are chosen first (possibly adversarially), then the random function is drawn independently, then it is applied, and only then can we bound the collision probability at 1/m -- the adversary never gets to see the seed before committing to their keys.

lessons.label: Hash Flooding: Randomization as a Security Property

sections.heading: From O(1) to O(n^2): the algorithmic complexity attack
sections.body: A hash table's famous O(1) average insert time is an AVERAGE, not a guarantee -- it holds only when keys spread roughly evenly across buckets. If an attacker can choose keys that all hash to the SAME bucket, every insert degrades to O(chain length), and inserting n such keys costs O(1+2+...+n) = O(n^2) total instead of O(n). Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach first formalized this as a practical denial-of-service vector in their 2003 USENIX Security paper 'Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks,' demonstrating it against Perl's hash tables and other systems of the era. The core requirement for the attack is simply that the hash function be FIXED and known (or reverse-engineerable) ahead of time, so an attacker can precompute a large batch of colliding keys offline and submit them all at once.

sections.heading: 28C3, 2011: the attack goes mainstream against the modern web
sections.body: The vulnerability re-entered the spotlight dramatically at the 28th Chaos Communication Congress (28C3) in December 2011, when researchers Alexander Klink and Julian Waelde presented 'Effective Denial of Service attacks against web application platforms.' They showed that most popular web platforms parsed incoming HTTP POST form data directly into a hash table (PHP's $_POST superglobal, Java's HashMap-backed form parsers, Python, Ruby, and ASP.NET's request-parameter collections all did this), and all of them used hash functions with predictable, non-randomized collision patterns. A single crafted POST body containing tens of thousands of colliding keys could pin a web server's CPU at 100% for a long stretch -- ASP.NET was hit especially hard, prompting Microsoft to issue an out-of-band, unscheduled security patch (MS11-100) within days, an unusually urgent response reflecting that a single modest HTTP request could take a server offline.

sections.heading: SipHash: the randomized-keyed fix that became a language default
sections.body: The fix the field converged on is exactly the randomization principle from the previous lesson, applied as a security property rather than only a performance one: hash strings with a function keyed by a secret, per-process random seed, so an attacker cannot precompute colliding keys without knowing the seed. Jean-Philippe Aumasson and Daniel J. Bernstein designed SipHash for this purpose, publishing it in 2012 as 'SipHash: a fast short-input PRF' -- a keyed pseudorandom function tuned to be fast enough for hash-table use (unlike a full cryptographic hash such as SHA-256) while remaining unpredictable to an attacker who does not know the key. SipHash became the default hash function for strings in Python starting with Python 3.4 (specified in PEP 456, 2013-2014) and is the default hasher backing Rust's standard HashMap. The lesson generalizes the one before it: universal hashing was originally motivated by average-case data-structure performance, but the SAME mathematical property -- an unpredictable function drawn from a keyed family -- is precisely what closes a real-world, actively exploited denial-of-service vulnerability class.

lessons.workedExample: Before the fix, an attacker studying an open-source web framework's source code finds it uses an unkeyed hash function h(s) for its request-parameter table. Because h is fixed and public, the attacker can compute offline, on their own machine, a list of 65,536 distinct strings that all hash to the same bucket under h -- a purely mechanical search exploiting h's known internals, unrelated to any password or secret. Submitting a single POST request with those 65,536 form fields forces the server's parser to perform 65,536 inserts into one degenerate bucket, costing roughly 65,536^2 / 2 comparisons -- billions of operations -- pinning a CPU core for tens of seconds to minutes from one request a few hundred kilobytes in size. After adopting SipHash with a random per-process key generated at startup, the same precomputed collision list hashes to essentially random, spread-out buckets, because the attacker cannot predict the runtime key -- the attack script that worked offline produces no effect at all against the patched server.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing security literacy will want the causal chain spelled out precisely: WHY does a fixed hash function let an attacker precompute collisions (because the function's behavior is fully determined once known), and WHY does keyed randomization fix it (because the attacker cannot know the runtime key when precomputing offline). Naming Crosby-Wallach (2003) for the original algorithmic-complexity-attack framing, Klink-Waelde's 28C3 2011 talk for the concrete multi-platform exploit, and SipHash (Aumasson-Bernstein 2012) as the adopted fix shows the student understands this as a real, dated engineering response to a real incident, not an abstract textbook worry.

questions.prompt: What is the precondition that makes a hash-flooding denial-of-service attack possible against a hash table?

options.text: The table must use open addressing rather than chaining
The hash function is fixed and known (or reverse-engineerable) ahead of time, letting an attacker precompute colliding keys
The server must be running out of disk space
The table must contain fewer than 100 entries

explanations.a: Both chaining and open-addressing hash tables can be driven to worst-case performance by engineered collisions; the storage scheme is not the root precondition.
explanations.b: Correct -- if the hash function's mapping from keys to buckets is fixed and knowable, an attacker can compute a large batch of colliding keys entirely offline before ever contacting the server.
explanations.c: Disk space is irrelevant; this is a CPU-time attack driven by pathological in-memory hash-table chain lengths.
explanations.d: The attack scales WORSE with more entries (O(n^2)), so it is more effective, not only possible, at larger n; small tables are not immune, just less impactful.

questions.prompt: What made the December 2011 28C3 disclosure by Klink and Waelde especially severe compared to the 2003 Crosby-Wallach result?

options.text: It showed the attack worked against nothing in particular
It demonstrated the attack against mainstream web platforms (PHP, Java, Python, Ruby, ASP.NET) via ordinary POST request parsing, prompting an emergency Microsoft patch
It was purely theoretical with no working exploit
It only affected hash functions used in cryptographic signatures

explanations.a: The disclosure was highly specific, naming exact platforms and the exact request-parsing code path that was vulnerable.
explanations.b: Correct -- Klink and Waelde showed practical exploits against PHP, Java, Python, Ruby, and ASP.NET, with ASP.NET's severity prompting Microsoft's out-of-band patch MS11-100.
explanations.c: It was demonstrated with working proof-of-concept exploits against real, deployed platforms, not left theoretical.
explanations.d: The vulnerable hash functions were ordinary hash-table hash functions used for data structures, unrelated to cryptographic signature schemes.

questions.prompt: Match each milestone to its correct date and contribution.

right.text: 2003 -- formalized algorithmic complexity attacks against hash tables
2011 -- 28C3 talk demonstrating hash flooding against major web platforms
2012 -- published SipHash as the keyed-PRF fix

questions.explanation: Crosby and Wallach's 2003 USENIX paper introduced algorithmic complexity attacks; Klink and Waelde's December 2011 28C3 talk demonstrated the attack against mainstream web platforms; Aumasson and Bernstein published SipHash in 2012 as the adopted, now widely deployed fix.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the hash-flooding story chronologically.

items.text: Crosby and Wallach formalize algorithmic complexity attacks against hash tables (2003)
Klink and Waelde demonstrate practical hash-flooding DoS against major web platforms at 28C3 (December 2011)
Microsoft issues the out-of-band patch MS11-100 for ASP.NET
Python adopts SipHash as its default string hash (PEP 456, Python 3.4)

questions.explanation: The theoretical foundation (2003) came first, followed by the concrete multi-platform demonstration at 28C3 (Dec 2011), the urgent Microsoft patch that followed within days of that disclosure, and finally the broader adoption of SipHash as a language-level default a couple of years later.

lessons.label: Bloom Filters and the False-Positive Budget

sections.heading: Bloom's 1970 design: trading certainty for space
sections.body: Burton Howard Bloom introduced the structure in his 1970 Communications of the ACM paper 'Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors.' A Bloom filter is an m-bit array, initially all zeros, plus k independent hash functions each mapping an element to one of the m bit positions. To INSERT an element, compute all k hash positions and set each of those bits to 1. To QUERY whether an element might be present, compute the same k positions and check whether all k bits are set: if any is 0, the element is DEFINITELY not in the set (a true negative, guaranteed); if all k are 1, the element is PROBABLY in the set, but this could be a false positive caused by the coincidental union of other elements' bits. This asymmetry -- zero false negatives, a tunable rate of false positives -- is the entire design trade: you accept a small, controllable error rate in one direction in exchange for a data structure that is often 10x or more smaller than storing the actual elements or a standard hash set.

sections.heading: The false-positive formula and the optimal number of hash functions
sections.body: After inserting n elements into an m-bit filter using k hash functions, the probability that a specific bit remains 0 is approximately e^(-kn/m) (each of the kn hash-and-set operations independently misses that bit with probability (1-1/m), and (1-1/m)^(kn) is approximated by e^(-kn/m) for large m). The false-positive rate -- the probability all k bits for a NEW, absent element happen to already be set -- is therefore approximately (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. Differentiating this expression with respect to k and setting the result to zero gives the optimal number of hash functions: k = (m/n) * ln(2), where ln(2) is approximately 0.693. Plugging this optimal k back into the false-positive formula and solving for the bits-per-element ratio needed to hit a target false-positive rate p shows m/n = -ln(p) / (ln 2)^2; for a target p = 1%, this works out to roughly 9.6 bits of filter space per inserted element -- far less than storing even a compact hash of each element, which is the entire appeal at scale.

sections.heading: The permanent asymmetry: no deletion, no false negatives, and where filters get deployed
sections.body: Because setting a bit to 1 for one element may be relied upon by another element's query, a plain Bloom filter cannot support deletion -- clearing a bit could silently reintroduce false negatives for other elements. The standard fix, the Counting Bloom Filter, replaces each bit with a small counter (often 4 bits) incremented on insert and decremented on delete, at proportionally higher memory cost. This structure has become a workhorse in systems that need a fast, space-cheap 'is this probably here' check before paying for an expensive lookup: Google Chrome's Safe Browsing feature historically used a Bloom filter to check URLs against a malware/phishing blocklist without downloading the full list; Bitcoin's Simplified Payment Verification (SPV) clients, formalized in BIP 37, use Bloom filters so a lightweight wallet can ask a full node for only the transactions it might care about without revealing exactly which addresses it is tracking; and storage engines including Apache Cassandra and Google's LevelDB attach a Bloom filter to each on-disk SSTable so a lookup for a key that is NOT in that file can be rejected in memory, entirely avoiding a disk read.

lessons.workedExample: A system needs to track n = 10,000 elements with a target false-positive rate of p = 1%. Using m/n = -ln(0.01) / (ln 2)^2 = 4.605 / 0.4805 = about 9.585 bits per element, the filter needs m = 10,000 x 9.585 = 95,850 bits, or roughly 12 kilobytes -- versus, say, 10,000 x 8 bytes = 80 kilobytes to store 8-byte hashes of each element directly, an over 6x space saving. The optimal number of hash functions is k = (m/n) x ln(2) = 9.585 x 0.693 = about 6.64, so the implementation rounds to k=7 hash functions. If instead the same 12 KB filter used only k=1 hash function, the false-positive rate would rise to roughly 1 - e^(-n/m) = 1 - e^(-0.1043) = about 9.9% -- nearly 10x worse than the 1% target for the identical amount of memory -- illustrating why the optimal-k formula, not an arbitrarily chosen k, is what makes the space budget actually deliver the promised error rate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing Bloom filters typically asks two things: what happens on a false positive (answer: you fall back to the real, authoritative check, e.g. a disk read or a full download, so correctness is preserved at a performance cost) and why you can't just delete an element (answer: bits are shared across elements, so clearing one could create a false NEGATIVE for another, which the design forbids -- the fix, if needed, is a Counting Bloom Filter with per-slot counters instead of single bits). A student who can also produce the ~9.6-bits-per-element number for a 1% target, rather than a vague 'Bloom filters are space-efficient,' shows they engaged with the actual trade-off curve Bloom derived in 1970.

questions.prompt: What can a Bloom filter guarantee about a negative query result (all-zeros found among the k checked bits)?

options.text: The element is definitely NOT in the set -- true negatives are guaranteed
The element is probably not in the set, but could be a false negative
The element was recently deleted
The filter needs to be resized

explanations.a: Correct -- if any of the k bits is 0, the element could never have set all k bits during insertion, so it is guaranteed to be absent; Bloom filters never produce false negatives.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual guarantee -- false POSITIVES are possible (finding all bits set for an absent element), but a negative result is always a true negative.
explanations.c: Standard Bloom filters do not support deletion at all; a negative result says nothing about deletion history.
explanations.d: A negative query result is a normal, correct outcome and implies nothing about needing to resize the structure.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many bits of filter space per inserted element are needed to achieve a 1% false-positive rate, using the optimal number of hash functions?

options.text: About 1 bit per element
About 9.6 bits per element
About 64 bits per element
About 100 bits per element

explanations.a: 1 bit per element is far too little -- it would produce a false-positive rate close to 100%, not 1%.
explanations.b: Correct -- solving m/n = -ln(p)/(ln 2)^2 for p=0.01 gives approximately 9.585, or about 9.6 bits per element, a widely cited figure for Bloom filter sizing.
explanations.c: 64 bits per element is roughly what a full 8-byte hash per element would cost, which is far more space than a Bloom filter needs for this error rate.
explanations.d: 100 bits per element would achieve a far lower false-positive rate than 1%, wasting space relative to the target.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world system to how it uses a Bloom filter.

right.text: Checks URLs against a malware/phishing blocklist without downloading the full list
Lets a lightweight wallet request only potentially relevant transactions from a full node
Rejects a key lookup in memory, avoiding an unnecessary disk read for a key not in that file

questions.explanation: Chrome historically used a Bloom filter for local blocklist checks; Bitcoin SPV clients under BIP 37 use one to filter relevant transactions without revealing the full watch-list; Cassandra and LevelDB attach one per SSTable to skip disk reads for absent keys.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in deriving the ~9.6-bits-per-element figure for a 1% target false-positive rate.

items.text: Write the false-positive rate as approximately (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k
Differentiate with respect to k and solve to find the optimal k = (m/n) ln 2
Substitute the optimal k back into the false-positive formula
Solve for m/n at the target p=0.01, yielding approximately 9.6 bits per element

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from the general false-positive-rate formula, optimizes over k to find the best number of hash functions for a given m/n, substitutes that optimum back in, and finally solves for the bits-per-element ratio needed to hit a specific target false-positive rate such as 1%.

lessons.label: One Run Is Not a Result

sections.heading: A random variable, not a number
sections.body: A deterministic algorithm run on a fixed input always produces the same runtime and the same output. A randomized algorithm — one whose internal coin flips (a random pivot in quicksort, a random tie-break in a greedy heuristic, a random restart point in local search) affect its behavior — produces a runtime and often a solution quality that are themselves random variables. Randomized quicksort on a fixed array of n=10,000 distinct elements might take 140,000 comparisons on one run and 210,000 on the next, purely because the pivot choices differed, even though the input never changed. Reporting '187,000 comparisons' as though it were a physical constant of the algorithm is a category error: it is one draw from a distribution, and a single draw tells you almost nothing about the shape, center, or spread of that distribution. The deliverable of any honest experiment with a randomized algorithm is therefore a distribution — described with a center, a spread, and ideally the full shape — never a lone figure quoted to false precision.

sections.heading: Median and IQR over mean and standard deviation, and why n >= 30
sections.body: Because many algorithmic runtime distributions are right-skewed (a few catastrophically slow runs pull the tail out far longer than they pull typical runs), the median and interquartile range (IQR: the gap between the 25th and 75th percentile) are usually more informative and more robust to outliers than the mean and standard deviation. A box plot displays exactly this: the box spans the IQR, the line inside marks the median, and whiskers or individual points show the outlying runs. Many empirical-algorithmics practitioners use roughly n >= 30 independent seeds as a rough starting point for stabilizing a median/IQR estimate on well-behaved distributions — below that, the sample median and IQR themselves bounce around from one batch of seeds to the next, so a comparison based on 5 or 10 seeds is barely more trustworthy than a comparison based on one. But as the next lesson shows, distributions with heavy tails may need far more seeds, or a different diagnostic entirely, before the summary can be trusted. Reporting the full histogram alongside the box plot matters too: a histogram of quicksort's comparison counts across many seeds on the same array reveals whether the distribution is a clean, narrow bell curve (the theoretical 1.39 n log2 n expectation for randomized quicksort, with tight concentration around it) or whether it has a long tail, multiple modes, or visible structure that a box plot's five-number summary would flatten out and hide.

sections.heading: Is the spread bigger than the claim?
sections.body: The single most common empirical-algorithmics mistake a science-fair judge will look for is a claim like 'my heuristic is faster' backed by two single numbers, one per algorithm, with no measure of run-to-run variability at all. The correct question to ask of any such claim is: how does the difference between the two algorithms' typical (median) performance compare to the spread (IQR, or the range across seeds) WITHIN each algorithm? If algorithm A's IQR is [120, 340] and algorithm B's IQR is [150, 310], the two boxes overlap heavily and the 'A beats B' claim is not supported by that data — the seed-to-seed noise is larger than the effect being claimed. Only when the boxes are cleanly separated (or, better, when a proper statistical test confirms the separation is unlikely under chance, a topic developed later in this unit) does a performance claim about randomized algorithms deserve to be believed.

lessons.workedExample: A student times randomized quicksort on the same 5,000-element random array across 40 independent seeds and records the comparison count each run. The 40 values range from about 61,000 to 118,000, with a median near 72,000 and an IQR of roughly [64,000, 80,000]. Plotting a histogram shows a roughly bell-shaped cluster around the median with a mild right tail — consistent with the exact expected comparison count C(n) = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n approx 71,000 for n=5,000 (notably lower than the cruder asymptotic estimate of 1.39 x 5,000 x log2(5,000) approx 85,400, which ignores the -4n correction term). If the student had reported only their FIRST run (say, 118,000, an upper-tail draw) as 'the' comparison count, they would have overstated the typical cost by nearly 65% purely from seed noise, with no indication that 39 other seeds told a very different story.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating any randomized-algorithms project will almost always ask 'how many trials did you run, and what did the variability look like?' A student who can produce a box plot or histogram across >= 30 seeds, and who can explicitly compare the spread to the size of the effect they are claiming, demonstrates they understand that randomized algorithms are measured, not computed, quantities. A student who reports one timing per algorithm invites the immediate follow-up 'was that just luck?' — and has no way to answer it.

questions.prompt: Why is reporting a single run's comparison count for randomized quicksort misleading?

options.text: Because quicksort is deterministic, so the number should always be identical anyway
Because the comparison count is a random variable across seeds, and one draw does not reveal its center or spread
Because comparison counts cannot be measured accurately in practice
Because only runtime in seconds matters, not comparison counts

explanations.a: Randomized quicksort's pivot choices are randomized, so runs on the identical input still vary from run to run — it is not deterministic in this sense.
explanations.b: Correct — the pivot sequence is random each run, making the comparison count a random variable; a single draw says nothing reliable about its typical value or its variability.
explanations.c: Comparison counts are straightforward to instrument and count exactly in code; measurement precision is not the issue here.
explanations.d: Comparison counts are a valid, hardware-independent proxy for cost; the issue is treating one draw as the whole distribution, not which metric is chosen.

questions.prompt: A student has box plots for algorithms A and B whose IQRs overlap substantially, with medians only slightly different. What should they conclude?

options.text: A is definitively faster than B because its median is lower
The observed median difference is not clearly distinguishable from seed-to-seed noise, since the spreads overlap heavily
B is definitively faster because box plots always favor the algorithm with the smaller box
The box plots are irrelevant and only the mean should be trusted

explanations.a: A lower median alone, with heavily overlapping spread, does not establish a real difference — the noise could easily explain it.
explanations.b: Correct — when within-algorithm spread is as large as or larger than the between-algorithm difference, the claim of superiority is not supported by the data as presented.
explanations.c: Box size (spread) does not by itself declare a winner; it is compared against the location difference, and a smaller box is not automatically better.
explanations.d: The mean is generally less robust than the median/IQR for skewed runtime distributions, so discarding the box plot in favor of the mean is backwards.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in a rigorous empirical comparison of two randomized algorithms on one input, from first to last.

items.text: Run each algorithm across >= 30 independent random seeds on the same input
Record the full set of runtime (or quality) measurements per algorithm
Compute median and IQR (and plot a histogram) for each algorithm's distribution
Compare the between-algorithm difference in medians to the within-algorithm spread before claiming one is better

questions.explanation: You must first generate enough independent runs (>= 30 seeds), then record all the raw measurements, then summarize each algorithm's distribution (median, IQR, histogram shape), and only then compare the size of the claimed effect to the measured spread before drawing a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each summary statistic or plot to what it tells you about a randomized algorithm's performance.

right.text: The typical (middle) value, robust to a few extreme outlier runs
The spread of the central 50% of runs, used to judge run-to-run variability
The complete shape of the distribution, revealing skew, multiple modes, or tails a five-number summary would hide

questions.explanation: The median gives a robust center, the IQR quantifies typical spread, and only the full histogram reveals shape details (skew, multi-modality, tail behavior) that summary statistics alone cannot show.

lessons.label: Heavy Tails and Why the Mean Lies

sections.heading: Gomes, Selman, and the discovery of heavy-tailed search
sections.body: In 1997, Carla Gomes, Bart Selman, and Nuno Crato (with related work by Gomes, Selman, McAloon, and Tretkoff) reported something surprising about randomized complete backtracking search algorithms on combinatorial problems like SAT and CSP scheduling: the runtime distributions were often HEAVY-TAILED, meaning the probability of an extremely long run decays much more slowly than an exponential or normal distribution would predict — closer to a power-law (Pareto-like) decay. Their 1997 CP conference paper 'Heavy-Tailed Distributions in Combinatorial Search' and the 1998 AAAI paper 'Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization' (with Selman and Kautz) established this empirically across quasigroup completion, graph coloring, and scheduling benchmarks. The practical shock is this: with a true heavy tail, the algorithm's runtime distribution can behave as though it has infinite or undefined mean and variance — not because any single run takes literally forever, but because occasional catastrophically long runs are common enough, and long enough, that the sample mean over any realistic number of trials never settles down. Add one more unlucky sample to your batch and the running average can jump substantially, even after hundreds of runs.

sections.heading: Reading the log-log survival plot
sections.body: The diagnostic tool for heavy tails is the SURVIVAL plot (also called the complementary CDF): plot P(runtime > t) against t on LOG-LOG axes (both axes logarithmically scaled). For a well-behaved (thin-tailed) distribution like an exponential, this survival curve on log-log axes bends sharply downward and drops off quickly. For a heavy (power-law-like) tail, the survival curve instead approaches a STRAIGHT LINE over a wide range of t on the log-log plot — because a power law P(runtime > t) approx c * t^(-alpha) becomes log(P) approx log(c) - alpha*log(t), which is linear in log(t). Recognizing that straight-line signature on a log-log survival plot is the single clearest visual test for heavy-tailed behavior; a downward-curving (concave) line instead signals a thin tail where the sample mean is trustworthy. The slope alpha of that line also tells you how heavy the tail is: smaller alpha (shallower slope) means an even heavier tail and even less-well-behaved sample statistics.

sections.heading: The fix the plot itself points to: randomized rapid restarts
sections.body: Gomes and Selman's key applied insight was that heavy-tailed behavior in randomized backtracking arises largely from occasional 'bad' early branching choices that commit the search down a barren subtree; once committed, completeness forces the algorithm to exhaustively exhaust that subtree before backing out, producing the extreme-tail runs. The fix — RAPID RANDOM RESTARTS — is to periodically abandon a run that has not found a solution within a fixed CUTOFF and restart from scratch with fresh random choices, discarding all the sunk work in the bad subtree. Because each fresh restart is an independent draw from the same heavy-tailed distribution, restarting frequently converts the algorithm's overall expected time-to-solution from potentially unbounded (dominated by the rare catastrophic tail) to well-behaved and typically much shorter, at the modest cost of repeating cheap early work. This restart strategy, validated on quasigroup completion, graph coloring, and scheduling benchmarks in Gomes and Selman's work, is now standard practice in modern complete SAT solvers, and the log-log survival plot is exactly the tool used to confirm restarts have removed the heavy tail after the fact.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs a randomized backtracking solver on a hard quasigroup-completion instance 200 times with different seeds, recording each run's time-to-solution. Most runs finish in under 2 seconds, but a handful take 40, 90, and even 300 seconds. Plotting P(runtime > t) versus t on log-log axes shows a straight declining line from around t=1 second out past t=100 seconds — the heavy-tail signature. The running sample mean, plotted against number of trials included, keeps jumping upward every time one of the rare long runs is added, never flattening out, while the median stays stable around 1.5 seconds throughout. Adding a restart every 5 seconds of no progress collapses the tail: the new survival plot curves sharply downward past t=5 seconds instead of continuing as a straight line, and the sample mean now stabilizes after only about 30 trials.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the field will ask why the student reported the median (or a restart-cutoff time) rather than the mean, and whether the student checked for heavy tails at all before trusting any average. Naming Gomes and Selman's finding and showing a log-log survival plot with the characteristic straight-line tail — plus the before/after effect of adding restarts — demonstrates the student diagnosed the actual statistical pathology in their data rather than assuming a well-behaved distribution by default.

questions.prompt: On a log-log plot of P(runtime > t) vs. t, what visual pattern signals heavy-tailed (power-law-like) runtime behavior?

options.text: A curve that bends sharply downward and drops off quickly
A roughly straight declining line over a wide range of t
A perfectly flat horizontal line
A curve that rises as t increases

explanations.a: A sharp downward bend on log-log axes is the signature of a thin-tailed (e.g. exponential) distribution, the opposite of heavy-tailed.
explanations.b: Correct — a power-law survival function is linear in log-log coordinates, so a straight declining line over a wide range of t is the heavy-tail signature.
explanations.c: A flat line would mean the probability of exceeding t never decreases, which is not a valid survival function for a proper distribution.
explanations.d: Survival functions P(runtime > t) are non-increasing in t by definition; they cannot rise.

questions.prompt: Why does the sample mean of a heavy-tailed runtime distribution fail to stabilize even after hundreds of trials, while the median stays stable?

options.text: Because the median is calculated incorrectly by most software
Because rare, extremely long runs occur often enough and are large enough to keep shifting the running average, while the median is insensitive to extreme values
Because the mean requires more trials than the median by mathematical definition, regardless of distribution shape
Because heavy-tailed distributions have no runs shorter than the median

explanations.a: The median is a standard, well-defined statistic; there is no computational error implied here.
explanations.b: Correct — in a heavy tail, occasional huge runtimes are frequent and extreme enough that each one meaningfully shifts the running average, whereas the median only depends on the middle-ranked value and ignores how extreme the tail values are.
explanations.c: Sample size requirements depend on distribution shape, not on some fixed rule that mean always needs more trials than median.
explanations.d: The median simply marks the 50th percentile; runs shorter than it are common in any distribution, heavy-tailed or not.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description from Gomes and Selman's heavy-tailed search research.

right.text: Occasional very bad early branching commits the complete search to exhaustively clear a barren subtree
Abandoning and re-attempting a run after a fixed cutoff, discarding sunk work in a bad subtree
A distribution whose tail decays slower than exponential, roughly power-law, seen empirically in randomized backtracking by Gomes, Selman, and colleagues

questions.explanation: Gomes and Selman found that randomized complete backtracking search often has heavy-tailed runtimes (power-law-like decay), traced this to occasional catastrophic early branching mistakes in complete search, and showed that rapid random restarts eliminate the pathology by discarding bad subtrees early.

questions.prompt: Order the investigative steps a student should take when suspecting heavy-tailed search behavior, from first to last.

items.text: Run the randomized solver many times and record each run's time-to-solution
Plot P(runtime > t) vs. t on log-log axes and check for a straight-line region
If a straight line appears, treat the sample mean as unreliable and prefer the median
Add rapid random restarts with a cutoff and re-plot the survival curve to confirm the tail is gone

questions.explanation: You must first collect many independent runtimes, then diagnose heavy tails via the log-log survival plot's straight-line signature, then adjust which statistic you trust (median over mean) if the signature is present, and finally apply and verify the restart fix.

lessons.label: Solution-Quality and Convergence Curves

sections.heading: Best-so-far curves and their built-in trap
sections.body: When a metaheuristic (simulated annealing, a genetic algorithm, tabu search, ant colony optimization) searches for a good solution to an optimization problem, the standard way to visualize its progress is a BEST-SO-FAR curve: at each iteration or elapsed time t, plot the best objective value found by any point up to t. Because this curve tracks a running best (a running minimum for a minimization problem, a running maximum for maximization), it is, by mathematical construction, MONOTONE — it can only improve or stay flat, never get worse, no matter how the underlying search is actually behaving moment to moment. This creates a subtle but important trap: a best-so-far curve always LOOKS like the algorithm is 'working', even if the underlying search has been effectively stuck doing nothing useful for the last 90% of the run. A flat plateau at the end of the curve is visually indistinguishable, on a single algorithm's plot alone, between two very different realities: (1) the search has converged to the true optimum and further search cannot improve it, or (2) the search is trapped at a local optimum and would need a fundamentally different move (a restart, a bigger perturbation, a different neighborhood) to escape.

sections.heading: The required baseline: random-restart hill climbing
sections.body: Because a lone best-so-far curve cannot distinguish real convergence from a stuck local optimum, the field's best practice calls for overlaying a BASELINE curve from the simplest possible competing method: random-restart hill climbing (repeatedly running greedy local search from a fresh random starting point and keeping the best result across restarts, with no sophisticated escape mechanism at all). If a sophisticated metaheuristic's best-so-far curve does not clearly and reproducibly beat random-restart hill climbing's best-so-far curve at the SAME computational budget, the sophistication is not earning its keep — the fancy algorithm may simply be doing an expensive version of what plain restarts achieve for free. Yet this baseline comparison is skipped surprisingly often, which is exactly why its absence is one of the most common red flags in student and even published heuristic papers.

sections.heading: Anytime profiles and reading a plateau correctly
sections.body: An ANYTIME PROFILE generalizes the single best-so-far curve into a picture of solution quality achievable at every possible time budget, often averaged (median, with IQR band) over many independent runs — this is the proper way to report best-so-far behavior for a RANDOMIZED algorithm, since any single run's curve is (per the earlier lesson) just one draw. When reading such a plot, a long plateau at the end of the median curve should never be read alone as 'the algorithm has converged to the optimal answer' — it should instead prompt three questions: has this same plateau value been independently reached by multiple different algorithms or by a known lower bound (corroboration), does the plateau persist even after a large jump in the computational budget (stability), and does the IQR band across seeds also collapse to near-zero at the plateau (consensus across runs)? Only when a plateau is corroborated, stable, and consensual does it support a claim of convergence; a plateau in a single run, or one where different seeds plateau at visibly different heights, is much more likely to be several independent local optima.

lessons.workedExample: A student develops a new local-search heuristic for the Traveling Salesman Problem and plots its best-so-far tour length against elapsed time on a 200-city instance, showing a curve that drops quickly then flattens after 30 seconds at a tour length of 15,200. Read alone, this looks like convergence. But overlaying random-restart hill climbing on the same instance and budget shows IT ALSO flattens near 15,400 after about 25 seconds — barely worse. Running the new heuristic across 30 seeds and plotting the median with an IQR band reveals the band is still fairly wide (14,900 to 15,600) even at 60 seconds, meaning different seeds are settling at meaningfully different plateaus — evidence of multiple local optima, not proof of a converged global answer, and only a modest, possibly noise-level improvement over the trivial baseline.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen many science-fair optimization projects will look immediately for the random-restart hill climbing baseline overlay, precisely because a monotone best-so-far curve alone always looks impressive regardless of whether the algorithm is doing anything clever. A student who proactively shows the baseline comparison, reports median-plus-IQR anytime profiles across many seeds rather than one curve, and correctly refuses to call a plateau 'converged' without corroboration and cross-seed consensus demonstrates they understand the visual trap rather than being fooled by their own chart.

questions.prompt: Why is a best-so-far curve, by itself, unable to distinguish true convergence from a local-optimum plateau?

options.text: Because best-so-far curves are only meaningful for deterministic algorithms
Because the curve is mathematically monotone by construction, so it always looks like steady improvement or a stable plateau regardless of what is really happening underneath
Because best-so-far curves cannot be plotted against elapsed time, only against iteration count
Because the objective value is not comparable across different runs

explanations.a: Best-so-far curves are commonly used for stochastic metaheuristics precisely because they summarize noisy progress; the issue is not that they're restricted to deterministic algorithms.
explanations.b: Correct — because the curve tracks a running best, it can never worsen, so a flat plateau at the end looks the same whether the true optimum was reached or the search is merely stuck.
explanations.c: Best-so-far curves can be plotted against either elapsed time or iteration count; that is not the source of the ambiguity.
explanations.d: Objective values from the same problem instance are directly comparable across runs; the ambiguity is about interpreting a monotone curve's plateau, not comparability.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of overlaying a random-restart hill climbing curve alongside a new metaheuristic's best-so-far curve?

options.text: To make the plot visually busier and more impressive
To provide a minimal-sophistication baseline, so that the new method's added complexity can be shown to actually earn better performance at the same budget
Because random-restart hill climbing always finds the global optimum
To replace the need for multiple random seeds

explanations.a: The baseline is functional, not decorative — it is the standard check for whether sophistication is justified.
explanations.b: Correct — if the new heuristic cannot clearly beat the simplest possible competitor at equal budget, its added complexity is not demonstrated to be worthwhile.
explanations.c: Random-restart hill climbing is a weak baseline precisely because it has no sophisticated way to escape local optima; it does not generally find the global optimum.
explanations.d: The baseline addresses a different concern (is complexity earning its keep) from seed variability (is the result reproducible); both are still needed.

questions.prompt: Order the checks needed before declaring that a plateau in a median anytime-profile curve represents true convergence, from first to last.

items.text: Confirm the plateau value is corroborated by another algorithm or a known lower bound
Confirm the plateau persists even after substantially increasing the computational budget
Confirm the IQR band across seeds also collapses near the plateau, showing cross-seed consensus
Only then describe the plateau as evidence of convergence rather than a local optimum

questions.explanation: A plateau only supports a convergence claim once it is corroborated by an independent source, shown stable under a larger budget, and shown consistent across seeds (narrow IQR) — skipping any of these leaves open the possibility the plateau is just a local optimum.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition in convergence-curve analysis.

right.text: The running best objective value found up to time t; monotone by construction
Median (with IQR band) of best-so-far performance across many independent seeds at every time budget
Greedy local search repeated from fresh random starts with no escape mechanism, used as a minimal-sophistication comparison point

questions.explanation: A best-so-far curve is one run's monotone running-best trace; an anytime profile aggregates many such runs (median plus IQR) to reveal how solution quality typically develops with time budget; random-restart hill climbing is the standard weak baseline any sophisticated metaheuristic must beat.

lessons.label: Run-Time Distributions and Performance Profiles

sections.heading: RTDs: P(solved by time t) on a single instance
sections.body: Holger Hoos and Thomas Stuetzle formalized the RUN-TIME DISTRIBUTION (RTD) methodology for stochastic local search algorithms, documented extensively in their book 'Stochastic Local Search: Foundations and Applications' (2004) and earlier papers. An RTD is an empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF): run the same randomized algorithm many independent times on the SAME problem instance, record each run's time-to-solution, sort those times, and plot the fraction of runs solved BY time t against t. The result is a non-decreasing curve from 0 to 1 that answers the practically crucial question 'if I give this algorithm a time budget of t, what is the probability it succeeds?' — a question a single mean or median runtime cannot answer on its own. Hoos and Stuetzle found that for many stochastic local search algorithms on hard random SAT instances, the RTD closely resembles an EXPONENTIAL distribution, which has the memoryless property: the probability of solving in the next unit of time is roughly constant regardless of how long the algorithm has already run. This memoryless behavior is exactly what makes rapid-restart strategies (see the heavy-tails lesson) effective and what makes simple parallelization by running independent copies effective, since restarting an exponential-RTD process gains nothing but also loses nothing.

sections.heading: Crossing curves: the winner depends on the cutoff
sections.body: When comparing two solvers' RTDs on the same instance, the two ECDF curves frequently CROSS: solver A may reach a 50% success probability faster than solver B, while solver B eventually overtakes A and reaches 95% or 100% success probability sooner. This is not a plotting artifact — it reflects genuinely different strategies, such as one solver making fast, high-variance progress with a heavier tail versus another making slower but steadier progress with a lighter tail. The direct consequence is that the question 'which solver is better' has NO single answer independent of context: the answer depends entirely on the cutoff time budget available in the application. A solver that dominates at a 1-second budget can be strictly worse at a 60-second budget, and a report that quotes only one cutoff (or, worse, only a mean or median with no cutoff structure at all) can quietly cherry-pick whichever solver looks best at that one arbitrary point, hiding the crossover from the reader entirely.

sections.heading: Dolan-Moré performance profiles and honestly reporting censored runs
sections.body: Elizabeth Dolan and Jorge Moré's 2002 paper 'Benchmarking Optimization Software with Performance Profiles' (Mathematical Programming, vol. 91) extended the single-instance RTD idea to the harder problem of comparing solvers across an ENTIRE BENCHMARK SET of many different problem instances at once. For each instance, compute each solver's performance ratio against the best solver on that instance; the performance profile then plots, for each solver, the fraction of the whole benchmark set on which its ratio is within a factor tau of the best, as tau increases — giving a compact picture of both efficiency (who wins most often, read at tau=1) and robustness (who eventually solves nearly everything, read as tau grows large). A run that TIMES OUT without finding a solution is CENSORED data, not missing data, and both the RTD and performance-profile methodologies require it to be recorded and plotted as such (e.g., as a run counted in the denominator but never crossing the 'solved' threshold, or assigned a very large or infinite ratio) rather than silently dropped from the average — dropping timeouts systematically removes exactly the hardest cases and inflates every solver's apparent performance, especially the solver that times out most often.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two SAT solvers on a benchmark of 50 hard instances. On instance #17, Solver A's RTD (from 100 independent runs) reaches 50% solved by 2 seconds but only reaches 80% solved even after 100 seconds; Solver B's RTD reaches 50% solved only at 8 seconds but reaches 99% by 100 seconds — the curves cross near t=20 seconds. Reporting only mean runtime with a 10-second cutoff and dropping the 20% of Solver A runs that never finished would make Solver A look clearly faster; correctly treating those as censored (never solved within budget) and building the RTD instead reveals Solver A is only better under tight time budgets. Aggregating properly with a Dolan-Moré performance profile across all 50 instances (each solver's ratio to the best on that instance, versus tau) shows Solver A wins on efficiency (best at tau=1 on more instances) while Solver B wins on robustness (near 100% solved by tau=4), a nuance a single summary number would have erased entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge familiar with empirical algorithmics will ask specifically what happened to the runs that timed out, since dropping them is one of the most common and most misleading shortcuts in student benchmark reports.
