It prevents an attacker who knows the hash algorithm from precomputing inputs that all collide, since the attacker doesn't know the key
It guarantees zero collisions ever occur
It removes the need for a hash function entirely

explanations.a: Keying does not change memory usage; it changes the unpredictability of the mapping from keys to buckets.
explanations.b: Correct — because attacker-supplied data is exactly the input the defender cannot randomize, the defense instead randomizes the (secret) function applied to that data.
explanations.c: SipHash still has collisions; it just makes constructing them without knowing the key computationally infeasible.
explanations.d: SipHash is itself a hash function; it does not eliminate hashing.

questions.prompt: Match each production system to the randomized or approximate technique it relies on.

left.text: Chrome Safe Browsing / Cassandra SSTable reads

right.text: Bloom filters for approximate membership
Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R) for bounded-memory uniform sampling
Miller-Rabin randomized primality testing

questions.explanation: Chrome's Safe Browsing feature and Cassandra/LevelDB-style databases use Bloom filters to skip expensive lookups for keys that are provably absent. Telemetry and log pipelines use reservoir sampling to keep a uniform sample from an unbounded stream in O(k) memory. OpenSSL and GnuPG use Miller-Rabin to certify random candidate numbers as prime with vanishingly small error probability.

questions.prompt: Order these events in a single Miller-Rabin-based RSA key generation run, from first to last.

items.text: Generate a large random odd candidate number
Run Miller-Rabin for several rounds with independently random bases
If any round reports 'composite,' discard the candidate and generate a new one
If all rounds report 'probably prime,' accept the number as a key component

questions.explanation: Key generation repeatedly draws a random odd candidate, subjects it to multiple independent Miller-Rabin rounds, discards and retries on any composite verdict, and only accepts a candidate once it survives every round — driving the false-positive probability down to roughly 4^-r for r rounds.

lessons.label: Case Study: Simulated Annealing for VLSI Placement and Timetabling

sections.heading: The 1983 origin: annealing metaphor meets chip placement
sections.body: In 1983, IBM researchers Scott Kirkpatrick, C. Daniel Gelatt, and Mario Vecchi published 'Optimization by Simulated Annealing' in Science (vol. 220, pp. 671-680), proposing that the physics of slow metal cooling — atoms settling into a low-energy crystal lattice when temperature drops gradually, rather than freezing into a defect-riddled glass when quenched fast — could be simulated as a general-purpose optimizer. Their algorithm accepts a candidate move that WORSENS the objective with probability exp(-deltaE/T), where deltaE is the increase in cost and T is a control 'temperature' that starts high and is lowered on a schedule toward zero. Early on, the system accepts many uphill moves and explores broadly; as T falls, it accepts fewer, converging toward a local optimum without ever being provably guaranteed the global one. Kirkpatrick's own paper demonstrated the technique on exactly the problem IBM cared about commercially: placing components and routing wire on integrated circuits (and circuit boards) to minimize total wire length and layout area, a combinatorial problem with a state space too large to search exhaustively and no usable gradient, since swapping two component positions changes the cost discontinuously.

sections.heading: Same algorithm, harder constraints: school and exam timetabling
sections.body: Decades later, the same acceptance rule shows up as one of the strongest general approaches to school timetabling and exam scheduling, problems formalized and benchmarked by the International Timetabling Competition (ITC) series (ITC-2002, ITC-2007, ITC-2019), which supplies real-world-derived instances so researchers can compare methods on identical data. Timetabling objectives are built from two tiers: HARD constraints that a valid schedule may never violate (a teacher cannot be in two rooms at once; a student cannot sit two exams simultaneously) and SOFT constraints that are merely undesirable and get penalty weights (a student having three exams in one day; a class ending after 4pm). The overall cost function sums weighted soft-constraint violations while hard constraints are typically enforced by the move generator itself (a 'swap' move that would violate a hard constraint is never proposed) or penalized so heavily that any feasible solution beats any infeasible one. Choosing those weights is itself an engineering decision with real consequences for what the algorithm treats as an acceptable trade-off.

sections.heading: Why annealing keeps winning on this kind of objective
sections.body: Both chip placement and timetabling share a signature that rules out gradient-based and most exact methods: the objective is a discrete, non-differentiable sum of many weighted terms, the feasible region has no clean convex or linear relaxation to exploit (these problems' LP relaxations are weak, with large integrality gaps, so branch-and-bound explores an exponential number of nodes even at moderate problem sizes), and local moves (swap two exam slots, swap two component positions) change the cost by an amount that is cheap to compute incrementally without re-evaluating the whole objective. Simulated annealing needs only that incremental delta and a cooling schedule — it does not need convexity, differentiability, or even a well-behaved neighborhood structure — which is exactly why it remains a first-choice baseline more than 40 years after Kirkpatrick's paper, on problems the exact-methods community has still not solved with certainty at realistic sizes.

lessons.workedExample: A team building an exam-scheduling annealer defines cost = 1000*(hard violations) + 5*(students with same-day exams) + 2*(students with back-to-back exams) + 1*(exams scheduled in the last slot of the day). They start at T=50, propose random single-exam slot swaps, accept improving swaps always and worsening ones with probability exp(-deltaE/T), and multiply T by 0.995 after every 10 proposed moves. Early iterations accept many same-day-exam-creating swaps because T is high; by iteration 20,000, T has dropped enough that only genuinely improving swaps survive, and the schedule has converged to a small number of same-day conflicts. Because the hard-violation weight (1000) dwarfs every soft weight, the search never settles on an infeasible timetable even during high-temperature exploration, as long as at least one lower-cost feasible neighbor is reachable.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will ask how the weights (1000, 5, 2, 1 in the worked example) were chosen, because arbitrary weighting can make an algorithm look like it is solving the real problem while actually optimizing a distorted proxy for it — this is the central methodological risk in any weighted-constraint formulation. A strong answer explains that hard-constraint weights should exceed the maximum possible sum of soft-constraint penalties (so no infeasible solution can ever look cheaper than a feasible one), and that soft weights should be justified by a stated institutional priority (e.g., 'same-day exams matter more than late-day exams because of measured student fatigue'), not tuned until the output looks nice.

questions.prompt: In simulated annealing, what does the temperature parameter T primarily control?

options.text: The number of variables in the objective function
The probability of accepting a move that makes the objective worse
The exact global optimum the algorithm will find
Whether hard constraints are enforced at all

explanations.a: The number of variables is fixed by the problem instance, not by T.
explanations.b: Correct — the Metropolis acceptance rule exp(-deltaE/T) governs how often the search accepts uphill moves, which is high at high T and low as T cools toward zero.
explanations.c: Annealing has no guarantee of finding the global optimum at any temperature; it is a heuristic, not an exact method.
explanations.d: Hard constraints are typically enforced by the move generator or a dominant penalty weight, independent of the temperature schedule.

questions.prompt: Why did Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi's 1983 chip-placement application, and modern school-timetabling systems, both reach for simulated annealing rather than a gradient-based optimizer?

options.text: Gradient methods are always slower than annealing regardless of the problem
Both objectives are discrete and non-differentiable with no usable relaxation, so there is no gradient to follow
Annealing is guaranteed to find the exact global optimum, unlike gradient descent
Gradient-based methods cannot be implemented on IBM hardware

explanations.a: Speed is problem-dependent; the real issue is applicability, not raw speed.
explanations.b: Correct — swapping two components or two exam slots changes the cost discontinuously, so there is no derivative to exploit, and integer relaxations of these problems tend to be weak or intractable at realistic sizes.
explanations.c: Annealing offers no such guarantee; it converges toward a local optimum as temperature cools, with no certificate of global optimality.
explanations.d: This is a hardware-agnostic algorithmic choice, unrelated to any specific manufacturer's machines.

questions.prompt: Match each timetabling term to its correct description.

right.text: Must never be violated in a valid solution (e.g., no double-booked room)
Undesirable but tolerable; contributes a weighted penalty to the cost function
A set of real-world-derived competition instances used to compare timetabling methods on identical data

questions.explanation: Hard constraints define feasibility and must always hold; soft constraints are weighted penalties that shape quality among feasible solutions; the International Timetabling Competition series provides the shared benchmark instances the field uses to compare approaches like simulated annealing against each other.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a single simulated annealing run for VLSI placement, from first to last.

items.text: Start at a high temperature T with an initial (often random) component placement
Propose a local move, such as swapping two components' positions
Accept the move if it improves cost, or with probability exp(-deltaE/T) if it worsens cost
Gradually lower T according to a cooling schedule
Stop when T reaches (near) zero and the layout has converged

questions.explanation: Annealing begins hot with an initial placement, repeatedly proposes and probabilistically accepts local moves under the Metropolis rule, cools the temperature over many such iterations, and terminates once the temperature schedule reaches its floor and the layout stabilizes.

lessons.label: Case Study: Evolutionary Design Beyond Software

sections.heading: NASA's ST5 evolved antenna: evolution flies in space
sections.body: In 2006, NASA flew three copies of an antenna, designated ST5-33-142-7, on its Space Technology 5 (ST5) mission — the first computer-evolved hardware ever to fly in space. The design work, led by Jason Lohn, Gregory Hornby, and Derek Linden at NASA Ames, used two evolutionary representations: one genetic-algorithm-style encoding with fixed, non-branching antenna arms, and one genetic-programming-style tree encoding that allowed the arms to branch. Both were evolved against a demanding, competing set of requirements: a wide beamwidth for a circularly polarized signal combined with wide impedance bandwidth, a combination that is genuinely hard to hand-design well. The evolved antennas — small, oddly bent, asymmetric shapes that no human antenna engineer would have sketched — matched or exceeded the performance of a conventionally hand-designed antenna produced by the mission's contractor, while also reducing fabrication time and design-cycle length. This was evolutionary search used not as a curiosity but as the production design process for a component that had to survive launch and operate correctly in orbit with no possibility of a fix.

sections.heading: Adrian Thompson's 1996 FPGA: evolution exploits the physical chip itself
sections.body: A decade earlier, at the University of Sussex, Adrian Thompson ran a more unsettling experiment. Using a Xilinx XC6216 FPGA with roughly 24,000 available logic gates, he evolved a circuit — using genetic algorithms operating directly on the chip's configuration bits — to discriminate between a 1 kHz and a 10 kHz square wave, with no clock signal driving it. The evolved solution used only about 100 gates, and when Thompson examined the working circuit he found something strange: a handful of logic cells had NO logical connection to the functional circuit — no wire path by which they could influence the output — and yet disabling any one of them destroyed the circuit's ability to discriminate the tones. Evolution had exploited unintended physical effects of that specific piece of silicon — electromagnetic or capacitive crosstalk between physically adjacent cells, and possibly analog, temperature-sensitive quirks of that individual chip — rather than any documented digital logic function. The circuit worked reliably only on the exact physical FPGA it evolved on; copies of the configuration bitstream loaded onto a different (even nominally identical) chip of the same model often failed to discriminate the tones correctly, because the exploited physical quirks were unique to that one piece of hardware.

sections.heading: From one-off demos to routine practice: neuroevolution and AutoML
sections.body: Both cases were once framed as remarkable one-off demonstrations; three decades later the same search principle is routine infrastructure. NEAT (NeuroEvolving Augmenting Topologies), introduced by Kenneth Stanley and Risto Miikkulainen in 2002, evolves both the weights and the CONNECTIVITY STRUCTURE of neural networks simultaneously, starting from minimal networks and adding complexity only when it earns its keep — a direct descendant of the same 'let search discover a shape no one specified' philosophy. Modern AutoML and neural architecture search (NAS) pipelines apply evolutionary or reinforcement-learning search over network architectures at industrial scale (Google's evolved image classifiers being an early widely cited example), searching a design space too large for humans to explore by hand, exactly as Thompson's and NASA's search spaces were too large to hand-design confidently.

sections.heading: The other side of the coin: fragility and unexplainability
sections.body: The common lesson across all four systems is that evolutionary search finds designs that WORK without finding designs anyone can fully EXPLAIN or trust to generalize. Thompson's circuit is the starkest case — it depended on undocumented physical properties of one chip and could not be safely ported. NASA mitigated this risk by testing physical prototypes extensively and by choosing a domain (antenna geometry) with fewer exotic exploitable side-channels than a live silicon substrate. NEAT and NAS-discovered networks routinely include connections that are difficult to interpret post hoc even though they measurably improve performance. Any team proposing evolutionary or neuroevolutionary design for a fair project should be ready to say explicitly how they tested that the evolved solution generalizes beyond the exact conditions (or exact hardware) it was evolved under.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a student evolves a small neural network with a NEAT-style algorithm to control a simulated robot arm, and it discovers a controller that performs excellently in simulation. Following Thompson's cautionary example, before claiming success the student should ask: does the controller rely on some artifact of the SPECIFIC simulator (a physics-engine rounding quirk, a fixed random seed baked into the training environment, an exploit of the simulator's collision-detection edge cases) rather than the actual physical dynamics it is meant to control? The disciplined test is the same one NASA effectively ran on the ST5 antenna: validate the evolved solution against conditions it was NOT evolved under — a different simulator build, added sensor noise, or (ideally) a physical prototype — before trusting that its performance reflects genuine problem-solving rather than overfitting to one substrate's idiosyncrasies.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge encountering an evolutionary-design project will almost always ask some version of 'how do you know your evolved solution isn't just exploiting a quirk of your specific setup?' — Thompson's FPGA result is the canonical cautionary tale, and a student who can cite it (chip-specific exploitation of undocumented crosstalk, failure to port to nominally identical hardware) shows they understand that evolutionary search optimizes exactly the fitness function and environment given to it, nothing more and nothing less. Judges reward projects that proactively test generalization beyond the training substrate, rather than only reporting in-sample fitness.

questions.prompt: Why did Adrian Thompson's evolved 1996 FPGA tone-discriminator circuit typically fail to work correctly when its configuration was copied onto a different, nominally identical chip?

options.text: The configuration bitstream was corrupted during copying
Evolution had exploited undocumented physical quirks (such as crosstalk between cells) unique to the exact chip it evolved on
FPGAs cannot store more than one configuration at a time
The 1 kHz and 10 kHz test tones were different on each chip

explanations.a: There is no indication of data corruption; the bitstream itself was faithfully reproduced.
explanations.b: Correct — some functioning cells had no logical connection to the output path, meaning evolution relied on physical side effects (crosstalk, analog quirks) specific to that one piece of silicon rather than documented digital logic.
explanations.c: This is unrelated to the phenomenon; the issue was about which physical chip ran a given configuration, not storage capacity.
explanations.d: The test signal was standardized; the chip's behavior, not the input, differed.

questions.prompt: What made the antenna design problem for NASA's ST5 mission a good candidate for evolutionary search rather than conventional hand design?

options.text: NASA had no antenna engineers available
The requirement combined wide circularly-polarized beamwidth with wide impedance bandwidth, a demanding joint constraint that is hard to hand-design well
Evolved antennas are always cheaper regardless of the requirements
The mission required a antenna with zero manufacturing tolerance

explanations.a: NASA and its contractor did produce a conventional hand-designed antenna for comparison; the evolved design matched or exceeded it.
explanations.b: Correct — combining wide beamwidth for circular polarization with wide impedance bandwidth is a genuinely difficult joint constraint, which is exactly the kind of large, awkward design space evolutionary search is suited to explore.
explanations.c: Cost savings were a reported benefit in this case, not a universal property of evolved designs.
explanations.d: Manufacturing tolerance was not the stated driver of the choice to use evolutionary design.

questions.prompt: Match each evolutionary design system to its distinguishing feature.

right.text: First computer-evolved hardware to fly in space, 2006
Exploited undocumented physical crosstalk unique to one chip
Evolves both connection weights and network topology simultaneously, starting from minimal structure

questions.explanation: The ST5 antenna, evolved by Lohn, Hornby, and Linden, flew on three ST5 spacecraft in 2006. Thompson's 1996 FPGA circuit relied on undocumented, chip-specific physical crosstalk. NEAT, introduced by Stanley and Miikkulainen in 2002, jointly evolves weights and topology, growing complexity only as needed.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Thompson's 1996 evolvable-hardware experiment, from first to last.

items.text: A genetic algorithm evolves configuration bitstreams directly on the physical FPGA
A circuit emerges that successfully discriminates 1 kHz from 10 kHz square waves using about 100 gates
Thompson inspects the circuit and finds cells with no logical path to the output
Disabling one of those seemingly disconnected cells breaks the circuit's function

questions.explanation: Evolution ran directly on the physical chip's configuration, producing a working discriminator; only upon inspection did Thompson find functionally isolated-looking cells, and only by disabling them did he confirm they were secretly essential through an undocumented physical channel.

lessons.label: Randomized Algorithms Under Attack

sections.heading: Crosby and Wallach, 2003: when the average case is the attack surface
sections.body: Randomized algorithm analysis usually promises good EXPECTED performance, and expected performance is exactly what breaks when an adversary can choose the input. In 2003, Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach presented 'Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks' at the USENIX Security Symposium, showing that hash tables using a FIXED, publicly known hash function — the norm at the time in Perl, and in software like the Squid web proxy and the Bro intrusion detection system — could be driven from average-case O(1) lookups to worst-case O(n) chained lookups by an attacker who simply computed inputs that all hash to the same bucket. Their demonstration against Bro was concrete: using bandwidth well within reach of a dial-up modem, six minutes of carefully crafted packets pushed a dedicated Bro server into dropping as much as 71% of its traffic while pinning its CPU at maximum. The insight generalized far beyond one tool — any data structure whose 'random-looking' behavior actually comes from a fixed, guessable function is not random at all from an attacker's perspective.

sections.heading: HashDoS and Bloom filter poisoning: the same weakness, different targets
sections.body: The same idea resurfaced publicly in 2011 as 'HashDoS,' presented at the Chaos Communication Congress (28C3) by Alexander Klink and Julian Walde, who showed that the default, unkeyed hash functions in PHP, Java, Python (pre-3.4), and several other languages' hash tables were all vulnerable to the same collision-flooding technique Crosby and Wallach had described eight years earlier — a single crafted HTTP POST body with thousands of colliding form-field names could pin a web server's CPU. Bloom filters have a related but distinct weak point: because a Bloom filter's false-positive behavior depends entirely on its k hash functions and bit-array size, an attacker who can predict or reverse-engineer those hash functions can craft inputs that deliberately set the same bits a legitimate item would set — 'poisoning' the filter into reporting false positives for content it never actually saw, or conversely, mapping many attacker-chosen queries to a saturated filter to defeat its space-saving purpose entirely.

sections.heading: Debian's 2008 OpenSSL bug: randomness that quietly wasn't
sections.body: The most consequential randomness failure in this space did not come from an attacker exploiting a fixed function, but from a well-intentioned code change removing one. In 2006, a Debian package maintainer, acting on warnings from memory-checking tools (Valgrind and Purify) about uninitialized-memory use, removed two lines of code from Debian's OpenSSL that fed entropy into the pseudorandom number generator. Discovered and disclosed by Luciano Bello in May 2008 as CVE-2008-0166, the bug meant that for roughly two years, every cryptographic key generated by that OpenSSL build derived its randomness almost entirely from the process ID, which on Linux ranges only from 1 to 32,768 — meaning there were only about 32,767 possible keys for a given key size and architecture. Any SSH key, SSL certificate, or other credential generated on an affected Debian or Ubuntu system during that window was one of a small, fully enumerable set, and attackers could simply generate every possible key and check for a match.

sections.heading: The fix, and the general principle
sections.body: All three failure modes share one remedy: make the function or seed a SECRET that the attacker cannot predict or reconstruct, rather than relying on the function merely looking complicated. Keyed hash functions like SipHash (adopted by Python's PEP 456 and Rust's standard HashMap specifically in response to HashDoS-class attacks) close the collision-flooding hole by giving each process a random key an attacker cannot know in advance. Cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators (CSPRNGs), properly seeded from OS-level entropy sources rather than predictable values like a PID or timestamp, close the Debian-style hole. The general principle that ties the whole lesson together: when a randomized algorithm's correctness or security argument depends on the adversary NOT knowing the random choices, the seed or key is not an implementation detail — it is part of the algorithm's correctness proof, and any process that weakens it (whether an attacker crafting collisions or a well-meaning maintainer deleting 'unnecessary' entropy code) breaks the guarantee just as surely as a logic bug would.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine a web application storing submitted form fields in a plain hash table keyed by field name, using a fixed, non-keyed hash function shipped with the language runtime. An attacker who knows that hash function (it is public, after all — it's in the source code or documentation) can, offline, compute thousands of distinct field names that all hash into the same bucket. Submitting one request containing those field names forces the server to perform thousands of O(n) linked-list-style lookups into one bucket instead of O(1) lookups, exactly as Crosby and Wallach demonstrated against Bro in 2003 and as HashDoS demonstrated against PHP and Java in 2011. Switching the hash table to a SipHash-keyed implementation seeded with a random value the attacker cannot observe defeats this: the attacker no longer knows which field names will collide, because the function computing the buckets is now a secret unique to that running process.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read about hash-flooding or the Debian bug will probe whether a student treats randomness as decoration or as part of the security argument itself — a common wrong answer is 'we used a hash function so it's fine,' when the actual question is whether that hash function's KEY or SEED is secret from the adversary. The Debian case is a particularly good example to cite because it shows the failure mode isn't always a clever attacker: a plausible-sounding code cleanup silently deleted the entropy source, and the bug survived nearly two years in production before discovery, which is a strong argument for treating any change near a random-number-generating code path as security-critical and worth extra review.

questions.prompt: What made Crosby and Wallach's 2003 algorithmic complexity attacks possible against hash tables in Perl, Squid, and Bro?

options.text: The hash tables used too much memory
The hash function was fixed and publicly known, letting an attacker precompute inputs that all collide into one bucket
The hash tables did not support deletion
Bro's network interface card had a hardware defect

explanations.a: Memory usage was not the vulnerability; the attack targeted computational complexity of lookups.
explanations.b: Correct — with a fixed, known hash function, an attacker can compute many inputs that map to the same bucket offline, then submit them to force O(n) worst-case chained lookups instead of O(1).
explanations.c: Deletion support is unrelated to this class of attack.
explanations.d: The vulnerability was algorithmic (a software design choice), not a hardware fault.

questions.prompt: In the 2008 Debian OpenSSL bug (CVE-2008-0166), what reduced the effective key space to about 32,767 possibilities for a given key size and architecture?

options.text: An attacker had stolen the private entropy source from Debian's servers
Removing entropy-gathering code left the process ID (ranging 1-32,768 on Linux) as effectively the only source of randomness in key generation
OpenSSL was configured to only generate 128-bit keys
The bug only affected keys generated on exactly May 13, 2008

explanations.a: There was no theft involved; the flaw was an accidental code change that removed legitimate entropy sources.
explanations.b: Correct — with the entropy-gathering lines removed, the PID became the dominant variable input, and since Linux PIDs range only 1 to 32,768, the number of distinct keys per architecture and key length collapsed to that small range.
explanations.c: Key size was unrelated; the flaw affected the RANDOMNESS feeding key generation regardless of the requested key length.
explanations.d: The bug affected any key generated by the flawed OpenSSL package from around September 2006 until the 2008 disclosure, not a single date.

questions.prompt: Match each attack or failure to its correct description.

right.text: Generalized Crosby and Wallach's collision-flooding attack to PHP, Java, and other languages' default hash tables
Exploits predictable Bloom filter hash functions to force false positives or saturate the filter
Accidental removal of entropy-gathering code left keys derived almost entirely from a small, guessable process ID range

questions.explanation: HashDoS extended the 2003 collision-flooding technique to widely used web-facing languages in 2011. Bloom filter poisoning relies on predicting the filter's hash functions to force incorrect membership answers. The Debian bug came from removing legitimate entropy sources, collapsing the effective key space to the range of Linux process IDs.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the timeline of hash-table collision-flooding attacks and their defenses.

items.text: Crosby and Wallach publish algorithmic complexity attacks against Perl, Squid, and Bro (2003)
Klink and Walde present HashDoS, generalizing the attack to PHP, Java, and other languages (2011)
Python adopts SipHash as its default string/bytes hash via PEP 456 (Python 3.4)
Rust ships SipHash-based hashing as its standard HashMap's default hasher

questions.explanation: The original 2003 Crosby-Wallach paper identified the vulnerability class; the 2011 HashDoS talk showed it was still widespread across mainstream languages; language ecosystems then responded by adopting keyed hash functions like SipHash as their defaults, with Python doing so via PEP 456 and Rust's standard library following the same keyed-hashing principle.

lessons.label: Designing a Fair-Ready Randomized or Heuristic Experiment

sections.heading: Pick a hard instance family and at least two honest competitors
sections.body: A randomized or heuristic algorithms project needs a problem where the difficulty is real and adjustable, not an easy instance dressed up to look hard: classic choices include instances of the traveling salesperson problem at varying city counts, graph coloring on generated random or structured graphs, bin packing, or a scheduling/timetabling instance in the spirit of the ITC benchmark tradition. Implement at least two methods, and critically, one of them must be a SIMPLE, HONESTLY TUNED BASELINE — a greedy construction heuristic, a basic hill-climber, or a straightforward randomized restart — not a strawman. The single most common flaw a judge will catch is a beautifully tuned proposed method compared against a lazily implemented baseline; the comparison is only informative if both sides received comparable engineering effort.

sections.heading: Fix the budget, not the wall-clock time
sections.body: Comparing methods by wall-clock running time confounds algorithmic quality with implementation quality (a poorly optimized version of a good algorithm loses to a well-optimized bad one) and with whatever machine happened to run the test. The fair-ready fix is to fix an EQUAL BUDGET of function evaluations (or objective-function calls, or candidate moves considered) across every method and every run, and measure solution quality reached within that shared budget — this isolates the algorithmic behavior being studied from hardware and implementation-efficiency effects. Report the machine used anyway, since even function-evaluation counts can be affected by cache behavior and instance representation, but the headline comparison should be evaluations-to-quality, not seconds-to-quality.

sections.heading: Run enough seeds, and show the distribution, not one lucky run
sections.body: Because randomized and heuristic methods produce a different result on every run, a single run proves almost nothing — it could be the algorithm's best day or its worst. The accepted minimum is at least 30 independent random seeds per method per instance, which is enough for basic distributional statistics (mean, median, variance) to stabilize and for standard significance tests to have reasonable power. Present results as RUN-TIME DISTRIBUTIONS (RTDs) — plotting, for each method, the fraction of runs that have reached a target quality by a given evaluation count — and/or BOX PLOTS of final quality across all 30+ seeds, which visually communicate spread and outliers in a way a single mean number cannot. Then run a WILCOXON SIGNED-RANK TEST (or Mann-Whitney U for unpaired seeds) comparing the two methods' results and report the resulting p-value — this is the standard non-parametric test for 'is method A's distribution of outcomes actually different from method B's,' and it does not assume the results are normally distributed, which randomized-algorithm outcomes frequently are not.

sections.heading: Log everything, and rehearse the hard questions
sections.body: Every seed value, every parameter (cooling schedule, mutation rate, population size, tuning method), the hardware used, and the exact instance files must be logged and reproducible — a result a judge cannot re-derive from the logs is a result they should not trust, and this is exactly the standard the field itself increasingly enforces. Before presenting, rehearse three questions judges reliably ask: 'How do you know that gap between methods isn't just noise?' (answer with the Wilcoxon p-value and the box plot spread, not a gut feeling); 'Did you tune the baseline as hard as you tuned your own method?' (answer by describing the baseline's tuning process explicitly, not just asserting fairness); and 'Is that your best run, or your median?' (answer by always reporting the median and interquartile range across all 30+ seeds, never cherry-picking the best of many runs as if it were typical).

lessons.workedExample: A student compares simulated annealing against a greedy-with-restarts baseline on 100-city random Euclidean TSP instances. They fix the budget at 200,000 tour-cost evaluations for both methods, run each on the same 40 instances with 30 different random seeds per instance (1,200 runs per method), and plot an RTD showing the fraction of runs reaching within 5% of the best-known tour length by evaluation count — simulated annealing reaches that target in fewer evaluations on the RTD curve. A box plot of final tour length across all 1,200 runs per method shows annealing's median is lower with a tighter interquartile range. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing paired per-instance median results gives p = 0.003, below the conventional 0.05 threshold, supporting that the gap is unlikely to be random noise. The student logs every seed, the cooling schedule parameters, and the exact machine (a specific CPU model) used for the evaluation-count-vs-wall-clock sanity check.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges evaluating any randomized or heuristic project treat statistical rigor as the dividing line between a science-fair-credible result and an anecdote — a project reporting 'my algorithm got a better score' from one or a handful of runs, with no seed count, no variance measure, and no significance test, reads as unverifiable regardless of how sophisticated the algorithm itself is. Conversely, a project that visibly fixes the evaluation budget, reports 30+ seeds with RTDs or box plots, states a Wilcoxon p-value, and can answer 'was the baseline tuned fairly?' without hesitation signals that the student understands empirical algorithm evaluation is itself a discipline with standards, not just a place to report whichever number came out best.

questions.prompt: Why should a fair-ready comparison between a randomized algorithm and a baseline fix an equal number of function evaluations rather than an equal wall-clock time?

options.text: Function evaluations are always faster to measure than wall-clock time
Fixing evaluations isolates algorithmic behavior from confounds like implementation efficiency and the specific machine used
Wall-clock time cannot be measured for randomized algorithms
Evaluation counts are required by law for science fair projects

explanations.a: Ease of measurement isn't the reason; the reason is what confound each choice controls for.
explanations.b: Correct — wall-clock time bundles algorithmic quality with implementation quality and hardware, while a fixed evaluation budget isolates how much solution quality the algorithm itself extracts per unit of search effort.
explanations.c: Wall-clock time is perfectly measurable for randomized algorithms; it's just a poor basis for a fair comparison.
explanations.d: There is no such legal requirement; this is a methodological best practice, not a rule imposed externally.

questions.prompt: Why run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test rather than just comparing the two methods' mean final scores?

options.text: Means are impossible to compute for randomized algorithm output
The Wilcoxon test is non-parametric, so it doesn't assume the results are normally distributed, and it quantifies whether an observed gap is likely to be noise
Wilcoxon tests are only used for ordering questions, never for statistics
Mean scores are always identical for randomized algorithms, so a test is unnecessary

explanations.a: Means are computable; the issue is that comparing raw means alone doesn't tell you if a difference is statistically meaningful.
explanations.b: Correct — the Wilcoxon signed-rank test does not require a normality assumption, which matters because heuristic algorithm output distributions are frequently skewed, and it directly answers whether the observed gap between methods exceeds what random variation would produce.
explanations.c: This test is a standard statistical significance test, unrelated to the 'ordering' checkpoint question type used elsewhere in this material.
explanations.d: Mean scores from randomized algorithms vary run to run; they are not identical, which is precisely why a significance test is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each judge question to the experimental design element that answers it convincingly.

left.text: 'How do you know that gap isn't noise?'
'Did you tune the baseline as hard as your method?'
'Is that your best run, or your median?'

right.text: A reported Wilcoxon signed-rank p-value plus a box plot of spread across 30+ seeds
An explicit, documented tuning process applied equally to the baseline
Reporting the median and interquartile range across all seeds, not a single cherry-picked run

questions.explanation: Each hard judge question maps to a specific piece of methodology: statistical significance testing answers the noise question, a documented equal-effort tuning process answers the baseline-fairness question, and reporting medians (not best-of-many) answers the cherry-picking question.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in designing and running a fair-ready randomized/heuristic algorithms experiment.

items.text: Choose a hard, adjustable instance family and implement at least two methods, including a fairly tuned baseline
Fix an equal function-evaluation budget for every method and run
Run each method on at least 30 independent random seeds per instance
Plot run-time distributions and/or box plots of final quality across all seeds
Run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test and report the p-value alongside the plots

questions.explanation: A sound experiment starts by choosing the problem and honest competitors, fixes the evaluation budget so comparisons are apples-to-apples, gathers enough seeds (30+) for distributional stability, visualizes the resulting spread with RTDs or box plots, and finally quantifies whether the visual gap is statistically significant with a Wilcoxon test.
